PART TWO  ANNOTATED INTERPRETATION 

There has been a marked lack of uniformity among the authorities in this country on the purpose of the Negotiable Instruments Law and the proper technique of interpreting the Act' but the weight of authority and the better view seem to follow the opinion of Mr. Eaton, Ex-president of the Conference, which is reprinted here:2 "The courts of the country know the origin and history of the Negotiable Instruments Law, that it is largely derived in its form and provisions from the English act upon the subject, that the great and leading object of the act, not only with the principal commercial states of the Union that have adopted it but also with the Congress of the United States in adopting it for the District of Columbia, was to establish a uniform system of law to govern negotiable instruments wherever they may circulate or be negotiated. Our courts know that it was not only uniformity of rules and principles that was designed, but also to embody in a codified form, as fully as possible, all the law upon the subject, to avoid conflict of decisions and the effect of mere local laws and usages that had heretofore prevailed. The great object sought to be accomplished by the enactment of the statute was to free the negotiable instrument, as far as possible, from all latent or local infirmities that would otherwise inhere in it, to the prejudice and disappointment of innocent holders, as against all the parties to the instrument professedly bound thereby. "The object of this codification of the law with respect to negotiable instruments was to relieve the courts of the duty of citation of conflicting cases and discussion of the discordant 

1 See Beutel "Necessity of a New Technique in Interpreting the ," 6 Tulane Law Review 1. 

2 Reprinted by permission of the Michigan Law Review from 12 id. 

88, 90 ff. 98

INTERPRETATION 

views entertained by courts and text writers of the greatest ability upon these questions, and to render certain and unambiguous that which had theretofore been doubtful and obscure, so that the business of the commercial world, largely transacted through the agency of negotiable paper, might be conducted in obedience to a written law emanating from a source whose authority admits of no question. "Where a statute is intended to embody in a code a particular branch of the law, and has specifically dealt with any point, the law on that point should be ascertained by interpreting the language used, instead of doing as before the statute was passed -roaming over a vast number of authorities in order to discover what the law is by extracting it by a minute, critical examination of prior decisions. If such a statute is to have read into it the law prior to its enactment, the value of codifying the law on the subject of negotiable instruments will be greatly impaired, if not destroyed, and the very object for which it was enacted will be frustrated. Where the language of such an act is clear, it must control, whatever may have been the prior statutes and decisions on the subject. Where there is a substantial doubt as to the meaning of the language used, the old law is a valuable source of information. "While the general purpose was to preserve the existing law, so far as it was uniform, yet in many respects in which there was a conflict or doubt, under the authorities, the language of the statute lays down rules which are not to be ignored simply because in some respects a change in the law is effected. "The primary purpose of the adoption of the negotiable instruments code was to obtain uniformity of decision where before there was great diversity. The state legislatures having enacted the code in the identical language of each other (or nearly so it would be unfortunate, indeed fatal, to such uniformity, if courts, under the pretext of judicial interpretation or construction, were so to vary and violate the plain provisions of the code as to undo and overthrow the very purpose of the code. "The statute was enacted for the purpose of furnishing in itself, a certain guide for the determination of all questions covered thereby relating to commercial paper, and therefore, so far it speaks without ambiguity as to any such questions, reference to case law as it existed prior to the enactment is unnec-

essary and is liable to be misleading. The Negotiable Instruments 

Law is not merely a legislative codification of judicial rules previously existing in this state, making that written law which was before unwritten. It is, so far as it goes, an incorporation into written law of the common law of the state, so to speak, the lawmerchant generally as recognized, with such changes or modifications and additions as to make a system harmonizing, so far as practicable, with that prevailing in other states. "It ought to be interpreted in such a way as to give effect to the beneficient design of the Legislature in passing an Act for the promotion of harmony upon an important branch of the law. Simplicity and clearness are ends especially to be sought. The language of the Act is to be construed with reference to the object to be attained. Its words are to be given their natural and common meaning, and the prevailing principles of statutory interpretation are to be employed. Care should be taken to adhere as closely as possible to the obvious meaning of the Act, without resort to that which had theretofore been the law of any particular commonwealth, unless necessary to dissolve obscurity or doubt, especially in instances where there was a difference in the law in the different states." Desirability of broad In addition to Mr. Eaton's argument above, there is a growconstruction ing demand in this country for broad construction of statutes, that is, that statutes expressing general principles of law be extended both by implication and analogy, in the same manner in which a common law lawyer uses a case, even though such an extension may result in a change in previous common law concepts growing out of decided cases.

Support for the extension of legislative principles rather than superseded judge-made law to new situations will be found in the article "Common Law and Legislation," by Roscoe Pound, 21 Harv. L. In a Massachusetts case, involving a note made in New York, N the New York law was not proved by the production of any statutes, but a New York case was presented, decided before the issue of the note, which cited the New York  Held, the N. Corporate bearer bonds, shown on their face to have been issued in New York, were sent to a guardian in California as a gift to his wards. The guardian improperly pledged the bonds to secure his personal debt to the defendant, which took without notice. The bonds were negotiable under the law of New York if it had been proved, and under the existing California law, but not under the California law at the time they were issued. 

Held, the defendant could not retain the bonds as negotiable instruments. In the absence of evidence of the New York law, it was assumed to be the same as that of California at the time of issue.  Popp v. Exchange Bank, 189 Cal. 296, 208 Pac. 113.

Since the non-negotiability of such bonds in California de pended upon a special peculiarity of California law, the judges must have known that they were negotiable in New York. A note in 11 Cal. Law Rev. 114 cites cases holding that the effect of such a transfer is determined by the law of the place of transfer, but such was not the view of the principal case, which applied the assumed law of the place of issue.

A conditional contract for the sale of an automobile agreed that as against an assignee of the seller, the buyer should be precluded from attacking the validity of the contract for fraud, duress, mistake, want or failure of consideration, or upon any other ground. Parties may not impart negotiability to a writing, not in itself a negotiable instrument under the general law merchant or statutes. The usage of business men to consider an instrument in this form negotiable can not overcome the positive provision of sec. 1. American Nat. Bank v. 

Sommerville, 191 Cal. 364, 216 Pac. 376. The contrary view is urged in a note in 33 Yale L. J. 302, "Partial negotiability of irregular instruments." There seems no public policy to prevent the clearly-expressed intention of the parties from taking effect.

A note payable on its face at a fixed date is not made nonnegotiable by provisions in the accompanying mortgage for acceleration upon default of any part of the principal or interest or upon failure to pay any lawful assessment upon the premises. Such provisions relate wholly to the security. The note being negotiable, the mortgage passes free of defenses to a holder in due course. Westlake v. Cooper, 69 Okla. 212, 171 

Pac. 859, L. R. A. 1918D, 522. 

In Bollenbach v. Ludlum, 84 Okla. 14, 201 Pac. 982, the court explained the two preceding cases, and said that the holder of an ordinary note secured by a mortgage with an acceleration clause has two alternative remedies. (1) If he sues on the note and to foreclose the mortgage in the same action, a default accelerates both note and mortgage. (2) If he sues upon the note without reference to the mortgage, the note is not accelerated and matures at the time specified on its face. If he elects the first alternative and the acceleration is automatic, notice of dishonor must be given to indorsers upon default and it is not sufficient that it is given upon commencement of the action. 

A note payable at a specified time, signed by husband and wife, made no reference to the chattel mortgage securing it, which was delivered at the same time and provided that the mortgagee upon taking possession of the property might, at its option, regard the debt as due at once. The wife did not sign the mortgage. Held, if she knew of its terms, the acceleration provision in the mortgage was enforceable against the wife in an action on the note.  Union Bank & Trust Co. v. Himmelbauer, 56 Mont. 82, 181 Pac. 332, 57 

Mont. 438, 188 Pac. 940. But on a later appeal, 68 Mont. 42, 216 Pac. 791, the acceleration provision was held not to be binding on the wife, because she did not sign or know of the mortgage.

A deed of land provided that part of the price should be taken in notes and that there should be an abatement of the price if any deficiency in the area were discovered. Each note stated that it was secured by a vendor's lien on the land. A bona fide purchaser for value of one of the notes had no notice of the abatement provision in the deed. Held, he could recover on the note to its full amount and was not subject to the abatement provision. The note and security agreement were not to be construed together, citing Thorp v. Mindeman, supra, and he was not put on inquiry as to the terms of the vendor's lien by the reference in the note. It was also held that if he sought to enforce his rights under the vendor's lien against the land, he would be subject to the abatement provision. The court recognized that a holder in due course of the note could enforce the lien free from equities, but stated that the abatement provision was a contractual right and more than an equity. The 

 was not cited. Shanabarger v. Phares, 86 W. Va. 64, 103 S. E. 349. The lien was grantor's lien rather than a vendor's, legal title having passed. See 3 Pomeroy's Equity

The court held, following Shanabarger v. Phares, supra, that a holder in due course of the notes could enforce the grantor's lien free from equities of payments by the maker to the payee subsequent

§1 (2) to the negotiation, but was subject to the defense of payments made by the grantee-maker in discharge of prior liens under the provision of the deed.

A note stating on its face that it was given for rent of a specified house as per contract of even date herewith, and that it was void if the property was destroyed before maturity, was not negotiable. Hight v. McCulloch, 150 Tenn. 117, 263 S. W. 794.

On the effect of a lease attached to rent notes, see First State 

Bank & T. Co. v. Crain, 157 La. 427, 102 So. 513, 38 A. L. R. 

347, stated under sec. 3(2).

A note which complied with the formal requisites was said to be rendered non-negotiable by a collateral written agreement for renewal at the option of the maker, when suit was brought by an indorsee who knew of the writing. Nat. City Bank v. 

Kirk (Ind. App.), 134 N. E. 772. This reasoning is clearly wrong, since negotiability depends on the form of the instrument itself, but the case is sound in denying recovery since the writing constituted an equitable defense against an indorsee with notice.

Action by alleged holder in due course against the maker of a note containing the following provisions: "This note is given. for the purchase money of said stocks and the same is not transferable or assignable without the said certificate of stock attached thereto. Said stock is to be delivered up to the makers hereof upon payment of this note. This note becomes void if transferred, sold or assigned without the said certificate of stock attached thereto." Held, the note is non-negotiable. Mason v. 

Flowers, 91 Fla. 224, 107 So. 334.

A draft in the ordinary form contained the following words after the sum: "400 c A. R. L. No. 3362 via A. R. L. B. L. 

direct." These words, under the custom and usage of business, notify the payee that a certain number of cases had been shipped by a certain line, and that the bill of lading went direct to the payee. Held, that the draft was an unconditional order and negotiable. Waddell v. Hanover Nat. Bank, 48 Misc. R. 578, 97 

N. Y. S. 305.

A note promising to pay at a certain time, but providing for an extension until a certain suit is determined, but not to exceed one year, is an absolute promise to pay not dependent on the outcome of the suit.  Jewett Lumber Co. v. Martin Conroy Co., 171 Ia. 513, 152 N. W. 493.

A note payable in six installments, maturing at different times within thirteen months, is not rendered non-negotiable by a provision that "a discount of six per cent. will be allowed if paid in full within fifteen days from date." In Oklahoma, under the law merchant, a note payable in installments three months apart, which contained a stipulation that if paid within fifteen days from date, a discount of six per cent, would be allowed, was held indefinite and uncertain at the time of its execution as to the amount payable and was therefore not negotiable, and it has been held in that state that this rule has not been changed by the Negotiable Instruments Law

§1 (2) which does not purpose to prescribe a different rule. First 

Nat. Bank v. Watson, 56 Okla. 495, 155 Pac. 1152. But see the Oklahoma cases under sec. 2. 

An order to pay A, or order, "$300.00, or what may be due on my deposit book," is conditional. National Sav. Bank v.

A writing directed to a savings bank, stating "Dear Sir, I want to draw all of my money out, $634.55. Oblige, Yours truly," signed by the depositor and delivered to a third person, was not a negotiable instrument when the bank rules stipulated that the bank book must be presented at the bank with an order before any legal obligation to pay could arise.

Ashless Coal Co. v. Davis, 183 Ky. 406, 209 S. W. 532.

Trust receipts by which a bank agreed to deliver shares of stock deposited with it to the order of the depositor upon return of the receipt were not negotiable instruments. The N. I. L. was not cited. Hearne v. Gillette, 151 La. 79, 91 So. 634.

When a note was payable on its face in money, parol evidence was not admissible that it was to be paid partly in merchandise. The N. I. L. was not cited. Harmon v. Harmon, 131

A contemporaneous oral agreement that the note was to be paid by a redelivery of the cattle sold is inadmissible under the parol evidence rule. Cox v. Parsons, 165 Va. 575, 183 S. E. 440, 165 Va. 582, 183 S. E. 443.

For instruments payable in particular money, including gold clause cases, see sec. 6(5).

A note payable in bonds is not negotiable. Moore v. Clines, 247 Ky. 605, 57 S. W. (2d) 509.

Interim certificates issued by a trust company, stating that the bearer was entitled on surrender of the certificate to receive a corporate bearer bond of a certain corporation, were stolen and sold to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. 

Held, the purchaser was not entitled to receive the bonds from the trust company. Their negotiability could not be determined by any custom of the commercial and business world in its treatment of such certificates, but by the , under which they were not negotiable because not containing an unconditional promise or order to pay a sum certain in money and not payable on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time. 

Babcock v. Nat. Surety Co., 106 Misc. 149, 175 N. Y. Supp.

See notes in 11 Corn. L. Q. 60, 24 Mich. L. Rev. 54, 35 Yale L. J. 877, 39 Harv. L. R. 875, 74 U. Pa. L. Rev. 727.

32% Liberty Loan full-paid interim certificates, issued by the Secretary of the Treasury, which state that payment in full has been made for Liberty bonds and that upon surrender of the certificates to a specified bank the bearer thereof will be entitled to receive bonds when prepared, are negotiable instruments. A bona fide purchaser for value for such a certificate is entitled to receive the bond, and not the person from whom the certificate was stolen. Although these instruments are not payable at a certain time or in money, in accordance with the N. I. L., the negotiability of such securities must be determined without inquiry into the statutes of the state or the common law. Congress under its power to raise money could delegate to the Secretary of the Treasury the right to make interim certificates negotiable, and the terms of these certificates had that effect. Security Nat. Bank v. People's Bank, 287 Mo. 464, 230 

S. W. 87.

Pleading 

County officials made a note payable "to M." The plaintiff bank, when offered the note as collateral, called M's attention to the fact that it was not negotiable on its face. M then obtained from the officials a letter that the words "or order" had been omitted and that he had authority to insert them in the note. They also wrote a letter to the Trust Company that the note should read "M, or order." In reliance on these letters, the bank took the note as collateral, indorsed by M. Held, the bank could recover from the maker of the note, free from any defenses good against M. While the note was on its face non-negotiable, the officials had power to correct the mistaken omission. The original omission of the words put the bank on notice, but it made inquiry and the subsequent letters rendered it a holder in due course. Road Improvement Dist. v. Southern 

Trust Co., 152 Ark. 422, 239 S. W. 8.

The payee's name was inserted in the blank on the printed form of a note from which the words "to the order of" immediately preceding the blank were stricken out, but the word "negotiable" immediately following it was retained. Held, the note was not negotiable. No intention within sec. 10 was shown to make it conform to the requirements of the  Charleston Nat. Bank v. Lemkuhl-Shepherd Co., 97 W. Va. 284, 125 

S. E. 241.

The complaint alleged that defendant "for value received, duly made, executed and delivered to plaintiff her promissory note in writing for $2,500." Held, that this was an action on a non-negotiable note, since it was not alleged to be payable to order or to bearer, and that consideration must therefore be alleged and proved. Also that the words "value received," is not a sufficient allegation of consideration. Martial Armand & 

Co. v. Creighton, 167 N. Y. Supp. 333.

When complaint upon a note did not allege that it was payable to bearer or order, the instrument declared upon was non-negotiable and hence there was, under New York law, no presumption of consideration, so that the failure to allege a consideration rendered the complaint fatally defective. Spear v. Assoc. Producing, etc., Corp., 120 Misc. Rep. 518, 199 N. Y. 

Supp. 84. See the note in 9 Corn. L. Q. 182.

2 cos the note, and a replication alleging merely that plaintiff bought Pleading for value before maturity and without notice was demurrable. 

Whateley v. Muscogee Bank, 197 Ala. 402, 72 So. 1018; Oneonta 

Trust & Banking Co. v. Box, 15 Ala. App. 440, 73 So. 759, citing sec. 184.

A note provided that if the note or any interest coupon was not paid at maturity, the whole debt should bear interest at an increased rate from the date of maturity of the coupon last paid. Alliance Trust Co. v. Jackson, 74 Okla. 257, 180

Miscellaneous interest cases

When a certificate of deposit maturing after six months provided for interest if the money was left for six months and stated that no interest would be paid after maturity, parol evidence was not admissible to show an agreement to pay interest for one year. One judge dissented.  

Verdi v. Helper State Bank, 57 Utah 502, 196 Pac. 225, 15 A.

If a note does not provide for interest, and the principal is paid in full by indorsers and accepted in full payment, the holder may not recover interest from the maker or indorsers. 

The N. I. L. was not cited. Paul Revere Trust Co. v. Castle, 231 Mass. 129, 120 N. E. 352.

A note was payable in twelve months from date, and provided, "In case • we make a general assignment for the benefit of creditors, * this note shall become due and payable immediately"; if not so paid, the payee was authorized to sell collateral securities, the proceeds to be applied "to the payment of any or all the liabilities aforesaid, with interest thereon to maturity." The maker assigned for creditors, and the payee realized upon the collateral six months after the date of the note. Held, the payee's right to interest ceased thereupon, and he was not entitled to interest for the remaining six months until the specified date of payment. The N. I. L. was not cited. Gaston v. Boston Penny Savings Bank, 233 Mass. 

23, 123 N. E. 101.

The holder of a note may, with the assent of the maker, make a gift of the right to receive the interest, separated from the ownership of the note. The N. I. L. was not cited. Read v.

Attorney's The word "or" in this subsection is not material, and an negotiability agreement to pay "attorney's fees and all costs of collection" does not impair negotiability, since the two phrases mean the same thing. Wood v. Ferguson, 71 Mont. 540, 230 Pac. 592; 

Philadelphia Nat. Bank v. Buckman, 314 Pa. 343, 171 Atl. 589.

So also agreement to pay attorney's fees and "all costs of collection," held not to impair negotiability. Anaheim Nat. Bank v. 

Dolph, 201 Cal. 17, 255 Pac. 184; Golden State Bank v. Dolph, 201 Cal. 767, 255 Pac. 187; First National Bank of Olive v.

But the provision "We agree to pay all costs, charges and expenses, including reasonable attorney's fees incurred by the payee in any foreclosure or other legal proceedings for the collection of the debt and in any other litigation or controversy arising from or connected with this note" rendered a note non-negotiable. Nussenfeld v. Smith (Conn.), 148 Atl. 388. 

A provision in a promissory note for attorney's fees "if collected by attorney, or if suit is brought on this note," is a promise to pay attorney's fees for collection only after dishonor, and does not impair the negotiability of the note. First Natl. Bank of Shawano v. Miller, 139 Wis. 126, 120 N. W. 820; Pugh v. 

Dawson, 95 Cal. App. 505, 273 Pac. 39.

A stipulation in a note for a reasonable attorney's fee in case of suit, does not render the note non-negotiable. McCormick v.

Severn, 36 Utah 6, 102 Pac. 626, 20 Ann. Cas. 1368; Potts v.

Nor does a provision that "if payment is not made at maturity, an additional amount of $10 and 10% of the principal and interest of this note shall be added to same as collection fees." The clause merely obliges the maker to indemnify the holder if costs of collection are incurred, and is not a penalty which must be paid in any event in case of dishonor. McClain v. Continental Supply Co., 66 Okla. 225, 168 Pac. 815. 

A note provided for attorney's fees, "If not paid promptly."

Held, this means, if not paid at maturity, and is valid. The 

N. I. L. was not cited, and it is not clear whether the note was negotiable. Easley v. Deer, 69 Ind. App. 264, 121 N. E. 542.

The holder of a note containing provision for attorney's fees is entitled to recover them, even though the note was purchased and suit brought maliciously for the purpose of suing without notice. Amuny v. Seaboard Bank & Trust Co. (Tex. Comm. 

App.), 23 S. W. (2d) 287.

Semble, the attorney's fee is due if the unpaid note is placed in the hands of an attorney for collection, although no suit is brought. 111, 75 Pac. 953; Security State Bank v. Fussell, 36 Okla. 527, 129 Pac. 746, contra as to the first point.

Tender of payment of note before proper demand is made by the holder cuts off attorney's fees. Urbish v. Rutledge (Tex. 

Civ. App.), 299 S. W. 921.

A note agreed to pay attorney's fees if it was not paid punctually and if an attorney was employed. Held, bringing suit was not a prerequisite to the collection of a fee.  Maxey v. Somerton State Bank, 22 Ariz. 371, 197 Pac. 894, 14 A. L. R. 1117.

If the note contains a clause for attorney's fees, if suit is brought, or if attorneys are employed to collect it, and the note is placed in the hands of attorney to collect, the maker is liable. for the fees whether the note is paid in cash or a new note is executed in lieu of the past due note. The N. I. L. was not cited. Williams v. Dockwiler, 19 N. M. 623, 145 Pac. 475.

Judge or jury A stipulation in a note to pay "all costs of collection," authorizes the collection in an action on the note of a reasonable attorney's fee. Letcher v. Wrightsman, 60 Okla. 14, 158 Pac. 1152. 

A stipulation in a note for ten per cent. attorney's fees if the note is placed in the hands of an attorney for collection, is a stipulation for liquidated damages and such fees are recoverable, in an action on the note, without proof they were incurred. First 

Nat. Bk. of Vicksburg v. Mayer, 129 La. 891, 57 So. 308; W. K.

Henderson Iron Works Supply Co. v. Meriwether Supply Co., 

178 La. 516, 152 So. 69. And where the note provides for ten per cent. attorney's fees, it cannot be shown as a defense that the plaintiff contracted with his attorney for a smaller amount. 

Bank of Lumpkin, et al. v. Farmers' State Bank, 35 Ga. App. 

340, 133 S. E. 307, vacating a former judgment in 33 Ga. App. 

117, 126 S. E. 280. But in Florence Oil, etc., Co. v. Hiawatha 

Gas, etc., Co., 55 Colo. 378, 135 Pac. 454, it was said that when the question is properly raised, the holder can only recover such part of the stipulated amount as will reimburse him for the reasonable and necessary attorney's fees he has been compelled to pay or has become liable for in enforcing collection of the note. It was also said in this case that the adoption of this provision in the  is an implied recognition that such stipulations are valid, there being no statute to the contrary. 

A demand note provided for attorney's fees in case of suit. 

A demand of payment should be made to entitle the holder to recover attorney's fees as special damages. Hodges v. Blaylock, 82 Ore. 179, 161 Pac. 396; Holstead v. Lewis (La. App.), 160 

So. 834.

Under the law of Maryland a clause in a note agreeing to pay five per cent. commission for collecting it, if not paid when due, was construed to mean such commissions to the extent of five per cent. in case the holder reasonably had to incur liability for and pay such commissions, but not otherwise. Chestertown Bank v. Walker, 163 Fed. 510, 90 C. C. A. 140. The N. I. L. was not cited in this case.

Attorneys' fees so stipulated are special damages and cannot be assessed as part of the costs. Murphy v. F. D. Cornell Co., 110 Cal. App. 452, 294 Pac. 490.

A promise to pay attorney's fees means a reasonable fee, and the amount should be left to the jury.  Beck v. Odell (Ind.), 14 O. N. E. 527, superseding (Ind. App.), 127 N. E. 852.

When a note provided for a reasonable attorney's fees, reasonableness was a question for the jury. The N. I. L. was not cited. Hillside State Bank v. Christensen (Wyo.), 229 Pac. 105; 

McCreary v. Stevens (Miss.), 126 So. 4; C. I. T. Corporation v. 

Studebaker Sales of Kentucky, 251 Ky. 349, 65 S. W. (2d) 84.

§2 (5) Contra, the reasonableness of attorney's fees is for the court and not for the jury.  Read Phosphate Co. v. Jenkins, 120 S. C. 337, 113 S. E. 317.

A court can determine the reasonableness of attorney's fees not only in equity under its general equitable powers, but at law under its power to control its officers. The  was not cited. Bank of Enoree v. Yarborough, 120 S. C. 385, 113 S. E. 313. 

Under the power of the court to control attorney's fees, they may be disallowed under circumstances rendering their recovery inequitable. When the payee, in a note secured by a mortgage, led the maker to believe that there would be no immediate foreclosure, he was not liable to pay attorney's fees to an indorsee after maturity, who took the notes subject to all equities against the payee at the time of assignment. The N. I. L. was not cited. Graves v. Burch, 26 Wyo. 192, 181 Pac. 354, 5 A. L. R. 1216.

If a note provides for an attorney's fee, the amount thereof must be proved, and the court will not take judicial notice of what constitutes a reasonable fee. Winslow Gas Co. v. Plost, 69 

Ind. App. 611, 122 N. E. 594, semble; Getman v. Hayhow, 103 

Okla. 161, 229 Pac. 559; Atkinson v. Neblett, 144 Va. 220, 132 

S. E. 326; contra, Burtt v. Schoening, et al, 138 Wash. 187, 244 

Pac. 381. blank 

A provision in a note for an attorney's fees, but leaving Amount blank the amount thereof, amounts to a promise to pay a reasonable sum as an attorney's fee, and does not render the note non-negotiable. Where plaintiff employed an attorney, it is sufficient to show what is a reasonable fee, and it is not necessary to prove an express agreement as to fees, or that plaintiff paid the attorney before suit. McCormick v. Swem, 36 Utah 6, 102 

Pac. 626.

If authority is given to fill blanks when the instrument is delivered, a reasonable sum may be inserted without voiding the instrument. Kramer v. Schnitzer, 268 Ill. 603, 109 N. E. 695. pay A note on a printed blank stated that the maker "agrees to dollars for attorney's fees, etc." A pen line was drawn through the blank. Held, that no attorney's fees were recoverable. The N. I. L. was not cited. Scandinavian-American 

Bank v. Long, 75 Wash. 270, 134 Pac. 913.

But where the amount was merely left blank, the maker was liable for reasonable fees, to be fixed by the court. Hawley v. 

Isaacson, 117 Wash. 197, 200 Pac. 1109, not citing the N. I. L.

Remedy to recover fee

The reasonable attorney's fees under the contract of the maker and indorser of a note to pay such fees, if recoverable at all. are recoverable as part of the contractual obligation and not as part of the costs. Schillinger v. Leary, 201 Ala. 256, 77 So. 846.

An attorney's fee provided for in a note is a constituent part of the obligation, enforceable by or in behalf of the holder, and is not to be considered as a distinct obligation or penalty to be enforced in behalf of the attorney or as a separate cause of action. The liability of one who assumes payment of such note includes liability for the attorney's fee.  Merrimon v. Parkey, 136 Tenn. 645, 191 S. W. 327.

If plaintiff secures a judgment on the note without providing for the costs of collection and attorney's fees, he can not recover them in another action, the contract having become merged in the judgment. The  was not cited. Sands v. Roller, 118 

Va. 191, 86 S. E. 857.

But it was held in First State Bank v. Cohasset Wooden 

Ware Co., 136 Minn. 103, 161 N. W. 398, not citing the N. I. L., that a general denial does not put in issue the reasonable value of attorney's fees stipulated for in the note. The claim therefor is not part of the cause of action on the note. They do not accrue until the services are performed and their value may then be determined by the court on application. 

So, when a note provided for an attorney's fee if it was collected by suit, the fee did not become due until after the institution of suit, so that it could not be included in the judgment but must be recovered in a separate action. The N. I. L. was not cited. Anderson v. Terhune, 206 Ill. App. 348. 

Where the note expressly stipulates that "attorney's fees in addition to other costs" might be recovered in the event of suit, attorney's fees were properly taxable as costs although not enumerated in Rev. Code, sec. 7169, declaring the items properly taxable as costs. The N. I. L. was not cited. Bovee v. Helland, 52 Mont. 51, 156 Pac. 416.

The note provided for an attorney's fee of ten per cent. The trial court did not submit the question of attorney's fee to the jury, who returned a verdict only for the amount of principal and interest. Held, that it was not error to add ten per cent, in rendering judgment. Futoransky v. Pope, 57 Okla. 755, 157

Pac. 905. Where the matter of the attorney's fee was submitted to the jury and the verdict was specifically for an amount without including attorney's fees. Held, it was error for the trial court not to add the stipulated ten per cent. for attorney's fees, and if it fails to do so the supreme court is justified in

§ 2 (5) so doing. Continental Gin Co. v. Sullivan, 48 Okla. 332, 150 

Pac. 209. recover The right to recover attorney's fees stipulated for in the note Who may passes to the indorsee with the note.  

Winn Parish Bank v. White Sulphur Co., 133 La. 282, 62 So. 

907. 

The right to recover attorney's fees and costs stipulated for in the note passes to a holder and constitutes a valid claim upon property mortgaged to secure the instrument. University of 

Richmond v. Stone, 148 Va. 686, 139 S. E. 257.

On the question whether a holder in due course can enforce a provision for attorney's fees free from defenses, see notes in

An indorser is liable for attorney's fees when he waives due diligence and states that he personally charges himself with the payment of this note and the debt evidenced thereby, since this substantially amounts to an assumption of liability coextensive with that of the maker. The N. I. L. was not cited. Farmers 

State Bank v. Haun, 30 Wyo. 322, 222 Pac. 45; Taylor v. Continental Supply Co., 16 Fed. (2d) 578.

When the parties to a note agreed that in case suit was brought to enforce payment thereof, they would pay a reasonable attorney's fee, an indorser was liable for the fee incurred by the indorsee in the suit against himself but not for that incurred in a prior unsuccessful suit against the maker. Sec. 2 was not cited. Highleyman v. McDowell Motor Car Co., 202 Mo. 

App. 221, 216 S. W. 52.

The indorsee of a note containing a stipulation for an attorney's fee sued his indorser and the maker and recovered a judgment in which no attorney's fee was included. The indorser paid the judgment and sued the maker for the amount of the note and costs and an attorney's fee. Held, that he could not recover the attorney's fee. If the action was on the assigned judgment it carried no fee. If on the note, it was a suit on the rote as paid, because assigned it could not be after it was merged in a judgment. The N. I. L. was not cited. Balkema v. Grolinund, 92 Wash. 326, 159 Pac. 127.

A note contained a provision that the makers and indorsers agreed to pay cost of collection or ten per cent. attorney's fee if payment was not made at maturity. An accommodation in-

In an action brought in the federal court of West Virginia on a note delivered and payable in Virginia to a Virginia bank and executed by residents of West Virginia, it was held that the federal court was not obliged to follow state court decisions in 

West Virginia refusing to enforce as illegal a provision for attorney's fees for collection, valid in Virginia since the question was one of general commercial law.  Citizens Nat. Bank of Orange, Va. v. Waugh (C. C. A. 

4th), 78 F. (2d) 325, 100 A. L. R. 939.

In an action by payee against maker and endorser, the notes were signed in Kentucky and mailed to Tennessee. Pursuant to a contract made in Tennessee, the notes were made payable in 

Tennessee. There was a provision for eight per cent. interest, which amount was legal in Tennessee, but not in Kentucky. The notes contained a provision for ten per cent. attorney's fees, which was permissible in Tennessee but not in Kentucky. Held, the notes were Tennessee contracts and governed by the laws of Tennessee, therefore the eight per cent. interest is enforceable, but the ten per cent. attorney's fee was not allowed, since such contracts are agreements to pay penalties, and tend to oppression of debtors and encourage litigation, contrary to the public policy of Tennessee. For this reason, such contracts when made in a foreign state, will not be enforced in Kentucky. Miller Bros. Co. v. Blackburn Coal Co., 212 Ky. 447, 279 S. W. 618.

A note containing a stipulation for attorney's fees made in West Virginia, where such stipulation is void, and payable in Virginia, where the stipulation is valid, was sued on in West Virginia. Held, stipulation is void since it is against the public policy of West Virginia. Campen Bros. v. Stewart, 106 W. Va. 

App. 247, 145 S. E. 381, limiting and disapproving People's 

State Bank of Crown Point, Inc. v. Jeffries, 99 W. Va. 399, 129 

S. E. 462.

The indorsee then brought suit to reform the note, in accordance with an alleged agreement for the liability of an indorser of negotiable paper, by inserting a warranty of payment at maturity. Held, for the defendant. The prior judg-

Sec. 3. When Promise is Unconditional. 

An unqualified order or promise to pay is unconditional within the meaning of this act, though coupled with— 

Cross Reference: §§ 1(2), 5, 126, 141, 184, 185, 196. 

(1) An indication of a particular fund out of which reimbursement is to be made, or a particular account to be debited with the amount; or

Cross Reference: §§ 5(1),(4), 6(5), 10, 17, 87, 127, 189. 

(2) A statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument.

Cross Reference: §§ 191, 4, 5, 5(1), 10, 17, 25. 

But an order or promise to pay out of a particular fund is not unconditional.

Cross Reference: §§ 5, 6(5), 10, 17.

A promissory note had printed on its face a trust agreement and on its back a conditional sales contract. The note contained the words, "this note is subject to and part of said contract," but the contract was not complete, all material blanks being unfilled. Held, negotiability of the note was unimpaired because it was on its face subject to a plainly non-existent contract, therefore unconditional. Jones v. First Nat. Corporate bonds "sub- 

Ever since the case of King Cattle v. Joseph, 158 Minn. 481,

Ject to 198 N. W. 437, it has been well established that the  mortgage" applies to corporate bonds. See cases cited under sec. 1, p. 108ff. supra. Until recently it was also well settled that corporate bonds containing the clause "subject to a mortgage or indenture" were non-negotiable. But during the last few years a number of cases following Enoch v. Brandon, 249 N. Y. 263, 164 N. E. 45, have departed from this rule with the result that, although it is perfectly clear under N. I. L. 1(2) that a nego tiable instrument "must contain an unconditional promise," the cases on the point are now in hopeless confusion. 

Under N. I. L. 3(2) it is clear that a statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument is unobjectionable. 

And bonds containing the following clause: "For the nature and extent of the security, rights of the holders of bonds, and the terms and conditions upon which the bonds are issued and secured, reference is made to the said mortgage," have properly been held negotiable. Bank of California v. National City Company, 138 Wash. 517, 244 Pac. 250; Weber v. Keith Railway 

Equipment Company, 248 Ill. App. 258; Siebenhauer v. Bank of California Nat. Ass'n, 211 Cal. 239, 294 Pac. 1062. Contra, St. Louis-Carterville Coal Co. v. Southern Coal & Mining Co., 194 Mo. App. 598, 186 S. W. 1152. These cases seem to achieve the limit to which reference can be carried without becoming conditional incorporation.

The following clause, which seems clearly to render the in- Corporate strument containing it conditional, has been held not to affect to mortgage" negotiability: "To which deed of trust reference is hereby made with the same effect as though recited at length herein, for the description of the property mortgaged, the nature and extent of the security, the rights of the holders of the bonds, and the terms and conditions upon which the bonds are issued, held and secured." Pollard v. Tobin, 211 Wis. 405, 247 N. W. 453, 9 Wis. L. Rev. 87; Marine Nat. Exchange Bank of Milwaukee v. Kallzimmers Mfg. Co., 293 U. S. 357, 79 L. Ed. 427, 55 S. C.

713; Detroit Trust Co. v. Detroit City Service Co., 262 Mich. 14, 247 N. W. 76, 31 Mich. L. Rev. 984.

A promissory note given for a chattel, and stipulating that the title to the chattel shall remain in the vendor-payee until the note is paid, is not conditional, and the maker is liable thereon although the chattel was destroyed before the maturity of the note. The  was not mentioned. Whitlock v.

In a suit by holder against maker, it was held that recitation in notes that "this note is given in payment of machinery purchased by contract between these parties ** and is given in accordance with same, and secured by the lien thereby created and hereby recognized *" is no more than a "statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument" and does not qualify the promise to pay. C. H. Mountjoy Parts Co. v. 

San Antonio Nat. Bank (Tex. Civ. App.), 12 S. W. (2d) 609.

The indorsee of a note, negotiable in form, had knowledge that it was given in connection with a contract which provided that the note was in part payment of a chattel, title to which was retained until payment of the note. The court considered that the situation was the same as if the terms of the contract had been written into the note, but held the note negotiable. The power of the payee to retake the chattel on dishonor did not affect the absolute promise to pay, but gave the payee a choice of remedies at maturity. People's Bank v. 

Porter, 58 Cal. App. 41, 208 Pac. 200. See the discussion of chattel notes under the N. I. L. in 11 Cal. L. Rev. 37 and 71 U. 

Pa. L. Rev. 167.

A note payable to the order of X which contains a provision that it is given subject to the approval of X for property received of X, and that the title to said property shall remain in X until the note is paid, is not negotiable. Worden Grocery 

Co. v. Blanding, 161 Mich. 254, 126 N. W. 212. The court did not cite the N. I. L., and followed the case of Sloan v. 

McCarty, 134 Mass. 245, upon this disputed question.

Miscellaneous memoranda

A remitter desiring to forward money to the plaintiff purchased a cashier's check containing the following clause: "For the account of" plaintiff payable to the bank where the plaintiff had kept an account. The bank failed and the plaintiff claims the fund as a preferred creditor on the grounds that the words constituted the payee bank a trustee. Held, such words are a mere statement of the transaction and created no trust. 

Equitable Trust Co. of New York v. Roehling, 275 U. S. 248, 48 Sup. Ct. 58, 72 L. Ed. 264, 76 U. Pa. L. Rev. 455, 28 Colum. 

L. Rev. 377, 6 Tex. L. Rev. 381, 8 B. U. L. Rev. 130. 

An acceptance containing the following provision: "This acceptance covers 220 radio cabinets and benches which are absolutely guaranteed and are to be replaced by the manufacturer if found damaged when cartons are opened," held negotiable, since guarantee did not constitute condition upon which trade acceptance was made payable, but constituted purely a collateral understanding between the drawer and drawee, and did not affect the obligation to make payment. Coffin v. D. W. May, Inc. (N. J.), 140 Atl. 331. "I shall pay to the order of the American Hoist & Derrick 

Co., on, etc., $2,340, for amount of the second installment agreed on of a crane of their manufacture, purchased on this date, according to specifications of their representative, Held, a negotiable note. Merchants Nat. Bk. v. Santa Maria 

Sugar Co., 162 App. Div. 248, 147 N. Y. Supp. 498. #99 When a note as originally written contained a memorandum that it was for the fulfillment of a certain agreement, this was a mere statement of the transaction which gave rise to the instrument and was material, so that the erasure of these words did not constitute an alteration of the instrument vitiating it in the hands of the holder in due course. Mason v. Shaffer, 82 W. Va. 632, 96 S. E. 1023.

When checks bear a memorandum of a certain contract, they may be applied by the payee upon other contracts under a parol agreement allowing this to be done without regard to such entries.  Long v. U. S. Fidelity 

& Guaranty Co., 178 N. C. 503, 101 S. E. 11.

A check sent in payment of a disputed claim bore the words "in payment of contract in full for painting," etc. The payee cancelled the words "in full" and cashed the check. Held, the check operated as an accord and satisfaction despite the erasure. 

The  was not cited. Beck Electric Const. Co. v. Nat. 

Contracting Co., 143 Minn. 190, 173 N. W. 413. 

A check to the order of X with the words in the lower leftheld hand corner "For Wilkes, this check may not be paid unless the unconditional object for which it is drawn is stated," is not conditional. If

§3 (2) 

the object is not stated, it is not a check, but if it is stated, the order to pay is absolute. Brown v. Cow Creek Sheep Co., 21 

Wyo. 1, 126 Pac. 886. "Original indorser certifies that he is the owner of commodity for which this check is given and has full authority to sell same," printed on the back of a check, was held not to render it non-negotiable. P. J. Williams Industries v. First State Bank of Lyford (Tex. Civ. App.), 38 S. W. (2d) 1109.

A note provided upon its face: "this note is collateral to a stock subscription of even date herewith." Held, the note is non-negotiable, since it incorporates the contract and renders. payment conditional. Ivory v. Lamoreaux, 241 Mich. 226, 217

N. W. 54. Two judges dissented, basing their dissent on section 

3. 76 U. Pa. L. Rev. 867.

A certificate of deposit was payable upon return with interest at two per cent. if left six months, "subject to the rules of the savings department." These rules, not on the certificate, required thirty days' notice before the withdrawal of a deposit.

Held, a negotiable instrument. It is not payable out of a particular fund, for it carries the credit of the bank, and not merely of the savings department. It is unconditional, for the rules of the savings department are provided for by the banking law and serve as a protection to the bank; the time of payment must inevitably happen. The amount is certain. White v. Wadhams, 204 Mich. 381, 170 N. W. 60.

A note is negotiable which states that it is for the purchase of a stallion, and that the payee warrants him to be possessed of specified qualities. An indorsee is not thereby put on inquiry as to breaches of the warranty. Critcher v. Ballard, 180 N. C. 111, 104 S. E. 134. 

A note for $1,183, partly printed and partly typewritten, stated that it was negotiable. Below the signatures and on the margin appeared in lead pencil the words, "Given to secure the difference between $15,000 and $13,820." Held, the indorsee could hold the makers free from defenses. The note was negotiable since the memorandum simply stated the transaction that gave rise to the instrument and did not make it payable upon a contingency. It did not indicate that the note was collateral for some other obligation, although such was actually the case and the principal obligation had been discharged. Under sec. 56 actual notice must be brought home to the holder, and the rule in other matters as to notice through mere information putting one on inquiry does not apply to commercial paper, so that the notation on the margin was not notice. Morehead v. Cummins, 207 Mo. App. 64, 230 S. W. 656.

§3 (2) Detachment of memorandum An instrument contained an order for specified goods, and at the end of it was a promissory note in negotiable form, the sig- from note natures to which were the only signatures to the instrument. 

The note was capable of being detached, and was detached and transferred by defendant. Held, that the instrument as originally written was not a promissory note; that the detachment of the note part was a material alteration, and that defendant was guilty of forgery. State v. Mitton, 37 Mont. 366, 96 Pac. 926.

The defendant in ordering goods was presented with an "order form"; the first part was a detailed contract, which the defendant signed, providing that title should remain in the vendor till payment; below on the same paper was the wording of a negotiable installment note, which the defendant also signed. The seller detached the note portion and sued. Held, the note was not negotiable because of the reservation of title, and its detachment and transformation into an apparently negotiable note was a material alteration which avoided the instrument.  Toledo Scale Co. v. Gogo, 186 Mich. 442, 152 N. W. 1046, Anno. Cas. 1917E, 601, with note on "Effect of detaching from promissory note contract or memorandum attached thereto."

A note covering the price of an order of goods was attached to the order and separated from it by a perforated line. The order stated that the payee was authorized to detach the note when the order was accepted and shipped. Notwithstanding the maker's countermand of the order, the goods were shipped and the note was detached and indorsed to a bank which was a holder in due course. The bank indorsed it to the plaintiff for value without recourse after maturity. Held, the maker was liable to the holder, and a verdict for the holder should have been directed. The  was not cited. Stevens v. 

Khetter, 110 S. C. 271, 96 S. E. 406.

The defendant signed a demand promissory note and a contract which recited that the note should be used only as collateral. Note and contract were printed on the same sheet of paper, and separated by a perforated line. The note was detached, and negotiated to the plaintiff as collateral. The plaintiff recovered. Although not a bona fide purchaser, the detachment of the note did not constitute a defense since the defendant knew that he was executing a negotiable note and it was used as he agreed. The N. I. L. was not cited. Shattuck v. Reed, 221 Mich. 155, 190 N. W. 649.

A conditional sales contract included an agreement in the form of a negotiable promissory note separated by a perforated line so that it could be detached from the remainder of the agreement. It was detached and sold to the plaintiff. Held, in a suit by the holder against the maker that it was non-negotiable, that the detachment was a material alteration and that

An instrument which begins with an order for goods at a cerheld condi- tain price, to be shipped to a city in another state at a certain time, and ends with a promise to pay the price at a certain place 180 days after date, is not a negotiable promissory note, since the promise was conditional on acceptance of the order and shipment of the goods. Neylus v. Port, 46 Pa. Super. Ct. 428. 

A note for $5,000, payable to the order of a bank, stated on the margin at the top that it was given to "reimburse" the bank for a specified certificate of deposit for $5,000, due at the maturity of the note. The note was held to be conditional and not negotiable. It showed on its face that it was given for the bank's promise to pay at a future time and not for money received from the bank or in connection with an actual deposit. "Reimburse" means to pay back, and implied a condition that the bank should have paid out something to be restored. Negotiability depends on the wording of the instrument, and can not be affected by subsequent facts. Three judges dissented on the ground that the memorandum was "a statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument." Every promissory note, whether negotiable or not, is given to reimburse somebody for something; it may be for credit only, so that the express use of the word should not impair negotiability. One of the majority concurred in the decision partly on the ground that the plaintiff was not a holder in due course even if the note was negotiable. Sacred Heart Church Bldg. Comm. v. Manson, 203 Ala. 256, 82 So. 498.

The dissent is the better view. The certificate of deposit was a negotiable instrument, as the majority admitted, so that the maker of the note received something of immediate value, and even a non-negotiable credit would have been a good business reason for the issue of the note. Words on a note which appear to be statements of a transaction should be construed as such if reasonably possible. There is no need for courts to imply conditions in order instruments from words which do not clearly involve conditions, for it is easy for the parties to insert them expressly if they desire them. See the adverse criticism of the decision in 8 Cal. L. Rev. 172, 19 Colum. L. Rev. 509.

The fact that a note otherwise negotiable in form was written on the same piece of paper as a conditional escrow agreement did not render the note non-negotiable.  Williams v. Silverstein (Cal. App.), 293 Pac. 102, 213 

Cal. 269, 2 P. (2d) 165, 6 U. of Cin. L. Rev. 87.

The defendant made a note to the plaintiff due one day of a particular after date, secured by stock in a corporation and stated to be 

Instruments payable "out "Payable in dividends to be declared" by the corporation. Several years later, the defendant gave the plaintiff a renewal note due one day after date for a smaller amount secured by a larger amount of the same stock and stating "dividends on said stock are to be used for payment of this note as received." Dividends subsequently ceased. After holding that the renewal note was without consideration, the court ruled that the first note was ambiguous and that parol evidence was admissible between the immediate parties to clear up this ambiguity and show that it did not carry the general credit of the maker, but only the credit of a particular fund, the dividends. The  was not cited, and did not apply to the first note, which was issued before its enactment. Boardman v. Frick, 95 W. Va. 

263, 120 S. E. 883. 

See the note in 30 W. Va. L. Q. 204. Extrinsic evidence is not properly admissible to show negotiability, which must be determined from the four corners of the instrument. However, even if the ambiguity of the first note made it not negotiable, the plaintiff could still have recovered upon it as a simple contract if it could be construed as payable out of the maker's general credit, and parol evidence was helpful on this question of construction. The second note was more probably negotiable, the fund being perhaps merely a source of reimbursement. 

A note was not negotiable which stated that it was made upon the condition that it was to be paid out of the first money received from the sale of certain lots, and if sufficient was not received by or before maturity, then the note was to be renewed or a new note given. Rector v. Strauss, 134 Ark. 374, 203 S. W. 

1024. This case is distinguished and limited by Road Impr.

A bond of a joint stock company which exempted the stockholders from personal liability was held a negotiable instrument not payable out of a particular fund. Hibbs v. Brown, 190 N. 

Y. 167, 82 N. E. 1108. So also Charles Nelson Co. v. Morton (Cal. It is submitted that these three cases show that the provisions of the act requiring the instrument not to be payable "out of a particular fund" are not synonymous with the old common law rule that the instrument must rest on the "general credit of the maker," but properly adopt the commercial point of view that an instrument exempt-

84 ing a portion of the general credit is still not based on a particular fund and is therefore negotiable.

Lorimer v.

A stipulation in a mortgage accompanying a note that the maker is not to be personally liable on the note and the mortgaged property only is to be looked to for payment, does not render the note non-negotiable. Tennent v. Caffery, 163 La. 976, 113 So. 167.

12, 11 A. L. R. 623.

A note payable to a bank provided that the bank should have a lien upon the deposit of the maker and that in the event of insolvency of the maker, the note should become due immediately without demand. Before the fixed maturity of the note, a receiver was appointed for the maker and the bank claimed a lien upon its deposit. Held, although a bank has no right to apply a deposit to a debt of the depositor until such debt matures, it had so matured in this case by virtue of the acceleration clause. "Insolvency" bears its usual sense of inability to pay debts.  Wright v. Seaboard 

Steel & Manganese Corp., 272 Fed. 807 (C. C. A., N. Y.). 

Where the instrument provided for acceleration at the option of the holder upon nonpayment of interest, held in equity, the holder must make demand before exercising the option by bringing suit. Parker v. Mazur (Tex. Civ. App.), 13 S. W. (2d) 174, and note 14 Corn. L. Q. 478. Contra, the bringing of suit at law is sufficient to support the allegation that the option had

§ 4 (2) 

been exercised. Pope v. Woolford Realty Co., 35 Ga. App. 284, 134 S. E. 174; Moore v. Kenemeyer (Tex. Civ. App.), 271 S. W. 

653. But where the acceleration on nonpayment is not optional on the holder, no demand is necessary before bringing suit. 

Hartge v. Capelato, 136 Wash. 538, 241 Pac. 5. 

provisions of notes

Each of three notes falling due in successive years contained Acceleration a provision that if any note was not paid at maturity, then all in series the notes were to mature at the option of the holder. On the day after default of the first note maturing, the indorsee brought suit against the maker and the indorser-payee without giving the latter notice of dishonor. Held, the indorser was discharged on all three notes. Suit was not equivalent to notice, but constituted an election by the indorsee to treat all the notes as due. 

Semble, the notes were negotiable. Farmers Bank & T. Co. v. 

Dent, 206 Ky. 405, 267 S. W. 202.

A statement in a series of separate notes that on default of payment in any one, all shall become due, does not impair negotiability. Havens v. Foskett, 81 Cal. App. 653, 254 Pac. 642.

The defendant made four notes due on successive dates, "or in case of my removal or attempt to remove from the county."

The payee sued under the Code before the specified maturities, but alleged that the defendant had removed. The answer denied such removal, alleged equitable defenses of duress and want of consideration, and prayed that the plaintiff be enjoined from negotiating or suing, and for cancellation. The defendant moved that the equitable issues be tried first. Held, motion denied; the law issues should be tried first. One judge dissented on the ground that if the defendant won on the law issues, the action would merely abate as premature; and the payee could then take the notes, which were negotiable and thus not yet matured, and could negotiate them to a holder in due course, cutting off the defenses. Lynch v. Schemmel, 176 Ia. 499, 155 

N. W. 1019. The dissenting opinion is approved in 2 Ia. L. 

Bull. 151. Where a series of notes provided that upon default in the payment of any one of the notes the remaining notes were to become immediately due and payable, it was held that the holders had the option of accelerating the maturity or allowing the notes to run the full period. Candee Smith & Howland Co. v. Bendish 

Contracting Co., 265 N. Y. Supp. 737, 148 Misc. 262.

Acceleration provisions Notes, payable at a certain time, but secured by a mortgage executed as part of the same transaction, and reciting that the in mortgages whole debt shall be due in case of sale or removal of the property by the mortgagor without the consent of the mortgagee, or in case the mortgagee deems himself insecure, are uncertain as to time and amount of payment and are therefore not negotiable. Iowa Nat. Bank v. Carter, 144 Ia. 715, 123 N. W. 237.

A note payable at a specified day stated that it was secured by a chattel mortgage. A note reading, "one day after date I promise to pay to be paid at my death," was not a good note. Zimmerman v. 

Zimmerman, 262 Pa. 540, 106 Atl. 198. The N. I. L. was not cited, and the note was not negotiable in any event as it contained no words of negotiability. Certainty of time seems clearly violated by its terms. It is suggested in 17 Mich. L. Rev. 702, that the note might have been construed as valid by the insertion of "or," but such a method would throw commercial paper into the vague realm of testamentary interpretation and mislead prospective purchasers into buying freak instruments with the hope of a liberal judicial construction which might not be given. Whatever the hardship in individual cases, it is much more just in the end to brand all uncertain instruments as bad. Furthermore, a note payable "one day after date or at my death" is also uncertain, for which is its maturity for purposes of presentment and notice, letting in equities, etc.?

ANNOTATIONS 

Although the act is silent on the negotiability of mortgages and other contracts collateral to negotiable instruments, it seems that such contracts can be drawn so as to meet its requirements by taking advantage of the provisions of this section. See Cook v. Parks, 46 Ga. App. 749, 169 S. E. 208, where a chattel mortgage was held a negotiable instrument subject to all the provisions of this act. On the power of a holder in due course of a negotiable instrument to take advantage of these incidental provisions free from defenses of prior parties, see 34 Harv. L. Rev. 

90; W. E. Britton, "Assignment of Mortgages securing Negotiable Notes," 10 Ill. L. Rev. 337. See also cases under secs. 1 and 57. "No action" clauses in securities There seems to be no reason why the provisions of section 5 corporate cannot be incorporated into bonds so as to limit the right of action to sue. It has been held that such limitations alone do not destroy negotiability. Pflueger v. Broadway Trust & Savings Bank, 351 Ill. 170, 184 N. W. 610, 31 Mich. L. Rev. 986; 

Paepke v. Paine, 253 Mich. 636, 235 N. W. 871, 75 A. L. R. 

1205; Cunningham v. Pressed Steel Co., 238 A. D. 624, 265 

N. Y. Supp. 256, affd. 263 N. Y. 671, 189 N. E. 750, 32 Mich. 

L. Rev. 403, 2 U. of Pitt. L. Rev. 75.

For a further discussion of these cases, see sections 3(2), supra, and 51, infra. "An instrument which contains an order or promise to do any act in addition to the payment of money is not negotiable" 

Cross Reference: 88 1 to 4, 6 to 9, 2, 3, 57, 126, 184.

A note otherwise negotiable in form but promising to pay money and wheat, is not negotiable. Thomson v. Koch, 62 Wash. 

438, 113 Pac. 1110.

A stipulation in an otherwise negotiable instrument that it constitutes a lien upon the maker's crop, and a promise that "no part of the crop shall be mortgaged or sold" renders the instrument non-negotiable. Rohr v. Jeffery, 128 Kan. 541, 278 

Pac. 725. 

A long instrument designated a "subscription" contained towards the middle language, which, if apart, would constitute

5 cas acts a negotiable promissory note to the order of a school. The Additional document also related to a scholarship in the school and contained promises to study two hours per week, etc. Held, not a promissory note, because it contained promises to do acts in addition to the payment of money. Page v. Wooster, 213 Ill. 

App. 239. Accord, Midwest Collection Bur. v. Greenwald, 214 

Ill. App. 468.

A note agreeing to pay taxes assessed upon the note or its mortgage security is not negotiable. Coolidge v. Saltmarsh, 96 

Wash. 541, 165 Pac. 508; Hubbard v. Robert Wallace Co., 201 

Ia. 1143, 208 N. W. 730, 45 A. L. R. 1065 and exhaustive note at 1074; Schumacher v. Miller (Conn.), 150 Atl. 524; Mazurkiewicz v. Dowholonek (Conn.), 149 Atl. 234.

A note contained a provision accelerating the maturity if the maker failed to pay taxes, rates or assessments on the property mortgaged to secure the note, or allowed taxes to be levied against the holder on account of the note. Held, that this bound the maker to pay the taxes, etc., and was a promise to do other things in addition to the promise to pay a certain sum of money and rendered the note non-negotiable. Bright v. Offield, 81 

Wash. 442, 143 Pac. 159, followed in Keir v. Staufer, 52 S. D. 

223, 217 N. W. 211.

It is submitted that the instruments in such cases as these do not contain absolute promises to do additional acts, but merely acceleration clauses in case such acts are not done, and therefore they are negotiable within the meaning of sec. 4(2). 

The test of negotiability ought to be whether or not the promisee would have a cause of action for breach of contract if the act is not done. It is clear that no such right exists under this form of instrument. The force of Bright v. Offield is consider ably lessened if it is not overruled by Bank of California v. 

National City Co., 138 Wash. 517, 244 Pac. 690, affd. and modified, 141 Wash. 243, 251 Pac. 561, 25 Mich. L. Rev. 794, where an instrument containing the following provision was held negotiable: "All interest which shall accrue hereon shall be paid without deduction of any amount for income tax which the Pacific Company [maker] shall be required or permitted to retain therefrom to pay under law."

A certificate of indebtedness containing in addition to a promise to pay money an agreement to keep free from incumbrance property, on which the value of collateral pledged for security of the instrument, depends, is not a negotiable instrument. The certificate was issued before the Negotiable Instruments Law was adopted in New Jersey, but the court said that sec. 5 of that act was the same as the common law. Strickland v. National Salt Co., 79 N. J. Eq. 182, 81 Atl. 828. An opposite result as to the negotiability of the same form of certificate was reached in the Federal Circuit Court of Appeals, Second Cir cuit (N. Y.), where the  was in force before the date

§ 180 

 acts 

Additional of the certificate, but the point in question does not appear to have been raised or discussed in that case. National Salt Co. v. Ingraham, 143 Fed. 805, 74 C. C. A. 479. But see ib., 122 

Fed. 40, 58 C. C. A. 356.

An instrument containing a promise to keep the machine, in payment for which it was given, in repair, is non-negotiable. 

Albany State Bank v. Anthony, 121 Oreg. 277, 254 Pac. 806.

So also a promise to insure the property pledged as security renders the instrument non-negotiable. First State Savings 

Bank v. Russell, 244 Mich. 298, 221 N. W. 142. 

Promise to furnish additional collateral But where the mortgage securing the note provides that the mortgagor is to insure the property, the note is not rendered non-negotiable when the mortgage terms are not incorporated therein. Northwestern Finance Co. v. Crouch, 258 Mich. 411, 242 N. W. 771.

A note containing the following stipulation, "We further agree to hold all fertilizers bought for us in trust *** for mortgagees and subject to their orders," and also a stipulation promising to give ten days' notice for the appointment of auditors to examine accounts, was held non-negotiable. First Nat. Bank of Dothan v. Elba Hardware & Furniture Co., 223 Ala. 493, 137 So. 173. 

A provision that if collateral declines in value the maker will furnish additional securities and that in default thereof the note shall become due and payable, renders the note non-negotiable. 

Hibernia Bank v. Dresser, 132 La. 532, 61 So. 561; Holliday

A note providing for a confession of judgment "after maturity" was negotiable though the words "if not paid" were not added. Sec. 5 was not cited. Metropolitan State Bank v. Mc-

Confession of maturity judgment before of laws A note, dated and payable in Illinois and authorizing any Conflict attorney to confess judgment on behalf of the maker "at any time hereafter," was prepared by the payee in Illinois and sent to the maker in Indiana, who there signed it and deposited it in the mail addressed to the payee. After maturity the payee obtained a judgment by confession in Illinois, and sued on this judgment in Indiana, where the law did not authorize the performance of contracts in this form, although permitting confession of judgment under some conditions. Held, the Illinois judgment was entitled to full faith and credit. The note was executed when it was mailed in Indiana, but was performable

Conflict in Illinois, and Illinois law must govern its performance. Such contracts are not against public policy in Indiana. One judge dissented.  Egley v. Bennett & 

Co. (Ind.), 145 N. E. 830, superseding 144 N. E. 533, which superseded (Ind. App.), 139 N. E. 385. See the notes in 38

The law of Texas prohibits powers to confess judgment before bringing suit, while Pennsylvania allows them. The defendant issued a judgment note in Dallas, Texas. Judgment was confessed in Pennsylvania. In a suit in Texas on the Pennsylvania judgment it was held that the judgment was void. 

Bernard Gloecker Co. v. Boker Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 52 S. W. (2d) 912.

§ 5 (3) (3) "Waives the benefit of any law intended for the advantage or protection of the obligor" 

Cross Reference: 88 2, 17, 23, 61, 70 to 78, 82(3), 89, 109 to 112, 120, 122, 124, 142, 144, 145, 152 to 157, 175, 186.

Instruments, otherwise negotiable in form, sometimes contain a provision "that the maker and indorsers severally waive presentment and notice of protest, and consent that time of payment may be extended without notice" or that "no extension of time of payment with or without our knowledge by the receipt of interest or otherwise shall release us or either of us from the obligation of payment," or "that after maturity this note may be extended from time to time by any one or more of us without the knowledge or consent of any of the others of us and after such extension the liability of all parties shall remain as if no such extension had been made" or similar provisions. They seem intended merely to prevent the discharge of secondary parties by extensions of time, but not to alter the specified date of maturity, unless there is an expressed agreement between maker and holder for such an extension subsequent to the execution of the note. These waivers clearly fall within sec. 5(3), and in the great majority of cases since the Negotiable Instruments

Law, such provisions have been held not to impair the negotiability of the instrument.

Kan. 564, 171 Pac. 636, not citing sec. 5(4), a note was held negotiable in which the makers, sureties, indorsers and guarantors waived presentation and notice and consented that the time of payment might be extended without notice to any of the sureties. Rossville State Bank v. Heslet, supra, was distinguished on the ground that there were no sureties on the note in the principal case. And in Leach v. Urschel, 112 Kan. 629, 212 Pac. 

111, a note was held negotiable despite a similar waiver of protest unaccompanied by a provision for extension of time. 

In Cedar Rapids Nat. Bank v. Weber, 180 Ia. 966, 164 N. 

W. 233, L. R. A. 1918A, 432, a clause reading: "All parties to this note, including sureties, indorsers, and guarantors, hereby severally waive presentment for payment, notice of nonpayment and protest, and consent to extensions of time on this note" was construed to mean that the payee or holder was bound in advance to consent to any extension of time which the maker might demand and, as no period of extension was fixed, the note was uncertain as to time and therefore not negotiable. Sed quaere? This construction seems forced. An extension could hardly be made otherwise than by agreement of the holder and maker at some certain time and for some definite time, and the clause was evidently intended to operate as a waiver by the parties secondarily liable. See First Nat. Bank v. Stover, 21 N. M. 

453, 155 Pac. 905, Ann. Cas. 1918B, 145, L. R. A. 1916D, 1280. 

See also 3 Corn. L. Q. 125; 4 Ia. L. Bull. 123. 

In Quinn v. Bane, 182 Ia. 843, 164 N. W. 788, the court held that because of its holding in Cedar Rapids Nat. Bank v. 

Weber, supra, that a clause giving the consent of the payee or holder to extensions made the note non-negotiable, it must hold the note in suit to be non-negotiable. But in this note the provision was different. It read "The maker, sureties, and guar-

§ 5 (3) antors of this note severally waive presentment for payment, notice of nonpayment, protest, notice of protest, and diligence in bringing suit against any party hereto, and consent that the time of payment may be extended from time to time without notice thereof.” Quinn v. Bane was followed in Manhard v. 

First Nat. Bank (Ia.), 165 N. W. 185, without discussion; 

Security Sav. Bank v. Capp, 193 Ia. 278, 186 N. W. 927; and in Farmers Nat. Bank v. Stanton, 191 Ia. 433, 182 N. W. 647, 17 A. L. R. 857, not citing , in which joint makers authorized the holder "to extend the time of payment 

time to time without impairing our several or joint liabilities."

The court refused to find that the maker's knowledge of the payee's intention to transfer this non-negotiable note estopped him to set up a defense when sued by a bona fide transferee for value; see the note on such estoppel in 17 A. L. R. 862.

The court in these Iowa cases seems to have been influenced by the case of Woodbury v. Roberts, 59 Ia. 348, in which case the note had a caluse that "the makers and indorsers of this obligation further expressly agree that the payee, or his assigns, may extend the time of payment thereof from time to time indefinitely as he or they may see fit."

But this note was a trick, since the payee and the maker were the same person. The maker therefore had power to extend his own note indefinitely so that its payment was optional as he could extend it forever. 

A note beginning, "September 1, 1916, * we jointly and severally promise to pay," provided that after it was due the time of payment might be extended from time to time "by any one or more of us" without the knowledge or consent of the others, and that the makers should continue liable as if no such extension had been made. There was only one maker. 

Held, the note was not negotiable, because not payable at a fixed or determinable future time. Wayne County Nat. Bank v. Cook, 73 Ind. App. 404, 127 N. E. 773. This decision seems erroneous, but was followed in Smith v. Zabel, 86 Ind. App. 

310, 157 N. E. 551, 3 Ind. L. J. 397, 26 Mich. L. Rev. 568, where a clause reading "No extension of time shall release either of us" was held to destroy negotiability. The holder had a right to payment on the date specified. The clause gave the maker no option of extension as against the holder, but was inserted to prevent an extension granted by the holder from releasing other makers who were expected to sign, but did not. Cf. American 

Bank & Trust Co. v. Ragsdale, 74 Ind. App. 367, 129 N. E. 59, not under N. I. L. -Minority view

The words "without defalcation" in a negotiable bill or note are now mere surplusage and without meaning, under the Negotiable Instruments Law, and hence do not constitute a waiver of rights of set-off or counterclaim. The  was cited only generally. First Nat. Bank of Rocky Ford v. Lewis, 57 Colo. 125, 139 Pac. 1102; Ex parte Rice, 161 S. C. 77, 159

S. E. 492, 79 A. L. R. 123. Sed quaere. It does not follow because in some states promissory notes, in the absence of such a clause, were not negotiable in the sense of cutting off defenses between the original parties, as against a holder in due course, that when the words are used in a note, which is fully negotiable without them, they may not have the effect of waiving rights of set-off or counterclaim, which could otherwise be asserted as against one who took with notice or after maturity. The Negotiable Instruments Law, in sec. 5-3, recognizes the use, in negotiable instruments, of provisions which waive the benefit of any law intended for the advantage or protection of the obligor, and statutes of set-off and counterclaim seem to come within the description of such laws. For the history of this provision for payment "without defalcation," which is still used in some states, the following cases may be consulted. London v. Tiffany, 5 W. & S. 367; Houk v. Foley, 2 P. & W. 245, 4 Halsted's Law 

120; Youngs v. Little, 3 Green's Law 1; Cumberland Bank v. 

Hann, 3 Harrison 222; McDonald v. Lee's Admr., 12 La. 435; 

Council Bluffs v. Cuppey, 41 Ia. 104.

The provision "without discount or offset" is equivalent to "without defalcation" and does not render uncertain the amount to be paid or impair negotiability. Waiver of exemptions and

85 (4) consent to the extension of the jurisdiction of justices of the peace in the note are also permitted. Perry Nat. Bank v. Engnell, 198 Ia. 26, 199 N. W. 283. (4) "Gives the holder an election to require something to be done in lieu of payment of money"

Cross Reference: 88 3, 6(5), 17. 

A provision in a bond, otherwise negotiable, entitling the holder, at his option, to receive money or stock of the corporation-maker, does not destroy the negotiability of the bond. Pratt v. Higginson, 230 Mass. 256, 119 N. E, 661, 1 A. L. R. 714.

A note providing that title to the property for which it was given should remain in the payee, and upon nonpayment at maturity the property was to be repossessed by the payee, did not impair negotiability since it gave the holder an election to take the property in lieu of payment of money. Sandlin v. 

Maury Nat. Bank, 210 Ala. 349, 98 So. 190.

The negotiability of notes was not impaired by a provision that the payee could retake the chattel for which the notes were given if they were not paid. People's Bank v. Porter, 58 Cal. 

App. 41, 208 Pac. 200. 

Where the maker has the option to deliver cash or bonds, the promise is not negotiable. Louisa National Bank v. Paintsville Nat. Bank, 260 Ky. 327, 85 S. W. (2d) 668, 100 A. L. R. 819. "But nothing in this section shall validate any provision or stipulation otherwise illegal"

An agreement on a note authorizing suit in any court in the state, waiving the defendant's right to be sued in the county of residence only, is valid. The N. I. L. was not cited. Thompson v. Union Springs Guano Co., 202 Ala. 327, 80 So. 409; 

Brown v. Alabama Chemical Co., 207 Ala. 215, 92 So. 260. But see Stewart v. Capitol Fertilizer Co., 207 Ala. 596, 93 So. 641.

(4) "Bears a seal"

198; Bolliel v. Fetter, 314 Pa. 284, 171 Atl. 466.
