Foreign The case contains an exhaustive and valuable discussion of Instruments the place of foreign money under the law merchant. Some of therein the court's reasoning is open to question. It is clear that the 

 does not make foreign paper money negotiable, since the law of the country where it was issued necessarily governs. 

In any event, it is incorrect to say that foreign money is money in this country. The limited and uncertain willingness to receive it takes it out of that category. The actual decision, however, is clearly sound. Instruments which are negotiable under the law that created them are negotiable everywhere. 

Furthermore, foreign paper money, in which a government promises to pay its own coin to bearer in its own country, falls within our principles of negotiability, since the holder can exchange the paper for what is legal tender at the place of payment.

The dictum, if it means that an instrument payable in this country in foreign money is negotiable, was not law in New 

York before the act. Thompson v. Sloan, 23 Wend. 71. How ever, if the money in which the instrument is payable circulates as legal tender or its equivalent at the place of payment, it is immaterial that the money is foreign at the forum or at the place of making. Black v. Ward, 27 Mich. 191.

An able argument in opposition to Thompson v. Sloan, supra, that even an instrument payable in money which is foreign at the place of payment should be negotiable, is presented by Herman Oliphant in "The Theory of Money in the Law of 

Commercial Instruments," 29 Yale L. J. 606. The opposing view is stated by R. N. Perkins, "May a Promissory Note be 

Payable in Foreign Money?" 5 Iowa L. Bull. 209, criticizing adversely the reasoning in Brown v. Perera, supra. See also 

M. B. Carroll, Drafts payable abroad in Dollars, 20 Ill. L. Rev. 

193; and sec. 152, infra. The question, whether a bona fide purchaser of foreign specie should be protected in this country, is discussed in 33 Harv. L. Rev. 259. If a coin is not received as money but as an antiquity and bought for more than its face value, the bona fide purchaser would doubtless not be protected. 

Moss v. Hancock [1899], 2 Q. B. 111. 

Banknotes of the Imperial Russian Bank bought in 1918 were held not to be money, but to be commodities within the statute of frauds, inasmuch as the notes were not backed by the credit of a responsible government and did not pass current anywhere as money. Brown v. Perera, supra, was distinguished.

Reisfeld v. Jacobs, 107 Misc. Rep. 1, 176 N. Y. Supp. 223. 

A note is negotiable, which was made and payable in Brazil in Brazilian reis at a specified rate of exchange into British sterling. Hebblethwaite v. Flint, 185 App. Div. 249, 173 N. Y. 

Supp. 81.

In an action on a bill of exchange drawn and accepted in London and payable there in pounds sterling, judgment will

§7 (1) be entered in dollars at the rate of exchange at the date of the judgment and not at the date of maturity.  Liberty Natl. Bank v. Burr, 270 Fed. 251 (Pa.). 

See the English case under sec. 2(4).

An American railroad corporation issued bonds for 500 francs each, with coupons for 10 francs, payable at a Paris banking house, or at the option of the holder at designated banks in Belgium and Switzerland, without deduction for American or existing French taxes. The bonds were printed in French and 

English. The place of execution or delivery was not stated, but the entire issue was purchased by a French banking house. 

The bonds stated that all questions were to be determined according to the law of the United States. The plaintiff, a holder in due course of several bonds, presented the coupons at the designated Swiss bank and demanded payment in Swiss franes. 

The bank tendered French francs, which had a much lower value and were refused. Held, judgment for the value of the coupons in French francs at time of presentation. The  was not cited. Levy v. Cleveland, etc., Ry. Co., 210 App. Div. 

422, 206 N. Y. Supp. 261, reversing 121 Misc. Rep. 681, 202 

N. Y. Supp. 396, which was approved in 37 Harv. L. Rev. 1132.

(6) "The holder of an office for the time being"

Cross Reference: §§ 9(3), 10, 14, 42, 191. 

This subsection changes the common law, under which a promise to pay to "the secretary for the time being" of an unincorporated association was not negotiable, Cowie v. Stirling, 6 E. & B. 333, affirming 3 E. & B. 832. Such an instrument is capable of three interpretations. (1) The payee may be the man who shall be secretary at maturity, designated by description and not by name. The note is then not negotiable, because until maturity it is uncertain who the payee is. Nobody has power to indorse, hence the note is unfitted to circulate. (2) 

The payee may be the man who is secretary at issue of the note, designated by description. The note is then negotiable, King v. Box, 6 Taunt. 325, but the note was not thus construed at common law when the man was not named as well as described. 

This interpretation is unsatisfactory, because the same man will continue to be payee although he has ceased to be secretary before maturity or negotiation of the note. (3) There may be "a floating promise" to the person who happens to be the secretary at any particular moment. This construction carries. out the probable intention of the parties, and ought to render the note negotiable. The payee is certain, since it is always possible to determine the person who is to indorse or collect the instrument at the given instant. This view is commercially desirable, since it enables an unincorporated association to become the beneficial owner of a note and to vest the control of it in the officer who for the time being is in charge of the finances of the association. See F. W. Maitland, "The Unincorporated Body" and "Trust and Corporation," 3 Collected 

Papers 271, 321. However, this interpretation was held by Lord

Campbell, in Cowie v. Stirling, supra, to prevent negotiability. 

The N. I. L. renders a note in this form negotiable, but does not decide which of the three interpretations is to be adopted. 

It is to be hoped that the third will be taken by the courts, because of its commercial desirability. This view receives support from the definition of "person" in sec. 191 as including an unincorporated body of persons, for the legislature has thus indicated an absence of hostility to vesting the ownership of a negotiable instrument in an unincorporated group. Since the

89 group itself may be named as payee, it seems equally possible to name its financial officer pro tem. Cf. sec. 42. "Where the instrument is payable to order the payee must be named or otherwise indicated therein with reasonable certainty"

(2) "When it is payable to a person named therein or bearer" 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 10, 17(4), 140.

A note on which the words, "to the order of the bearer," were all typewritten was not payable to bearer or transferable by delivery; but was held a negotiable note transferable by the indorsement of a specific payee, who was not named but sufficiently described. Semble, if after the printed words on a check, "to the order of," the word "bearer" was filled in by writing, the check would possibly be transferable by delivery, since the signer would express his intention by the writing and pay little attention to the printed words. American Nat. Bank v. Kerley, 109 Oreg. 155, 220 Pac. 116, 32 A. L. R. 262.

The court presumably meant that the specific payee was the individual to whom the note was originally delivered by the makers; but it is difficult to see how "the bearer" indicated him with reasonable certainty to a subsequent purchaser not present at the delivery. According to the court's view, nobody but the original recipient of the note could indorse it on, yet how could a prospective purchaser learn that the first indorser was such a recipient except by the kind of inquiry into extrinsic facts which the law of commercial paper seeks to avoid? The authorities cited for the court's position that "bearer" may be a description of the payee, are obviously discussing instruments transferable by delivery. It would seem that the note was either transferable by delivery, or else non-negotiable for want of a sufficient description of the payee. See the notes in 

37 Harv. L. Rev. 764; 22 Mich. L. Rev. 837; 4 Oreg. L. Rev. 

148; 72 U. Pa. L. Rev. 317, all disapproving the court's view.

A note payable to a named payee or bearer may be negotiated without indorsement of the named payee. City Nat. Bank & 

Trust Co. of Corpus Christi v. Pyramid Asbestos & Roofing Co. 

(Tex. Civ. App.), 39 S. W. (2d) 101.

For an interesting article on the comparative law of this subject, see Philip W. Thayer, "Fictitious Payees in Bills of

A note payable to "The X Company," which was a firm name under which several persons were doing business, is not payable to a fictitious payee. Write Away Pen Co. v. Buckner, 188 Mo. 

App. 259, 175 S. W. 81. And so if payable to the name under which one person did business. Hill v. McCrow, 88 Oreg. 299, 170 Pac. 306.

Gibford, who had done business with the defendants under the trade-name "Gibford Chemical Co.," fraudulently obtained. notes from the defendants payable to Gibford Chemical Co. He indorsed this name by himself as agent, and sold the notes to the plaintiff. No corporation of this name existed. The trial court directed a verdict for the defendants on the ground that the notes were payable to a fictitious person, such fact being unknown to the makers. The Supreme Court held that the makers were not precluded by their knowledge of the tradename from setting up the fictitious nature of the payee if they relied upon fraudulent representations of Gibford that his business had been taken over by a corporation of that name; but that this reliance was a question for the jury, and the verdict was set aside. If the defendants intended Gibford to be the payee under the trade-name, they were liable, as the indorsement was then genuine.

Plaintiff, whose real name was Storch, had, on account of trouble with his wife, assumed the name of Krause, and defendant gave a note to plaintiff payable to the order of Krause. 

Held, that this was not a case of fictitious payee and that plaintiff, suing in his own name of Storch, could recover against defendant. Sockland v. Storch, 123 Ark. 253, 185 S. W. 262, Ann. Cas. 1918A, 668. 

A draft drawn by the shipper of goods and intended to be payable to the plaintiff bank, which took the draft in good faith for value before maturity, was made out on a printed form in which the payee was the X bank, which had been consolidated with the plaintiff bank and taken its name. Through inadvertence the parties failed to substitute the plaintiff's name for that of the X bank by a rubber stamp, ordinarily used. Held, the plaintiff was a holder in due course of the draft, which could be construed as payable to bearer, since the payee was a nonexisting person, and therefore no indorsement was necessary. Or else the plaintiff, being the legal successor of the X bank, was entitled to use its name. First Wisconsin Nat. Bank v. People's Nat. Bank, 136 Va. 276, 118 S. E. 82, 36 A. L. R. 736. 

The second ground seems preferable, since the fiction, if there was such, was not known to the drawer. The court also relied on sec. 43, and stated that the plaintiff had the right to insert its own name as payee.

The plaintiff, being indebted to the Claremont Storage Warehouse, Inc., sent an envelope addressed to the "Claremont Storage & Warehouse Co.," containing the plaintiff's check payable to "Clearmount Storage Co." The check was indorsed by some unauthorized person and paid to a collecting bank by the defendant drawee bank. Held, the drawee bank was liable to the drawer. The check was not payable to bearer, since the name of the payee was a misnomer and not fictitious. Joseph Milling 

Co. v. First Bank, 109 Oreg. 1, 216 Pac. 560, 29 A. L. R. 358, with note.

The final clause of subsec. 3 raises at least two difficulties. (1) Must the knowledge be actual or may it be imputed? 

Certainly if the drawer or maker is a corporation, it can not be actual, and the intention of the agent who signs the instrument to pick out a fictitious payee is decisive. Cases to this effect are collected in the second group, infra. Doubtless, the same principle would govern if the agent signed on behalf of a natural employer. Is the intention of any agent other than the actual signer significant? This question arises in Robertson Banking 

Co. v. Brasfield, infra, p. 209, and other cases in the first group; see also the cases in the third group. (2) A second difficulty is, who is the person who makes the instrument payable to a payee,--the clerk who after investigating the creditors of a corporation and the amount due them prepares the checks, or the treasurer who goes through the mechanical task of signing his name, trusting in the honesty of the clerk "And such fact was known to the person making so

The view advocated is supported by the great weight of authority, as set forth in cases in the first group. 

There is, however, some authority the other way, e. g., the

One Keefe, a claim and returned goods clerk in the plaintiff's department store, with the aid of a confederate, prepared and checked false bills for goods purporting to be sold to plaintiff by various sellers, some of whom did not exist, got the bills approved by other clerks and took them to the proper officer who directed a check to be drawn to the order of the supposed sellers, and Keefe took the checks to deliver to the supposed sellers, indorsed the payees' names, and got a friend also to indorse them, and obtained payment from his friend's bank to which the checks were paid by the defendants, the drawee banks. 

These fraudulent operations covered a period of over five years, more than one hundred and seventy operations and involved over $50,000. A loan broker applied to the plaintiff for a loan to "D. W.

The broker indorsed the name of D. W. Johnson upon the check, and deposited it in an account in that name in a bank which collected the check from the defendant drawee. The broker subsequently checked out the whole deposit. Held, the plaintiff depositor could recover the amount of the check from the drawee bank. The indorsement was a forgery. The check was not payable to bearer because the fictitious nature of the payee was not known to the drawer. Even if the broker was the agent of the drawer, his knowledge would not be imputed to the drawer. Sec. 61 did not make the drawer admit that any other person than the named payee could legally indorse the check.

X purchased from the American Express Co. four drafts drawn by the company on itself, two payable to a fictitious corporation and two to what may have been the name of an actual firm, but X apparently did not intend this firm to have any interest in the drafts. His indorsements were forged or unauthorized, and inoperative under sec. 23. The bank had no title; the payment was due to another. A note in 21 Colum. L. Rev. 597 suggests that a different result might be reached on the theory that X was the remitter of the drafts and the real party in interest; the identity of the payees was immaterial to the drawer, who intended the instru ment to be transferable by the remitter free of prior equities, and the way to effectuate this intention is to give the remitter a power to negotiate by indorsing the fictitious names. It is impossible, however, to assimilate the case to the impersonation cases (p. 349 ff, infra), where the drawer intends the instrument to be payable to the person before him, whatever the name he assumes, since X was not intended here to be the payee. And, although the drawer was willing that the remitter should select any payees he pleased, he exercised this power when the names given by him were filled in. Either those persons must indorse, or if they did not exist nobody could. The decision is sound.

The time slips for workmen of the plaintiff city were issued by a clerk, and checks signed by the Commissioner of Finance were made out in accordance with payrolls based on these slips and signed by another official. He would indorse the name of the payee on each of the fraudulent checks and get them cashed at business places, whence they were passed through various banks, paid by the defendant drawee bank, and charged to the city's account. The New York agents of the plaintiff insurance company were authorized to draw drafts upon the plaintiff for the payment of losses. The drafts stated that upon acceptance by the company the defendant bank would pay the amount to the order of the policyholder. A clerk, Carty, in the agents' office, in charge of the adjustment of losses, presented to the agents proofs of loss of fires, which had not taken place, on properties covered by policies in the company issued by the agents. The agents drew drafts payable to the names of these policyholders for the amounts of the supposed losses and delivered them to Carty. 

He indorsed the names of the payees and deposited them in banks, which forwarded them for acceptance to the plaintiff company. The plaintiff accepted them without investigation as to the genuineness of the indorsements, and the defendant bank paid them and charged the plaintiff's account. Held, the indorsements of the payees were forged, and the company could recover the amounts of the drafts from the bank. The checks were not payable to bearer, for the payees were not fictitious but actual policyholders, and no fiction was known to the agents, the drawers. The duty to ascertain the genuineness of indorsements rested upon the bank when paying, and not upon the company when accepting. No such duty was thrown upon the

company by instructions on the drafts, that when an indorsement was made by an agent or representative of the payee evidence of his authority must accompany the draft unless previously filed with the plaintiff. His acts in checking the records of the agents and the company to see if they corresponded could not be imputed to his employer or the plaintiff so as to bar recovery, for an examination by an honest clerk would not have revealed the forgeries. Effect of drawer's

In a similar case it was held that the fraudulent knowledge negligence of the fictitious payee by the swindling clerk was not imputed to his employer, the drawer, but that it was error for the court to charge the jury that the drawer was not required to examine the indorsements on the checks to ascertain if they were genuine, since this instruction invaded the province of the jury. The law requires a depositor to exercise due care in examining his account and vouchers to know whether or not the balance shown to his credit is correct, and he is charged with whatever knowledge he would have acquired by making such an examination in a reasonably careful manner. By delegating the examination to the delinquent clerk the employer was chargeable with knowledge of whatever information would have been disclosed to an honest clerk by reasonably careful examination, and this was a question for the jury. Fletcher Am. Nat. Bank v. Crescent Paper Co., 193 Ind. 329, 139 N. E. 664. Accord, City of 

Indianapolis v. Nat. City Bank, 80 Ind. App. 677, 138 N. E. 791, 141 N. E. 249.

In Litchfield Shuttle Co. v. Cumberland Valley Nat. Bank, 134 Tenn. 379, 183 S. W. 1006, the court reached the same result but by a different process of reasoning. The manager of plaintiff having authority to draw and issue checks, fraudulently and for his own purposes drew checks payable to persons with whom plaintiff had business dealings, but the manager himself indorsed the checks in the names of the payees and either collected them from defendant, the drawee bank, or negotiated them to other persons to whom the bank paid them. The court held that the bank was not liable to the plaintiff because under sec. 65 the manager by negotiating the instruments warranted that they were genuine and that by sec. 23 he and his principal were precluded from setting up the forgery of the names of the payees.

Plaintiffs' agent drew drafts on plaintiffs payable to real persons but not intending them to have any interest therein, indorsed the names of the payees and negotiated the drafts to a holder in due course and plaintiffs paid the drafts to the defendant collecting bank. Held, the drafts were payable to bearer, that a good title passed to the purchaser and that the plaintiffs could not recover. The court relied partly on the negligence of the plaintiffs, who had permitted the agent to pay sellers of grain in cash and then reimburse himself by drawing drafts on the plaintiffs payable to such sellers, whose names he indorsed without their authority and then collected the drafts from the defendant bank, which paid them without objection from the plaintiffs or receiving any information from them of the agent's practice. Bartlett v. First Nat. Bank, 247 Ill. 490, 93 N. E. 337; Noel v. Security Bank of Chicago, 163 Ill. App. 82, accord.

A later Illinois case held that this element of negligence was not essential to the decision in Bartlett v. First Nat. Bank, supra, and reached the same result, denying recovery although the plaintiff did not know of the agent's practice of indorsing drafts without the authority of the payees. The court rested squarely on sec. 9-3, and held that when the agent drew drafts in which he did not intend the payees to have any interest, they were payable to bearer. Three judges dissented. The administrator of an estate, having been duly authorized, drew checks payable to the distributees out of the estate's account, then forged the payee's indorsement and misappropriated the funds secured by cashing the check. Held, that the drawee bank was not liable to the estate, since the checks must be regarded as payable to bearer under sec. 9(3). The court stated that it was immaterial whether the person named as payee was actually entitled to the check, or had an interest therein; the sole test was whether the drawer of the check intended the payee to be fictitious. Fiction known to one of sev A building and loan association was accustomed to lend to its eral officers shareholders, taking their notes and giving them checks drawn signing on the defendant bank. The treasurer, S, from time to time falsely represented to the other officers that one of the shareholders had applied for a loan. S signed the name of the pretended borrower to a note for the amount. A check payable to the name of this shareholder was made out by the secretary, and signed on behalf of the association by the president, the secretary, and S as treasurer. It was then handed to S for delivery to the supposed borrower. Instead, S indorsed the shareholder's name and then his own, and cashed the checks for his own benefit with the defendant drawee, which charged the association's account. After payment of such checks and balancing the association's account, the bank would return the bank book and vouchers to S, the treasurer. These fraudulent transactions involved thirty-two checks over a period of more than four years. The association made no objection to the

§ 9 (3) 

account until more than year after the return of the last of these checks. Held, the drawee bank was not liable to the association for the amounts of the checks. Although the bank paid upon forged indorsements of the payees, the exercise of reasonable diligence by the officers of the depositor, other than S, in examining the vouchers would have shown that all the checks were paid to S individually and would have led to a detection of the fraud in its early stages. It is no excuse that this duty to examine the vouchers was delegated to the officer who committed the forgeries. The court refused to decide whether a statute exempting a bank from liability to a depositor for payment of a forged check, unless the forgery was reported within a year, applied to forged indorsements.  Pannonia Bldg. & Loan Assn. v. West Side Trust Co., 93 N. J. L. 377, 108 Atl. 240.

The reasoning of the court is open to question. The duty to examine vouchers seems satisfied when the depositor has ascertained that the balance on his books corresponds with the bank. 

Forgery of the drawer's signature or an increase in the amount of the check necessarily upsets the balance on the depositor's books. Forgery of the indorsement has no such effect. Therefore, depositors do not ordinarily examine the indorsements on vouchers, and failure to do so hardly constitutes a want of the care shown by an average reasonable man under the circumstances, so as to bar recovery from the bank. Welsh v. German 

Am. Bank, 73 N. Y. 424; United Security L. & T. Co. v. Central 

Nat. Bank, 185 Pa. 586, and other cases cited in Brady on 

Checks § 151, are contra to the principal case.

However, it is possible to support the decision upon a different ground, that the indorsements were not forged. Who was the payee of such a check? There are three possible views. (1) It was the actual shareholder whose name was given by S. If so, the indorsement was forged, and the depositor should have recovered unless barred by negligence. (2) The payee was S, who had assumed the stockholder's name. The association's primary intent was to pay the person signing the application and the note, i. e., S, and the secondary intent to pay to the shareholder named may be ignored. The case on this view is like the fraudulent impersonation cases under sec. 23, infra, such as First 

Nat. Bank v. Exchange Nat. Bank, 170 N. Y. 88, 62 N. E. 1089.

If S was the payee, the indorsement was genuine, and the denial of recovery was sound. (3) The check was payable to bearer under sec. 9(3), because the payee was fictitious, and this fact was known to S, one of the signers of the check. The difficulty in this view is, can the fiction be said to be "known to the person making it so payable" when it was unknown to two out of the three officers signing. When one officer signs, knowing of the fiction, his knowledge is imputed to his principal, under Snyder Corn Exchange Nat. Bank, supra, but quaere if this holds good

The treasurer of a corporation, practically in sole charge of its affairs, signed the corporate name to checks payable to the names of persons whom the corporation did not owe and who had no interest in the checks, procured the countersignature of the president, indorsed the payees' names and his own, and deposited the checks to his personal account in the defendant bank, which in good faith allowed him to withdraw the amount thereof. Held, the drawee bank, after paying the checks, could not recover the amount from the collecting bank in an action for money had and received under mistake. Since the countersignature of the president was required by the drawee bank, and not by any by-law of the drawer corporation for its protection, the corporation must be considered the drawer of the check with knowledge of the fictitious payees within sec. 9-3, so that the checks were payable to bearer and the defendant had a good title. Hackensack Trust Co. v. Hudson Trust Co., 189

This section in the first edition was based on the case of Lane v. Krekle, 22 Ia. 404, in which, however, the note was payable to a fictitious person "or bearer,' so that, of course, the title would pass by delivery whether there was an indorsement of the name of the fictitious payee or not. 

But the court did give an obiter opinion to the same effect as that expressed in sec. 139 of Mr. Daniel's book. Then Kohn v.

§ 9 (3) 

In the last edition of Mr. Daniel's book no other cases to this effect are cited except certain English cases which, however, rest on the Bills of Exchange Act, sec. 7 (3), which provides that, "Where the payee is a fictitious or nonexisting person the bill may be treated as payable to bearer," which lays down an absolute rule without regard to the knowledge or intention of the drawer.

With the exception of the dictum in Lane v. Krekle and the judgment in Kohn v. Watkins, the American rule has been that an instrument payable to a fictitious or nonexisting person is payable to bearer only when this fact is known to the person making it so payable. Armstrong v. Bank, 46 Ohio St. 

512, 22 N. E. 866, 6 L. R. A. 625, 15 Am. St. Rep. 655; Chism v. Bank, 96 Tenn. 641, 36 S. W. 387, 32 L. R. A. 778 (indorsement to fictitious person, the indorser being ignorant of the fiction); Fifth Nat. Bank v. Central Nat. Bank, 82 Hun. 559, affirmed 152 N. Y. 636; Shipman v. Bank, 126 N. Y. 318, 27 N. 

E. 371, 12 L. R. A. 791. And in Jordan Marsh & Co. v. Nat.

Shawmut Bank, supra, the Supreme Court of Massachusetts said that at common law as well as under sec. 9(3) of the Negotiable 

Instruments Law, an instrument payable to a fictitious payee is not payable to bearer unless the maker knows that the payee is fictitious or nonexisting.

It also seems illogical to say that an instrument is payable to bearer because the maker is estopped to assert that the payee is fictitious. How does it follow that anyone should take title by mere delivery when he takes an instrument which on its face is made payable to the name of a person and therefore by its terms called for an indorsement?

If a man with knowledge of the fiction signs and puts into circulation an instrument payable to a fictitious or nonexisting person, it may well be held that, as he knows that there is no one who comes within the description of the payee, and therefore no one to indorse the instrument according to its tenor, and yet intends that the title shall pass and that it shall circulate, he intends or should be estopped to deny that he intends that it shall circulate without indorsement, and by mere delivery, just like an instrument drawn payable to bearer. (In point of fact the maker really intends to make the instrument payable to himself under the fictitious name, and he actually indorses it in that name, and almost no case has been found in which such an instrument was negotiated without an indorsement in the name of the payee.)"

But when a maker believes that the payee is a real person, even if his signing and putting into circulation the instrument payable to a fictitious or nonexisting payee is held to be an 5 Mr. McKeehan in his discussion of sec. 9(3) cites three New York cases of unindorsed instruments, before the

9(5) and N. I. L. 40. But it should be noted that N. I. L. 9(5) merely states what are the formal requisites of bearer paper, but says nothing about the manner in which it is negotiated.

§ 10  

This problem is covered in detail by  34 and 40 which, unlike the English Act, specify the manner in which such paper is negotiated. The conflict, if any, in the section of the N. I. L. is not between 9(5) and 40, but between 34 and 40. For a discussion of the means of negotiating bearer paper with indorsements thereon, and the effect of the cases of Smith v. Clarke and 

Parker v. Roberts, see sec. 40, infra.

A note endorsed in blank by the payee which was in the possession of the bank commissioner of a defunct bank. Held, in view of N. I. L., secs. 33, 34 and 191, an "order note" bearing a blank indorsement is payable to bearer, therefore there was a presumption that the note was the property of the defunct bank. Austin v. Wasaff (Tex. Civ. App.), 284 S. W. 694.

The indorsement in blank of a non-negotiable promissory note does not make it negotiable, and the indorser is liable only as an assignor. Wettlaufer v. Baxter, 137 Ky. 362, 125 S. W. 741, 26 L. R. A. (N.S.) 804; Johnson v. Lassiter, 155 N. C. 50, 71 

S. E. 23; Newland v. Moore, 173 N. C. 728, 92 S. E. 367; Foley v. Hardy, 119 Kan. 183, 237 Pac. 925, 42 A. L. R. 1064 and note.

So also an otherwise non-negotiable certificate of deposit with the words "payable upon return of the certificate properly indorsed" is not rendered negotiable by indorsement in blank. 

Central State Bank v. Central Mercantile Bank of New York, 

248 N. Y. 428, 162 N. E. 475; Aufderheide v. Moeller, 221 Mo. 

App. 442, 281 S. W. 965.

Sec. 10. Terms, When Sufficient. 

The instrument need not follow the language of this act, but any terms are sufficient which clearly indicate an intention to conform to the requirements hereof.¹

A note containing provision that it is payable "to the order of" the payee therein named, "is" negotiable since it contained words of negotiability. It is immaterial whether words of negotiability precede or follow name of payee. Metropolitan Discount Co. v. Wardlaw, 37 Ga. App. 423, 140 S. E. 525.

A certificate of deposit reciting that "X has deposited in the Y bank three thousand dollars to the credit of himself, payable in current funds on return of this certificate properly indorsed on July 1, 1909," is a negotiable instrument under the N. I. L.

§ 14 Sec. 13. When Date May Be Inserted. 

Where an instrument expressed to be payable at a fixed period after date is issued undated, or where the acceptance of an instrument payable at a fixed period after sight is undated, any holder may insert therein the true date of issue or acceptance, and the instrument shall be payable accordingly. The insertion of a wrong date does not avoid the instrument in the hands of a subsequent holder in due course; but as to him, the date so inserted is to be regarded as the true date.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 4, 52, 86, 132, 135, 191, 7, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 53, 124, 125, 143, 196.

ANNOTATIONS 

Plaintiff purchased from the payee an undated note payable four months after date, on which were the indorsements of the payee and of several other accommodation indorsers. Plaintiff knew the date of issue of the note, but without authority filled in a later date. Held, that sec. 13 implies, at least, that the insertion of a wrong date in an undated instrument, by one having knowledge of the true date of issue, will avoid the instrument as to him, and that the indorsers were discharged. Bank of Houston v. Day, 145 Mo. App. 410, 122 S. W. 756. 

Where a note was issued without a date, and an unauthorized date was later filled in, it was held that a holder in due course under the altered date could recover because he purchased within a reasonable time after issue as provided under sec. 53. 

The court overlooked sec. 13 but the result is sound. Wilson v. 

Stark (Miss.), 112 So. 390.

Where the instrument is wanting in any material particular, the person in possession thereof has a prima facie authority to complete it by filling up the blanks therein.

ENGLAND- 

Bill payable to drawer's

An accepted bill of exchange payable to the order of the order drawer, and indorsed by the defendant with a space above his name, is "wanting in a material particular," and may be completed by the indorsement of the drawee-payee in the blank space, so that he may recover from the indorser according to the intention of the parties. The Lord Chancellor (Haldane) concurred in the result, but considered that the bill was complete when issued so that the drawer-payee could recover from the indorser without filling in his own name. McDonald & Co. v. 

Nash & Co. [1924], A. C. 625. Lord Haldane's view seems sound. The acceptor's obligation rendered the bill effective without the payee's indorsement and hence already complete. It did not resemble a note payable to the maker's order, which is incomplete until he indorses ( sec. 184) because until then no obligation exists upon the note. "In order, however, that any such instrument when completed may be enforced against any person who became a party thereto prior to its completion, it must be filled up strictly in accordance with the authority given and within a reasonable time" 

Burden of proof of

Burden of proof is on the defendant to show that the blanks authority were filled in without authority. Windahl v. Vanderbilt, 200 Ia. 

816, 203 N. W. 252; Bloom v. Horwitz, 100 Misc. Rep. 687, 166 

N. Y. Supp. 786.

But the burden is on the plaintiff, a party prior to the completion of an instrument signed in blank, to prove that the blanks were filled up within a reasonable time. Semble, that from October to the following June 9 is, if unexplained, more than a reasonable time. Madden v. Gaston, 137 App. Div. 294, 121 N. Y. Supp. 951.

8 14 

In Business Men's League v. Sregow, 153 N. Y. Supp. 231, a note, blank as to date, due date and payee, was signed by the defendants, the maker and two indorsers, without consideration, and delivered to R for his accommodation. R pledged it to plaintiff as collateral for a loan of $500. The note was excluded from evidence apparently on the ground that when it was delivered to R it was not filled in and there was no evidence either way as to authority to fill it in. Held, error. The court made no reference to the Negotiable Instruments Law, but held on the authority of old New York cases that the delivery of the note in blank gave implied authority to fill in and negotiate it, and the fact that it is filled in, in the presence of the purcheser, does not put him on inquiry as to the terms of the authority. 

The court seemed to be unaware that the old rule had been changed by sec. 14, 

The case, however, suggests interesting questions as to the burden of proof. First, is the mere delivery of the instrument signed in blank prima facie evidence that it was delivered in order that the paper may be converted into a negotiable instrument? It would probably be so held because of the form of the instrument, but see Smith v. Prosser [1907], 2 K. B. 735.

Second, the delivery for the purpose mentioned operates as a prima facie authority to fill up the instrument as such (that is, as a negotiable instrument), for any amount. Does this include a prima facie authority to fill in other blanks? Probably as to all missing requirements necessary to make it a negotiable instrument, since otherwise it would not be such an instrument. 

For the payee or one in privity with him to enforce a note executed in blank, against anyone a party thereto, before its completion, the evidence must show it was filled up in accordance with the authority given. Testimony of the maker that he gave no one authority to fill a blank will overcome any presumption of authority arising from the fact that it was delivered in blank. Equitable Trust Co. of New York v. Lyons, 72 Misc. Rep. 49, 129 N. Y. Supp. 79.

A bill in equity stating that the defendant was suing the plaintiff on notes indorsed by the plaintiff in blank and filled up by the defendant fraudulently and without consideration, was held not to state a ground for enjoining the pending actions and cancelling the notes, since there was an adequate defense at law.  Ciccarelli v. Hofmann, 90 

N. J. Eq. 94, 105 Atl. 795.

The presumption that a note was completed before it was signed and not afterwards, does not arise where the note is written in several inks and different hands. Exchange Bank v. Robinson, 185 Mo. App. 582, 172 S. W. 628.

A note with the payee's name blank, was signed by two makers, A and B. B gave it to A with instructions that the X "In accordance with the authority given"

§ 238 

"In accordance bank was not to be made payee.

The note was delivered by A with the given" authority to this bank for value, which filled in its name with A's consent. 

Held, if B was surety for A, sec. 14 governed and B was not liable; but if B gave the note to pay his debt to A, sec. 14 did not govern, since a principal may not repudiate the act of his agent as being in excess of authority, while he retains the fruit of the unauthorized act. First Nat. Bank v. Athey, 188 Ia. 

330, 174 N. W. 347.

This decision may rest upon the doctrine of ratification. If B regarded the debt as discharged after he knew of A's action, this constituted ratification of the filling in, which related back so as to cure the violation of instructions and render the blank "filled up strictly in accordance with the authority given" by the ratification. On the other hand, if B still insisted that the note should not have been used in this way, he did not retain the fruit of the unauthorized act, for B's debt to A remained unpaid. On this state of facts, B could not be held liable without disregard of the express provisions of sec. 14.

Defendant signed a note in blank on the statement that it was to be used to borrow money for a co-defendant who was jointly liable with the plaintiff to a bank. The note was filled up in the presence of the plaintiffs, who were made payees, and delivered to them, and they then paid the co-defendant's share of the debt to the bank. Held, that the note was filled up in accordance with the authority given, that the payees were holders for value and could recover on the note. Hermann's Exr. v. Gregory, 131 Ky. 819, 115 S. W. 809.

A note signed by defendant contained a power of attorney for confession of judgment for the amount of the note, and costs, and attorney's fees, the space for the amount of attorney's fees being left blank. Upon entering a confessed judgment the payee's attorney wrote in the blank space a sum equal to ten per cent. of the amount of the note. The judgment was vacated on motion, and at the trial the evidence showed that at the time of delivery the parties contemplated the insertion of such amount as might be necessary. Held, that the note was not void for alteration and was properly admitted in evidence. Kramer v. Schnitzer, 268 Ill. 603, 109 N. E. 695.

Two notes with the payee's name blank were given by the makers to X to enable him to raise money, with authority to fill in the blanks. X negotiated a loan from a bank and then filled in the bank's name as payee. The bank refused to take the notes in this form, but with the consent of X and X's wife it erased its name and substituted the wife's as payee, who indorsed. X then delivered the notes to the bank, which paid value. The makers were held liable to the bank. The fact that an alteration appears even if made by the plaintiff will not defeat recovery without proof that it was material and made after delivery. First Nat. Bank v. Patterson, 188 Ia. 1237, 177 N. W. 545.

When the amount of a check drawn in blank has been filled in accordance with the implied authority, a subsequent alteration of the amount avoided the check.  Keller v. State Bank, 292 Ill. 553, 127 N. E. 94, 9 A. L. 

R. 1082.

See the adverse criticism of the change in the common law in the United States by Hening, The Uniform Negotiable Instruments Law, 59 U. Pa. L. Rev. 471, 484ff. He argues that the

English common law was the same as ours until altered by the Bills of Exchange Act, and this alteration should not have been followed in the  Nevertheless, the statutory rule seems sound, for there is not sufficient reason for encouraging the circulation of incomplete commercial paper to make it desirable to protect even an innocent purchaser for value who knows of the blanks. 

In Grand Lodge, K. of P. v. State Bank, 79 Fla. 471, 84 So. 

528, where the agent of the maker of a note delivered it with the name of the payee in blank for value to the plaintiff, which filled in its own name, it was said that a holder for value of negotiable paper otherwise perfect has the right to fill in the name of the payee. This statement goes too far, because under the express language of secs. 14 and 52-1 the person taking the instrument with blanks is not a holder in due course and is put on inquiry as to the authority given by prior parties. The facts of the case, however, indicate that the filling in was ratified by the maker although not previously authorized. 

In Dumbrow v. Geld, 72 Misc. Rep. 400, 130 N. Y. Supp. 182, the defendant indorser signed a printed form which the maker afterward filled up and signed, adding a provision as to interest, although the printed form contained no provision therefor. It was held, that, as the plaintiff transferee knew that the note had been indorsed before it was filled in and signed by the maker, he was not a bona fide holder. The facts are not very fully reported, but the case seems to hold that a transferee can not be a holder in due course if he knew that the instrument had been signed in blank or in an incomplete state, although it had been filled up and was complete at the time he took it. Knowledge on the part of a purchaser that the instrument was incomplete when signed, but completed before the transfer, seems to be given as much effect to put him upon inquiry as if he had seen the instrument or taken it in an incomplete state. But the

§ 14 

language of sec. 52 may be contra, since "a holder in due course is a holder who has taken the instrument under the conditions (among others) that it is complete and regular upon its face." 

Accord, Bronson v. Stetson, 252 Mich. 6, 232 N. W. 741, 29 

Mich. L. Rev. 625. Sed quaere? If he would be a holder in good faith under sec. 56.

When a note payable to a trust company was signed by several makers, and blanks were later filled by one maker, S, with the date, the maturity, and the creation of a joint and several liability, in a manner contrary to instructions from his co-makers, and this fact was known to the payee's treasurer, the payee was not a holder in due course except against S. 

Tremont Trust Co. v. Noyes, 246 Mass. 197, 141 N. E. 93.

Defendant indorsed a note with the name of X inserted as payee, but otherwise blank, and gave the same to X to use in renewal of another note which defendant had indorsed for the accommodation of X. The affidavit of defense, in addition to the above facts, stated that X never indorsed the note, but that a partner of X filled up the note, signed the name of the firm as makers, indorsed the name of X and the firm name on the note, and negotiated it to a bank, which placed the proceeds to the credit of the firm. Held, that the indorsement of the firm name was an affirmation that the indorsement of X's name was by him or by his authority, that X was estopped thereby as well as by the receipt of the proceeds to deny the genuineness of his signature. Richards v. Street, 31 App. Cas. D. C. 427.

Sed quaere? If X had in fact indorsed the note or authorized the indorsement in his name, and after its completion it had been used for another purpose than intended by defendant, the defendant would nevertheless be bound to a holder in due course. 

But any estoppel against the firm as makers or as indorsers from having negotiated the note with the apparent indorsement of the payee, should not be available against third parties. The firm and each of its partners may be estopped to deny that the title passed, but the defendant has the right to insist that the title. could pass, as far as he is concerned, only by the indorsement of the payee named in the note before the defendant indorsed and delivered the blank form. Hortsman v. Henshaw, 11 How. 

177, cited by the court, does not cover such a case. If, in that case, the drawer after delivering the bill to the payee had come into wrongful possession of the bill, had forged the name of the payee and negotiated the bill and the drawee had accepted the bill and had been sued on the acceptance, while the drawer would be estopped, if he had been sued, to set up the forgery of the payee's name, the acceptor, surely, would not be estopped to show that plaintiff had no title, for the acceptor would still be liable to the payee.

Sec. 15. Incomplete Instrument Not Delivered. 

Where an incomplete instrument has not been delivered it will not, if completed and negotiated, without authority, be a valid contract in the hands of any holder, as against any person whose signature was placed thereon before delivery.¹

The defendant signed a number of promissory notes, blank as to date, payee and amount, and left them on his desk in his office, whence they were stolen, filled in and indorsed to the plaintiff for value, before maturity and without notice of any

defects. Held, that under sec. 15 the defendant is not liable on the notes. Sec. 16 applies only to complete instruments.

A blank check signed by the plaintiff was stolen by persons who filled in the amount and a fictitious name as payee, and presented it to the drawee bank which certified it. They indorsed the payee's name and passed the check to the defendant for value without notice, who collected the amount from the drawee. Held, the drawer having taken up the check from the bank could recover from the defendant in an action for money had and received. Delivery of an incomplete instrument was necessary to a valid inception of the contract. Although possession was prima facie evidence of delivery, the presumption could be rebutted. The provision of sec. 16 that a valid delivery is conclusively presumed when the instrument is in the hands of a holder in due course must be read in connection with sec. 15, and sec. 16 does not apply in the case of an incomplete instrument, completed and negotiated without authority. The drawer of an incomplete check owes no duty of care toward possible purchasers to prevent its getting unlawfully into circulation. 

Two judges dissented on the ground that the defendant was a holder in due course and delivery should be conclusively presumed. Linick v. Nutting & Co., 140 App. Div. 265, 125 N. Y.

Sec. 16. Delivery-When Effectual-When Pre sumed. 1 Every contract on a negotiable instrument is incomplete and revocable until delivery of the instrument for the purpose of giving effect thereto. As between immediate parties, and as regards a remote party other than a holder in due course, the delivery, in order to be effectual, must be made either by or under the authority of the party making, drawing, accepting or indorsing, as the case may be; and in such case the delivery may be shown to have been conditional, or for a special purpose only, and not for the purpose of transferring the property in the instrument. But where the instrument is in the hands of a holder in due course, a valid delivery thereof by all parties prior to him so as to make them liable to him is conclusively presumed. And where the instrument is no longer in the possession of a party whose signature appears thereon, a valid and intentional delivery by him is presumed until the contrary is proved. 2

ANNOTATIONS 

AMES: The doctrine of sec. 16, that one who has signed a negotiable instrument complete on its face is liable thereon to a holder in due course, although it was never delivered by him, but lost by him, or stolen from him, or even from someone else after his death, is somewhat startling at first. But it should commend itself on reflection.

Sec. 16 applies even to the case of an undelivered bill or note made payable to order, stolen by the payee, indorsed by him and negotiated to a holder in due course, thus codifying such extreme cases as Clarke v. Johnson, 54 Ill. 296, and Shipley v. 

Carroll, 45 Ill. 285. Ed.

A draft drawn on a New York bank by a South American branch bank and payable to a foreign corporation was attached in New York by a creditor of the payee corporation while the draft was in possession of the drawee bank, and before it had been delivered to the payee. A draft was drawn by a cashier payable to another bank and delivered to the defendant so as to enable him to take care of transactions with the payee bank by which he had obtained funds to discharge a large indebtedness to the cashier's bank, which the cashier had concealed from his directors. The defendant was indicted for receiving a draft secreted by the cashier. Held, defendant discharged. Nothing of value was secreted by the cashier or received by the defendant, since the draft had no value until it was delivered to the payee, after which the cashier parted with any control over it.

Horn v. Nicholas, 139 Tenn. 453, 201 S. W. 756, L. R. A. 1918E, 157.

The defendants signed as surety comakers a note payable to Delivery ordi- C. The plaintiff advanced money on the note, and a few days later procured an indorsement without recourse from C, who had not promised to lend any money to the principal maker and did not authorize the plaintiff to make the loan or in any other way possess an interest in the note. Held, the surety makers were not bound. They agreed to be liable to C, and could be bound only if their contracts were completed by a delivery to him. His indorsement without recourse did not constitute him a party. Chitwood v. Hatfield, 136 Mo. App. 688, 118 S. W. 1192. A married woman, domiciled in Tennessee where she was incapable of contracting, signed and delivered a note there which was dated in Tennessee, but payable in Virginia, where she was capable. The N. I. L. was not cited. In re Lucas's Estate, 272

The defendant drew checks to the order of plaintiff and handed them to plaintiff, who indorsed them each to a named person and gave them to defendant to mail to the respective indorsees, but defendant failed to do so. "Immediate parties" The delivery of a check to one of two or more payees will operate as a delivery to all.  Spaulding v. First Nat. Bank, 210 App. Div. 216, 205 N. Y. Supp.

ENGLAND 

A bill of exchange was indorsed and handed to the payee's bankers to be discounted. Some days later the bankers credited the payee's account with the bill. Held, that the property in the bill did not pass to the bankers until it was discounted by them. Dawson v. Isle [1906], 1 Ch. 633. 

"As between immediate parties, and as regards a remote party other than a holder in due course, the delivery, in order to be effectual, must be made either by or under the authority of the party making, drawing, accepting or indorsing, as the case may be; and in such case the delivery may be shown to have been conditional, or for a special purpose only, and not for the purpose of transferring the property in the instrument" 

Cross Reference: 88 19, 52, 60 to 63, 132 to 138, 191, 28, 29, 55, 58, 68, 196.

When a note is delivered by the maker to an intermediate person who gives it to the payee for value, the payee, is not an "immediate" party, although he is in proximity to the maker. 

Immediate means privity not proximity. Howard Nat. Bank v. 

Wilson, 96 Vt. 438, 120 Atl. 889. "Immediate parties,' in sec. 16, excludes a party who is a holder in due course. In such case these words must be confined to parties who are 'immediate' to the conditions or limitations placed upon the delivery in the sense of knowing or being chargeable with notice of them. A payee who is a holder in due course is not an immediate party in the sense of that section." Rugg, C. J., in Liberty Trust Co. v. Tilton, 217 Mass. 

462, 464, 105 N. E. 605, L. R. A. 1915B, 144.

The provisions of this section refer to a conditional or special delivery to the payee or holder, of which he is advised at the time, and not to a delivery by an obligor to an agent or intermediary for transmission to the payee. Therefore one who signed as surety-maker, relying on a false statement of the principalmaker that the signature of another ostensible surety was genuine, and upon the violated condition that other named persons were to sign cosureties before delivery to the payee, is liable to the payee who took the note for value in good faith without notice of the fraud or breach of agreement. Ex parte Goldberg & Stone, 191 Ala. 356, 67 So. 839.

The defendants, two sureties, signed a renewal note payable to the payee bank on the original note, on condition that the principal debtor also sign it. The bank did not procure his signature. On suit by the state bank examiner to enforce re-

newal note, held, the delivery was conditional and the defendants were not liable. Beard v. Austin State Banking Com'r. 

(Tex. Civ. App.), 297 S. W. 786. Contra: The directors of a bank at the instance of their cashier signed a note with the understanding that their names were to be used as officers of the bank and the bank's name was to be filled in above theirs as maker. The cashier did not fill in the note as instructed but sold it to the plaintiff who innocently gave value. Held, the plaintiff could not recover. Foster v. Security Bank & Trust 

Co. (Tex. Comm. App.), 288 S. W. 438, 36 Yale L. J. 1005, 22 

Ill. L. Rev. 765. conditional

Held: "void" as used in the agreement referred to a condition precedent, rather than to a condition subsequent, and thus is not objectionable under the parol evidence rule. Kuhn v. Simmons (Me.), 139 Atl. 474. 

The language of the section that the delivery may be shown to have been conditional, or for a special purpose, and not for the purpose of transferring the property in the instrument, is somewhat ambiguous. If the last clause qualifies both a conditional delivery and a delivery for a special purpose, it would seem that where the delivery is conditional and no property in the instrument passes, we have a case of the first kind and not of the second. But if the last clause modifies only delivery for a special purpose, then "conditional" as used in this sentence includes both conditions precedent and conditions subsequent. 

Under this interpretation evidence of either kind of condition would constitute a valid defense. From a business point of view this latter interpretation seems preferable, because it eliminates the academic common law distinction between the two types of conditions. See 5 Wigmore, Evidence (2d. ed.), §§ 2409, 2444, n. 6, which as a practical matter is often reduced to mere verbage which even the courts find themselves unable to follow consistently. (See Kuhn v. Simmons, supra, where the court in deciding a case under  16 held that words which clearly created a condition subsequent were admissible as a valid defense on the pretense that they created a condition precedent. 

Although the reasoning seems wrong the result is sound. Conditions subsequent were held a good defense in Wakonda State

On the other hand the following cases, in addition to those noted above, all but one of which cite the act, reach the result that parol evidence of delivery upon conditions subsequent is admissible. This seems to be the preferable construction of the act and gives the proper meaning to the term "property" as complete and unincumbered title as required by sec. 55.

Parol evidence was not admissible that notes were delivered by the maker to the payee, subject to an agreement for later adjustment of the amount due between the parties.

525, 528. Three judges dissented without opinion. A majority of the Appellate Division held the agreement could be shown as a condition precedent, 192 App. Div. 268, 320, 182 N. Y. 

Supp. 824, 856; but two judges dissented, 192 App. Div. 268, 340, 182 N. Y. Supp. 824, 871, considering it a condition subsequent within Jamestown Business College v. Allen, 172 N. Y. 

291, 64 N. E. 952. The Court of Appeals agreed with the dissenting judges below on this point, although affirming the decision of the majority on the different ground that there was partial failure of consideration. Sec. 16 was not cited.

Parol evidence is not admissible to vary the unqualified terms of a note by proving an agreement that it shall be paid in installments. Nalitzky v. Williams, 237 Fed. Rep. 802, 151 C. C. 

A. 44. A finding of the jury that the note was executed "with the understanding or agreement * that said note was not to become due and payable until" the completion of a building, will not support a judgment for the maker against the payee.

In an action upon a check the defendant testified that he gave the check in the suit on Sunday upon the express condition that it should not be used until the following Saturday. 

Nevertheless on Monday the defendant met the payee at the defendant's bank, and the payee said that he had come to have the check certified, whereupon the defendant stopped payment. 

Held, the defendant had a right to rescind the transaction and to stop the check. Stadtmauer v. Lukin, 126 Misc. Rep. 318, 213 

N. Y. Supp. 33. The N. I. L. was not cited.

A parol agreement to renew a note, made after its execution on good consideration, can not be set up as a defense in an action at law thereon. Semble, the maker may have redress in another action for breach of the renewal contract. The N. I. L. was not cited. West v. Jones, 7 Boyce (Del. Super.) 509, 108 Atl. 675.

A note in 29 Yale L. J. 924 considers that the agreement to renew should constitute an equitable defense. The objection to this view is that although the original note ought not to be discharged by the agreement, the suggested judgment for the defendant in the principal case would be res adjudicata in a future suit on the original note even if brought after the date for payment specified in the renewal contract. While such a parol agreement is admissible under the parol evidence rule because subsequent to the note, it should not be the basis of a final judgment, -Agreement varying time of payment

The plaintiff bank was about to sell cotton assigned it as collateral for A's past-due note, which exceeded the amount that could lawfully be lent to one person. A, expecting that cotton would rise, persuaded the bank to renew the loan, part of it being covered by a new note signed by A, and part by a note signed by the defendant, A's brother. At maturity of these notes, the bank sold the collateral, which had greatly declined in value and applied the proceeds to pay part of A's note. Held, the defendant was liable in full upon his note. Parol evidence was not admissible of an agreement that the collateral was to be held as security for both notes, so that the defendant would be entitled to share in the proceeds of the sale. One judge dissented on the ground that the agreement concerning the consideration did not vary the notes, which stated only a formal consideration. The majority did not cite the , and the dissenting judge did not think that sec. 16 had any application to this case. Nat. Loan & Exch. Bank v. Tolbert, 129 S. C. 503, 124 S. E. 772. A note in 23 Mich. L. Rev. 415 prefers the dissenting opinion.

Sec. 17. Construction Where Instrument is Ambig uous. 

Where the language of the instrument is ambiguous or there are omissions therein, the following rules of construction apply:- 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 73(3), 78, 110, 111, 130, 196. (1) Where the sum payable is expressed in words and also in figures and there is a discrepancy between the two, the sum denoted by the words is the sum payable; but if the words are ambiguous or uncertain, reference may be had to the figures to fix the amount; ¹ 1 

Cross Reference: § 10. 

(2) Where the instrument provides for the payment of interest, without specifying the date from which interest is to run, the interest runs from the date of the instrument, and if the instrument is undated, from the issue thereof;

Cross Reference: 88 191, 2(1), 10. 

1 The last clause of 1 is not in the corresponding section of the Eng lish Act. B. E. A. s. 9 (2).

§ (1) 280 

Marginal figures (3) Where the instrument is not dated, it will be considered to be dated as of the time it was issued; 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 6(1), 7(2), 10 to 15, 45. (4) Where there is a conflict between the written and printed provisions of the instrument, the written provisions prevail; 2

Cross Reference: 88 101, 10. 

(5) Where the instrument is so ambiguous that there is doubt whether it is a bill or note, the holder 2 may treat it as either at his election; 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 184, 191, 10, 130. 3 (6) Where a signature is so placed upon the instrument that it is not clear in what capacity the person making the same intended to sign, he is to be deemed an indorser; 2 

Cross Reference: 88 31, 63, 64, 67, 68, 125(4), 192. (7) Where an instrument containing the words "I promise to pay" is signed by two or more persons, they are deemed to be jointly and severally liable thereon.*

Where the amount of a check was expressed in figures as "250.00" and in words as "two hundred and 50/100ths Dollars," it was held that the sum expressed by the words con trolled. Farmers' State Bank of Dickinson v. Koffler, 232 N. W.

Altering the marginal figures of a check to make them correspond with the amount stated in written words, which are not ambiguous or uncertain, is not forgery. The People v. Lewinger, 252 Ill. 332, 96 N. E. 837, Ann. Cas. 1912D, 239. And an alteration of the marginal figures was held not to be forgery when no change was made in the words specifying the amount. 

McIntosh v. State, 23 Ga. App. 513, 98 3. E. 555, decided before the enactment of the N. I. L.

If the drawer of a check, intending to make it payable for $8.90, wrote marginal figures to that amount, but wrote words calling for eighty dollars and ninety cents, the drawer was liable for $80.90 even if the marginal figures were fraudulently raised to that amount. Produce Exchange Bank v. North Kansas, etc., Co. (Mo. App.), 212 S. W. 898.

A note stating the amount in marginal figures with a blank before "dollars" where the amount would ordinarily be inserted in words, was a negotiable instrument, and an indorsee for value before maturity without notice of defenses was held a holder in due course. Sec. 17 was not cited. Citizens Bank v. Jones, 127 

Wash. 294, 220 Pac. 787. The conflicting cases are collected in the opinion and in a note in 22 Mich. L. Rev. 607, approving the decision.

Semble, when a note contains the amount in marginal figures but the space for the amount in words is left blank, the holder in good faith may fill in the blank in the body within the limit of the amount shown by the marginal figures. Quaere, whether recovery may be had for the amount in the marginal figures without filling the blank? Missouri State L. Ins. Co. v. Allen (Mo. App.), 251 S. W. 751.

A bank is not justified in dishonoring a check which bears the figures "$365." although the amount written is "three sixty five dollars" since the marginal figures control in case of ambiguity. Nuzum v. Sheppard, 87 W. Va. 243, 104 S. E. 587, 11

Cross Reference: 88 191, 2(1), 10. 

A note is none the less negotiable because a blank is left for the rate of interest. In such case the legal rate applies. Franklin Nat. Bank v. Roberts Bros., 168 N. C. 473, 84 S. E. 706.

The expression "eight per cent per annum from annum until paid" is of the same legal effect as if it read "from blank until paid," so that the substitution of "date" for the second "annum" was not a material alteration. Temple v. Harrington, 90 Oreg. 295, 176 Pac. 430.

In Hill v. Hart, 23 N. M. 226, 167 Pac. 710, the court, after stating that there was no conflict between the written and printed portion of a note as to the time when interest began to run, said that if uncertainty existed, it could be cleared up by the introduction of parol evidence of the agreement between payee and maker. The plaintiff was a transferee from the payee without indorsement.

On a blank printed form of note the blanks were filled in on a typewriter. In the blank space for interest after the printed word "at" were typewritten "7 per cent. from date." A circle was drawn around the figure 7 with pen and ink and above it the figure 8 was made with pen and ink. Defendant contended that the note was not negotiable because of uncertainty in the rate of interest. Held, that the typewritten part must be considered as printed within the meaning of the statute, that the written rate prevails and that there is no uncertainty therein. 

Acme Coal Co. v. Northrup Nat. Bank, 23 Wyo. 66, 146 Pac. 

593, L. R. A. 1915D, 1084.

A note bearing the printed form "pay to the order of" was filled out in writing by the insertion of "L. F. Closman only." 

Held, not negotiable. The written "only" conflicts with the printed "order," and prevails over it. One judge dissented, saying there was no conflict since "only" meant that only

180, 166 N. W. 559, L. R. A. 1918D, 224, with note on effect of "only." See also the note in 86 Cent. L. J. 250, which considers that the single written word "only" is so slight a factor that it ought not wholly to eliminate what was printed.

Where a line has been drawn through the printed words, "to order of," the instrument is non-negotiable. Noall v. Dickinson, 49 Ida. 705, 292 Pac. 219.

Where a marginal notation is in the same typewriting as the body of the note and contradictory thereto, the main body controls. E. E. Rivet & Sons v. Durand, 53 R. I. 48, 163 Atl. 476. (7) "Where an instrument containing the words "I promise to pay" is signed by two or more persons, they are deemed to be jointly and severally liable thereon"

we "On demand after date I promise, etc.," signed by two, is joint and several, under sec. 17(7), and the holder may proceed against one party in equity and the other at law. Lewenstein v. Forman, 223 Mass. 325, 111 N. E. 962. 

Where husband and wife signed a note, reading "I promise to pay," in the position usually signed by makers, it was held that parol evidence was not admissible to show that wife signed as indorser. Burke v. Jacobson, 53 R. I. 91, 165 Atl. 363.

In an action by the superintendent of banks when the payee became insolvent, against the defendant on a note executed by the defendant and son, which recited, "I, we, or either of us, promise to pay," where the defendant at the time of making the note made a deposit in the payee bank receiving a certificate of deposit therefor, it was held, under  sec. 17(7), the note represented the joint and several liability of the makers. therefore the defendant could set off in satisfaction of the note a sufficiency of the time certificate of deposit of which he was still the holder. Powell v. Mobley, 166 Ga. 163, 142 S. E. 678. 

A note reading "I promise to pay" was signed by two makers.

A joint action was brought against both but one defendant died before judgment. Held, the liability was joint and several and the action could be continued against the surviving defendant

on his several liability while another action could be brought against the personal representative of the deceased maker. 

Baker County State Bank v. Jones, 86 Fla. 484, 98 So. 592. Cf., Continental Illinois Bank & Trust Co. v. Clement, 259 Mich.

In an action by the payee against the executor of the estate of X the note containing the words "I promise to pay" was signed by X and Y as makers. The defendant interposed a demurrer on the grounds that the instrument was a joint obligation. Held, the obligation, under  17(7), is joint and several and the demurrer was properly overruled. First Nat. 

Bank of Eugene v. Dodd, 118 Oreg. 1, 245 Pac. 503.

When the form of a note corresponded to the language of this subsection, the four makers were presumably joint and several. 

Each was liable to pay the whole amount, but if one paid more than his share he could have contribution from the others. Bronner v. Walrath, 208 App. Div. 758, 202 N. Y. Supp. 577.

Conversely, a note in plural form signed by one person is valid. Mrazek v. Tollar, 210 Ill. App. 384, not citing the N. I. L. 

Where a note contained the words "We promise to pay to ourselves" and also the statement in the body that "each" party waived his homestead rights, etc., it was held a joint obligation. Exchange Bank of Savannah v. Harper, 35 

Ga. App. 786, 134 S. E. 789. 

The plaintiff payee signed a note as co-maker with the defendant which provided, "I or we or either promise to pay."

The plaintiff signed a note jointly with her husband reading "I promise" and containing a collateral agreement depositing shares of stock "as security for payment of this or any other liabilities to said holder." The collateral which was owned solely by the wife was later sold at her order. Held, that the bank could not apply the proceeds to payment of other individual debts of the husband. Heffner v. Huntington, 311 Pa. 29, 166 Atl. 370. 

Where a note read, “X * does promise to pay," and was signed by X and defendant, it was held that defendant was deemed to be an indorser and not a maker, since the language on the instrument did not import an unconditional promise on his part to pay. O'Dess v. Gunter, 258 Mich. 667, 242 N. W. 804.

When an instrument payable to X was indorsed "X by Y with power of attorney," plaintiff, in order to prove his title, must show the authority of the agent to indorse. Scotland

Where agency is established, the power to indorse negotiable instruments depends on the question, what is the scope and purpose of the agency. Specific authority need not be given for the indorsement of each particular instrument. Guaranty Trust Co. v. Manhattan Co., 183 App. Div. 586, 170 N. Y. Supp. 81.

It is not essential to the regularity of an indorsement by an agent that his authority should appear on the instrument.

The maker of a note payable to a corporation is concerned with the authority of the agent who indorses the corporation's name transferring the note to plaintiff, only to the extent that the maker shall be protected if compelled to pay and shall not be required to pay one who is not the owner of the note or otherwise entitled to recover thereon. Citizens State Bank v. Skeffington (N. D.), 196 N. W. 953.

The by-laws of a corporation required all notes to be signed by the president and attested by the secretary with the corporate seal. Notes payable to the corporation were indorsed in its name by the secretary alone. Held, the corporation was liable. The by-law, having been almost completely ignored in practice, was waived, and also the action of the secretary was ratified by the directors.  Farmers State Bank v. 

Haun, 30 Wyo. 322, 222 Pac. 45, 224 Pac. 856.

So also where the secretary of a corporation was in the habit of indorsing all instruments payable to the corporation, it was held that the indorsement passed title notwithstanding a provision in the by-laws that the treasurer should sign also. Aronofsky v. Humes (R. I.), 147 Atl. 749.

The plaintiff's cashier was accustomed to indorse checks payable to the plaintiff with a rubber stamp which was not restrictive and deliver them to the defendant, who acted as banker for the plaintiff. The defendant cashed some of these checks and the cashier embezzled part of the proceeds. The plaintiff's auditors examined the defendant's accounts of transactions with the plaintiff and could have discovered the unrestricted nature of the indorsement. In an action by the plaintiff to recover the proceeds of checks collected by the defendant after such cashing, the trial court directed a verdict for the plaintiff. This was held error. The cashier's authority to indorse checks for cash-

indorse ing was a question for the jury, and could be found to exist from Authority to the course of dealing although there were no specific instructions from the plaintiff to the defendant regarding the scope of the cashier's powers. Crane v. Postal Tel. Cable Co., 48 App. D. C. 54. 

Where the plaintiff introduced in evidence an affidavit of payee bank's cashier, that the indorsement was that of the payee bank made by him as cashier with authority, it was held that under Missouri Rev. St. 1919, sec. 11762, which requires the board of directors of banks to give written authority to the cashier before the cashier can validly indorse notes, the plaintiff did not prove indorsement by the cashier's affidavit. The written record of authority should have been introduced. Newton County Bank v. Holderman (Mo. App.), 9 S. W. (2d) 852.

The fact that a joint payee retains his share of the proceeds of a note indorsed for him by his co-payee without authority does not mean that he has ratified the signature as his own. 

Johnson v. Watland, 208 Ia. 1370, 227 N. W. 410.

AMES: Under this section, an agent signing without authoragent ity of the principal is, by implication, liable on the instrument. signing in This is unjust and a departure from the English Act and the principal almost uniform current of judicial decisions by which the agent is liable only on his implied warranty of authority. It increases negotiability and enables plaintiff to prove with ease and certainty the amount to be recovered. 

In an article in 10 Law Notes (American) 104, a writer signing himself "L. P. M.," contends that the clause "he is not liable on the instrument if he was duly authorized," does not warrant the implication that the unauthorized agent is liable on the instrument.

Taking the words of this section alone the writer signing himself "L. P. M." is correct. The words "if he was duly authorized" only apply to the affirmative situation where authorization actually existed. The negative, lack of authorization, is not mentioned. Therefore, it would seem that the section is silent on the question of liability of the unauthorized agent, and under sec. 196 recourse must be had to the law merchant. 

However, an examination of secs. 24, 44, 17(6), 63 and 69 shows an intention of the act to hold all parties liable on the instrument whose signatures appear thereon. This conclusion is strengthened by the fact that the words quoted do not appear 2 The words "if he was duly authorized" are not in the English Act.

In light of the well-known rule of law that an authorized agent is not personally liable for his acts within the scope of his authority, the addition of such a phrase would be meaningless unless it intended by inference to cover the liability of the unauthorized agent. Since then the phrase is ambiguous, resort is properly had to the intention of the framers of the act. The authorities on this point are collected in the case of New Georgia Bank of Albany, Ga. v. J. & G. Lippman, 249 N. Y. 307, 164 N. E. 108, in which Cardozo, C. J., points out that the commissioners have clearly stated that they intended the unauthorized agent to be bound on the instrument.

As is pointed out there, this achieves a desirable commercial result in that it removes uncertainty as to damages and protects the holder. Although the words of this section are unfortunately phrased, this excellent decision sets at rest any doubt as to the proper interpretation. The case is noted in 77 U. of Pa. L. Rev.
