Liability of The plain language of this section, read with sec. 42, indiauthorized agent when cates that it was the intention of the draftsman and the commisprincipal sioners to clear up the unnecessary and unpardonable confusion Comment caused by the failure of some of the courts to exercise a little conflicting common sense and to recognize mercantile usage. Much of the the effect of difficulty found in this subject is purely manufactured and Sec. 20 would not trouble a business man for a moment. He would perceive no difference between notes signed, "The X Co. by A, Pres.," or signed, "The X Co., A, Pres.," or signed "X Co., A, Pres.," or "A, Pres., X Co.," or a note reading "The X Co. promises to pay" and signed "A, Pres." Yet courts have been found to make distinctions in such cases. For instance, in Reeve v. First Bank, 54 N. J. L. 208, 23 Atl. 853, 16 L. R. A. 143, a note signed "Warrick Glass Works, J. Price Warrick, Pres.," was properly held to be the note of the corporation, and not the note of Warrick or the joint note of Warrick and the corporation, so also in Aungst v. Creque, 72 Oh. St. 551, 74 N. E. 1073. 

Whereas in McCandless v. Belle Plaine Co., 78 Ia. 161, 42 N. W. 

635, 4 L. R. A. 396, it was held that such a note is the note of the signer, that oral evidence was not admissible to show that the corporation alone was intended and that both were liable. 

And in Day v. Ramsdell, 90 Ia. 731, 52 N. W. 208, a note reciting that, "We, the A. B. Co., promise to pay," but signed merely by two persons describing themselves as President and Secretary, was held to be their individual obligation. In 17 

Banking Law Journal, 305-306, it was properly said that "nine business men out of ten would regard such a note as that of the company," and it would hardly be an exaggeration to include the tenth man. The same New Jersey court that decided Reeve v. First Bank, supra, also said in the same case that a note signed "J. Price, Pres., Warrick Glass Works," nothing appearing in the body of the note to indicate who is the maker, is prima facie the note of J. Price. Here again a business man would regard this as a note of the company. In Miller v. Roach, 150 Mass. 140, 22 N. E. 634, 6 L. R. A. 71, a note reciting, "We

§ 20 

promise to pay," was signed "John Roach, Treas." Stamped on the paper was the impression of a large circular seal, around the edge of which was printed the name of a company so placed that the circumference passed through the final letter of Roach and the word treasurer. This was held to be the note of the company. Reed v. Fleming, 209 Ill. 390, 70 N. E. 667, accord. 

Whereas in Dutton v. Marsh, L. R. 6 Q. B. 361, where a note reciting, "We, the directors of the A. B. Co., promise, etc., was signed by four persons, one of whom added the word "Chairman' after his name, with the company's seal in the corner, it was held that the signers were individually liable, that the affixing of the seal was not enough to exclude personal liability and to show that it was the company's note. Distinctions have been made between the case of a note signed "A. B. Agent, C. D. 

Co.," and a note signed "A. B. Agent for C. D. Co.," it being held that in the former case A. B. was personally liable, in the latter that he was not. Barker v. Mechanic Ins. Co., 3 Wend. 94.

Here again a business man would see no distinction. He would regard both signatures as being made on behalf of the company. 

In some states where the name of a company is printed at the head or on the margin of the instrument and the note is signed "A. B., Pres., for instance, the instrument has been held to be sometimes presumptively, sometimes conclusively, the instrument of the company. Second Bank v. Midland Co., 155 Ind. 

581. In this case the opinion of the court contains a valuable discussion of the subject from the business point of view. See also 2 Thompson on Corporation, 2d ed., secs. 1897, 1898; Carpenter v. Farnsworth, 106 Mass. 561, where the court said (p. 

562): "The court has always laid hold of any indication on the face of the paper, however informally expressed, to enable it to carry out the intention of the parties.'

On the other hand, the contrary has been held in C. N. Bank v. Clark, 139 N. Y. 307, and First Nat. Bank v. Wallis, 150 

N. Y. 455. Some courts have treated the instruments in some of these cases as ambiguous and have admitted parol evidence to show the intention of the parties. Taylor v. Fluharty, 41 

Ida. 511, 239 Pac. 1049, not citing , adversely criticized in note 35 Yale L. J. 753. It is submitted that a court wishing to construe the language of sec. 20 in accordance with the evident intention of the draftsman and not disposed to interpret it with a desire to adhere to any former rule in the state, ought to find little difficulty in these cases. Sec. 20 is taken from sec. 26 of the Bills of Exchange Act, but is made stronger by the addition of the words "where the instrument contains," which are not to be found in the section of the Bills of Exchange Act. Notes signed by individuals with the addition of such words as agent, president, secretary and the like, without disclosing any principal, either in connection with the signatures or in the body of the instrument, naturally had to be treated

A note reading, "We promise to pay,' was signed "Briel holding agent 

Shoe Co., Fred C. Briel, Prest., J. H. Taylor, Mgr." It was held that this instrument imposed, prima facie, a personal liability upon Briel and Taylor, subject, however, to be shifted by pleading and proof. The court said that sec. 20 is declaratory of the law as it always has been in Alabama, citing a number of cases. 

Briel v. Exchange National Bank, 172 Ala. 475, 55 So. 808. It is submitted that this decision, which is contra to Jump v. Sparling, 218 Mass. 324, 105 N. E. 878, and above cited cases, is an example of the narrow spirit in which the interpretation of the act is sometimes approached. There was no claim in the case that the signers were not authorized by the corporation. It is clear that the signers added to their signatures words, indicating that they signed in a representative capacity, and that they disclosed their principal. If the principal had been named in the body of the instrument no doubt the court would have held differently, but the section does not require this. Also, if the signers had interpolated the word "by" between their names and their official designations, no doubt the court would have held differently. 

But the manner in which this instrument is signed is so common in the business world and so well understood to mean the same thing as if the word "by" had been interpolated, that it would seem that the courts, even without the aid of sec. 20, ought to treat this as prima facie the obligation of the principal, if not conclusively so. 99 On the second trial of this case it was found upon the evidence that it was the intention of the defendants, and so understood by the plaintiff, that the defendants B and G should be personally bound upon the note and judgment in favor of the plaintiff was affirmed by the Supreme Court. Briel v. Exchange Nat. 

Bank, 180 Ala. 576, 61 So. 277. Sed quaere as to the correctness of this finding upon the evidence adduced? And see Little v.

Although it is a well-established rule of the common law that a trustee or executor is personally liable on contracts made in the execution of his duties, and that the trust estate is not a legal entity, see A. W. Scott, Liabilities Incurred in the Administration of Trusts, 28 Harv. Law Rev. 724, especially 738 ff.

It seems that the  intended to change this rule, and adopt the business concept of the trustee as a representative of the estate. N. I. L. 191 defines "person" as a body of persons whether incorporated or not. This is clearly broad enough to cover the unincorporated businesses, business, trusts, and trust estates of all kinds. It should also be noted that sec. 20 adds the words "or in a representative capacity" which cover all such cases in addition to the agency relationship. Where a series of notes were signed by the "executors of his estate, Wm. O. Daly and John R. Courtright," as payment (as the case may be) on a legacy of William J. Daly." Held, that under N. I. L. sec. 20 the words "executors of his estate" referred to the said Daly estate; that the notes showed clearly on their faces that they were signed by the executors as executors and were in payment of a legacy; and that the defendant was not liable on the notes. The principal (the Daly Estate) was disclosed by the recitals of the notes. Cotton v. Courtright, 215 Ala. 474, 111 So. 7.

Where the executrix indorsed a note naming the estate, it was held that she was not personally liable and burden was on plaintiff to prove lack of authority to indorse. Carre v. Seaman 

(Del. Super.), 190 Atl. 564.

Sec. 21. Signature of Procuration-Effect of. 

A signature by "procuration" operates as notice that the agent has but a limited authority to sign, and the principal is bound only in case the agent in so signing acted within the actual limits of his authority.

Sec. 22. Effect of Indorsement by Infant or Corpo ration. 

The indorsement or assignment of the instrument by a corporation or by an infant passes the property therein, notwithstanding that from want of capacity the corporation or infant may incur no liability thereon.¹ 

Cross Reference: $8 42, 191, 16, 23, 40, 57, 60 to 62, 65(3), 114(2), 115(1), 130, 148(1), 196. "Where a bill is drawn or indorsed by an infant, minor, or corporation having no capacity or power to incur liability on a bill, the drawing or indorsement entitles the holder to receive payment of the bill and to enforce it against any other party thereto." B. E. A. s. 22 (2).

$318 

 Infant's indorsement

ANNOTATIONS 

AMES: The language of sec. 22, unlike that of the English 

Act, is ambiguous and may mean that the transfer of the infant is irrevocable, which would be an unjust change in the law where the indorsee knows of the infancy. 

BREWSTER: The language used in sec. 22 means the same thing as that of the English Act.

MCKEEHAN: The section makes no change in the law. An infant's indorsement always "passes the property." The section does not touch the question of his right to revest the title in himself. The English Act provides the same thing as sec. 22. 

Sec. 22 merely provides that the indorsement of an infant is not void and that his incapacity is not a defense in favor of prior parties, but does not take away the infant's right to disaffirm his indorsement and recover the instrument even against an innocent indorsee for value. Murray v. Thompson, 136 Tenn. 

118, 188 S. W. 578, L. R. A. 1917B, 1172; see 2 Tenn. L. Rev. 

138; Strother v. Lynchburgh Trust & Savings Bank (Va. 1931), 156 S. E. 426, 73 A. L. R. 166, 19 Georgetown L. Rev. 485.

Both of these cases take an unnecessarily narrow view of the purpose of this section. The cases cited by the Tennessee court relate to lunatics. The textbooks cited and the L. R. A. note contain no cases of negotiable paper to support the alleged "common-law rule" of the infant to rescind the transfer of negotiable paper as against a bona fide purchaser for value. 

The only case found is Taylor v. Croker, 4 Esp. 186, in which 

Lord Ellenborough stated that the infant could not disaffirm.

The Virginia case simply followed the former Tennessee court in its erroneous assumption that the infant's power to disaffirm liability necessarily required power to revest himself with title to the instrument. In the similar situation of money transferred by an infant, it seems certain that he could not recover the money from a holder in due course. It is submitted that in the case of ordinary negotiable paper a similar result should be reached, and the commercial policy in favor of the free circulation of such paper to innocent purchasers should override the somewhat antiquated policy of our law which gives such excessive protection to infants as often to result in what has been called "infantile paralysis." In the analogous situation of a chattel sold by an infant and resold to a bona fide purchaser, the common-law cases allowed the infant to recover the chattel, but sec. 24 of the Uniform Sales Act seems to declare the modern commercial policy of protection of the purchaser and repudiates the previous judge-made rule. (Williston on Sales, secs. 14, 342.) This modern policy should apply a fortiori to negotiable instruments, even though they are outside the terms of this section of the Sales Act. It is better to bring the negotiable instrument situation within the analogy of a broad legislative principle rather than within the judicial principle as to chattels,

§ 22 

which was undesirable while it lasted and has been superseded by a carefully drawn statute adopted by numerous states. Such a result is also proper under 196 if we regard the Sales Act as a codification of the Law Merchant. But as to the infant's liability to subsequent holders, see secs. 60 to 62 and 65(3). 

For authorities supporting extension of statutes by analogy, see Interpretation, supra, p. 101.

An infant's executor may disaffirm the transfer of bearer paper as against an immediate transferee. Bankers' Trust Co. v. Bank of Rockville Center Trust Co., 114 N. J. E. 391, 168 

Atl. 733, 89 A. L. R. 697. by lunatics incompetents It seems also that this section should be applied by analogy Indorsements to purchasers from lunatics, married women and other cases of and other incompetency, and a bona fide purchaser should be protected. 

Such was the holding of Fleming v. Consolidated Motor Sales 

Co., 74 Mont. 245, 240 Pac. 376. A contrary result was reached in Hellman Commercial Trust & Savings Bank v. Alden (Cal. 

App.), 268 Pac. 688, affirmed on the grounds of waiver of rights as to the issuing bank, 206 Cal. 592, 275 Pac. 794, but the case was controlled by specific sections of the California Civil Code entirely incapacitating an interdict. 

An indorsement by a deceased wife was held to be good evidence of a gift of the instrument to her husband.  Parker v. Stanley (Mo. App.), 21 S. W. (2d) 200.

Sec. 23. Forged Signature. 

When a signature is forged or made without the authority of the person whose signature it purports to be, it is wholly inoperative, and no right to retain the instrument, or to give a discharge therefor, or to enforce payment thereof against any party thereto, can be acquired through or under such signature, unless the party, against whom it is sought to enforce such right, is precluded from setting up the forgery or want of authority.'

The purported drawer of a forged check held it for seven forged days after its return by the drawee bank, which was then perchecks Drawer v. drawee- mitted to charge it to the drawer's account, and no notice was given to the drawee of the forgery until its discovery by the drawer thirty days later. In an action by the drawer against the drawee, held, there was evidence for the jury of the drawer's negligence, which would bar recovery. Bank of Black Rock v. 

Johnson & Son Tie Co., 148 Ark. 11, 229 S. W. 1. Accord, that the depositor's negligence bars recovery. Morgan v. U. S. Mtge. & Trust Co., 208 N. Y. 218, 101 N. E. 871; Tri-Bullien Sm. &

See the article by Dean H. W. Arant, "Forged Checksthe Duty of the Depositor to his Bank," 31 Yale L. J. 598.

When a power of attorney authorized the plaintiff's agent to draw checks up to a certain amount, the bank can not charge the plaintiff's account for checks drawn in excess of that amount. 

The depositor's recovery is not barred by his failure to examine the vouchers or report the forgery, since the power of attorney gave the bank notice that the agent himself would examine the monthly statements.  Farrell v. 

First Nat. Bank, 263 Fed. 778 (Pa.).

The plaintiffs' bookkeeper made a clumsy forgery of the firm's name on a check, which could readily have been discovered by the drawee bank if it had exercised ordinary care. He deposited the check in the payee bank to the plaintiffs' credit, and subsequently drew out the amount by other forged checks, so that the plaintiffs derived no benefit from the deposit. Held, the drawee bank was liable. The plaintiffs were not estopped by any failure to use care in checking up the monthly statement, although they were deceived into thinking that the accounts were correct because they were usually gone over in the presence of the fraudulent bookkeeper. The  was not cited. Stumpp v. Farmers L. & T. Co., 109 Misc. Rep. 24, 178 

N. Y. Supp. 811.

Plaintiff discounted a note executed without authority in the name of the X Association by a trustee, and gave therefor a check on defendant bank, payable to the order of the X Association. 

The check was presented by the trustee to defendant for certification and was certified. The trustee, without authority, and without the knowledge of the association, indorsed the check in the name of the association, and the defendant afterwards paid the check and charged it against plaintiff's account. Held, that no title to the check passed and that plaintiff could recover the amount from the defendant. Anglo-South American Bank v. 

Nat. City Bank, 161 App. Div. 268, 146 N. Y. Supp. 457, affirmed without opinion, 217 N. Y. 726. Accord, Scala v. Miners & Merchants Bank, 64 Colo. 185, 171 Pac. 752.

In auditing the account between a school district and a depository bank it was discovered that nineteen checks had been ashed a second time or forged. The checks were returned with "Paid" marked on them with a rubber stamp. This was erased and the checks recashed, and some were forged. The defense was the negligence of the school board treasurer in failing to make an earlier discovery of the fraud. Held, under the Pa.

School Code (Sec. 2601 of the School Code, P. L. 425 [Pa. St. 

1920, § 5357]), that the depository bank is placed in a different position than the depository of an ordinary account, and the bank is liable.  In re Georges T. P. 

School Dist. (Pa.), 150 Atl. 96. 

The drawer may recover from the drawee for an instrument paid on a forged indorsement. Labor Bank & Trust Co. v. 

Adams (Tex. Civ. App.), 23 S. W. (2d) 814; Schwarz v. Bank of Pittsburgh National Ass'n, 283 Pa. 200, 129 Atl. 52. The 

 was not cited. Accord, Farmers' State Bank in Merkel v. United States, 62 F. (2d) 178 (C. C. A. 5th). The N. I. L. 

Iwas not cited.

The drawee bank was not liable to its depositor for paying his check on forged indorsements when the money was used by the recipient for the depositor's benefit under a contract between them. The N. I. L. was not cited. Beeson-Moore Stave Co. v. 

Clark Cty. Bank, 160 Ark. 385, 254 S. W. 667; Yanocoe & Co.,

Inc. v. American Exchange Irving Trust Co. (App. Div.), 234 

'N. Y. Supp. 603. The N. I. L. was not cited.

So also on similar facts where the proceeds reached the person intended, the drawer could not recover. Federal Land Bank of Omaha v. Omaha Nat. Bank of Omaha (Neb.), 225 N. W. 

471, note 29 Mich. L. Rev. 219. The N. I. L. was not cited. 

Alent v. Bank of United States, 131 Misc. Rep. 370, 226 N. Y. 

Supp. 653; Couture v. Ocean Park Bank, 205 Cal. 338, 270 Pac. 

943. The N. I. L. was not cited.

Defendant drawee bank paid a check on the forged indorsement of the payee's name. Held, that the plaintiff, the drawer, was not estopped because the forger was the agent of the plaintiff, to whom the check was instrusted for delivery, although the agent had forged the name of the payee on previous checks, the plaintiff being ignorant of such prior forgeries. The drawer can recover even if negligent in examining indorsements, if no injury results to the drawee. National Surety

Mere negligence of the drawer is not enough to preclude him from recovery. It must be the proximate cause of the injury to the bank. Provident Sav. Bank & Trust Co. v. Western &

When the payee's name on a check was forged and the check deposited to the personal account of the forger, and paid by the drawee bank, the depositor's right of recovery against the bank was not barred by its failure to examine vouchers, since no discrepancy in the balance would be disclosed.  Spiegel Realty Corp. v. Gotham Nat. Bank, 121

On the security of a trust deed purporting to be executed by X's sister, the plaintiff gave X, who had applied for a loan of $3,000, a check payable to the sister's order. X took the check to the defendant drawee bank, indorsed it as agent for his sister, and deposited it with the defendant to his account, later checking out the proceeds. $1,000 was used to pay off an old loan from the plaintiff to X, secured by a mortgage which was discharged. The defendant charged the plaintiff's check to his account. The sister took no part in the application for a loan, her signature to the trust deed was forged, and she gave no authority to X to indorse her checks. Held, the plaintiff recovered $2,000. The drawee could not properly charge the plaintiff's account, except for the amount of the old loan, which did not constitute a loss to the plaintiff since the mortgage could be reinstated. Although the plaintiff may have been negligent in not making inquiries of the sister, this would not bar recovery; the payment was not on a forged indorsement, but the bank negligently assumed that X's genuine indorsement was authorized. The  was not cited. McKaughan v. Merchants 

Bank & Trust Co., 182 N. C. 543, 109 S. E. 355. 

A note in 1 N. Car. L. Rev. 40 argues that the drawer should not have recovered, on the ground that he made the loan to X and either meant him to be the payee or meant the payee to be fictitious, and used the sister's name in a nominal capacity. This seems doubtful since the plaintiff relied on the supposed security of the sister's land. The note also argues, and it would seem soundly, that if the drawer was not precluded from recovering, the amount should not have been limited to $2,000. When X wrongfully obtained the amount of the check he became a constructive trustee thereof for the bank. When he delivered $1,000 to the

plaintiff in payment of an antecedent debt, the plaintiff became a purchaser for value thereof free from equities of the bank. 

The possibility of reinstatement of the debt should be immaterial. So the drawer's loss by the wrongful payment of his check was not reduced by the receipt of the money from X, and he should have recovered the full amount of his check from the bank. 

The drawer's right to recover upon forged indorsements is conditioned upon his surrendering the forged instruments to the drawee for the purpose of further proceedings against other indorsers. Showers v. Merchants' Nat. Bank, 293 Pa. 241, 142 

Atl. 275, 42 Harv. L. Rev. 125, 38 Yale L. J. 257. 

A check sent by the drawer to the payees, a partnership, in payment for goods which had been returned as unsatisfactory before the receipt of the check, was handed to an employe of the payees for transmission to their main office. The employe indorsed the check with the name of the payees and his own name, and deposited it in the defendant bank where he had an account, which collected it from the drawee bank. Only the partners had authority to deposit firm checks and usually did so with a rubber stamp, which read, "For deposit only to the credit of (the firm)." The collecting bank was held liable to the drawer. Sec. 23 of the  was summarized but not cited by number. Gustin-Bacon Mfg. Co. v. First National Bank of

It is submitted that this is a misapplication of sec. 23 on which the court relied. That section relates to rights to retain the instrument or to give a discharge therefor or to enforce payment thereof against a party thereto. The plaintiff was not seeking to enforce a right on the instrument. The court seemed to think that plaintiff's right to recover rested on secs. 65 and 

66. But those sections do not relate to the indorsement of one presenting for payment but only to an indorsement for transfer to a purchaser. One who indorses in presenting for payment is not a warrantor and makes no promise. His indorsement is simply a receipt. See 17 Harv. Law Rev. 581, 582; and under sec. 66, infra. So the right of the drawee is the right which the common law gives him. Again, even assuming that secs. 65 and 

66 give the only right to recover in such a case, how was the

drawee precluded in this case from setting up the payment of money on mistake of fact. There could be no estoppel in the absence of evidence that the defendant had cha red his position by reason of the negligence of the drawee in failing to regard the direction of the drawer. Moreover, negligence on the part of the payor is not generally a bar to the recovery of money paid under a mistake. Kelly v. Solari, 9 M. & W. 54; Appleton 

Bank v. McGilway, 4 Gray 518.

In an action by a drawee bank against a collecting bank to recover money paid on checks with forged indorsements, the negligence of the drawer in failing to prevent or discover the forgeries is wholly immaterial. There is no privity between the drawer and the collecting bank and the drawer owes to it no duty of vigilance. Semble, there is no duty owed even to the drawee to examine the indorsements on vouchers. American Exch. Nat. Bank v. Yorkville Bank, 122 Misc. Rep. 616, 204 N. Y. Supp. 621, affd. by memo. 210 App. Div. 885, 206

A. L. R. 147, because there the drawer was a party; Continental Nat. Bank & Trust Co. of Chicago v. Olney Nat. Bank (C. C. A. 7th), 33 F. (2d) 437.

But the drawee did not recover when the names of the payees were indorsed by the drawer. This was a case of fictitious payees known to the drawer, so that the checks were payable to bearer and retention of payment by the defendant collecting bank could not be said to be inequitable. At common law there was a split of authority on ratification, and though there was a strong current of authority to the effect that a forgery could not be ratified, and a number of cases have so held since the , Hartlep v. Murphy, 197 

Ind. 222, 150 N. E. 312, 1 Ind. L. J. 103, not citing the N. I. L., it should be noticed that most of these cases do not cite the act. 

It is submitted that they should not be followed. The word "precluded" is broad enough to include ratification; and the usual argument against ratification of a forgery on grounds of public policy properly applies to criminal and not civil liability. This is the better rule on the agency point. See American 

Law Institute, Tentative Agency Restatement No. 1, sec. 100; 

Kaufman v. Helwick, 212 Ill. App. 10; Gluckman v. Darbery, 85 N. J. L. 457, 89 Atl. 1016, note 36 L. R. A. (N.S.) 1007;

In an action by the holder of a certificate of deposit against the issuing bank it appeared that the defendant bank's cashier had authority to issue certificates. In New York there is a statute,  sec. 326, to this effect: "Recovery on forged checks -No bank shall be liable to a depositor for the payment by it of a forged or raised check, unless within one year after the return to the depositor of the voucher of such payment, such depositor shall notify the bank that the check so paid was forged or raised." The plaintiff insurance company drew two checks upon the defendant bank payable to two policyholders and sent them to the plaintiff's agent for delivery to the payees. He forged their indorsements, indorsed his own name, deposited them to his personal account in a bank which collected them from the de-. fendant, and converted the proceeds. The plaintiff had sent the checks to its agent after learning of frauds by him, and although it knew that previous checks sent to him had not been received by the payees, it had failed to compare the indorsements on the vouchers with genuine signatures of the payees in its possession. The trial court directed a verdict for the plaintiff, which was reversed, because evidence should have been submitted to the jury on the issue whether the plaintiff was precluded from setting up the forgeries by its negligence in not discovering the agent's prior misconduct or informing the defendant of reasons for special caution. The usual rule that a depositor is not bound to examine the indorsements on vouchers did not apply to the prior forged checks, because it possessed better facilities for discovery of forgery than the drawee. The court also decided that the acts of the agent in forging indorsements and guaranteeing their genuineness by his own subsequent indorsements were outside his agency and did not estop the plaintiff from setting up the forgeries. Weisberger Co. v. Barberton Savings Bank, supra, was followed in Slattery & Co. v. Nat. City Bank, 114 Misc. 48, 186

N. Y. Supp. 679. The plaintiff brokerage firm had accounts with two persons named Harold E. Richards, one in Oklahoma and the other in Texas. The plaintiff closed its account with the 

Texas Richards. Subsequently securities were sold for the

Oklahoma Richards, and a check was drawn for the amount due payable to Harold E. Richards, but by mistake was forwarded to the Texas Richards, who knew he had no interest therein. He indorsed the check and had it cashed at a bank, which believed him to be the proper payee and sent the check to the defendant bank, its New York correspondent. The amount was paid to the defendant by the drawee bank and charged to the plaintiff's account. The Oklahoma Richards never received the proceeds of the check and prior to the commencement of suit assigned to the plaintiff drawer whatever claim he had. Held, the defendant was not liable for conversion of the check and the proceeds thereof. The plaintiff could not recover as assignee of the 

Oklahoma Richards since he had not title in the check for want of delivery to him. He could not recover as drawer on the ground of payment on a forged indorsement because the check was delivered to the Texas Richards as payee, who could give a good title to it by indorsement to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. The intent to make the check payable to the Oklahoma Richards was superseded by the actual delivery to the Texas Richards. Moreover, the plaintiff was estopped by its negligence to dispute the forgery if it existed. The same result was achieved in Market St. Title & Trust Co. v. Chetton 

Trust Co., 296 Pa. 230, 145 Atl. 848, 77 U. Pa. L. Rev. 1015.

Apart from the negligence point, these decisions seem clearly delivery unsound. On the negligence point quaere. The cases seem inconsistent with New York cases holding that the drawer of an instrument owes no duty of care to a subsequent purchaser to guard against wrongful filling of blank spaces. Nat. Exch. Bank v. Lester, 194 N. Y. 461, 87 N. E. 779. See also People's Trust 

Co. v. Smith, 215 N. Y. 488, 109 N. E. 561; Linick v. Nutting & Co., 140 App. Div. 265, 125 N. Y. Supp. 93. The principal decision, indeed, goes even farther than the cases imposing liability for negligence in connection with blank spaces, for a person does not reasonably anticipate that a wrongful use will be made of an order instrument by one who has no interest in it, simply because of a similarity of names. The result, however, renders complete protection to the holder who could not possibly have prevented the fraud. The decision is adversely criticized in 21 Colum. L. Rev. 576, 30 Yale L. J. 628. Contra, Thomas v. First Nat. Bank, 101 Miss. 500, 58 So. 478, before the ; Jones Bros. v. Citizens' Nat. Bank of Okmulgee, 106 Okla. 162, 233 Pac. 472.

The question of burden of proof for forgery is largely determined by practice acts of the various states. The answers to such problems are to be found in construing the two acts together.

Taking the N. I. L. alone it seems that there should be a presumption that the instrument is genuine. See secs. 11, 16, 24, 28, 45, 46, 59. The burden of proof of the genuineness of the signature should be the same as that of other defenses. See cases and discussions under secs. 23 and 59. Supreme Kingdom, Inc. v. Fourth Nat. Bank of Macon, 174 Ga. 779, 164 S. E. 204, not citing the N. I. L.

The following cases hold that the burden of proof of the nongenuineness of the signature is on the party who pleads it.

247; Security Finance Co. v. Baxter Drug Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 285 S. W. 1103. The N. I. L. was not cited.

The same result has been reached under practice acts where the plea is not verified. Terrill v. Fowler, 175 Ark. 1010, 1 S. W. (2d) 75; Sinclare Coal Co. v. Tabor-Grigg Coal Co. (Mo. App.), 272 S. W. 701; First State Bank of Mangum v. Lock, 113 Okla. 

30, 237 Pac. 606; Davis Inv. Co. v. Cratty (Me.), 143 Atl. 61. 

The N. I. L. was not cited.

In a suit by the payee against the person sought to be held as maker of a note signed by a mark, it was held that under a denial of the signature the burden of proof that the mark is that of the defendant is on the plaintiff. An answer denying defendant's signature to a note puts on plaintiff the burden of establishing that the note was signed by defendant or that the signature was ratified by him. The burden of evidence, as well as the burden of proof, begins, continues and ends with the proponent of the proposition that the signature is genuine. An instruction that if defendant did not sign the note he should have judgment, is not erroneous, because it did not also require the jury to find that the signature was affixed without the authority of defendant. Subsequently, the drawee bank, without disclosing the payment by the drawer, called upon the plaintiff to refund to it the amount of the draft and delivered the money to the defendant drawer. Held, the complaint was demurrable. The defendant was not bound at its peril to ascertain the genuiness of the signature of its depositor, Parker, when it appeared upon the check and the draft, not as drawer but as indorser. The plaintiff was equally bound to ascertain the genuineness of Parker's indorsement on the draft. 

The defendant was not guilty of negligence or of deceit, and was not liable to refund money paid under mistake, since the payment was voluntary and the mistake, if it existed, was not of fact, but of law. A check on a London bank drawn in Roumania was transferred by a forged indorsement in Austria, where such transfer gave a good title. Held, that the validity of the transfer is to be governed by the law of Austria, sec. 24, B. E. A., being only declaratory of English law and not controlling the general rule of international law. Embiricos v. Anglo-Austrian Bank [1905], 1 K. B. 677. 

Accord, United States v. Guaranty Trust Co. of New York, 69 F. (2d) 799, affd. 293 U. S. 340, 79 L. Ed. 415, 55 S. C. 221, 95 A. L. R. 651, with note, 83 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 681, 12 N. Y.

The defendant, a Belgian bank, received a check drawn by the United States Government payable to a corporation and indorsed specially by its president in the name of the corporation and also in his own name. It then collected the check through a Washington correspondent for the president's private account and subsequently paid him the proceeds. In a suit by the receivers of the corporation it was proved that under the Belgian law the bank was under no duty to the corporation in such a case. Held, that the law of the place of transfer governed, and although the indorsement in Belgium raised no duty, the collection in Washington as agent put the bank on notice of the rights of the corporation and judgment was directed for the receivers. 

So far as the conflict of laws point is concerned, the court seems clearly wrong. Since the defendant never was in the 

United States, it is not subject to the law of this country, and by the law of Belgium it is protected. However, it appears from the undisputed facts that the president had no power to indorse. This being so, the result is sound on the ground of forgery. See section 23. Weissman v. Banque de Bruxelles, 254 

N. Y. 488, 173 N. E. 835.

The English manager of a Ceylon tea corporation forged the rubber stamp signatures of two of its directors upon corporate checks, imitating the signature of one director in ordinary writing. He kept the stamp in a locked box in a locked drawer. During a brief absence of the director the clerk was entrusted with the keys. The checks were paid by the drawee bank. Fraudulent impersonation 

When a railroad issued a pay-check to an impostor, believing him to be an employe, and the impostor, after forging the employe's indorsement, transferred the check to the plaintiff for value without notice, held, the railroad was liable to the plaintiff. The court went on the ground that the railroad was precluded by its negligence from setting up the forgery. Missouri 

Pac. Ry. Co. v. Cohn Co., 164 Ark. 335, 261 S. W. 895, certiorari denied, 266 U. S. 627, 69 L. Ed. 219, 45 Sup. Ct. Rep. 126.

Plaintiff, a private banker, received a letter written by an impostor, but signed with the name of an army officer, whose name was on the army list, in which letter the plaintiff was asked to discount pay vouchers. The plaintiff assented and pay vouchers, which were forged, were received by the plaintiff, who mailed a letter to the supposed officer, addressing him by name and adding his official title, "Lt. Col. Coast Artillery Corps," and enclosing a check made payable in the same manner. check was indorsed by the impostor in the name of the payee 

This and, passing through other banks, was finally paid by the defendant, the drawee bank, and charged to the account of the plaintiff. Held, that the designation of the payee by his official title distinguished the case from other cases of fraudulent impersonation, and that the drawee bank was not entitled to charge the drawer's account. Mercantile Nat. Bank v. Silverman, 148 

App. Div. 1, 132 N. Y. Supp. 1017, affirmed without report, 210 

N. Y. 567, 104 N. E. 1134.

In these fraudulent impersonation cases, the maker or drawer of the instrument may be said to have a double intent. First, he intends to make the instrument payable to the person before him or to the person writing at the other end of the line, in case the negotiation is by correspondence. Second, he intends to make the instrument payable to the person whom he believes the stranger to be. The courts have almost unanimously held that the first is the controlling intent except where the named payee was already known to the maker or drawer, as in Cundy v. 

Lindsay, 3 A. C. 459, and Rossi v. Nat. Bank, 71 Mo. App. 150, supra, or was more particularly identified in some manner, e. g., by some designation, description or title as in the case of Mercantile Nat. Bank v. Silverman, 148 App. Div. 1, 132 N. Y. Supp. 

1017, supra, in which cases the courts treat the second as the controlling intent.

For full discussion of this subject by Professor Ames, Judge Brewster and Mr. McKeehan, see under sec. 23 in their articles, in the second edition of this work. 

The principle of these cases is adopted in Hartford v. Greenwich Bank, 157 App. Div. 448, 142 N. Y. Supp. 387. But query, whether the principle was correctly applied? The case is really one of fictitious payee, not known to the drawer to be such, as was stated in the opinion of the two dissenting judges. It is like the case of Jordan Marsh Co. v. National Shawmut Bank, 201 Mass. 397, 87 N.E. 740, 22 L. R. A. (N.S.) 250, and other

§ 23 impersonation cases cited under section 9(3), supra, and ought to have been Fraudulent decided in the same way. But the judgment was affirmed by the 

Court of Appeals in 215 N. Y. 726, 109 N. E. 1077, on the opinion of Scott, J., below. Hartford v. Greenwich Bank, supra, has been called a border line case, which should not be extended beyond the facts thereof and was not intended to overrule Shipman v. Bank, 126 N. Y. 318, 27 N. E. 371. United Cigar Stores 

Co. v. Am. Raw Silk Co., 184 App. Div. 217, 171 N. Y. Supp. 

480, affd. 229 N. Y. 532, 129 N. E. 904, sec. 9(3); Strang v. 

Westchester City Nat. Bank, 235 N. Y. 68, 138 N. E. 739. 

See also an elaborate note in 50 L. R. A. 75 to the case of Land

Title & Trust Co. v. Northwestern Nat. Bank, 196 Pa. 230, 46 

Atl. 420, affirmed after second trial, 211 Pa. 211, 60 Atl. 723, in which case a check payable to X was given by the drawer to one who falsely represented himself to be X, the owner of certain land, in return for a mortgage on the land, forged by the impostor in the name of X. The check was indorsed by the impostor in the name of X and collected through the defendant bank. It was held, the drawer could not recover from the defendant. The instrument in this case was made before the adoption of the 

Negotiable Instruments Law in the state, but the judgment is in accord with the great majority of the cases, both before and since the Act. Recovery against the bank was also denied in Marcus v. People's Nat. Bank, 57 Pa. Sup. Ct. 345, where the facts were similar to the Land Title & Trust Co. case, except that the impostor was not the supposed owner of the land, but a lawyer who represented that the owner was his client. It would seem that this fact should have varied the result, since the check was not payable to the impostor under another name, but to his supposed principal. The court said that the drawer impliedly represented by the check that the payee was an existing person and that as between two innocent parties, he who by his acting makes the loss possible must bear it.

N. Y. Supp. 209.

The bank accordingly sent a check to Polk's order, and B received the registered letter from the defendant postmaster by representing himself to be D. W. Polk. B cashed the check and converted the proceeds to his own use. Held, the postmaster was not liable to D. W. Polk. Semble, the bank was liable; and the postmaster would have been so if Polk himself had ordered the amount of the deposit sent by registered mail. Quaere, whether the bank could recover from the postmaster? Polk v. Garrison, 162 Ark. 

624, 258 S. W. 631, not citing the 

This quaere seems answered in Citizens' State Bank of Mc- 

Lean v. Fuller (Tex. Civ. App.), 274 S. W. 208. An impersonator wired the drawer bank to wire his balance in the drawer bank to the payee bank, and signed the wire O. C. F. The drawer bank then wired the payee bank "credit O. C. F. $230.50, we remit" and sent a draft to the payee bank for that amount. 

This draft was turned over to the impersonator, and by him cashed. The depositor "O. C. F." now sues both banks to recover the money paid the impersonator. Held, that no recovery could be had from the payee bank; but the drawer bank was liable to the true O. C. F. and the payee bank was liable to the drawer bank on account of its negligent identification of “O. 

C. F."

Defendant, a clerk of court, drew a check pursuant to a court order payable to the order of X and delivered it to Y, who represented himself to be X. Thereafter Y, still pretending to be X, forged X's indorsement in the presence of plaintiff, who in turn by way of identification indorsed the check "O.K." above his signature without further inquiry. After Y cashed the check at Z bank, payment was stopped, and Z bank charged the amount to plaintiff's account. Held, that plaintiff was estopped by his negligence in asserting any rights against defendant. Keel v. Wynne, 210 N. C. 426, 187 S. E. 571, 11 U. of 

Cin. L. Rev. 89, 15 N. C. L. Rev. 186. 

A swindler representing himself to be "J. W. Jones" drew a sight draft on the X bank and obtained in exchange a certificate of deposit from the defendant bank payable to "J. W. 

Jones." Held, although the payee was fictitious the certificate was not payable to bearer, and title could be passed to a holder in due course by the swindler's indorsement. Corinth Bank &

A certificate of deposit payable to A was stolen by X, who assumed A's name and in that name rented a room and a postoffice box. X indorsed the certificate and sold it by mail to a purchaser for value without notice in return for a cashier's check bought by the purchaser and payable to "A." The swindler indorsed the check in A's name and sold it to plaintiff, a holder in due course, who deposited it in the defendant bank, and it was paid by the drawer bank. After discovery of the fraud, the defendant repaid the amount of the check to the drawer bank and charged the plaintiff's account. Held, the plaintiff could recover the amount of the check. The swindler was the true payee of the check and the indorsement was not a forgery. The court quoted with approval from the third edition of this book. Uriola v. Twin Falls Bank & T. Co., 37 

Ida. 332, 215 Pac. 1080. 

See also, note 15 Cincin. L. Rev. 212, and sec. 43 and cases there cited.

The manager of a city garage and his clerk, who were in charge of time slips, added a number of fictitious names to the rolls. Checks were then drawn by the city finance department and returned to the garage for distribution. Each check carried on its back a place for signature of the payee "for identification only." The manager and clerk signed the fictitious names here and re-signed them at the banks which forwarded them to the drawee bank for collection. Held, the instruments were not payable to bearer and city could recover the amount paid thereon. 1 Every negotiable instrument is deemed prima facie to have been issued for a valuable consideration; ¹ and every person whose signature appears thereon to have become a party thereto for value.

By permission of Professor Williston, the following observa- 

Williston tions on the provisions of this chapter are quoted from his work on the Law of Contracts: 

1 Not in B. E. A., but sec. 30 (1) reads as follows: "Every party whose signature appears on the bill is prima facie deemed to have become a party thereto for value."

CONSIDERATION 

8 24 Professor 

"SEC. 108. The promises in negotiable paper require consid- Comments by eration between the promisor and his immediate promisee.-The Williston rule of the common law was well settled prior to the enactment of the Negotiable Instruments Law in accordance with the statement at the head of this section, so that a drawer or maker was not liable to the payee if he proved that the instrument was given without consideration.

Nor was an indorser liable to his immediate indorsee, nor either drawer, maker or indorser, even to a remote holder who was neither himself a holder for value, nor a successor to the rights of such a holder, except in the case of an acceptor whose promise even though made subsequent to the plaintiff's acquisition of the instrument is regarded as supported by the consideration received by the drawer. The 

Negotiable Instruments Law, sec. 24-28, was doubtless intended to codify the common law on the subject, and in the main unquestionably does so. There are, however, distinctions both at common law and under the statute between negotiable paper and ordinary simple written contracts with reference to consideration even as between immediate parties. In the first place 'every negotiable instrument is deemed prima facie to have been issued for a valuable consideration; and every person whose signature appears thereon to have become a party thereto for value,' though when evidence is introduced tending to show that no consideration was given, some courts hold that the ultimate burden of establishing its existence is upon the holder. 

There are, however, contrary decisions and under secs. 24 and 

28 of the Negotiable Instruments Law it seems clear that whatever the law may have been previously, the burden is now thrown upon the defendant not only of introducing some evidence of lack of consideration, but of ultimately establishing such lack by a preponderance of evidence. Further, though any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract is also sufficient for a promise on a negotiable instrument, some things are sufficient to support a promise on negotiable paper which are not sufficient consideration for other promises. Thus an ordinary oral or written promise to pay an antecedent debt does not create a new obligation; but a negotiable instrument is unquestionably sufficiently supported by an agreement to receive it in discharge of an antecedent debt. Whether an instrument, or a signature on an instrument, given to secure an antecedent debt of a third party is binding if the creditor makes no agreement to extend or discharge the indebtedness or to forbear action upon it is not clear under the statute. If under the statute such an instrument or signature is binding, the law to that extent has been changed; for prior to the enactment of the statute it was clear that after a negotiable instrument had been delivered for sufficient consideration, one who subsequently signed was not liable without new consideration. Another possible distinction from ordinary simple contracts should be observed. Whatever may be the rule

§ 360 

Comments by in regard to such contracts as to the person from whom con- Williston sideration must move, there is no doubt that an obligation upon Professor a negotiable instrument may be supported by consideration received by the obligor from some one other than the obligee, as well as by consideration furnished to some one other than the obligor." Burden of proof of "The presumption of consideration is a presumption of fact. consideration It extends to any fact which under the circumstances might defendant reasonably supply a consideration and it cannot be overthrown -on the except by proof of facts warranting the inference of no consideration of any kind. Consideration may arise in various ways and proof of absence of one kind does not necessarily disprove presence of another kind." American Nat. Bank of Mt. Carmel v. Woolard, 342 Ill. 148, 173 N. E. 787.

Although a plaintiff who unnecessarily sets forth consideraon burden tion in his complaint must prove it and does not get the benefit of proof of the presumption of consideration, this rule does not apply to a plaintiff merely because he files a note setting forth consideration as an exhibit with his complaint.  Torian v. Caldwell, 178 Ky. 509, 199 S. W. 35.

The drawer of a draft has the burden of overcoming the presumption of consideration established by the execution of the draft. Press v. Vollintine, 53 Wash. 137, 101 Pac. 706.

In an action by the payee against the maker of a negotiable note, where the defense was failure of consideration, and the burden of going forward with the evidence was on the defendant, it was held that the court's allowing the plaintiff the right to open and close was an error. James Conforti Const. Co. v. 

Neek Realty Corp., 125 Misc. Rep. 876, 212 N. Y. Supp. 393.

The payee by proving notes and offering them in evidence has established without further testimony a prima facie case entitling him to go to the jury. Wickham Havens, Inc. v. Haas, 7 N. J. Misc. 1035, 147 Atl. 741. Contra: Where an indorserdefendant has shown lack of consideration the presumption of this section does not entitle the case to be submitted to the jury. 

Spurway v. Read (Ia.), 231 N. W. 306.

In an action on a note by the payee against the maker where the defense was absence of consideration, it was held that the failure of the defendant to sustain the burden of proving his defense, after the introduction of the note in evidence by the plaintiff, warranted the court's action in directing a verdict for plaintiff. Booth v. Johnston (Ia.), 273 N. W. 847.

Kemppainen v. Suomi Temperance Society, 128 Oreg. 643, 275 Pac. 680.

In a suit by X against Y to cancel the mortgage it was held that, in the absence of proof by Y that he had assigned the original debt to the second corporation, the note and the mortgage were without consideration under sec. 28 and therefore judgment was entered cancelling them. 

The facts do not disclose whether or not the original note had been indorsed to Y. The case seems clearly wrong under secs. 

24, 25, and 29 because it places the burden on the defendant

Y to show consideration for the note whereas the plaintiff X should have had the burden of proving that the original instrument was without consideration. Bradstreet v. Crosbie, 123 

Okla. 269, 253 Pac. 63.

A tenant gave a note for the next year's rent. The lease was surrendered during the year. Held, his liability on the note was wholly discharged without apportionment of the rent. 

One judge dissented on the ground that the presumption of consideration threw upon the defendant the burden to prove failure of consideration. Willis v. Kronendonk, 58 Utah 592, 200 Pac. 1025, 18 A. L. R. 947, with note on rent obligations.

When a note and a contract relating to the same subjectmatter were executed together, they formed one transaction, and the payee must prove performance of the contract in order to recover upon the note. The presumption of consideration, under sec. 24, did not here exist, and the burden was not on the defendant to prove want of consideration, as in an action based on the note alone, since the contract was put in evidence as part of the payee's case. Seaman v. McNamara, 180 Wis. 609, 193 N. W. 377. 

A contract for the delivery of promissory notes, some of which were already overdue, in payment for a patent right, was ordered specifically performed. The remedy at law would be inadequate because the plaintiff would have the burden of proving consideration, whereas after the delivery of the note, the defendant in an action at law would have the burden. The 

 was not cited. Teschner v. Falkenwalde, 135 Md. 114, 108 Atl. 467.

It was held that in the absence of other evidence that it was an error to exclude cross examination of a holder on the question of whether or not he held the instrument for collection only. Sugg v. St. Mary's Oil Engine Co., 193 N. C. 814, 138 

S. E. 169.

§ 368 

 Sec. 25. Value-What Constitutes 

Value is any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract. An antecedent or pre-existing debt¹ constitutes value; and is deemed such whether the instrument is payable on demand or at a future time. 

Cross Reference: 88 27, 54, 191, 196, 24, 26, 28, 49, 52, 55, 88, 119 to 124.

ANNOTATIONS 

"Value is any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract" 

Cross Reference: 88 27, 196, 24, 26, 52, 191.

For comments of Professor Williston on this section, see supra, sec. 24. As suggested there any holder who has given consideration is, under the act, a holder for value, and the old common law distinction is abrogated by this and following sections. Thus the problem of whether or not a person is a holder for value resolves itself into a question of simple contract law. 

If he took the instrument in pursuance of a binding contract he is a holder for value.

What is sufficient "Value" and "no value" are very elastic terms, and merely consideration because the consideration for a note from the viewpoint of hindsight is of no value in a monetary sense, the maker of the note will not be relieved of liability.

The question of the rights and duties of a bank as holder for value of negotiable paper has been greatly complicated by the adoption in many states of the so-called Bank Collection Code, see p. 24, supra, and also by numerous individual statutes on the subject. The following discussion treats only of the effect of the N. I. L. These other statutes should also be consulted, especially in situations involving collection of checks. 

Although section 25 clearly provides that any consideration sufficient to support a simple contract constitutes value, the majority of the courts have tenaciously clung to the old common law rule that mere crediting of an account is not value.

It is submitted that this is an erroneous result and is in the teeth of the statute. Sections 25 to 28 clearly show the intent of the act to make value for a negotiable instrument synonymous with the commercial idea of a binding contract. It is perfectly clear that this was the interest of the framers. See Commissioners' note to this section in Part One, supra, where the Commissioners express the intent to adopt the English rule. The only implication to the contrary to be found in the act is sec. 54, see discussion under that section infra; but this section does not apply to credits because the credit itself is the full amount to be given. The holdings of these cases create an unfortunate commercial result. If the indorser of the instrument is indebted to the indorsee, the cases uniformly hold that credit on the books is sufficient to constitute value. See cases on pre-existing debt as value cited under the second sentence of this section, infra, p. 391ff. It is hard to understand how the same act of crediting the account can be value in one case and not in the other. 

A number of recent cases have reached the proper result that mere crediting the account is value. First Nat. Bank v. Cross & 

Nupper (La. App.), 157 So. 636 (discussing the act and refusing to follow Louisiana cases to the contrary); Blacher v.

A. L. R. 1366, 26 Mich. L. Rev. 209; Tapee v. Varley-Wolter

Bank of Winnett, 164 Okla. 127, 23 P. (2d) 190, not citing the 

N. I. L.; McAuley v. Morris Plan Bank of Virginia, 155 Va. 

777, 156 S. E. 418. See National City Bank of St. Louis v. 

Macon Creamery Co., 329 Mo. 639, 46 S. W. (2d) 127, 80 U. of

The drawer-payee of bills of exchange accepted by the defendant discounted them with the plaintiff's bank, which credited the proceeds to the drawer's account. The amount of the drafts was charged in the indirect-liability ledger against its account as indorser. When the drafts were dishonored at maturity, the bank charged them back to the account of the drawer on the direct-liability ledger and credited it with the amount on the indirect-liability ledger. This increased the existing overdraft in the drawer's account. Subsequently, the drawer gave the bank a promissory note for the amount of the drafts. 

Held, the bank was a holder for value, entitled to enforce the draft against the defendant acceptor. The transfers after dishonor were a mere bookkeeping arrangement, which did not vary the legal effect of the transaction. The drafts were presumptively not paid by the taking of the note, and the burden of proof upon the defendant to show such payment was not supported by any evidence. Union Electric Steel Co. v. Imperial 

Bank of Canada, 286 Fed. 857 (C. C. A., Pa.).

When the seller of goods drew drafts on the buyer for the price payable to a bank, to which it delivered the drafts with bills of lading attached, and the seller allowed the buyer to obtain possession of the goods without paying the drafts, the right of the bank to the price of the goods as against a creditor of the seller, who garnished the buyer, depends on the question whether the bank was a purchaser of the goods or merely took the drafts as security for the credit made to the drawer's account. The bank had a right to charge the amount of the drafts back to the drawer's account, and if it took the drafts as security and later charged the amounts back, it could not thereafter, with knowledge of the garnishment, regain priority by renewing the drawer's credit. CONSIDERATION 

The delivery of negotiable notes in the purchase of an instrument constitutes value although the notes have not been paid. 

Penbrook Trust Co. v. Wiegand (N. J. L.), 126 Atl. 404; Goodale v. Thorn, 199 Cal. 307, 249 Pac. 11.

A note obtained from the defendant maker by the payee's fraud was purchased without notice by the plaintiff, who gave his own note to the payee. The plaintiff after learning of the fraud made no attempt to delay payment of his own note until the controversy was adjusted, and concealed from the maker the fact that his note was outstanding until he had paid it in the hands of the payee. Held, the plaintiff could not recover from the defendant. While the giving of a negotiable note by the purchaser constitutes value, and he need not always refuse to pay it if the infirmity in the original note is contested, he must show the utmost good faith in endeavoring to avoid payment of his own note until the right of the holder against the maker of the original note is determined and in affording the maker of the original note every opportunity to avail himself of his defense. 

 Simmons v. Hodges, 250 Fed. 424, 162 C. C. A. 494 (Tex.). 

The plaintiff, a bona fide indorsee of a note, paid for it with a check. Eighteen days later he was told by the makers of the note that it had been obtained by the payee's fraud. Held, it was not incumbent upon the plaintiff to stop payment upon the check. Reitherman v. Wheeler (Mo. App.), 247 S. W. 222. 

The issue of a non-negotiable certificate of deposit by a bank in purchase of a note is not value if the bank receives notice of defenses before the certificate is paid. Minatare Bank v. 

Wilson, 112 Neb. 216, 199 N. W. 111; Clayton v. Bank of East 

Chattanooga, 204 Ala. 64, 85 So. 271. These cases are rightly criticized, 33 Yale L. J. 628.

The payee of notes, given by defendant upon an illegal consideration, transferred them to plaintiff bank for a certificate of deposit, issued by the bank. Held, that plaintiff was not a holder for value, it not appearing that the certificate of deposit had been paid. The  was not cited. Armstrong v. Walker, 200 

Ala. 364, 76 So. 280. If the certificate of deposit was negotiable, which, however, does not appear, the decision is clearly wrong. 

In Andrew v. Peterson, 214 Ia. 582, 243 N. W. 340, the issuance by a bank of a certificate of deposit, the court not stating whether it was negotiable, as payment for the purchase of a note was held to be value. The N. I. L. was not cited. 

Issuing a neogtiable certificate of deposit is parting with value, especially where it has been negotiated to a holder in due course and subsequently paid. Elmore Co. Bank v. Advent, 189 Ala. 418, 66 So. 509; Gypsum Valley Nat. Bank v. Dillenbeck, 111 Kan. 98, 205 Pac. 1022; Security State Bank v. Brown, 110 Neb. 237, 193 N. W. 336; Italian American Bank of Denver 

Delivery of paper as value commercial

§ 

388 v. Carosella, 81 Colo. 214, 254 Pac. 771; People's Sav. Bank of paper as value Blakesburg v. Smith (Iowa), 230 N. W. 565; Bank of High Hill

Delivery of commercial v. Rockey (Mo. App.), 277 S. W. 573; Pennoyer v. Dubois 

State Bank, 35 Wyo. 319, 249 Pac. 795, 25 Mich. L. Rev. 445.

When the plaintiff paid for a note in part by issuing its negotiable certificates of deposit and in part by placing credit in another bank as directed by the transferor, it was a purchaser for value, and it was immaterial whether the credit was exhausted or whether the certificates of deposit were still outstanding when the plaintiff received notice of the maker's de fenses. Ranchmen's Trust Co. v. Gill, 113 Kan. 261, 214 Pac. 

413. Contra, Castui v. Morrison, 232 Mich. 352, 205 N. W. 108.

The case was decided upon a mistaken idea of the effect of secs. 54 and 59, and is adversely criticized in an excellent note, 24 Mich. L. Rev. 714.

The payee who had obtained a check by fraud indorsed it to the plaintiff, who paid partly in cash and checks which were paid, and partly in a negotiable certificate of credit for $500 on the purchase price of an automobile. This certificate was still outstanding, assignable without the plaintiff's consent, and binding on it. Held, the plaintiff could recover from the drawer the full amount of the check. The liability incurred on the certificate was value. Montgomery Garage Co. v. Mfrs. Liabil ity Ins. Co., 94 N. J. L. 152, 109 Atl. 296, 22 A. L. R. 1224. 

When a bank took a note from the payee and issued in exchange a negotiable certificate of deposit, which it paid to the original recipient after receiving notice that the maker of the note had been defrauded, held, the maker was not liable to the bank, which was not a purchaser for value of the note. Miller v. Commercial State Sav. Bank, 227 Mich. 316, 198 N. W. 996.

The plaintiff was induced by fraud to make notes to a packing company. The defendant bank refused to buy the paper from the company, but took the plaintiff's note for the same amount payable to the bank, and his original notes were cancelled. The bank paid part of the amount to the company in cash and gave it a certificate of deposit for the balance payable to its order in "current funds. (This balance was perhaps paid in cash to the company and then exchanged for the certificate.) The certificate was indorsed to the X bank, a bona fide purchaser for value. The plaintiff sued the defendant bank to impress a trust upon the wrongdoer's deposit; the defendant impleaded the X bank. Held, the plaintiff could not recover from either bank. Even on the doubtful assumption that the certificate of deposit was non-negotiable, this would merely subject the holder thereof to the defenses of the maker and not to a trust in favor of the plaintiff, who was not a party to the certificate. The plaintiff deposited with brokers United Kingdom notes payable to bearer to protect a proposed margin account which was never in fact opened. The defendant, who had previously purchased notes of the same issue through the brokers and left them in their possession, requested delivery and received from the brokers five notes, two of which came from those deposited by the plaintiff with the brokers. The defendant had no notice of this fact. Held, the plaintiff could recover the value of his notes so delivered to the defendant. The duty of the brokers to deliver five notes to the defendant did not constitute an "antecedent or pre-existing debt" within sec. 25, and he was not a bona fide holder, since he was not purchasing negotiable commercial paper in due course for value at the time of the transaction but was merely receiving notes purchased theretofore. The title to the two notes was always in the plaintiff since any authority in the brokers to repledge would not arise until the plaintiff became indebted to the brokers. Rumery v. Brooks, 205 

App. Div. 283, 199 N. Y. Supp. 517.

The decision is questionable. Possession of bearer instruments is properly title, so that the brokers had title contrary to the court's reasoning. The obligation of the brokers to deliver notes to the defendant seems a debt within commercial understanding, unless the defendant by the terms of his purchase was entitled only to notes bearing a specific serial numbering. The decision shows the reluctance of the New York courts to depart from the New York common law view that an antecedent debt did not constitute value. The reasoning of the court, that if the defendant were compelled to return the notes to the rightful owner he would be entitled to a recredit with the brokers for their value or to the right to demand another allotment, has been equally applied as an argument that one taking for an ordinary antecedent debt gives no value since he can re-establish the debt on surrender of the instrument. 

In a Massachusetts case involving a note made in New York the New York statute enacting sec. 25 was construed to make payment of a pre-existing debt value. Allied Furriers Corporation v. Lisker, 244 Mass. 411, 138 N. E. 571.

Sec. 26. What Constitutes Holder for Value 

Where value has at any time been given for the instrument, the holder is deemed a holder for value in respect to all parties who become such prior to that time. 

Cross Reference: §§ 25, 27, 54, 191, 24, 28, 29, 186.

ANNOTATIONS 

See, Hunter, Holders for Value of Negotiable Paper, 22 Ill. 

L. Rev. 287.

§  

404 Where the defendant signed an instrument as an accommodation party, without any new value passing from the plaintiff payee; it was held a question for the jury whether or not the defendant signed pursuant to the original agreement. Merchants' State Bank of Velva v. Roline, 200 Ia. 1059, 205 N. W. 

863, 12 Iowa L. R. 69. 

Where defendant signed a note as accommodation maker after delivery to the payee without any new value passing from the payee, it was held that the payee could not recover from defendant, one who had become a party to the note after plaintiff became a holder for value. Cornell v. Johnson, 59 S. D. 617, 241 N. W. 740. It is submitted that the case is clearly wrong.

The defendant was intended as an accommodation party. It is to be noted that sec. 29 does not specify any time for the giving of value, but simply that an accommodation party is liable to holders for value. There is nothing in sec. 26 which warrants the negative inference that one who has given value is not a holder for value as to persons who became parties after that time. It is clear under sec. 27 that if the defendant had executed his own note and given it to the plaintiff as collateral under the same facts, he would be liable. The mere accident that he happened to sign the same note should make no difference.

An allegation in an answer that the note was executed and indorsed without any consideration is insufficient, the allegation of the complaint that the payee indorsed and delivered the note for value before maturity having been admitted. Rogers v. 

Morton, 46 Misc. Rep. 494, 95 N. Y. Supp. 49.

The payee of notes, who had put money in the hands of X to be loaned, received from X the notes signed by defendants and credited to X with the amounts in her accounts with him. Defendants defended on the ground that they had recived no consideration. Held, that plaintiff was a holder for value. Metzger v. Sigall, 83 Wash. 80, 145 Pac. 72.

The holder of a note for $2,000, surrendered it for a payment of $500, and a new note for $1,500 executed by the maker and indorsed by defendant. Held, that the holder of the new note was a holder for value. Van Norden Trust Co. v. L. Rosenberg, 62 Misc. Rep. 285, 114 N. Y. Supp. 1025.

Sec. 27. When Lien on Instrument Constitutes 

Value

Where the holder has a lien on the instrument, arising either from contract or by implication of law, he is deemed a holder for value to the extent of his lien.

In the case of In re Hopper-Morgan Co., 154 Fed. Rep. 249, it was held that both under the former law of New York and under this section, an accommodation note, given without any restriction upon its use, may be transferred merely as collateral security for an antecedent debt so as to make the indorsee a holder for value. Also that the assumption of the obligation of presenting the note for payment and giving notice of dishonor to indorsers was giving value, following Railroad Co. v. National 

Bank, 102 U. S. 14, and declining to follow the New York cases to the contrary, because they were not decisions of the highest court of the state. 

In Smith v. Nelson Land & Cattle Co., 212 Fed. Rep. 56, 122 

C. C. A. 512, involving other sections of the , the court held that where a question is governed by a Negotiable Instrument Law adopted by the state the federal court is bound to give force and effect to the statute if applicable.

An indorsee, who took a note to indemnify himself against Notes taken future loss on account of his pre-existing contingent liability to a third person in another transaction as surety for the indorser-payee, had a lien on the note for any loss subsequently for indemni- fication

408 Notes taken incurred as surety, unaffected by intervening notice of the for indemni- fication maker's defenses against the payee. Griswold v. Morrison, 53 

Cal. App. 93, 200 Pac. 62. See the comment in 22 Colum. L. 

Rev. 279.

Contra. W negotiated worthless checks to a bank through collusion with its bookkeeper. The plaintiff surety company, which had insured the bank against the dishonesty of the bookkeeper, agreed to reimburse the bank. The surety company, in seeking to recoup its loss, got W to indorse over a note payable to him and made by the defendant. The surety company subsequently repaid the bank. Held, the surety company was subject to the maker's defense against W, since it did not take the note for value. Its claim of value was based on the doctrine of subrogation, but at the time of the indorsement the company had made no payment to the bank, and until subrogation, the claim remained enforceable by the bank, and not by the surety company. 

It is not liability to pay, but an actual payment to the creditor, which confers the right to subrogation. That the surety company later became subrogated is immaterial. American Surety 

Co. v. Palmer, 240 N. Y. 63, 147 N. E. 359, reversing 211 App. 

Div. 33, 206 N. Y. Supp. 817, 10 Cornell L. Q. 356.

Sed quaere? The payment to the bank, though after the indorsement, was apparently made without notice of the maker's defense, and so completed the performance by the surety company of the requirements of a holder in due course. It is not necessary that value should be given simultaneously with the indorsement. Furthermore, it would seem that the surety company became a holder in due course at the time of the indorsement. Although it had not yet by payment to the bank acquired a present enforceable right against W, it was under a definite liability to the bank because of W's fault, and on discharge of that liability a right against W was sure to arise. The surety company was entitled to indemnify itself against this loss in advance. As a practical matter, the company changed its position on taking this note, since it naturally refrained from endeavoring to get other assets of W. There was from a business point of view an antecedent debt from W to the surety company, and it seems immaterial that suit could not be brought on it until the company paid the bank. The situation closely resembles that in Griswold v. Morrison, supra, in which the transfer of a note to indemnify the transferee against a contingent liability was held a taking for value. It does not seem a material distinction, that the transferee's liability in that case was incurred by indorsing the transferor's paper, whereas here the transferee was liable on its surety bond because of the transferor's wrong ful acts.

A note made by the defendant payable to C was indorsed by C to the plaintiff to indemnify him on another note which the plaintiff had signed for C's accommodation and which the plaintiff subsequently paid. A note for $200, obtained by fraud practiced by the payee upon the defendant maker, was indorsed and delivered by the payee to the plaintiff upon a contract that if the plaintiff would become surety for the payee on a note to a third person for $100 and if the plaintiff should be obliged to pay the note on which he was surety the said note for $200 should become the property of the plaintiff. The plaintiff was obliged to pay the note for $100 and sued the defendant upon his note for $200. Held, that the plaintiff had become the sole owner of the note made by the defendant and was not a mere lien holder, under sec. 27, and having no notice of infirmity in the paper he was a holder in due course and could recover the full amount. 

Jett v.

The plaintiff took over the liabilities of another bank, and as indemnification against loss, the note in question was indorsed to it. Held, that plaintiff was a holder for value and in due course. First Nat. Bank in Hazard v. Combs, 237 Ky. 834, 36 

S. W. (2d) 644.

§ 410 

 Rights of pledgee 

Where there is a defense to the instrument held as collateral the burden is on the pledgee to show the amount for which the instrument was pledged and in the absence of such proof judgment for the defendant is proper. John Davis & Co. v. Bedgisoff (Wash.), 283 Pac. 665; Farwell v. Tingle (Tex. Civ. App.), 280 

S. W. 232, not citing the 

A pledgee of a maker's own notes as collateral security for other notes of the maker is a holder for value of the collateral. 

First Nat. Bank of Ottawa v. Kay Bee Co., 366 Ill. 202, 7 N. E. (2d) 860.

A pledgee of a note for collateral security who sues the maker thereon at the request of the pledgor-payee, the note being unenforcible between the maker and the payee because of illegality, cannot recover unless he shows that his debt will be lost unless he recovers. Kincaid v. Lee County State Bank (Tex. Civ. App.), 4 S. W. (2d) 310.

Where the amount of the collateral was pledged in a number of instruments aggregating in value an amount much larger than the principal debt, it was held that the burden was on the holder to show that he would lose the principal debt, or part thereof, before he could recover. Harris v. Bucek (Tex. Civ. 

App.), 8 S. W. (2d) 565.

The defendant was the maker of a note payable to a bank which had failed, and which had pledged his note to the plaintiff as collateral security for a debt. The bank later paid a dividend to the plaintiff without asking for the return of any collateral. Held, that the fact that the defendant had a set-off against the payee bank was no defense in a suit on the note at law by the pledgees. Jones v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust 

Co., 110 Fla. 69, 147 So. 895.

So also where the holder has collected enough from other collateral to pay the pledge, he has no further right to collect on other collateral. Columbia Nat. Bank v. Stine, 135 Kan. 779, 12 P. (2d) 814.

A depositor in a bank after the bank has failed can set off his deposits in the bank against his note held by the bank as collateral security for the debt of another. Gab v. French Com'r. of Finance (Mo. App.), 279 S. W. 435.

The defendant's notes were pledged by the payee corporation to the plaintiff as collateral for the payee's own note. After the collateral notes had matured the plaintiff took a renewal of the principal note from a corporation which had taken over the payee's business, and retained the collateral notes. Held, the plaintiff was a purchaser before maturity of the collateral notes, and entitled to retain them. Since the renewal did not amount to a discharge of the payee's original obligation, the collateral was not released and the transaction did not constitute a repledging of the defendant's notes after maturity. The 

N. I. L. was cited without reference to any section. Gilland v. 

Honeywell, 103 Neb. 50, 170 N. W. 357.

The bona fide pledgee of a note which bore eight per cent. interest against which there was an equity in favor of the maker against the payee, was allowed to recover the amount of the pledgee's debt, but interest thereon only at the legal rate, in the absence of evidence as to the rate which the principal debt was to bear. Citizens Bank v. Limpright, 93 Wash. 361, 160 Pac. 1046.

Bearer bonds belonging to a married woman were wrongfully pledged by her husband to a bank which knew that the wife had purchased the bonds as her separate property. Bearer bonds belonging to a wife were pledged by her husband as collateral security for a note for $4,000 as well as the pay. ment of any other liability of the husband to the pledgee whether now existing or thereafter arising. He was not entitled to have the proceeds of the other collateral applied in payment of his note, since that was also collateral. The N. I. L. was not cited. Lamaille County
