Plaintiff's complaint set forth a negotiable note made by defendant to the order of one P for $10,000, and alleged that P indorsed the note, which was before maturity and for value purchased by plaintiff and that plaintiff was the legal owner and holder thereof. Defendant denied the indorsement and transfer of the note and alleged an equity against P and that plaintiff took the note with notice thereof. These allegations were traversed by the reply. It appeared in testimony that P borrowed $4,000 from one A giving his note therefor and delivered defendant's note indorsed in blank to A as collateral security. That thereafter A, for value, indorsed P's note and transferred it and defendant's note as accompanying collateral to plaintiff, all said transfers being before maturity of defendant's note. Held, that under the pleadings, the defendant, not having raised the question of collateral and the amount of the note for which it was pledged, was not entitled to rely on sec. 27, and the judgment for plaintiff for the full amount of defendant's note was sustained. Bailey v. 

Inland Empire Co., 75 Oreg. 309, 146 Pac. 991. The court said that since the distinction between suits in equity and actions at law was still maintained in Oregon, it was doubtful whether it could compel the plaintiff to litigate a question between the defendant and P, who not being a party to the action would not be bound by any judgment thereon. This case suggests the interesting question, whether, in spite of sec. 27, a court must not give the lienholder judgment for the full amount of the instrument, unless the party against whom the equity exists is made a party to the action in jurisdictions where that is permitted, or a bill in equity is filed against the maker and such party in jurisdictions where the distinction between law and equity is maintained.

Sec. 28. Effect of Absence or Failure of Considera tion

Absence or failure of consideration is matter of defense as against any person not a holder in due course; and partial failure of consideration is a defense pro tanto, whether the failure is an ascertained and liquidated amount or otherwise.' 

Cross Reference: §§ 52, 196, 24 to 27, 29, 54, 55, 58, 59.

Where pleas of no consideration and illegal consideration are made, it was held that the defendant may be compelled to elect upon which plea he desires to stand, because, if taken together, they are inconsistent. Harbour v. Turner (Ida.), 282 Pac. 79. 

For cases on burden of proof, see sec. 24, supra, p. 363ff. verdicts 

In McCormack v. Williams, 88 N. J. L. 170, 95 Atl. 978, the Directed court said that "in sec. 28 of our Negotiable Instruments Act it is expressly provided that the absence or failure of consideration shall be a matter of defense as against any person not a holder in due course, that is not a holder before maturity without notice of any invalidity in the instruments. This defense does not speak for itself. It has to be interposed and proved." In this case the defendant having set up want of consideration to the knowledge of the plaintiff as a defense, the plaintiff offered the notes in evidence and rested. The defendant and two other witnesses gave testimony which, if believed, showed that the notes lacked consideration. No witnesses were examined for the plaintiff. It was held that the trial judge erred in directing a verdict for the defendant. The notes gave inherent evidence of validity. That all the individual witnesses, who testified gave evidence tending to show their invalidity, no matter how strong that evidence, raised, in effect, a conflict of testimony, and conflicting testimony is always for the jury.

Where the evidence was clear that the defendant had executed her note in substitution of her husband's note, previously given in a stock purchase transaction, it was not error to direct a verdict for the payee on the issue of absence of consideration. 

Kiess v. Baldwin, 90 F. (2d) 392 (App. D. C.).

On an issue of failure of consideration, where there is some substantial evidence tending to prove such failure, it is error to direct a verdict for the plaintiff. Gardner Lumber Co. v. Bank of Commerce, 73 Fla. 276, 74 So. 313; Glass v. Virginia-Carolina 

Chemical Co., 73 Fla. 873, 74 So. 981; Lyne v. Central Trust 

Co. of Owensboro, 228 Ky. 802, 16 S. W. (2d) 452. The  was not cited in these cases.

In a suit between remote parties to a bill of exchange, as the payee or indorsee and the acceptor, to sustain the defense of no consideration, there must have been no consideration received by the defendant and plaintiff must have given no consideration. 

National Park Bank v. Saitta, 127 App. Div. 624, 111 N. Y. 

Supp. 927, affirmed without opinion, 196 N. Y. 548. The N. I. L. was not cited on this point. Or the plaintiff must have received notice of the failure or want of consideration. Internat. Banking Corp. v. Morcott Co., 184 N. Y. Supp. 747.

Defendant executed a note and mortgage to X company under an agreement whereby X agreed to discharge a prior note and mortgage on the same property. X transferred the note without indorsement to plaintiff, a bona fide purchaser. X went into the hands of a receiver subsequently without performing its part of the agreement. Held, in an action to foreclose the mortgage, that defendant was estopped from setting up the defense of failure of consideration on the equitable principle that as between two innocent persons the loss must be borne by the one whose action made it possible. This case is correctly criticized in 45 Harv. L. Rev. 1112. Kiley v. Bugge, 165 Wash. 677, 5 P. (2d) 1038.

One who takes a note with knowledge that the consideration has failed is not a holder in due course and the defense is good against him. The N. I. L. was not cited. Washington Trust

The N. I. L. was not cited. Burnes Nat. Bank v. Mueller-Keller Candy Co., 86 F. (2d) 252 (C. C. A. 8th).

Sec. 29. Liability of Accommodation Party 

An accommodation party is one who has signed the instrument as maker, drawer, acceptor or indorser, without receiving value therefor, and for the purpose of lending his name to some other person. Such a person is liable on the instrument to a holder for value, notwithstanding

CONSIDERATION 

§ 29 such holder at the time of taking the instrument knew him to be only an accommodation party. 

Cross Reference: 88 16, 19 to 21, 25 to 27, 60 to 64, 67, 132, 135, 136, 191, 24, 28, 49, 52, 55, 58, 68, 119(2). “An accommodation party is one who has signed the instrument as maker, drawer, acceptor or indorser, without receiving value therefor, and for the purpose of lending his name to some other person" 

Cross Reference: 88 16, 19 to 21, 25 to 27, 60 to 64, 67, 132, 135, 136, 191, 24, 28.

ANNOTATIONS 

AMES: The clause "without receiving value therefor" is inaccurate and misleading. If A gives B $10 to induce B to sign a note for $1,000 for A's accommodation, no one would doubt that B would be an accommodation party, yet if he is, the above clause is erroneous.

BREWSTER: The definition in sec. 29 is the same as in the cases, textbooks and law lexicons. 

MCKEEHAN: As stated by Mr. Arthur Cohen, "Without receiving value therefor" means without receiving value for the bill and not without receiving any consideration for lending his name. So B is an accommodation party if he received no value for the instrument, though he did receive $10 for signing his name to it.

Mr. McKeehan's seems proper and has been adopted, the courts holding that "Value" in this section relates to the value paid for the negotiation of the instrument and not to a payment made by the accommodated party to the defendant for lending his name by way of accommodation. McGhee Inv. Co. v. Kirsher, 71 Colo. 137, 204 Pac. 891; Morris County Brick Co. v. Austin, 79 N. J. L. 273, 75 Atl. 550; Carr v. Wainwright, 43 F. (2d) 

507, 9 Tex. L. Rev. 601.

Where it was agreed between the maker and the payee of a note that each should receive one-half the proceeds of the discount and pay one-half of the note, the maker was not an accommodation maker.  Reyburn v. Queen 

City Savings Bank & Trust Co., 171 Fed. 609, 96 C. C. A. 373.

A married woman made a note to pay for labor and materials used in the construction of houses by her husband on her property. Held, that she was not an accommodation maker. 

Brayer v. Edell, 163 N. Y. Supp. 989.

One is not shown to be an accommodation or an accommodated indorser by the mere fact that a car for the purchase price for which the note was given was purchased both for him and the maker of the note. Overland Auto Co. v. Winter (Mo. 

App.), 180 S. W. 561, affirmed, 277 Mo. 425, 210 S. W. 1.

It was held that the note was not an accommodation note. Smith v. Funston, 50 S. D. 175. 208 N. W. 776.

The payee of a raised check asked plaintiff, a depositor in the drawee bank, to introduce him to the bank. Plaintiff asked the teller if the check was good, to which he answered, "Perfectly, I believe." At the request of the teller the plaintiff indorsed the check and the bank paid it. Upon finding that the check was raised, the bank deducted the full amount of the check from plaintiff's account. Plaintiff sued the bank. Held, that plaintiff was an accommodation indorser, and, as such, liable to the bank, but only for the difference between the original amount and the raised amount. Smith v. State Bank, 54 Misc. Rep.

Nor did plaintiff receive the money or mislead the banker. He only identified the payee.

"Such a person is liable on the instrument to a holder for value, notwithstanding such holder at the time of taking the instrument knew him to be only an accommodation party" 

Cross Reference; 88 25 to 27, 191, 16, 24, 28, 49, 52, 55, 58, 59, 68, 119(2). "Holder for value" in this section does not apply to an accommodated payee who has purchased the instrument from a subsequent holder. See N. I. L. 121(2). Barnhill v. Ow, 145 

Kan. 696, 67 P. (2d) 546.

It has been agreed with some force that this section of the act is defective in that it allows a "holder for value," even though he is not a holder in due course, to recover from an accommodation maker, thus giving a holder of such paper greater rights than a holder of other paper. Taking this sentence literally and by itself there might be some justification for such a position; but when it is read in light of section 16 which makes delivery "for a special purpose" a defense against parties "other than a holder in due course," together with section 55 which makes "negotiation in breach of faith" a defect of title, and in light of section 58 which provides that "in the hands of a holder other than a holder in due course, a negotiable instrument is subject to the same defenses as if it were nonnegotiable," it is clear that such defect is entirely removed and amendment seems unnecessary. 

Where an accommodation note was procured by fraud, it was held that a purchaser for value with knowledge of the facts could not recover from the accommodation maker. The court cited with approval the above discussion. National City Bank Burden of proof

Although the present editor not agree with the necessity of the amendment advocated in the following comment by Professor Brannan, which appeared in full in 26 Harv. L. R. 

493, 494-500, and in the Fourth Edition of this book, pp. 286291, the following portion is repeated here because it clearly sets forth the proper interpretation of the act on the point involved. 

Comment by 

Professor on Marling "The Supreme Court of Wisconsin, in a recent case,¹ has Brannan held that under section 29 of the Negotiable Instruments Law, v. Jones an indorsee who pays value for an accommodation note, with knowledge of the accommodation, may recover against the accommodating maker, even though the negotiation was the first one and was after maturity, and the learned author of an able article commenting on certain sections of the Negotiable Instruments Law, upholds the judgment of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin as to the construction of the statute. "This construction of section 29 is based chiefly on the contrast between the use of the phrase 'holder for value' in section 

29, with the phrase 'holder in due course' used in section 28.

There is force in this argument, but it leads to absurd and unjust results, for the effect of it is to dispense with the necessity of the holder being a holder in due course in any respect except as to the giving of value. If the argument is sound, then the holder for value of accommodation paper occupies a position superior to that of any other purchaser of negotiable paper, since there is no other requirement for his recovery except that he be a holder for value. He will not be subject to any of the conditions prescribed by section 52 except that he shall have given value for the instrument. "If the Supreme Court of Wisconsin is right, then anyone who pays value for an accommodation instrument will be able to recover upon it even if the instrument was not complete and regular upon its face. It might have been obtained by fraudulent representations or by threats or undue influence. It might have been given upon an illegal consideration, e. g., given to effect a violation of the liquor law or to furnish a house of prostitution or to aid in a burglary or a murder. It might have been signed in blank with an agreement that it should be filled up for a certain sum, and yet be filled up by or in the presence of the transferee for a larger sum. "In all these cases under the interpretation of the Wisconsin court, the purchaser for value, although cognizant of the conditions under which the paper was executed, is entitled to recover because he is a holder for value and need not be a holder in due 

1 Marling v. Jones [1909], 138 Wis. 82, 119 N. W. 931. 

2 Professor Hening in 59 U. of P. Law Rev. 471, 532.

CONSIDERATION 

§ 29 Professor course. Again, an agreement between the accommodated party Comment by and the accommodating party that the instrument should not be negotiated after maturity would be no bar to recovery, even though such agreement was known to the purchaser after maturity. Even in the English cases and all the American cases except one, which adopt the English rule, such an agreement would be an equity attaching to the instrument in case the first negotiation was after maturity, but if the transferee need not be a holder in due course, he would not be affected by this agreement provided only that he hold for value. If it was really intended to make an accommodation note fully negotiable after maturity so as to cut off the defense of the accommodation party, why was it provided in section 58, which is not in the Bills of 

Exchange Act, that 'In the hands of any holder other than a holder in due course, a negotiable instrument is subject to the same defenses as if it were non-negotiable?'

This provision is so absolutely irreconcilable with the interpretation put on section 29 by the Wisconsin court as to justify the belief that the phrase 'holder for value' was used in section 29 without full appreciation of the possible inference from such use. "It may be urged that the foregoing argument tends to show not that an amendment of section 29 is necessary, but merely that the construction of the section by the Wisconsin court is erroneous. But when not only a Supreme Court, but also a learned teacher and writer interpret the section in the same way, is it not probable that other courts will follow their lead?

It is submitted, therefore, that it is the part of wisdom to remove all doubt by an amendment which will prevent the possibility of a construction which produces a result so contrary to mercantile understanding, and which will lead to such mischievous consequences as have been above described." "In Cottrell v. Watkins, 89 Va. 801, 817, another unfortunate consequence of the doctrine of such cases as Marling v. Jones was pointed out. The court said: "The doctrine itself, so far from upholding the integrity and ready circulation of commer-

Negotiation after The foregoing objections of Mr. Brannan to the wording of maturity this section seem justified by Marling v. Jones, 138 Wis. 82, recent cases 119 N. W. 931, 131 Am. St. Rep. 996, criticized in 57 U. of Pa. 

L. Rev. 662; Altfillisch v. McCarty, 49 S. D. 203, 207 N. W. 

67, 48 A. L. R. 1270, 24 Mich. L. Rev. 847, 10 Minn. L. Rev. 

613, criticized in 39 Harv. L. Rev. 893; and Vernon Center 

State Bank v. Mangelsen, 166 Minn. 472, 208 N. W. 186. These cases held that a purchaser after maturity could recover from an accommodation party. These are, however, the only cases found which take this view of the act, the first has been criticized by almost all reviewers, and the second is decided under a mistaken view of the application of the English rule, see 39 Harv. L. Rev. 893; and entirely overlooks the effect of the first sentence of sec. 58 which is not in the English act. All seem to overlook sec. 16.

The decided weight of authority under the act as shown by the following cases shows that a proper result should be reached under the present wording of the section. 

See also, cases under sec. 58.

The defendant finance company, at the request of the president of the bank, executed and delivered its accommodation note to the bank for the bank's accommodation. The bank thereafter sold out to the plaintiff and the note was delivered to the plaintiff nearly a year after its maturity. It was held that in view of  secs. 16, 52 and 58, the defense of want of consideration was available to the maker as against the plaintiff who was not holder in due course, even though it bought for value without notice. Pacific-Southwest Trust & Savings Bank v. 

Valley Finance Corp., 99 Cal. App. 728, 279 Pac. 222, petition for rehearing denied, 280 Pac. 134. 

In Rylee v. Wilkinson, 134 Miss. 633, 99 So. 901, the opinion discusses all the sections of the Act involved and quotes with approval the view expressed in the text above, that the use of the accommodation party's credit is meant to be limited by the maturity of the instrument.

This result was also reached in Weiser Nat. Bank v. Peters, 174 Ark. 984, 298 S. W. 878; Pan-American Bank of California v. Crawford, 108 Cal. App. 1, 291 Pac. 220, not citing N. I. L.;

If a corporation having general power to issue and to indorse negotiable paper for its own benefit in the course of its business, indorses for the accommodation of another, the corporation will be persumed to have acted within the scope of such general power and will be liable on its indorsement to a holder in due course. American Trust & Sav. Bank v. Bauer D. & I. Co., 205 

Ill. App. 255; Cox & Sons Co. v. Northampton Brewing Co., 245 Pa. 418, 91 Atl. 859, Ann. Cas. 1916A, 86; Morton v. 

Lovell Bldg. Co., 43 Wyo. 81, 297 Pac. 799. It is often said. that a corporation has no power to execute negotiable paper for accommodation and yet is liable on such paper to a holder in due course. It seems more proper to say that when the corporation has general power to execute negotiable paper, the issue of such paper for accommodation is an abuse and not a lack of power, and therefore, when the paper is issued without authority, the right of the holder to recover depends on whether he was ignorant of the fact that the paper was for accommodation and is otherwise a holder in due course.

Where the defense of the accommodating corporation is lack of capacity to sign accommodation paper, knowledge of the accommodation will defeat recovery by a holder for value. Rosenberg v. Bekenstein, 211 App. Div. 791, 208 N. Y. Supp. 309, reversing 200 N. Y. Supp. 296, the  was not cited; In re

McLean Store Fixtures Corporation, 70 F. (2d) 217 (C. C. A. 

1st).

Therefore, if the treasurer make a note in the name of the corporation without express authority for the accommodation of another and no such custom or usage is shown, the note is not enforceable, even in the hands of a holder in due course. The N. I. L. was not cited. Jacobus v. Jamestown Mantel Co., 211 N. Y. 154, 105 N.

Therefore in such a case the plaintiff must show both that he paid value and also that he did not know of the accommodation character of the instrument. Nat. Bank v. Snyder Co., 117 App. Div. 370, 102 N. Y. Supp. 478; Bradley

Co., infra, sec. 56.

A corporation, whose name was signed to a note by an agent for accommodation, was held liable to an indorsee who knew of the accommodation but was otherwise a holder in due course. 

The ordinary rule that accommodation contracts by a corporation are ultra vires was said to be superseded in this situation by the N. I. L. Sec. 37 was cited by an obvious mistake for sec. 

29. Putnam v. Ensign Oil Co., 272 Pa. 301, 116 Atl. 285. This holding is open to serious question. The reasoning of the court would apply to the signature of a firm name by a partner, which was known by the plaintiff to be for accommodation. While sec. 

29 was intended to declare the common law rule that accommodation in itself is not a defense against a holder for value who knows of the accommodation, it was hardly intended to abrogate settled principles of law as to accommodation contracts by corporations and partnerships. In these cases we have accommodation plus the additional defense of abuse of power and sec. 29 does not say that this additional defense can not be set up against a holder with notice thereof.

The possession and negotiation by the maker of a note with the indorsement of the payee imports that the indorsement was for accommodation, and neither sec. 29 nor sec. 22 give power to a corporation to make accommodation indorsements. Oppenheim v. Simon Reigel Cigar Co., 90 N. Y. Supp. 355.

The cashier of the defendant bank indorsed its name on a note made by a firm in which he was a partner and payable to the bank but never carried on its books. This fact was known to the plaintiff bank, which bought the note and deposited the proceeds to the firm's account. The defendant gave no specific

A corporation indorsed a note given by a stockholder to another stockholder in return for the transfer of the payee's stock to the maker and the forbearance of the payee's husband to sue the corporation on a claim for salary. Pathé Exchange v. McElroy (Mo. App.), 243 S. W. 430.

Farmers State Bank v. Haun, 30 Wyo. 322, 222

The note was solely for the accommodation of the cashier. ARTICLE III NEGOTIATION Sec. 30. What Constitutes Negotiation 

An instrument is negotiated when it is transferred from one person to another in such manner as to constitute the transferee the holder thereof. If payable to bearer it is negotiated by delivery; if payable to order it is negotiated by the indorsement of the holder completed by delivery.

This first sentence of the section states the general method of negotiation and the next sentence is only illustrative. Thus it is possible to have a negotiation by means other than those mentioned in the second sentence. For an example of this problem of statutory interpretation, see comment The Doctrine of 

Ejusdem Generis, 5 Tulane L. Rev. 266, and authorities there cited.

Under this section and sec. 191 an instrument is negotiated when it is delivered to the payee or to an indorsee. "Negotiated" is not confined to transfer after delivery to the payee.

After a note had been endorsed by the payee and delivered involving to a bank by way of pledge, the payee assigned his interest in the note to H by a writing not attached to the note. No notice of this assignment seems to have been given to the bank. Subsequently, a creditor of the payee garnished the bank and claimed the surplus in its hands from the proceeds of the note after the pledged debt was paid. Held, the assignee, H, was entitled to this surplus. It was not necessary that the assignment be accompanied by an indorsement to transfer the pledgeor's equity to the assignee, and delivery directly to him was not required since the instrument was no longer in the pledgeor's possession. 

Johnson v. Beickey, 64 Utah 43, 228 Pac. 189. The decision is adversely criticized in 34 Yale L. J. 200, which considers that H and the garnishing creditor were competing assignees, and that the creditor was entitled to priority because it gave the first notice to the pledgee in possession. The note considers that the objections to requiring notice from an assignee of equitable interests of long continuing character, as in Dearle v. Hall, 3 Russ. 1, do not apply to short term commercial paper in a known pledgee's hands. It seems doubtful, however, whether the note is correct in treating a garnishing creditor like an assignee. Dearle v. Hall, by the weight of authority, does not apply in favor of a garnishing or attaching creditor who gets merely what the debtor has. Ames, Cases on 

Trusts, 413n.; Scott, Cases on Trusts, 623n.; 1 Williston, Contracts, § 434.

The payee of a bill of exchange died. His wife, who was residuary legatee and executrix, indorsed the bill with the name

§ 30 of her husband, under which she was carrying on his business, and delivered it to the plaintiff. Held, he could not recover from the defendant acceptor. In the absence of evidence that the debts and specific legacies had been paid or that any steps had been taken by the executrix in the administration of the estate, she was not the owner of the bill at the time of its indorsement and had no authority, except in her capacity as executrix, to dispose of the same. There is no pretense that in making the transfer she was acting in a representative capacity or that the estate received the consideration for the transfer.  was not cited. Buck v. Kelly, 108 Misc. Rep. 408, 178

The purchasers of the property of a traction company, pending the receipt of the purchase money from another city, executed notes for the amount to a bank which issued a cashier's check payable to the order of the secretary of the traction company who indorsed it to the order of a trustee who indorsed it in blank.

A note given for railroad stock was indorsed by the payee to his principal whose money he held to be loaned on security, but the principal never saw the note, which was retained by the payee until his death. And the only knowledge which the principal had thereof was from entries in his pass book, his only transaction with the payee being a deposit of money to be loaned and the receipt of interest. Held, that there was no indorsement completed by delivery and that the principal had not the title to the instrument. Young v. Hayes, 183 Ia. 134, 165 N. W. 391.

In an action by a partnership, payee of a note, against a collecting bank for conversion of the note, the fact that the note bore an indorsement by the firm to one of the partners did not defeat recovery, since there was no evidence that the indorsement was completed by delivery and the firm was shown to be in possession of the note. The indorsement might have been stricken out under sec. 48 as not necessary to the title. Chapman v. First 

Nat. Bank, 26 Wyo. 138, 181 Pac. 360, 182 Pac. 91.

The registered owner of Liberty Bonds filled out and signed the form of transfer on the back thereof and delivered them to the transferee. The signature was witnessed by a notary public, but not by one of the officers before whom a registered owner was required to appear by the requirements of the 

Treasury Department "in order to effect the transfer" of registered bonds. The rule provided also, "Assignors must be identified to the satisfaction of the officer before whom the assignment is made as known and responsible persons." Held, title to the bonds passed to the transferee. The requirements do not restrict the passage of title as between the parties but only the right of the transferee to register the bonds in his own name and to obtain interest payments and a settlement at maturity.  In re Est. of Stockham, 193 Ia. 823, 186 N. W. 650, 22 A. L. R. 765, with note, "Assignment and transfer of government bonds."

Sec. 32. Indorsement Must Be of Entire Instrument 

The indorsement must be an indorsement of the entire instrument. An indorsement, which purports to transfer to the indorsee a part only of the amount payable, or which purports to transfer the instrument to two or more indorsees severally, does not operate as a negotiation of the instrument. But where the instrument has been paid in part, it may be indorsed as to the residue.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 30, 31, 41, 191, 8(5), 10, 49, 63, 64, 141, 142.

ANNOTATIONS 

A complaint stating that the payee indorsed a half interest in a note to plaintiff states no cause of action at law. Berkley v. 

Muller, 164 App. Div. 351, 149 N. Y. Supp. 620.

So, also, an affidavit for attachment stating the same facts, is insufficient. Ib. 

Where the defendant-maker executed a promissory note in payment for land after an indorsement of a portion of another note of defendant was unsatisfactory to the vendor, it was held that there was sufficient consideration for the second note since the assignment or indorsement of part interest in the first note was invalid under  sec. 32. Wright v. Shoenhair (Cal.), 280 Pac. 174.

Plaintiffs, makers of a note secured by mortgage, paid the note at maturity to the payee, received the note and the mortgage with a release indorsed thereon. The register of deeds refused to accept the release for record because the payee before maturity of the note had by separate instrument assigned a third interest in the mortgage to a third person, which assignment had been recorded. Plaintiffs, without payment of the one-third to the third person on demand by him, sued the payee to recover onethird the amount of the note. Held, that plaintiffs could not recover. Their payment to the payee was rightful and discharged them. The assignment of a part was not a negotiation and the assignee was not a holder in due course. But plaintiffs might in equity bring all parties into court and have a decree for cancellation of the mortgage. Offenstein v. Weygandt, 89 

Kan. 739, 132 Pac. 991.

Plaintiff was a bona fide indorsee of a note, but X furnished one-half the consideration for the purchase and had one-half in-

S. E. 64. 

A note secured by a real estate mortgage was payable to persons not partners. One payee was fraudulently induced to indorse "my one-half interest" to X without recourse, and by subsequent indorsements this interest was transferred to a real estate corporation. The other payee did not indorse. In a proceeding by the two payees to foreclose the mortgage, the real estate company was made a defendant and the makers paid the amount of the note into court. Held, the real estate company was entitled to the indorsing payee's share of the proceds in the note. The indorsement of part of the note did not constitute a negotiation so as to make the real estate company a holder in due course, but it was a bona fide assignee for value of a nonnegotiable chose in action and took free of equities of the in dorsing payee, although it would have been subject to any equit able defenses of the makers. Where a note on its face carries a complete indorsement, a parol agreement that the indorsee is to have only a part interest was held not within this section and holder had good title. Slay v. Wheeler (Tex. Civ. App.), 84 S. W. (2d) 841, 49 Harv. L. 

Rev. 647.

Where a note for the sum of $4100 payable to two payees was indorsed by both with the indorsement by one expressed to be to the extent of $1200, the note was not rendered nonnegotiable, since the indorsement was not one of a part of the instrument but a complete transfer and merely limited the in dorser's liability. Puckett v. Big Lake State Bank (Tex. Civ.

Sec. 33. Kinds of Indorsement

An indorsement may be either special or in blank; and it may also be either restrictive or qualified, or conditional.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 31, 34, 36, 38, 39, 191, 35, 37, 63, 64, 139. 

1 The English Act omits the words "qualified or conditional." B. E. A. s. 32 (6).

§ 478 

 ANNOTATIONS 

An allegation in a complaint to which was annexed the note sued on, that it was indorsed to the plaintiff, is sustained by showing that the note was indorsed in blank. It is immaterial whether plaintiff's ownership was derived through a special or a blank indorsement. Cleveland Co. v. Chitenden, 81 Conn. 667, 71 Atl. 935.

Sec. 34. Special Indorsement-Indorsement in 

Blank

A special indorsement specifies the person to whom, or to whose order, the instrument is to be payable; and the indorsement of such indorsee is necessary to the further negotiation of the instrument. An indorsement in blank specifies no indorsee, and an instrument so indorsed is payable to bearer, and may be negotiated by delivery. 1

Sec. 35. Blank Indorsement-How Changed to Spe cial Indorsement

The holder may convert a blank indorsement into a special indorsement by writing over the signature of the indorser in blank any contract consistent with the character of the indorsement.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 17(6), 31, 34, 63 to 66, 191, 10, 36, 124, 125. 

1 "By writing above the indorser's signature a direction to pay the bill to, or to the order of, himself or some other person." B. E. A. s. 34 (4).

 ANNOTATIONS 

Where a holder stamped over a blank indorsement a statement containing the following words, "I hereby guarantee payment of the within note or any renewal of the same," it was held that this was a material alteration: the indorser was discharged. First Nat. Bank of Perry v. Sweeny, 203 Ia. 35, 212 

N. W. 333. 

Writing above a blank indorsement the words "protest waived" is a material alteration, and if made without the consent of the indorser, avoids the indorsement. Sawyer State Bank v. Sutherland, 36 N. D. 493, 162 N. W. 696.

Sec. 36. When Indorsement Restrictive

An indorsement is restrictive, which either— (1) Prohibits the further negotiation of the instrument; or (2) Constitutes the indorsee the agent of the indorser; or (3) Vests the title in the indorsee in trust for or to the use of some other person.'¹

But the mere absence of words implying power to negotiate does not make an indorsement restrictive." 

Cross Reference: 88 30, 37, 191, 10, 16, 47.

In Werner Piano Co. v. Henderson & Reese, 121 Ark. 165, 180

S. W. 495, notes made by the defendants were indorsed by the payees, before maturity, as follows: "Pay to the order of the

The court said that the indorsement was a restrictive indorsement, making the indorsee the agent of the indorser, but the jury below found that plaintiff had notice by this indorsement of defenses of the maker and therefore was not an innocent purchaser. The court made the mistake of failing to distinguish between an indorsement for the use of the indorser and an indorsement for the use of a third person. In this case the indorsement was for the use of plaintiff, and the bank, the indorsee, became, not an agent for the indorser, but a trustee for the plaintiff. Moreover, it is difficult to see how a restrictive indorsement gives notice to the indorsee of defenses of the maker against the payee-indorser. But it would be correct to say that if the indorsement had been made by the payee for his own use, the defense would be good against the indorsee, not because he had notice thereof, but because he was only the agent or trustee of the payee-indorser.

Sec. 37. Effect of Restrictive Indorsement-Rights of Indorsee

A restrictive indorsement confers upon the indorsee the right— (1) To receive payment of the instrument;

§ (1) 486 

(2) To bring any action thereon that the indorser could bring; (3) To transfer his rights as such indorsee, where the form of the indorsement authorizes him to do so. 

But all subsequent indorsees acquire only the title of the first indorsee under the restrictive indorsement. 

Cross Reference: §§ 36, 47, 51, 58, 191, 10, 16, 30, 50, 52, 55.

AMES: Under clause 2 an indorser, even though for value can not be sued by an indorsee in trust for a third person, e. g., if A, the holder of a note, indorses "pay to B for use of C," B could not sue his indorser A even if A received value for his indorsement. This is unjust. 

BREWSTER: Equity would take care of the case supposed.

MCKEEHAN: It is plain that the indorsee in such a case should have a right of action against the indorser. How equity would take care of the case is not apparent. It has been suggested that the language of sec. 37 (2) is used in a permissive and not in a restrictive sense. By this construction the indorsee in trust could sue his indorser. in trust for

Indorsements The unjust result which Mr. Ames feared from subsec. 2, a third occurred in Gulbranson-Dickinson Co. v. Hopkins, 170 Wis. 326, person 175 N. W. 93. The payee being indebted to the plaintiff, delivered the notes to it before maturity as collateral, but indorsed them so as to make them payable to a bank "for credit account of" the plaintiff. The plaintiff, as the real party in interest under the Code, was allowed to sue the maker in its own name, but was held subject to the defense of failure of consideration as between the maker and payee, of which it had no notice. The

NEGOTIATION 

§ 37 (2) Indorsements in trust for a court conceded that the restrictive indorsement under sec. 36(3), unlike that under 36(2), transferred both the legal title and the third person beneficial interest in the instrument. The bank held title for the benefit of the plaintiff. However, it was stated that under sec. 47 the notes ceased to be negotiable because of the restrictive indorsement; and being non-negotiable, the plaintiff or the bank could not be a holder in due course, but was subject to any defense which might have been made against the notes in the hands of the payee. To the contention that the delivery of the notes by the bank to the plaintiff after dishonor united the legal and equitable title and thus constituted the plaintiff the owner as if the original indorsement had been unrestricted, the court replied that the plaintiff did not become holder until after maturity.

Apart from the language of the , this holding is clearly unsound. The restrictive indorsement created a trust for the plaintiff's benefit and gave notice of this trust to later purchasers, but it did not give notice of defenses of prior parties. 

Especially, it did not cut down the practical advantages which the plaintiff, whom it meant to benefit, would have had under an ordinary indorsement. While the plaintiff did not become legal owner until after maturity, the bank was a purchaser before maturity, for value given by the plaintiff, and should have been treated as a holder in due course, subject only to the trust in favor of the plaintiff. The plaintiff, which derived its title from a holder in due course, was as free from prior equities as the bank, regardless of the transfer after maturity, and this transfer discharged the trust, making the plaintiff in all respects an absolute owner. Hook v. Pratt, 78 N. Y. 341, 34 Am. Rep. 

539, so held before the N. I. L.

A proper interpretation of sec. 47 does not necessitate the result of the Gulbranson case. It should be noted that N. I. L. 

47 which is invoked here does not provide that an instrument is non-negotiable after it is restrictively indorsed or discharged. 

It merely provides that the instrument remains negotiable, until that event (having in mind, perhaps, conditional indorsements, secs. 33 and 39, conditional acceptances, sec. 141(1), qualified acceptances, sec. 142, and the like). Thereafter, the effect of transfer is governed by the appropriate sections, in this case secs. 36 and 37, and the equities of the case. Even if the negative inference is to be applied, it still does not follow that the act requires the result of the Gulbranson case. Section 191 provides, "In this act, unless the contents require otherwise, indorsement means indorsement coupled with delivery." When the term indorsement in sec. 47 is given this meaning it seems that the instrument would not lose its negotiability until after it was delivered to the restrictive indorsee. Thus the first restrictive indorsee under this interpretation might be a holder in due course if the form of the restrictive indorsement and the

§ (2)  

488 in trust for

Indorsements nature of the transaction were such as would permit it. Turna third ing, then, to secs. 36 and 37, it seems clear that such a case is person possible under sec. 36 (3). Mr. McKeehan's suggestion that sec. 

37 (2) is permissive and not exclusive is entirely logical. It is given further weight by the fact that the commissioners' notes show that this provision was for the purpose of overcoming the effect of Rock County Nat. Bank v. Hollister, 21 Minn. 385, which held that an indorsee for collection could not sue under the real party in interest statute. That sec. 37(2) is not exclusive is shown by the fact that, under the last sentence of sec. 37, indorsees subsequent to a restrictive indorsement get the title of the first indorsee and not that of the restrictive indorser. If the framers had intended sec. 37 (2) as exclusive "restrictive indorser" would have been inserted for "indorsee" in the last sentence. It should be noted further that the preliminary draft contained a provision that the trustee's indorsement cut off the rights of the beneficiary, showing clearly that sec. 37 was not intended to prevent the trustee himself from becoming a holder in due course as to prior parties. 

The result here suggested was reached on the grounds of estoppel in Atlantic City National Bank v. Commercial Lumber 

Co. (1931 N. J.), 155 Atl. 762, 32 Col. L. Rev. 130, 18 Va. L.

Rev. 199, where the court held that the first indorsee of a restrictively indorsed check indorsed "For Deposit" only could recover from the drawer who had a defense of failure of consideration. But the case must stand. For the proposition that the indorsee was a holder in due course, see sec. 58. 

The plaintiff deposited a check for collection to the Olney bank which indorsed it "Pay any Bank or Banker" to the defendant, who paid the Olney bank in full. The next day the 

Olney bank failed and the plaintiff now sues the defendant in equity for return of the checks. The Bank Collections Act provided that the indorsement to defendant was restrictive. Held, that defendant need not return the checks or their proceeds. 

Lipshulz v. Philadelphia Savings Fund Soc., 107 Pa. Super. Ct. 

481, 164 Atl. 74. This case also shows that sec. 37 (2) is permissive and not restrictive.

More support for this interpretation is to be found in Midwest Nat. Bank & Trust Co. v. Niles & Watters Sav. Bank, 190 

Ia. 752, 180 N. W. 880. In that case the payee of a check obtained by fraud offered it to the plaintiff bank to be cashed or deposited. After the bank had obtained a telegraphic acceptance or certification from the drawee (see sub. sec. 134), the payee indorsed "For deposit," signed his name, and delivered the check to the bank. The amount was credited to his account, and subsequently checked out. The drawee, which dishonored the check, was held liable as acceptor to the bank. The court did not decide whether the bank had notice of the fraud, but considered this immaterial, as there was no fraud in obtaining the

NEGOTIATION 

§ 37 (2) in trust for a acceptance and the action was against the acceptor and not the Indorsements defrauded drawer. The defendant contended that the indorse- third person ment was restrictive, and rendered the check subject to original defenses, but the court without deciding this question held that the bank was not claiming as indorsee but as the direct promisee under the acceptance, in reliance upon which it had paid value. 

Midwest Nat. Bank & Trust Co. v. Niles & Watters Sav. Bank, 

190 Ia. 752, 180 N. W. 880.

If the bank took with notice of the fraud, the decision is questionable. It would clearly be impossible for the bank then to hold the drawer, and it seems equally inequitable for the bank, knowing of the fraud upon him, to hold the drawee bank and thus charge the drawer's account. It would seem that the acceptor should be able to set up the drawer's defenses against anyone not a holder in due course. On the other hand, if the bank took without notice, the decision seems sound. The indorsement seems restrictive, but this should not prevent the indorsee from being a holder in due course with respect to the acceptor (or the drawer if there were no acceptance). The form of indorsement merely puts the indorsee on notice of the equities of the indorser, and here there were none. In the absence of actual notice of the drawer's equities, the bank on paying value became a holder in due course. On correct principles, the result is preferable to that in the Gulbranson case, supra. 

See Smith, The Concept of "Negotiability" as used in sec. 

47, 7 Texas L. Rev. 520, note in 1 B. U. L. Rev. 137, and the 

New Jersey cases of countermand of certification discussed under sec. 188. 

In Union Trust Co. v. Mathews, 258 Mich. 433, 242 N. W. 

781, the court held that where an instrument was indorsed specially to a trustee for the payee, the trustee gave value and met all the requirements of a holder in due course, that the trustee could not recover from the maker who had a defense of failure of consideration. Unfortunately the court put its original opinion on the ground that the trust agreement made the indorsement restrictive and that the rule of Gulbranson case, supra, applied. On rehearing the court admitted that the indorsement was not restrictive but failed to rephrase its reasoning, falling into the error that that interpretation of 37 applied. 

The Harvard Law Review also fell into the same error, 45 Harv. 

L. Rev. 738. The case is properly criticized in an excellent note in 31 Mich. L. Rev. 72, which points out that the real justification for the case rests in an attempt to prevent unjust enrichment to the beneficiary which on the particular facts of this case could not have happened.

The jury under these instructions found for the defendant. On appeal the upper court, taking the position that the plaintiff under the indorsement could get no better rights than the payee, affirmed judgment. Since the finding of the jury on the point of notice was adverse to the plaintiff it is submitted that the statements of the court on the effect of restrictive indorsement are not necessary to the decision and that the case was properly submitted below. It has often been held that indorsements "for collection" or collection for collection account" or "for deposit" or "for deposit and collection" do not pass the legal title to the indorsee. This is an error and arises from the fact that courts so holding fail to distinguish between the legal title to the instrument and the beneficial ownership thereof. The courts may well say that the title to the instrument remains in the indorser if they mean thereby only that he retains the beneficial ownership. But the legal title must be in the indorsee, otherwise he would not be able to sue on the instrument in his own name, see sec. 51, as has been held in some of the very courts which hold that he has no title, nor would he be able to indorse the instrument to another to collect, as in the common case of an instrument drawn upon or payable at a distant bank which must often be transferred several times before it reaches the place of payment. 

An indorsement for collection does not destroy the transferability of the instrument and it can be reindorsed so that the indorsee can sue in his own name. Fawsett v. Nat. Life Ins. 

Co., 97 Ill. 11; Haskell v. Avery, 181 Mass. 106, 63 N. E. 15; 

Robinson v. Gentry (Mo. App.), 106 S. W. (2d) 913. The 

 was not cited.

Bayer, 46 Oreg. 143, 79 Pac. 497, 114 Am. St. Rep. 858.

An indorsee "for collection" can not hold the acceptor where the drawer paid the amount of the bill before maturity to the indorser and released the acceptor, although said indorsee has paid the amount to the indorser. Under sec. 35, Bills of Exchange Act, such indorsee gets no property in the bill. Williams, Deacon & Co. v. Shadbolt, 1 Cababe & Ellis, 529. 

An indorsee for collection who has remitted the amount of a draft to the indorsing bank in which the drawer had placed it for deposit can sue the drawer upon dishonor and proper protest, etc. Cairo Nat. Bank of Cairo, Ill. v. Banton Co. (Mo. 

App.), 287 S. W. 839.

Sec. 38. Qualified Indorsement

A qualified indorsement constitutes the indorser a mere assignor of the title to the instrument. It may be made by adding to the indorser's signature the words "without recourse," or any words of similar import.

Such an indorsement does not impair the negotiable character of the instrument.¹

The holder of a note and mortgage transferred them together, indorsing the note and stating in the assignment of the mortgage that the transfer of the notes was without recourse. Sec. 39. Conditional Indorsement

Where an indorsement is conditional, a party required to pay the instrument may disregard the condition, and make payment to the indorsee or his transferee, whether the condition has been fulfilled or not. But any person to whom an instrument so indorsed is negotiated, will hold the same, or the proceeds thereof, subject to the rights of the person indorsing conditionally. 

Cross Reference: 88 31, 191, 3 to 5, 10, 16, 17, 33, 40, 49, 65, 66, 88, 141.

Sec. 40. Indorsement of Instrument Payable to Bearer

Where an instrument, payable to bearer, is indorsed specially, it may nevertheless be further negotiated by delivery; but the person indorsing specially is liable as indorser to only such holders as make title through his indorsement.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 9, 30, 31, 34, 191, 8, 9(5), 16, 35, 39, 47, 48, 56, 67, 88, 191.

ANNOTATIONS 

2 Read by itself and given a broad interpretation, this section seems to cover two situations: (1) where paper originally payable to order is indorsed in blank and later indorsed specially; (2) where paper originally payable to bearer is indorsed specially. In both cases at common law it was held that such paper could be further negotiated by delivery. This also seems to have been the intent of the framers of the Act, for the Commissioners' note cited both Smith v. Clarke and Johnson v. Mitchell, the two leading cases on this point. But if one examines carefully the rest of the Act as applied to the first set of facts given above, it will appear that such a broad interpretation of section 40 is in conflict not only with the plain meaning of sections 34, 9(5), 30 and 49, but also with the expressed intent of the Commissioners as set out in the notes under those sections. Thus where an instrument originally payable to order has been indorsed in blank, making it a bearer instrument under section 9(5), and later indorsed specially, section 34 provides that "the indorsement of such indorsee is necessary to further negotiate the instrument," a square conflict with section 40. It should be noted also that an instrument in this condition is no longer within the definition of a bearer instrument given in section 9(5), because the last indorsement is no longer in blank.

The Commissioners' notes to these two sections show the clear intent to adopt the rule of the B. E. A. And, as Chalmers

And under section 49 although a transfer of such instrument passes title, the transferee cannot become a holder in due course until the instrument is actually indorsed. 

If, therefore, section 40 is given its broad interpretation, it would necessarily conflict with these other sections and the plain intent of the framers in adopting them. 

It is a well established rule of statutory construction that where there is a possible conflict between sections, the meaning should be adopted which reconciles as many sections as possible. 

Therefore, section 40 should not be applied to paper originally payable to order.

The second situation, that where the paper was originally payable to bearer, is quite different. As noted above, there is no provision in section 8 that instruments indorsed specially are payable to order; such paper by definition [ 9(1)] is payable to bearer and by the last sentence of section 30 remains negotiable by delivery. The only possible conflict here is between section 34, which provides that indorsement of such paper is necessary for further negotiation, and section 40, which provides that it is not. Under these circumstances section 40 should control, otherwise it becomes entirely meaningless. 

There is considerable evidence to the effect that this was the intention of the Commission. Eaton' categorically states that such was their intention and contemporary writers sustain him.

The view of Mr. McKeehan, expressed in the fourth edition of this work, that Smith v. Clarke is still in force despite sec. 

9(5) gains slight support from Parker v. Roberts, 243 Mass. 174, 137 N. E. 295. A blank indorsement of a note by the payee was followed by two special indorsements, by the A bank to the B bank, and by the B bank to "any bank or banker." The second special indorsement was stamped, "Cancelled." The plaintiff was in possession of the note and did not allege or prove title through any bank, but alleged that the payee indorsed in blank and that he himself was the holder. The defendant maker pleaded want of consideration and fraud. Held, the plaintiff was a holder in due course free from defenses. His presumption of title by possession was not rebutted, and he was not obliged to trace title through the special indorsers. Under sec. 9(5) the plaintiff's possession and the blank indorsement would establish title if no further indorsement appeared. But the two further indorsements might be struck out under sec. 48 as not necessary to his title, and the note would then be transferable by delivery and in effect payable to bearer. The case is adversely criticized by G. W. Goble, "Effect of a special indorsement on a bearer instrument," 5 Ill. L. Q. 247; and in 23 Colum. L. Rev. 488.

The decision may be just on the facts, even if Smith v. Clarke is abrogated. The plaintiff, according to the facts of the case set out in the finding of the court below, probably took by delivery directly from the payee, and there was testimony of the payee, himself a lawyer, to support this conclusion. Under the circumstances, the plaintiff had title under section 49 and was entitled by section 48 to strike out the subsequent indorsements. The court's discussion of section 48 is, therefore, entirely relevant. The case, also, is to be distinguished from the usual situation where there are blank indorsements followed by special indorsements, because in this case, the indorsements being for collection would not constitute notice to the plaintiff of any rights in the special indorsees. The fact that he might have taken from the payee is sufficient to support affirmance of the judgment in the court below. It should also be noted in this respect that neither section 30 nor 34 prohibit negotiation back to prior holders of paper with special or restrictive indorsements, still left thereon. See sections 48 and 50.

Sec. 41. Indorsement Where Payable to Two or 

More Persons 

Where an instrument is payable to the order of two or more payees or indorsees who are not partners, all must indorse, unless the one indorsing has authority to indorse for the others. 

Cross Reference: 88 8(4), 19, 31, 191, 8(5), 10, 17(7), 20 to 23, 32, 49, 59, 68.

Sec. 42. Effect of Instrument Drawn or Indorsed to a Person as Cashier

Where an instrument is drawn or indorsed to a person as "Cashier" or other fiscal officer of a bank or corporation, it is deemed prima facie to be payable to the bank or corporation of which he is such officer, and may be negotiated by either the indorsement of the bank or corporation, or the indorsement of the officer.¹

The thief forged the indorsement of Smith and was paid the check by the defendant, and the plaintiff paid it. The plaintiff later discovered the fraud and sued the defendant. Held, there was no impersonation; the indorsement was forged, and the plaintiff could recover. Bank of Italy v. First

The payee on a note was "Stutz Motor Car Co. of America, Inc."

The indorsement by the intended payee was "Stutz 

Motor Car Co. of America, Inc., Stutz Atlanta Motor Co. by 

Fred S. Wilson, State Distributor." In an action by the alleged holder against the certifying bank it was held that under  sec. 43 title passed by the indorsement. Atlanta & Lowry Nat. 

Bank v. First Nat. Bank of Carrollton, 38 Ga. App. 768, 145 

S. E. 521, 42 Harv. L. Rev. 699, 13 Minn. L. Rev. 501.

The mere fact that the payee named in the note is "Cascade Country Club," and the indorsement thereon is "Cascade Country Club, Inc., W. H. Emrick, Pres." does not indicate that the payee and the indorser are not the same persons, or overcome the presumption that the indorsement is genuine. Dean v. 

Felton, 125 Oreg. 122, 266 Pac. 236. 

Where the payee corporation "Bureau Marketing Service" is described in the instrument as "Bureau Mkt. Service, Osceola, Iowa" the indorsement "Bureau Marketing Service, Esther

Agan" was sufficient. Bureau Marketing Service of Osceola v. 

Lewis, 220 Ia. 662, 263 N. W. 7. 

Where a check was made payable to "X and Y Oil Trust" the indorsement "X and Y, by X" was held insufficient. Young v. Hembree (Okla.), 73 P. (2d) 393.

The drawer purchased goods from a thief and gave his check therefor. The thief directed that the check be made to "Rip 

Gordon" and the check was so made, the drawer thinking him to be "Rip Gordon," whereas his name was Hollis. The defendant took the check for value indorsed by Hollis as "Rip

Gordon," and presented it to the drawee bank who paid it. 

Before the drawee charged it to the drawer's account payment was stopped by the drawer and the drawee bank brings this action against the defendant on grounds that the signature, "Rip Gordon," was a forgery. It was held that the indorsement was not a forgery. Milner v. First Nat. Bank of Waynesboro, 38 Ga. App. 668, 145 S. E. 101. 

When a draft was inadvertently made payable to a bank which had consolidated with the plaintiff bank, the plaintiff had the right to insert its own name as the payee. An indorsement under the wrong designation within sec. 43 was not necessary under the circumstances. First Wisconsin Nat. Bank v. Peoples 

Nat. Bank, 136 Va. 276, 118 S. E. 82, 36 A. L. R. 736.

The plaintiff entered into a charter-party with a steamship company for the use of the steamship Belvernon, which the company was to purchase, and as part payment drew his check to "steamship Belvernon and owners." The check was forwarded to the company's brokers, who were authorized to indorse for them, and indorsed "Steamship Belvernon and owners J. C. F. 

Agents." The boat was never acquired by the company but the check was paid by the defendant drawer. In a suit to recover it was held that payment under this indorsement was proper.

Sec. 44. Indorsement in Representative Capacity 

Where any person is under obligation to indorse in a representative capacity, he may indorse in such terms as to negative personal liability. 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 31, 63, 191, 10, 18 to 21, 30, 42, 64.

ANNOTATIONS 

A note payable to "the order of ourselves" was signed "First 

United Presbyterian Church, Pres. J. E., Treas. E. A. S.," and was indorsed "First United Presbyterian Church, J. E. Pres., E. A. S. Treasurer. Finance Committee, J. E., E. A. S., J.

McK.' It was not contended that the defendants J. E. and E. 

A. S. were liable as makers, but that they and also J. McK. were liable as indorsers. Held, that this form of indorsement negatived personal liability of the defendants. Chelsea Exchange 

Bank v. First U. P. Church, 89 Misc. Rep. 616, 152 N. Y. Supp. 201. 

A note payable to "A, Executor" was indorsed in the same form to the plaintiff. Held, A was not individually liable upon his indorsement. Its form, together with other facts known to the plaintiff indorsee were evidence that A did not intend to assume personal liability. Wolff v. Flateau, 206 App. Div. 134, 

200 N. Y. Supp. 646.

Sec. 45. Time of Indorsement-Presumption 

Except where an indorsement bears date after the maturity of the instrument, every negotiation is deemed prima facie to have been effected before the instrument was overdue. 

Cross Reference: 88 30, 31, 85, 191, 11, 13, 16, 17(3), 24, 46, 58, 59, 68.

§ 45 

NEGOTIATION ANNOTATIONS 

The mere production of the note with the indorsement on it and testimony that it was transferred in due course of business supports the finding that it was indorsed before maturity. Milan v. Graham, 131 Me. 220, 160 Atl. 581.

The negotiation of an instrument by indorsement without date establishes prima facie that it was negotiated before maturity, and one who denies that the holder of such instrument is a holder in due course has the burden of proof. This burden is not discharged by mere proof of demand for payment one day after maturity. Cook v. Tannery, 109 Okla. 85, 234 Pac. 590.

The fact that an indorsement appears to be in much fresher ink than the face of a demand note is not sufficient to overcome the presumption that it was indorsed before it was overdue. 

Gibbons v. Longino & Reid, 153 Miss. 749, 121 So. 490.

This section merely enacts the common law, under which the presumption was held to be of slight value. Guthrie v. Gibson, 67 Colo. 94, 184 Pac. 989.

The burden of coming forward with evidence that the indorsement of a payee was made after maturity is upon the maker, at least if the defense is payment before maturity. Union Station 

Trust Co. v. Bostick, 133 Miss. 627, 98 So. 105.

If the maker of a note in a suit by the indorsee introduces evidence of the payee's defective title, the indorsee can not rest upon the presumption that the indorsement to him was before maturity, but will lose unless he offers evidence of that fact. 

Jones v. Brandt, 173 Wis. 539, 181 N. W. 813. See also, cases under sec. 59.

Where there is evidence of fraud and that the instrument was in the hands of a third party after maturity, that is sufficient to rebut the presumption of this section and send the case to the jury. Price Real Estate & Insurance Co. v. Jones, 191 

N. C. 176, 131 S. E. 587.

Contra: Where an innocent party is the holder of an altered instrument originally payable on demand but altered by the addition of a date of maturity and indorsed in blank, it was held that under sec. 45 he was presumed to be a holder in due course. Gibbons v. Longino & Reid, 153 Miss. 749, 121 So. 490.

Where the plaintiff took the instrument after maturity, but no evidence was offered as to when prior indorsements were made, it was held that the presumption of sec. 45 warranted the application of sec. 58 and the plaintiff had all the rights of a holder in due course. No defect of title of a prior party was shown and therefore sec. 59 was not involved. Hahn v. Eckel, 154 Tenn. 444, 289 S. W. 496.

In an action by the indorsee of a note against the maker, it was no defense that the date of the indorsement had been altered, when the date both before and after alteration was prior to the maturity of the note. Wheeler v. Stone (Tex. Civ. App.), 261 

S. W. 1082.

§ 510 

 Sec. 46. Place of Indorsement-Presumption 

Except where the contrary appears, every indorsement is presumed prima facie to have been made at the place where the instrument is dated.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 31, 191, 6(3), 11, 16, 17(3), 24, 45, 59, 68.

ANNOTATIONS 

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, a note is held to be made at the place where it is dated. The  was not cited on this point. Finch v. Calkins, 183 Mich. 298, 149 N. W. 1037.

A married woman, accommodation indorser of a note dated and payable in New York, is estopped as against a holder in due course to show that the indorsement was made in New Jersey, where it would be void. Chemical Nat. Bank v. Kellogg, 183 N. Y. 92, 75 N. E. 1103, 2 L. R. A. (N.S.) 299, 111 Am. St. 

Rep. 717. Accord, Walling v. Cushman, 238 Mass. 62, 130 N. 

E. 175. 

And so when a married woman was the maker of a note dated and payable in Illinois she was estopped to show that it was executed in Wisconsin, where she was incapable of signing as surety for her husband.  Jefferis v. Kanawha Fuel Co., 182 Wis. 203, 196 N. W. 238.

A note issued in Kentucky by a resident was indorsed by the payee to his wife in Oklahoma, where they were domiciled. 

Transfers between husband and wife were valid in Oklahoma, but invalid in Kentucky unless recorded. It is not stated whether the instrument was dated in Kentucky. Held, the indorsee wife was entitled to recover from the maker in an action in Kentucky. The N. I. L. was not cited. Fogarty v. Neal, 201 Ky. 

85, 255 S. W. 1049. See the note in 12 Ky. L. J. 245.

Notes made in Georgia were indorsed by the defendant for the accommodation of the payee. She was not entitled to notice if her indorsement was governed by the law of Georgia which had not then adopted the N. I. L., but if the indorsement was made in South Carolina, notice was required by the N. I. L. 

Held, the plaintiff, a holder in due course, was entitled to act upon the assumption that the notes were indorsed in Georgia, the place at which they bore date. Sec. 46 was not cited. Mayfield v. Equitable Trust Co., 295 Fed. 109 (C. C. A., S. C.).

Sec. 47. Continuation of Negotiable Character 

An instrument negotiable in its origin continues to be negotiable until it has been restrictively indorsed or discharged by payment or otherwise. 

Cross Reference: 881 to 6, 37, 51, 119, 122, 124, 125, 191, 40, 48 to 50, 52, 57, 58, 89, 120, 121, 188.

An indorsement to A for the benefit of B is restrictive under this section, renders the instrument non-negotiable, and makes the indorsee or his successors subject to defenses good against the restrictive indorser. Gulbranson-Dickinson Co. v. Hopkins, 170 Wis. 326, 175 N. W. 93. See discussion under sec. 37 (2);

When a note is negotiable in form, its negotiability is not impaired by this printed provision on the back, preceding a special indorsement by the payee, "For value received, I hereby guarantee the payment of the within note, and any renewal of the same, and hereby waive protest, demand and notice of demand and nonpayment and suit against the maker, and consent that the payment of this note may be extended from time to time without affecting any liability thereon." Union Nat. Bank v. Mayfield, 71 Okla. 22, 174 Pac. 1034, 2 A. L. R. 135.

Although by prior California decisions the execution of a mortgage at the time a note is made destroys its negotiability in the hands of a purchaser with notice of the mortgage,' a note duly executed as a negotiable instrument continues negotiable despite the subsequent execution of a mortgage to the payee, which was assigned to the indorsee. In an action on the note, the indorsee was not subject to defenses of the maker against the payee of which the plaintiff had no notice. Semble, the defenses might have barred an action to enforce the mortgage. 

Pitman v. Walker, 187 Cal. 667, 203 Pac. 739.

An overdue promissory note is still negotiable within a statute exempting from attachment debts secured by bills of exchange or negotiable promissory notes, and hence the amount due thereon is exempt from foreign attachment. Sec. 47, , is consistent with this view. Oakdale Mfg. Co. v. Clarke, 29

Sec. 48. Striking Out Indorsement 

The holder may at any time strike out any indorsement which is not necessary to his title. The indorser whose indorsement is struck out, and all indorsers subsequent to him, are thereby relieved from liability on the instrument.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 31, 63, 121, 191, 9, 10, 35, 40, 47, 50, 51, 53, 120.

ANNOTATIONS 

An indorsee indorsed the note to a bank for collection, and upon its dishonor received it back. Held, such indorsee in possession of the note was a "holder" under sec. 191, and that he could sue upon it without striking out his indorsement. Mere possession was sufficient evidence of ownership to support the suit (sec. 51). New Haven Mfg. Co. v. New Haven Pulp Co., 76 Conn. 126, 55 Atl. 604. Accord, Monahan v. Watson, 61 Cal.

Pac. 652; Prewett v. First Nat. Bank of Ha-German, 45 Ida. 

451, 262 Pac. 1057, 1058. 

One in possession of negotiable paper, indorsed in blank by the payee, is prima facie the owner thereof, and the mere erasure of subsequent indorsements does not destroy this presumption. 

King v. Bellamy, 82 Kan. 301, 108 Pac. 117. The  was not cited in this case.

Where a special indorsee of a note has indorsed it restrictively, he may later indorse it in blank and negotiate it by delivery without striking out the restrictive indorsement, such an instrument being still a negotiable chose. Succession of

Sec. 49. Transfer Without Indorsement-Effect of 

Where the holder of an instrument payable to his order transfers it for value without indorsing it, the transfer vests in the transferee such title as the transferor had therein, and the transferee acquires, in addition, the right to have the indorsement of the transferor. But for the purpose of determining whether the transferee is a holder in due course, the negotiation takes effect as of the time when the indorsement is actually made.¹

Both authorities overlook the fact that the statute does not say "only such title." 

Sec. 49 is not applicable to a note payable to bearer. Marlar v.

Where an instrument was transferred to the plaintiff after maturity, for value and without indorsement, it was held that subsequent payment to the transferor discharged the instrument.

Transferee without from accom- It has been held in Scotland that under the Bills of Exchange Act, sec. 31(4), which is the same as sec. 49, , the indorsement transferee for value, but without indorsement, of a bill accepted modated for the accommodation of the drawer-payee gets the title of the payee transferor and may hold the acceptor without first getting an indorsement. Hood v. Stewart, 17 Session Cases (4th Series) 749.

As observed by Professor Ames (in his discussion of sec. 49, and see supra), if the American courts should follow this Scotch case his objection to sec. 49 would disappear. Sec. 49 changes the law to the extent that a transfer for value, even without indorsement, of an instrument, payable to order, passes the legal title, although subject to equities. But accommodation, as against a transferee for value, is not, properly speaking, an equity, but only a defense against the accommodated party and transferees without value. The Scotch precedent ought therefore to be followed. See also the English cases, infra, p. 528.

A non-negotiable note given by the maker for the accommodation of the payee was pledged to secure a renewal note without indorsement and without notice of the accommodation. Held, the maker was liable to the payee, and was estopped to set up the defense that the note was given only to secure the original loan and not renewals.  Earle v. Fletcher 

American Nat. Bank of Indianapolis, 70 Ind. App. 559, 123 N. 

E. 706. The general principle of this case agrees with the

Scotch case cited above, but the payee's violation of the accommodation agreement would seem a defense against one not a holder in due course.

After the defendant had been induced by fraud of Y to make a note payable to Y, the payee's name was changed without the defendant's consent to P, a person unknown to the defendant, in a manner obvious on the face of the note. Held, the plaintiff could recover. In Roy v. Duff, 170 Ia. 319, 152 N. W. 606, it was held that under secs. 16, 30, 49 and 52 the possession of a note, payable to order, but not indorsed, is prima facie evidence of the possessor's right to maintain an action against the maker, but that mere possession without indorsement or a showing of delivery or payment of consideration was not a prima facie evidence of ownership as against the payee, and was an insufficient showing of the passing of title to the possessor. Only the latter point was involved, since the action was by the administrator of the legal owner of unindorsed notes to recover them from one who was in possession, but could not show delivery or gift by the intestate or payment of consideration for the notes. But the court in deciding for the plaintiff made the distinction above mentioned. The same distinction is made on similar facts, without citing the , in Reynolds v. Nat. It is submitted that the distinction made in Roy v. Duff and other cases, supra, is not valid and that mere possession of an unindorsed note payable to order is not prima facie evidence of ownership against the maker. It is as much to the interest of the maker as of the payee, that the possessor should be obliged to give evidence to show that the instrument was transferred to him by the legal owner, since otherwise the maker might be obliged to pay a second time. But there is little room for doubt that, under the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Law, the mere possession by a third person of an unindorsed note payable to order is not prima facie evidence of ownership, either as against the payee or the maker and so is the weight of authority. 

As already pointed out, Roy v. Duff and the other cases cited as contra to this position do not squarely involve the point. The question was directly raised and decided, in accordance with the position taken by the preceding paragraph, in Escamilla v. Pingree, 44 Utah 421, 141 Pac. 103, L. R. A. 1915B, 475, although no reference was made to the Negotiable Instruments Law then in force in the state, and in Capitol Hill State Bank v. Rawlins 

Nat. Bank, 24 Wyo. 423, 160 Pac. 1171, 11 A. L. R. 937, in which case the court discussed the question at length as affected by secs. 59, 191, 30 and 49, and held that in an action by the possessor of an unindorsed certificate of deposit, payable to order, against the maker, the mere fact of possession was not evidence of title. Such a person is not the "bearer" of the instrument, because by sec. 191 "bearer" means the person in possession of a bill or note which is payable to bearer. Nor is he a holder, because by the same section "holder means the payee or indorsee of a bill or note who is in possession of it or the bearer thereof." But sec. 49 creates an anomalous situation in providing that where the holder of an instrument, payable to his order, transfers it for value, without indorsing it, the transfer vests in the transferee such title as the transferor had therein, but for the purpose of determining whether the transferee is a holder in due course, the negotiation takes effect as of the time when an indorsement is actually made. The section vests in the transferee the legal title of the transferor, but subject to equities until an indorsement is made. Kiefer v. Tolbert, 128 Minn. 519, 151 N. W. 529. ()

Yet the transferee is not a holder because not within the definition of holder in sec. 191. It is evident that no presumption of a prima facie title can arise in favor of a plaintiff, who, although he is in possession, is not a payee, indorsee or bearer, and that in order to bring himself within the description of transferee under sec. 49 he must show that a holder transferred it to him for value.

A contrary result was reached in Manhattan Chamber of 

Commerce v. Gallagher, 123 Kan. 155, 254 Pac. 345, 26 Mich. L.

Rev. 98. A well reasoned opinion in which the court points out that the foregoing discussion is a narrow interpretation of the act. The court properly observed that the possessor of an unindorsed instrument is not a holder and is therefore not within the presumptions of the act in favor of holders; but such a person may be an owner under sec. 49, and since the act is silent as to the presumption in the case of owners, and since there was a split at common law, the court drew an analogy from the law of property wherein the presumption of ownership is in favor of the possessor and held that mere presentation of such unindorsed instruments in evidence was sufficient grounds for recovery thereon. A similar result was reached in Doniger v. 

Lasoff, 125 Misc. Rep. 838, 211 N. Y. Supp. 486, which did not cite the  

The courts in these cases overlook the fact that although the act is silent on this particular point the entire spirit of the act is to give effect to the contract on the face of the instrument and the presumptions are always in favor of their correctness; see secs. 11, 13, 14, 24, 46 and 68. In a case such as this the face of the instrument would indicate that title was in a person other than the possessor, and the burden should therefore be upon him to show his ownership. This result is in accord with the commercial custom of demanding indorsements and since it is the weight of authority as indicated by the cases below it should be followed.

The view taken in the text is also supported by Yost v. Eckart, 209 Ill. App. 30; Harponola Co. v. Conkin, 205 Ky. 736, 266 S. 

W. 626; McCune v. Daniels (Mo. App.), 251 S. W. 458; First

Certified check 

In Meuer v. Phenix Nat. Bank, 94 App. Div. 331, 88 N. Y. rights of Supp. 83, affd. by memo. 183 N. Y. 511, 76 N. E. 1100, the without transferee without indorsement of a check who had it certified Indorsement and changed his position in reliance upon the certification, retransferee covered from the bank in the absence of equities between the drawer and payee. Semble, the certification discharged the drawer.

Semble, a drawee bank, which without fraud, forgery or mistake, certifies a check after it has been transferred without the payee's indorsement, is liable to the transferee, and the drawer and indorsers being discharged may not induce the drawee bank to withhold payment although there was failure of consideration between the payee and the plaintiff. The court also said that the drawer and indorsers would not be able to rely on equities of their own. Lipten v. Columbia Trust Co., 194 App. Div. 384, 185 N. Y. Supp. 198.

Sed quaere? The provisions of sec. 188 can not effect the discharge of the drawer and indorsers since the certification was not obtained by a holder. The tentative suggestion of the court that a "transferee" is referred to as a holder in sec. 54, has little merit in view of the precise definition of "holder" in sec. 

191, and the provisions of secs. 30, 51 and 52. The court, however argues that if certification is not obtained by a holder within sec. 188, the provisions of the law merchant will, under sec. 196, apply, for instance, to certification obtained by the drawer which is not within the express provision of any section of the N. I. L. It is contended that under the law merchant certification discharges the secondary parties whether the transferee was an indorsee or not. This seems doubtful when the instrument was subject to equities. These are not cut off by a transfer without indorsement, and make it as inequitable for the transferee to obtain certification as it would be for him to recover a judgment against prior parties in an action at law. Thus, if a thief stole a check from the payee and had it certified, the drawer would not be discharged as against the payee, and the thief would not be able to recover from the certifying bank.
