§ 49 Certification properly imports a promise to pay the lawful owner Certified of the check and not the particular person who procures the rights of certification. check- transferee without indorsement

Of course, if the transferor without indorsement authorized the certification or had no equities against the transferee, the latter would have the same rights under the certification as if it had been obtained by the transferor, Freund v. Importers, etc., Bank 76 N. Y. 352; Meuer v. Phenix Nat. Bank, supra; cf. 

Lynch v. First Nat. Bank, 107 N. Y. 179, 13 N. E. 775, a questionable decision. But if the transferor had equities, the certifying bank should be able to set them up against the transferee without indorsement, at least when expressly authorized to do so by the transferor. Meridian Bank v. First Bank, 7 Ind. App. 322, 33 

N. E. 247, 34 N. E. 608, semble.

If the payee was subject to equities of the drawer, the certifying bank should be able to set these up against the transferee without indorsement if it could do so against the payee, had he obtained the certification. See Times Sq. Auto Co. v. Rutherford 

Nat. Bank, 77 N. J. L. 649, 73 Atl. 479, discussed under sec. 188; 

Goshen Nat. Bank v. Bingham, 118 N. Y. 349, 23 N. E. 180. Even if the certifying bank is held liable to the payee in such a situation, as in the doubtful Times Sq. Auto Co. case, on the ground that the drawer was discharged when the payee got certification so that the drawer's equities became immaterial, it is doubtful if certification by the transferee without indorsement should give him the same questionable right of recovery since he is not a holder. He could not recover from the drawer. If the bank paid him without certification, he would be liable for the proceeds in an action by the drawer. Therefore, it is unjust that he should hold the certifying bank, and have the amount of the check charged to the drawer's account. Pac. 149. bonds limiting the right A considerable amount of litigation recently has arisen over Corporate the so-called "no action" clauses in corporate bonds or mortgages. While it seems that such clauses could be effectively drawn within the requirements of N. I. L. 5, no such attempt seems to have been made by the draftsmen of the bonds, and the section is seldom, if ever, referred to by the courts. to sue The arrangement of clauses of this kind fall into two general classes: (1) where the limitation of the right of action is placed in the bond itself; and (2) where they are found in the mortgage but not in the bond.

If the clause is set out completely in the bond itself, there seems to be no difficulty in giving complete effect to its provisions. For an excellent note on the validity of these clauses in general, see 108 A. L. R. 88. 

If, on the other hand, the clause is as follows: "The holder of this bond shall have no right of action except as provided in the mortgage," it has been held that where the bond is nonnegotiable, the clause is effective. Moody v. Pacific S. S. Co., 174 Wash. 256, 24 P. (2d) 609.

Where the clause is set out in the mortgage but not in the bond a number of varying situations arise.

If the bond is made subject to the mortgage, and, therefore, held non-negotiable, the courts seem to agree that the clause in the mortgage is effective to limit the right of action on the bond. Colsky v. Eyres Storage & Distributing Co., 178 Wash. 

404, 34 P. (2d) 1114; Ledgerwood v. Hale & Kilburn Corp., 47

F. (2d) 319. 

But where the bond contains a reference to the mortgage which amounts to a mere statement of the transaction which gives rise to the instrument, it seems that the right to sue on

§ 

538 

Corporate the bond should not be limited by any clause in the mortgage.

limiting Cunningham v. Pressed Steel Co., 238 A. D. 624, 265 N. Y. S. 

bonds to sue 

256, affd. 263 N. Y. 671, 189 N. E. 750, 32 Mich. L. Rev. 403, 2 U. of Pitt. L. Rev. 75. Contra, Rittenhouse v. Lukens Steel 

Co., 116 Pa. Super. 303, 176 Atl. 543, 2 U. of Pitt. L. Rev. 25.

The greatest difficulty arises in those cases where the bond has been made expressly subject to the mortgage, but where the courts, nevertheless, have held such bonds negotiable. (See discussion of these cases under sec. 3(2), supra.) In these cases the courts have taken the position that since the clauses in the bond deal merely with security rights in case of foreclosure, the "no action" clause does not limit the right of action on the bond. 

Oswianza v. Wengler & Mandell, 358 Ill. 302, 193 N. E. 123, not citing the , 83 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 679. Mendelson v. 

Realty Mort. Corporation, 257 Mich. 442, 241 N. W. 154. It is submitted that these cases are improperly decided. First, as discussed under sec. 3(2), such instruments should be held nonnegotiable, and being so held, the clause should be effective. However, if the courts insist on holding them negotiable, they seem logically driven to the weird conclusion that the "no action" clause is ineffective even though the intent of the parties to the contrary is plainly set forth in both the bond and the mortgage. 

Where the bond or the mortgage contains a negotiability-bycontract clause a further difficulty arises. Some courts have taken the position that the right to sue on the bond is an essential characteristic of negotiability, and the right to sue cannot be cut off by a "no action" clause. Benson v. Schwerin, 285 

Ill. App. 121, 1 N. E. (2d) 813, reaches this result.

There seems to be no reason why the parties could not limit the right of action and still keep the bond negotiable. The promise remains unconditional, but one of the remedies merely is limited. Limitations of this kind seem to be approved by section 5. 

The "no action" clause also has been held to limit the right to sue on coupons. St. Louis-Carterville Coal Company v. 

Southern Coal & Mining Company, 194 Mo. App. 598, 186 S. W. 

1152. This result would seem to be proper only if the coupons carry such non-action clause on their face, or are made subject to the bond or mortgage, in which case it seems the coupon itself should be non-negotiable unless it also carries a negotiability by contract clause. 

The right to sue on the mortgage should, of course, be governed by the provisions of that instrument. And it seems that "no action" clauses in the mortgage should be effective to limit foreclosure proceedings. See note, 108 A. L. R. 88 ff.

For a further discussion of this subject see the Law Review articles cited with the cases set out supra and Ohi, "Whether a 

No Action Clause of a Trust Deed or Mortgage Can be In corporated in a Bond or Note by Reference," 2 John Marshall

L. R. 172.

An express trustee in possession of a note indorsed in blank Miscellanemay sue in his own name. Fransham v. Tow Bros., 196 Ia. 1082, 196 N. W. 71. 

In Gaffney v. Gordon, 34 F. (2d) 491 the court held that a holder of negotiable notes suing in representative capacity as trustee for creditors had to allege and prove these facts. The court evidently overlooked sec. 51.

When the plaintiffs were payees of notes, the allegation of their ownership was unnecessary.  Gibson v. Hannay, 198 Ia. 930, 200 N. W. 579.

Joint payees may properly sue as coplaintiffs though not partners. The  was not cited. Krause v. Spurgeon (Mo.

The possession of a note by the payee after the maker's death raises a presumption of ownership. The N. I. L. was not cited. 

Johnston v. Apple, 98 Oreg. 278, 193 Pac. 1024.

Under the N. I. L. the indorsee of a negotiable instrument under seal may sue in assumpsit. Cracowaner v. Carlton Nat. 

Bank (Fla.), 124 So. 275, 43 Harv. L. Rev. 654.

The payee of a note in possession thereof is presumed to be the owner and can maintain suit although the note bears his indorsement. Union Guano Co. v. Garrison, 130 S. C. 404, 126 

S. E. 133, the N. I. L. was not cited; Tompkins v. Rain, 26 N. M.

A restrictive indorser may bring suit on the instrument if at the time of suit he has possession of the note, although his indorsement has not been stricken out. And possession of the note by such an indorser is prima facie evidence of his legal title. 

Vermont Evaporator Co. v. Taft, 107 Vt. 400, 181 Atl. 100, 2

was not cited.

An indorsee may sue in his own name but is not obliged to, and may sue in the name of the payee to his own use. Hanratty v. Dougherty, 71 Pa. Super. Ct. 248, not citing the N. I. L.

A note indorsed in blank was negotiated to the plaintiff corporation, which was subsequently consolidated with another corporation. Held, the plaintiff corporation was not the proper party to sue on the note. The N. I. L. was not cited. Citizens

A maker of a note payable to a bank can not contest the validity of a bank consolidation by which the note was negotiated to the plaintiff bank. Nat. Bank of Rochester v. Erion-Haines 

Realty Co., 213 App. Div. 54, 209 N. Y. Supp. 522, affg. 123 

Misc. Rep. 893, 206 N. Y. Supp. 452.

A note payable to a partnership under the firm name was dated before a change of partners. After the change, it was delivered in return for goods then received from the firm. Held, the partners in the changed firm were presumptively owners of the note.  Trop v. Gramercy 

Chocolate Co., 187 App. Div. 523, 175 N. Y. Supp. 766, reversing 

173 N. Y. Supp. 467.

The maker of promissory notes payable to himself indorsed them in blank, and delivered them to a married man in payment for an automobile purchased from the wife. The husband also indorsed them in blank and delivered them to the wife, who delivered them to the plaintiff for value after maturity. The maker set up the defense that since contracts between husband and wife as parties to negotiable instruments are not valid in Massachusetts, the husband's indorsement to the wife was void, so that the plaintiff could not sue in his own name. Held, defense bad. The maker's indorsement under sec. 9-5 rendered the notes payable to bearer even though there were subsequent indorsements in blank, which need not be considered so far as concerns passing title. If the husband indorsed as agent for the wife, there was no invalidity; and if he wished to add his own liability as indorser, that could be done. The plaintiff as holder for value could sue in his own name, although he bought after maturity. He did not trace his title to any contract between husband and wife. He could strike out the husband's indorsement as not necessary to his title, under sec. 48, if this were essential, but it is not. Leavitt v. Wintman, 234 Mass. 248, 125 N. E. 390.

A note held by the plaintiff, a married woman, as holder in due course, was indorsed by her before maturity to a corporation in payment of her pre-existing indebtedness to it, which was charged on its books to her husband. After dishonor, the corporation delivered the note to the husband, charging it against certain dividends to which he was entitled. He handed the note to his wife, who sued the maker. Held, she is entitled to sue as holder. The evidence warrants the conclusion that the husband received the note as her agent and delivered it to her as her own. In any event, the wife, as the person in possession with the assent of the husband, may maintain suit. Bovarnick v. Davis, 235 Mass. 195, 126 N. E. 380.

The payee indorsed notes to the plaintiff, a holder in due course. After maturity the plaintiff handed the notes to the payee's executor without receiving payment and the executor delivered the notes to his attorneys, who instituted suit in the

52 

 § cos plaintiff indorsee's name. Held, a verdict for the plaintiff was Miscellaneous properly directed. Title was not transferred to the executor. 

The notes were produced at the trial and were in the possession of the plaintiff, who was a holder. Alexander v. Reiter, 99 N. 

J. L. 447, 123 Atl. 869. Since the executor was undoubtedly a holder, it is questionable whether the indorsee can also be considered such, unless under the circumstances the possession of the executor was the possession of the indorsee. It would seem that action should preferably have been brought in the name of the executor. The desirability of this is indicated by the possible existence of equities against the payee. 

Payment by the bank of a certified check indorsed in blank by the drawer-payee discharges the check, and repayment to the bank by the one who received payment, when threatened with suit, will not entitle him to sue the bank on its certification, although he was a holder in due course and the check was returned to him. The money repaid passes to the credit of the depositor and the bank is liable to him for it. Poess v. Twelfth 

Ward Bank, 43 Misc. Rep. 45, 86 N. Y. Supp. 857. 

Where a promissory note was attached and sold under an execution against the holder, the purchaser may sue thereon in his own name, whether the indorsement by the sheriff was regular or irregular, and whether it was indorsed or not. Fishburn v. Londershausen, 50 Oreg. 363, 92 Pac. 1060, 14 L. R. A. (N.S.) 1234. 

See also, R. B. Turner, Depositor of Demand Paper as "Purchaser," 37 Yale L. J. 874; W. L. Townsend, Bank Depositor of Commercial Paper, 7 N. Y. U. L. Q. Rev. 293, id. 618.

Sec. 52. What Constitutes a Holder in Due Course. 

A holder in due course is a holder who has taken the instrument under the following conditions:- 

Cross Reference: 88 59, 191, 14, 16, 57. (1) That is complete and regular upon its face; 

Cross Reference: 881 to 12, 13 to 15, 31, 124, 126, 128, 132, 184, 17, 43, 48, 142. (2) That he became the holder of it before it was overdue, and without notice that it had been previously dishonored, if such was the fact; 

Cross Reference: §§ 53, 56, 83, 85, 86, 191, 45, 47, 59, 124, 194. (3) That he took it in good faith and for value; 

Cross Reference: 88 24 to 29, 54, 191, 56, 59. (4) That at the time it was negotiated to him he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating it.' 

Cross Reference: 88 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 21 to 23, 30, 49, 55, 56, 124, 125, 47, 59. 

1 The English Act omits the words "infirmity in the instrument." 

B. E. A. s. 29 (1) (b). cases

$ 542 

 Pleading and procedure 

ANNOTATIONS 

Secs. 52, 55, 56 and 59 vary the ordinary rule of procedure requiring him who alleges a fact to prove it, but they are not unconstitutional as an invasion of the judicial power by the legislature. Johnson County Sav. Bank v. Walker, 79 Conn. 

348, 65 Atl. 132.

An allegation in an answer that plaintiff is not a holder in due course is a conclusion of law and insufficient to show which of the conditions named in sec. 52 has not been complied with. 

Rogers v. Morton, 46 Misc. Rep. 494, 95 N. Y. Supp. 49.

In an action by the indorsee of a note against the maker, the defendant's answer averring fraud is demurrable for failure to deny the averment of the complaint that the payee for value received, in due course of business, and before maturity, assigned and transferred the note to the plaintiff. Lapp v. Merchants Nat. Bank, 74 Ind. App. 527, 123 N. E. 231, rehearing denied, 124 N. E. 707.

Judges, in defining a holder in due course in their instructions to juries, should employ the text of the  whenever possible, rather than ancient or newly-created phrases, the meaning of which is uncertain. Matteson v. Trask, 63 Mont. 160, 206 

Pac. 428; People's Bank & Trust Co. v. Duncan, 194 N. C. 692, 140 S. E. 610. 

The evidence tended to show that plaintiff took for value a check drawn by defendant, but knowing that it had been delivered to the payee upon a condition which had not been fulfilled and that payment had been stopped. Held, error to direct a verdict for the plaintiff, as the question whether plaintiff was a holder in due course within secs. 52, 55, 56, N. I. L., is for the jury. Groh's Sons v. Schneider, 34 Misc. Rep. 195, 68 N. Y. 

Supp. 862. 

In an action by a holder against the maker of a promissory note, the defense was failure of consideration. The uncontradicted evidence of witnesses whose credibility was not questioned showed that the plaintiff was a bona fide holder of the note, and that he purchased it for value before maturity without knowledge of any equity of the defendant, and of facts indicating bad faith in taking it. It was held that it was an error for the court to refuse to direct for the plaintiff. Minden State Bank v. 

Sawin, 113 Neb. 691, 204 N. W. 793.

In an action by the holder against the maker, who alleges fraud on the part of the payee, there was uncontradicted evidence showing that the plaintiff took the note for value, before maturity, and without notice of facts from which bad faith could be inferred, it was held that the lower court erred in not directing a verdict for the plaintiff. Mack v. Dailey (U. S. C. C. 

A. N. Y.), 3 F. (2d) 534.

When the indorsee of a note testified that he paid $2,000 for it in cash, but the payee testified that he had not deposited the

§ 52 

amount paid him in any bank, and the maker had received no inquiry from the indorsee with reference to the validity of the note, and the indorsee's testimony with respect to inquiries sent to banks about the maker's solvency was not corroborated, a verdict that the indorsee was not a holder in due course was not set aside. Wheeler v. Stone (Tex. Civ. App.), 261 S. W. 1082.

Whether the payee may be a holder in due course under the , as he was at common law, is a question upon which the courts are in serious conflict. There can be no doubt that a proper interpretation of the act read as a whole leads to the conclusion that a payee may be a holder in due course under any circumstance in which he meets the requirements of sec. 52. 

The argument of Professor Brannan in an earlier edition of this work has never been successfully answered and is here repeated: "Section 191 defines 'holder' as the payee or indorsee of a bill or note, who is in possession of it, or the bearer thereof. 

Sec. 52 defines a holder in due course as 'a holder who has taken the instrument under the following conditions: 1. That it is complete and regular on its face. 2. That he became the holder of it before it was overdue, and without notice that it had been previously dishonored, if such was the fact. 3. That he took it in good faith and for value. 4. That at the time it was negotiated to him he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating it.' "Since 'holder,' as defined in sec. 191, includes a payee who is in possession, the word holder in the first clause of sec. 52 and in the second subsection may be replaced by the definition in sec. 191 so as to read 'a holder in due course is a payee or indorsee who is in possession,' etc. "Now as to subsec. 4. Was the instrument negotiated to this holder who is a payee in possession? Is 'negotiation' limited to transfer by indorsement? By sec. 30 'an instrument is negotiated when it is transferred from one person to another in such manner as to constitute the transferee the holder thereof.' It is not prescribed in this section that the transferor shall be a holder but only a 'person.' It is only necessary to transfer the instrument so as to constitute the transferee a holder. As a 'payee who is in possession' is by sec. 191 a holder, it is clear that a maker or drawer, for instance, or person intrusted with the instrument though not himself a holder, negotiates it when he transfers it to the payee. "The last sentence of sec. 30, 'if payable to order it is negotiated by the indorsement of the holder completed by delivery,' must be construed to refer to negotiation after the instrument has come into the hands of the payee or other holder (indorsee). 

Reading the definition of 'holder' in sec. 191 into the paragraph it will read, 'if payable to order it is negotiated by the indorsement of the 'payee' or indorsee who is in possession.' 

May the holder in due be a course?

$ 544 

 "The Supreme Court of Massachusetts, in Liberty Trust Co. 

holder in due V. Tilton, 217 Mass. 462, 465, 105 N. E. 605, L. R. A. 1915B, 144, May the payee be a course? speaking of this sentence of sec. 30, said that 'it was not intended to include all the ways in which an instrument might be negotiated nor to restrict the comprehensive terms of the preceding sentence. Plainly, under these two secs. (30 and 191), a negotiable instrument payable to a named payee is negotiated when the physical possession of it is handed for value to the person named as payee. One effect of the last sentence of sec. 30 is to describe the method by which the person who first becomes holder may pass it. It does not comprehend all the ways by which an instrument may be negotiated.' "The error of the Iowa court [Vander Ploeg v. Van Zuuk, 135 

Ia. 350, 112 N. W. 807, 13 L. R. A. (N.S.) 490] seems to have arisen from the failure to distinguish between proximity and privity of the parties, as was said by Professor Hening [59 

U. of P. L. Rev. 471, 480]. Under the law merchant there was no incongruity in permitting a payee to recover against the maker or acceptor when the payee was an innocent party deceived by the agent of the maker or acceptor. Mere proximity of the names on commercial paper is not conclusive as to privity; no more than apparent remoteness on the face of the paper is conclusive as to the absence of privity. The substance of the agreement is regarded and not the form of its expression on the commercial paper.' "Speaking of the meaning of the words 'immediate parties' in sec. 16, , it was said by Rugg, C. J., in Liberty Trust 

Co. v. Tilton, 217 Mass. 462, 464, supra, that 'immediate parties' in that connection exclude a party who is a holder in due course. 

In such case these words must be confined to parties who are 'immediate' to the conditions or limitations placed upon the delivery in the sense of knowing or being chargeable with notice of them. The payee who is a holder in due course is not an immediate party in the sense of that section. This result follows from holding that a payee may be a 'holder in due course,' as defined in sec. 52, because he could become such holder only on condition.' 4. That at the time it was negotiated to him he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument.' Thus he could not be such holder unless the paper was 'negotiated' to him. Therefore the word 'negotiated' was held to describe the means by which a payee might acquire a note. It was given its common legal significance of concluded by bargain or agreement. A promissory note, complete as to form and payable to a named person, may be negotiated to that person by being sold to him or taken by him for value. This is the common and popular signification of the word. It was the sense in which it was used in the law merchant before the Negotiable Instruments Act. Its meaning has not been changed by the act.'"

The cases holding to the contrary, that the payee can not be a holder in due course, are based on an unnecessarily narrow

§ 52 

interpretation of single sections, usually section 30, or 16, the adoption of which requires that section 191 and the first section of sec. 30 be read out of the act. Thus it is clear that the framers of the act intended that a payee should be a holder in due course. But even conceding, for the sake of argument, that there is some ambiguity the preponderant weight of authority under the act, both by cases and by jurisdiction, is clearly to the effect that a payee may be a holder in due course. This fact alone should cause all courts, in the interest of uniformity, which is the major purpose of the act, to adopt this view. 

For reviews of the cases on this question, see 15 A. L. R. 437; 

21 A. L. R. 1365; 26 A. L. R. 769; 32 A. L. R. 289; 68 A. L. R. 

962, collecting common-law authorities as well; and the various law review notes cited below and under sec. 14. The A. L. R. notes favor the negative interpretation of the Act, but would give protection to the payee on principles of estoppel and bona fide purchase for value. An article by Professor Underhill 

Moore in 20 Colum. L. Rev. 749 on "The Right of the Remitter of a Bill or Note," while agreeing with the affirmative view, suggests that cases supporting that view have not always sufficiently considered the element of notice to the payee of defenses, from the form of the instrument, the relation of the transferor (remitter) to the person issuing the instrument, and other surrounding circumstances. The negative view is favored by A. M. 

Hamilton, "Holder in Due Course," 24 Jurid. Rev. 41. The affirmative view is favored by Professor L. W. Feezer in an exhaustive article in 9 Minn. L. Rev. 101, which contains a discriminating consideration of the minority decisions; by R. W. 

Aigler, "Payees as Holders in Due Course," 36 Yale L. J. 608 (1927), which gives an excellent historical study; by F. K. 

Beutel, "The Rights of a Remitter," 12 Minn. L. Rev. 584, 600, where it pointed out that in cases where a remitter is involved the argument in the minority cases that the instrument can not be negotiated (in the restricted sense) to the payee is without legal or historical foundation; and by William E. Britton, "The 

Payee as a Holder in Due Course," 1 U. of Chi. L. Rev. 728.

The conflicting authorities are grouped below by states: first, those supporting the affirmative view; secondly, those support. ing the negative view; thirdly, those where the authorities require special mention. The defendant was induced by the fraudulent representations of B to subscribe for the stock of the X Co., of which B was agent, and which was organized to purchase the property of the plaintiff company. The court in both opinions held that the plaintiff though a bona fide holder for value was not a holder in due course, because subsec. 4 of sec. 52 requires negotiation to such holder. Under sec. 30 "negotiated" is a highly technical term, and means a transfer which takes place after the instrument has become an obligation by a person in whose hands it is an obligation. 

This highly artificial reasoning is ably criticized by a note in 1 Wis. L. Rev. 421, which points out that since the payee clearly comes within the rest of the language of sec. 52, the word "negotiated" is not entitled to an excess of emphasis which overthrows the recognized principle of the law merchant,-that one who takes for value and in good faith should be able to rely upon his apparent ownership of the instrument. A note in 6 

Minn. L. Rev. 156 shows that negotiation under sec. 30 includes a transfer from one person to another, and not merely from one holder to another. It does not require the transferror to be a holder. See also, 70 U. Pa. L. Rev. 52.

If the definition of "holder" in sec. 191 be incorporated into sec. 52, the latter reads, "A holder in due course is a payee or indorsee of a bill or note, who is in possession of it or the bearer thereof, who has taken the instrument under the following conditions, etc."

Those conditions may be fulfilled by a payee as well as by an indorsee. The use of "negotiated" in subsec. 4 is no objection, since sec. 30 was not intended to include all the ways in which an instrument might be negotiated, but simply recites the two usual and ordinary ways. The following case recognized that the Jurisdictions payee might be a holder in due course in situations like those in the Massachusetts cases, supra, p. 547, but reached the opposite result on the facts. requiring special mention A drew a check on defendant bank payable to plaintiff and gave it to a messenger to have it certified and give to plaintiff in payment for revenue stamps. Defendant certified the check, B stole it and posing as A's messenger delivered it to plaintiff, who gave full value for it. Plaintiff sued defendant. Held, that even assuming that plaintiff acted in good faith, yet plaintiff was not a holder in due course and that it can not recover. Empire Trust 

Co. v. Manhattan Co., 97 Misc. Rep. 694, 162 N. Y. Supp. 629. 

Determination affirmed, no opinion, 180 App. Div. 891; see criticism in 30 Harvard Law Rev. 515.

It is submitted that this case is wrong. Plaintiff was a holder of the check because it was the payee who was in possession of it (sec. 191). Plaintiff was a holder in due course, if the check was negotiated to it (sec. 30), because plaintiff clearly came within the definition of holder in due course in all other respects (sec. 

52). The check was negotiated to plaintiff because it was transferred to plaintiff in such manner as to constitute plaintiff the holder, for plaintiff was the payee and by the transfer to it the plaintiff came into possession of the check (sec. 30). "The section carefully abstains from prescribing that the transferor must be a holder," per Fletcher Moulton, L. J. [1907], 1 K. B. 

794, 808, so that even a thief can transfer to any one a bearer instrument and to the payee an instrument payable to his order. 

These conclusions are not vitiated by sec. 16, for plaintiff, being by all the definitions a holder in due course, a valid and intentional delivery by all parties prior to him is conclusively presumed. This result is not prevented by the first clause of sec. 16 which requires a delivery as between immediate parties, and as regards a remote party other than a holder in due course. 

Was plaintiff an immediate party? No, because "immediate parties" excludes a holder in due course. "Immediate parties" means parties who are immediate to the conditions or limitations placed on the delivery in the sense of knowing or being chargeable with notice of them. Liberty Trust Co. v. Tilton, supra, pp. 544, 545, and upon the assumption that he acted in good faith, plaintiff did not come within this category. "Immediate" means privity not proximity. A payee is in proximity to the maker, but he may or may not be in privity with or immediate to the maker. Whether we say that, as to a holder in due course, delivery is immaterial or that, as the statute puts it, delivery is conclusively presumed, the result is the same. If a complete negotiable instrument gets out of the hands of the maker, it matters not whether this occurs by an absolute or conditional delivery or by no delivery at all, as in the case of theft from the maker. If it comes to the hands of one who can show him-

§ 554 

requiring Jurisdictions self to be a holder in due course, the maker is bound, and that special a payee is capable of being a holder in due course has been almost mention universally held at common law, and according to the great weight of authority the Negotiable Instruments Law has made no change in this respect.

It is to be regretted that the Appellate Division gave no opinion in the case under discussion (Empire Trust Co. v. Manhattan Co.). When Appellate Courts affirm judgments without an opinion, and without even adopting the opinion of the lower court, one is led to suspect that the court must have had difficulty in finding reasons for its judgment of affirmance. 

It is possible, however, that the Appellate Division affirmed the judgment because the jury found that the plaintiff had acted in bad faith and the trial justice in the city court stated, that he felt that this verdict on the question of fact was justified. 

The affirmance, therefore, can not be regarded as adopting the conclusion of the Supreme Court Appellate Term on the question of law. It would indeed be regrettable if a court of the greatest commercial state had taken a position so contrary to the great weight of authority, both at common law and under the Negotiable Instruments Law. In any event the case is not an authority for the proposition that a payee can not be a holder in due course under the Negotiable Instruments Law.

On the contrary, the Supreme Court conceded that he may be, as was held by the Supreme Court conceded that he may be, as was held by the Supreme Court of Massachusetts in the case

ENGLAND 

In Lloyds Bank v. Cooke [1907], 1 K. B. 794 (C. A.), the payee of notes issued in blank and wrongfully filled up recovered from the maker. This leading case unfortunately failed to settle whether the language of the B. E. A. included the payee as a holder in due course. Fletcher Moulton, L. J., based recovery squarely on the B. E. A.; but the two other judges held that the defendant was liable under the common law doctrine of estoppel, which was still in force since the B. 

E. A., so that the rights of the parties under the provisions of the Act need not be ascertained. The court did not expressly overrule Herdman v. Wheeler [1902], 1 K. B. 361; see 

14 Harv. L. Rev. 579, but it seems clear that this case must have been decided in favor of the payee, had it occurred after Lloyds 

Bank v. Cooke. See the references to it in Paine v. Bevan, 30 

T. L. R. 395, arguendo; Lilly v. Farrar, 17 Rep. Jud. Off. Quebec C. B. R. 554; Herdman v. Wheeler and the dictum in Lewis v. Clay, 67 L. J. Q. B. (N.S.) 224, have not been judicially cited since Lloyds Bank v. Cooke, and must be considered as discredited and practically overruled. A contrary opinion is expressed in 32 A. L. R. 299.

The payee was stated to be a holder in due course in Glenie v. Bruce Smith [1908], 1 K. B. 263 (C. A.); Talbot v. Von 

Boris [1911], 1 K. B. 854, 865 (C. A.). Cf. Smith v. Prosser [1907], 2 K. B. 735 (C. A.). 

B, representing himself as agent for a firm of motor car manufacturers, whom he falsely stated to be backed by the defendant furniture dealers, asked the plaintiffs to become local sales agents for the motor cars and fraudulently obtained a large check, which was crossed and marked "not negotiable," as a deposit upon cars to be shipped to the plaintiffs. He delivered the check to the defendant company in settlement of his indebtedness to it. 

The defendant took the check in good faith, and did not deal with B. as an agent of the plaintiffs. There were some direct communications between the defendant and the plaintiffs respecting the form of the check. The defendant cashed the check

requiring mention Jurisdictions before the fraud was discovered. Held, reversing the judgment special below, that the defendant was not liable to the plaintiffs for money had and received to their use, or paid for a consideration that had failed, or paid under a mistake of fact. Jones v. War ing & Gillow [1925], 2 K. B. 612 (C. A.). On appeal the House of Lords, 1926 A. C. 670, reversed the case and held that the plaintiffs could recover. There was some discussion of the question of the payee being a holder in due course, and, although the court as a whole put the decision on other grounds, two of the lords expressed the opinion that he could not be. However, it is submitted that this case can not be authority for the point because crossed checks marked "not negotiable" are distinctly made non-negotiable by sec. 81 of the B. E. A., and under the express wording of this section the defendants acquired no better title than B.

The drawee of a draft is not a holder in due course under this section. American Hominy Co. v. Milliken Nat. Bank, 273 Fed. 

550 (III.). 

It is possible for a person to meet all the requirements of this section and still not be able to recover on the instrument. Baach v. Bank of Pocahontas (Va. 1931), 160 S. E. 68, 76 A. L. R. 

1324 with note. See excellent note 80 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 447.

No person can be a holder in due course of an instrument payable to a named payee or order, without the indorsement of the payee. Fourth Nat. Bank of Macon v. Lattimore, 168 Ga. 

547, 148 S. E. 396.

The pledgee for value in good faith of a complete unmatured note, without notice of equities, is a holder in due course. Anderson v. Union Bank, 117 Va. 1, 83 S. E. 1080; Colona v. Parksley 

Nat. Bank, 120 Va. 812, 92 S. E. 979. 

In Union Trust Co. v. Mathews, 258 Mich. 433, 242 N. W. 

781, the court held that where an instrument was indorsed specially to a trustee for the payee, the trustee gave value and met all the requirements of a holder in due course, that the trustee could not recover from the maker who had a defense of failure of consideration. See discussion under sec. 37, supra.

A note payable to the maker's order was indorsed in blank to a bank. The note was afterwards altered by inserting "payable with interest." The bank made a deed of trust of all its property including the note to secure its creditors. Held, that in Virginia a pre-existing debt is a valuable consideration for a deed of trust to secure it, and that the trustee was a holder in due course and could recover on the note according to its original tenor, under sec. 124. Trustees of American Bank v. Mc-

money to S, who bought the note. The payee of an accommodation note indorsed it before maturity to A for goods to be furnished at once and in the future.

A bank purchased a note in the usual course of business at the usual rate of discount. Held, that a notice to the maker stating that the note was at the bank "for collection" was not an admission that the bank was not a holder in due course. The 

 was not cited. Bank of Baraboo v. Laird, 150 Wis.

Plaintiff bank was the holder in due course of a note against which the maker claimed to have a defense of fraud. Upon the maturity of the note, the indorser deposited bonds with the plaintiff "as security for the debt and costs and as collateral for the payment of the note" and requested plaintiff to sue the maker, which plaintiff did. Held, that plaintiff can not sue as an innocent holder and can not recover against the maker.  First Nat. Bank v. Fox, 40 App. Cas. D. C. 

430. Sed quaere? The plaintiff's title was the same as when first acquired, that is, the legal title and the beneficial ownership, since it had not been paid. The maker's remedy was to file a bill in equity against the bank and the fraudulent indorser and have the security applied to pay the note. If plaintiff were a naked trustee for the indorser this could be set up by the maker as an equitable defense, but plaintiff was not a trustee, but sued in its own right as owner. The court spoke of a law of New York "when a bank holds security they are not entitled to sue the indorser and collect as an innocent holder." No reference was given and the law has not been found. The effect of sec. 121, N. I. L., is to give the holder the right to sue the maker, although the holder has been secured or paid by the party secondarily liable. Peoples Nat. Bank v. Rice, 149 N. Y. App. Div. 18, 133 

N. Y. Supp. 622. See also, Twelfth Ward Bank v. Brooks, 63 

N. Y. App. Div. 220, 71 N. Y. Supp. 220; Capitol Nat. Bank v. Robinson, 41 Wash. 454, 83 Pac. 1021.

Instruments held "com- regular" The fact that the words "payable with interest" are written plete and on a blank space after the words "value received," in the same handwriting as the other written parts of the note, does not prevent the note being complete and regular on its face. Trustees of American Bank v. McComb, 105 Va. 473, 54 S. E. 14.

In an action by a holder before maturity against the maker, who defends on the ground that the due date was altered by the payee, from January 1st to December 1st, and this being a material alteration, the plaintiff cannot recover, it was held that the plaintiff can recover on the instrument, as per original terms, under sec. 124, because he is a holder in due course. The court inspected the instrument and found the alteration was not apparent hence it was complete and regular. Chamberlain v. Geer, 135 Wash. 340, 237 Pac. 719.

Where a printed name of a payee was stricken out and another payee's name inserted in writing, the president of the holder bank testified that that was common practice. It was held that the note was complete and regular on its face. Clapper v. Gamble (C. C. A.), 28 F. (2d) 755.

On similar facts a payee was held a holder in due course of an altered instrument where no custom was shown. Saxon v. 

McGill, 179 Ark. 415, 16 S. W. (2d) 987.

An instrument which carries two per cent. interest is complete and regular upon its face, although the usual rate is three per cent. White v. Wadhams, 204 Mich. 381, 170 N. W. 60.

A note containing a provision for higher rate of interest after maturity than before, which was invalid but did not impair negotiability, was complete and regular upon its face. Allen v. 

Cooling (Minn.), 200 N. W. 849. A note in 23 Mich. Law Rev. 

655, suggests that inasmuch as ordinary factors impairing negotiability are governed by sec. 1, and blanks are governed by sec. 14, there is no need to invoke sec. 52(1) except in extraordinary cases.

A note stating the amount in marginal figures, with a blank space before "dollars, "where the amount would ordinarily be inserted in words, was complete and regular upon its face. 

Citizens Bank v. Jones, 127 Wash. 294, 220 Pac. 787.

The preferable view is that the acceptance was already complete and payable at a time certain.

An accepted bill with no drawee is not complete and regular upon its face, and an indorsee is not a holder in due course. 

Clay & Funkhouser Banking Co. v. Dobyns, 213 Mo. App. 468, 255 S. W. 946.

In the absence of defenses, a holder might have power under sec. 14 to fill in the acceptor's name as drawee of a bill of exchange, and there is authority that he could hold the acceptor as maker of a note without any filling in. Peto v, Reynolds, 9 Ex. 410. However, when there were defenses, if the instrument be considered a bill, the blank for the drawee's name would constitute notice of the defenses under sec. 14; and it would be sheer quibbling if such notice from the blank could be avoided by calling this queerlooking instrument a promissory note. promissory note. There is no policy for giving the buyer of such a freakish instrument the protection accorded to the purchaser of normal commercial paper.

A note given to an individual payee stated that certain stock certificates had been delivered to plaintiff bank as trustee to secure the payment of this note and any other liabilities of A, the maker, to the holder thereof. No collateral was then delivered, but a few days subsequently the maker delivered the certificates, not to the bank but to the payee, in return for a receipt for the certificates, "held as collateral for A's note," giving date, amount and maturity. The plaintiff bank, which acquired the note as indorsee for value before maturity without notice of the receipt, and received the certificates from the payee, sought to establish and foreclose a lien upon the collateral as to other notes of the maker of which the plaintiff was payee. Held, the bank could apply the collateral only upon the note indorsed to it. (1)

Under the Iowa decisions, the plaintiff was not a holder in due course of the notes held by it as payee, and the defense of the receipt was not cut off as to these. (2) It was not a holder in due course of the note indorsed to it. Since it described the stock as delivered to a trustee, whereas it was received from the possession of the payee, this was an apparent violation of the terms of the note which made it not "regular upon its face." 

The indorsee would have learned of the existence of the receipt if it had made inquiries of the maker or had disclosed to the payee its intention to appropriate the collateral to other indebtedness. The  was cited generally. Commercial Nat. Bank v. May, 187 Ia. 888, 174 N. W. 646.

The decision seems unduly narrow, since the receipt merely connected the collateral with the note, without negativing the "other indebtedness' clause. The delivery of the certificates to the payee instead of a trustee seems an immaterial change in the arrangement, insufficient to impose constructive notice upon the plaintiff.

If the pledgee of a note renews the principal debt by accepting the paper of a third person in exchange for the original paper of the pledgeor, but retains the collateral note which the pledgee originally took in due course, the pledgee is now a holder of the collateral note as of the time of renewal, and since it was then matured, the pledgee is no longer a holder in due course thereof but is subject to the maker's defenses against the payee, the original pledgeor. A note obtained from the defendant by the fraud of the payee was indorsed by him in blank and delivered to M who pledged it to the plaintiff bank. Held, it was a question for the jury whether the delivery to M was an absolute surrender of the bank's lien or was intended to enable M, as the bank's agent, to place the note in another bank for collection. The latter alternative would not deprive the bank of its original title as a holder in due course; but the former alternative would render the bank's second taking a new acquisition of the note after maturity, so that it would be subject to the maker's defenses. 574 "Negotiated" (4) "That at the time it was negotiated to him he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating it" 

Cross Reference: §§ 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 21 to 23, 30, 49, 55, 56, 124, 125, 47, 59.

The  in defining things that may be wrong with an instrument uses three terms, defenses, infirmities and defects of title. It has been objected that these terms are an unnecessary duplication, see 4th. edition of this work p. 419, and there is much to be said in favor of this position. But a careful examination of the act as a whole will indicate that each term may have its specific place. Defects of title are defined by sec. 55 to cover all those situations which at common law were known as equi defenses, and also to cover those equities of ownership where there was breach of faith in negotiation. (For a discussion of the term equity of defense and equities of ownership see 

31 Harv. L. Rev. 1140, 5 Tulane L. Rev. 287.) The term defenses seems to include common law defenses, outside of those covered in sec. 55, such as mistake, absence and failure of consideration, sec. 28; incapacity, sec. 22; lack of authority, sec. 19, etc. Infirmities then must include things that are wrong with the instrument itself as distinguished from those things that are lacking in the contracts on the instrument. Such infirmities are to be found in situations arising under secs. 13, 14, 15, 16 (usually defects of title), 21, 23, 124 and 125. The conclusion that these situations were not intended by the framers of the act to be included in either the terms of defects of title or defenses as used in sec. 57, but were to be classed as infirmities as used in 52-4, is substantiated by the fact that the sections above specifically provide for the rights of holders in due course who acquire the instruments under these facts, thus supplementing the rights given by sec. 57.

Notice acquired by the purchaser after he has bought the note does not prevent him from being a holder in due course. The 

N. I. L. was not cited. Citizens Union Nat. Bank v. Thweatt, 166 Ark. 269, 265 S. W. 955.

On the meaning of "negotiated" and the bearing of this subsection upon the question whether the payee may be a holder in due course, see supra, pp. 543 to 560, also sec. 30.

& Trust Co. v. Cowgill, 85 F. (2d) 255 (App. D. C.). The case is clearly wrong on the point of negotiation. See sec. 30. 

One is not to be deemed a holder in due course of a note unless it has been "negotiated" and transferred to him, either by indorsement or delivery, and one who merely claims an equitable interest can not be deemed a holder in due course so as to take free from defects under sec. 57. The plaintiff made a contract for the building of a house on his lot by a lumber company, which was to be paid partly from the proceeds of a first mortgage, partly by a second mortgage, and the balance in cash. As security the plaintiff delivered a deed of his land, which was to be reconveyed free of incumbrances when the contract payments were received. As part of the same transaction the plaintiff gave his note for the contract price to the lumber company to enable it to obtain funds for carrying out the contract. The defendant bank, with knowledge of the written contract, discounted the note for the lumber company and accepted a conveyance from it of the plaintiff's land. The bank refused to reconvey the land after completion of the building unless paid the entire amount of the note in cash. Held, the plaintiff was entitled to a reconveyance upon making payment in accordance with the terms of the contract, but since the bank had made no promise to reconvey free of incumbrances, it could reconvey the land subject to a mechanic's lien. The bank as purchaser was not affected by equities that might never come into being and which arose subsequently to its purchase. Pellegrino v. First Nat. Bank, 210 App. Div. 584, 206 N. Y. Supp. 716, modifying 123 Misc. Rep. 506, 205 N. Y. 

Supp. 715.

The result of the case is not entirely satisfactory. If an indorsee of the note was merely an assignee of the contract rights of the lumber company, why was a note given at all? Since the purpose of the note was to obtain funds for carrying out of the contract, the note might have well been considered an independent obligation on which the plaintiff was an accommo-

§ 52 (4) dation maker and liable to the bank as holder for value. Under this view, the bank held the land not as security for performance of the contract, but to secure the payment of the note. 

The defendant gave a note to a building company which had contracted to erect buildings on her property. The note was indorsed by the payee for value before maturity to the plaintiff, which had notice of the contract and the fact that the buildings had not yet been built. They were never erected. The plaintiff was held not a holder in due course because it had notice of the infirmity in the instrument. Commercial Germania Trust & Sav. Bank v. Southwestern Surety Ins. Co., 145 La. 367, 82 So. 

373. Unless the indorsee knew that the payee would break its contract, the case seems squarely opposed to numerous decisions holding that notice of an executory agreement by the payee does not subject the indorsee to the defense of subsequent failure of consideration. See page 652, infra.

Upon evidence that the note, which was payable on demand, was transferred to the plaintiff, with indorsements showing payment nearly in full and with knowledge on his part that there was a dispute between the maker and the payee as to the amount due thereon, the plaintiff was held not a holder in due course. 

Brophy Grocery Co. v. Wilson, 45 Mont. 489, 124 Pac. 510.

(See under sec. 30, supra.) 

The result of the case might be aided by sec. 28, which was not cited, allowing a recovery pro tanto, in case of a partial failure of consideration.

Negotiable bonds were stolen from the plaintiff who immediately caused notices to this effect to be circulated to all dealers.

First, actual notice,  52(4); then, "Knowledge of such facts that taking the instrument amounted to bad faith," N. I. L. 

56. It is the weight of authority under this latter section that negligent failure to investigate unknown facts is not bad faith; but this should be distinguished from negligent failure to recall a known fact, which is the case here, and which clearly falls under the former test. In the instant case, the fact of notice is admitted, but it was negligently forgotten. This may be good faith; but it certainly should not be classed as absence of notice. 

The case should be distinguished from Raphael v. Bank of England (1855), 33 Eng. Law & Eq. 276, 17 C. B. 161, cited by the court, where the notice was reasonably forgotten after the lapse of over a year. The holding is criticized in note, 10 Tulane

Sec. 54. Notice Before Full Amount Paid. 

Where the transferee receives notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating the same before he has paid the full amount agreed to be paid therefor, he will be deemed a holder in due course only to the extent of the amount heretofore paid by him.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 13, 14, 15, 16, 21 to 23, 25, 30, 52, 55, 56, 191, 19, 22, 24, 26, 27, 45, 59.

ANNOTATIONS 

The words "before he has paid the full amount agreed to be paid therefor" read by themselves are susceptible of two meanings: (1) before the transferee has given the ultimate cash for the instrument or (2) before he has completed the transaction involved.

If the first interpretation be adopted then giving credit by banks, giving negotiable instruments, and other promises to pay in the future, would not constitute value and the holder would be a holder in due course only in so far as he had liquidated his obligation before notice of the infirmity. This is the position which had been taken by many courts before the act and some since; but it is submitted that it is contrary to the spirit of the act and the specific purpose of secs. 25, 26 and 27, which clearly adopt the business point of view that a credit transaction may be complete payment. The cases are collected under sec. 25 and infra.

The second interpretation was undoubtedly in the mind of the draftsman, because his notes show that he cited as his authority Dresser v. Mo., etc., R. R. Construction Co., 93 U. S. 92, which was a case of an installment purchase with a down payment and notice before the balance was paid. 

The second interpretation seems the proper one, namely that section 54 applies only where the transferee has received notice of the infirmity before he has finished the particular type of settlement agreed upon for the exchange of the instrument. Thus 

1 Not in B. E. A.

§ 54 

sec. 54 would apply where the instrument was transferred in return for installment payments as in Commercial Credit Co. v. 

Nissen, 49 S. 303, 207 N. W. 61; or in cases where credit was contracted for but not yet completed as in American Nat. Bank v. Kerley, 109 Oreg. 155, 220 Pac. 116, 32 A. L. R. 262; or Callahan v. Stewart Land Co., 113 Kan. 577, 215 Pac. 831; but it would not apply to cases like Howells State Bank v. Hekrdle, 113 Neb. 561, 203 N. W. 1005, which it is submitted are improperly decided.

This narrow construction of sec. 54 is the only way in which it can be reconciled with secs. 25 and 27 and is in accord with the modern commercial views of payment. This interpretation was adopted among others in Griswold v. Morrison, 53 Cal. App. 

93, 200 Pac. 62; and Peoples Savings Bank of Blakesburg v. 

Smith (Ia.), 230 N. W. 565. See also "Value in the Transfer of 

Negotiable Instruments," 33 Yale L. J. 628, and cases and comments infra and under sec. 25. 

Of course there may be cases in which such a result would lead to unjust enrichment. Where such cases develop relief should be sought in an equitable action against the proceeds of the instrument where all parties are joined, and not in the ordinary suit at law, which would result in interference with bona fide commercial transactions. The possibility of such cases, and their complicated nature, suggested by Cartier v. Morrison and 

Pennoyer v. Dubois State Bank, discussed, pp. 590, 591, infra. 

The following comment of Professor Brannan points out another possible double interpretation: 

This section codifies the law, but it is submitted that the theory which it expresses is erroneous and contrary to the principle underlying sec. 57. Suppose a note for $200 against which the maker has an equity of fraud as against the payee. It is sold by the payee for $150 to the plaintiff, a bona fide purchaser without notice, upon terms of payment of $100 cash and $50 in a month. Within the month plaintiff is notified of the equity. 

How much should plaintiff recover of the maker? The section says $100, thereby depriving plaintiff of the benefit of his bargain. On the other hand suppose plaintiff had paid the whole consideration of $150 before receiving notice. In this case plaintiff, under sec. 57, recovers $200, the full amount of the note, thus receiving the benefit of his bargain. There is no reason for the difference except that there had been a conflict of authority as to the second case but not as to the first. purchaser for value

Legally, the plaintiff being a bona fide should recover the full amount of the note. But the fraudulent payee was constructive trustee of the note for the defendant maker. In exchange for the note the payee received from the plaintiff $100 cash and plaintiff's obligation to pay $50 in a 

2 Dresser v. Railway Construction Co., 93 U. S. 92.

§ 590 

Burden of proof month. The payee then held this obligation and the $100 in trust for the maker. When the plaintiff is notified of the trust, his obligation is not increased in amount, only he must not pay the unpaid amount to the payee, but must hold it for the maker, who is the beneficiary, and if he pays the trustee after notice he can not recover that amount from the maker. The result is that plaintiff should recover $200, the full amount of the note, less any part of the amount he agreed to pay but has not paid before notice. That amount is $50. The plaintiff therefore should recover $200 less $50, or $150. The case may be more briefly put in this way. The plaintiff is the holder in due course of a note for $200 and is legally entitled to recover that amount. 

But after notice of the trust he must hold subject to that trust his obligation to pay $50 to the trustee, and the maker is entitled to an equitable set-off of that amount as against plaintiff's legal right of action for $200.

Despite the force of Professor Brannan's argument in the preceding paragraphs, the rule of sec. 54 accords, not only with the common law of negotiable instruments, but also with the law of trusts in the analogous situation where a trustee in breach of trust conveys the legal title to the res to a bona fide purchaser, who subsequently learns of the breach before he has paid a balance of the agreed purchase price and is given only a lien on the res for the amount already paid. Ames, Cases on Trusts, 287; Scott, Cases on Trusts, 655n. Thus sec. 54 carries out an established principle that a bona fide purchaser must complete his side of the transaction by acquiring legal title and paying the full price (before maturity, in the case of negotiable instruments), before he is considered to be in a sufficiently meritorious position to cut off equities. It was not clear, however, that sec. 

57 could not be properly interpreted to give the purchaser the value of his bargain to the extent which he has paid. Thus in 

Professor Brannan's case he might be allowed to recover $133.33, which would be in accordance with the principle of sec. 57. 

The defendant made a note payable to X who negotiated it before maturity to Y. The defendant later made a renewal note payable to himself, indorsed it and gave it to X instead of giv ing it to Y. X transferred it to the plaintiff, before maturity. 

Plaintiff gave X certificates of deposit which were negotiated to third parties. Before payment on the certificates plaintiff knew of the defendant's equity. It was held that plaintiff had the burden of proving that the holder of the certificates whom he paid was a holder in due course, and since he did not offer evidence on that issue he cannot recover. Cartier v. Morrison, 232 

Mich. 352, 205 N. W. 108. The court cited secs. 54, 55 and 59 on this point. This is a misconception of the meaning of secs. 

54 and 59, the negotiable certificates themselves were the full amount agreed to be paid by the plaintiff for the instrument in

§ 54 

proof suit. By the preponderant weight of authority the issue of such Burden of paper is value. Goodale v. Thorn, 199 Cal. 307, 249 Pac. 11 and cases under sec. 25. It is admitted that the plaintiff purchased bona fide and the only question in the case is value; therefore the presumption of sec. 59 and the possible defect in X's title to the certificate under sec. 55 do not apply. 

This case is disapproved in Pennoyer v. Dubois State Bank, 35 Wyo. 319, 249 Pac. 795, 25 Mich. L. Rev. 445, where the equities of such situations and the effect of the sections involved are fully discussed in an excellent decision on the following facts and argument:

Plaintiff was indorsee of the note in suit. As consideration for the note it gave the payee a negotiable certificate of deposit. 

The payee transferred the certificate to the First Nat. Bank of 

Cody. Testimony was given by the plaintiff that it had no notice of the alleged fraud of the payee at the time that it gave the certificate; but it offered no proof to show that at the time of payment it had no notice. It was held, in view of  sec. 

59, the plaintiff had the burden of proving that it did not come within sec. 54, but the plaintiff could rely upon N. I. L. secs. 

45 and 59, which put forth presumptions that the Bank of Cody was a holder in due course of the certificate of deposit, and thereby obligated the plaintiff to allow the certificate to be paid. 

This took the case from coming under sec. 54, because that section is applicable when the holder is under no absolute obligation to pay when he receives notice of the defect in title. If any unjust enrichment to the Bank of Cody which might protect the defendant's equities was possible the burden was on the defendant to prove it.

In an attachment of the proceeds of a draft, by the drawee against the bank, payee of the draft, the bank showed that it had credited the drawer's account for the amount of the draft, and the plaintiff set up a claim against the drawer, but did not prove that he had not checked out the amount of the draft. It was held that the holder of a draft payable to him is presumed to have paid value for it, and the burden of showing equities to the contrary is upon him who asserts right to the proceeds thereof or sets up a defense against it; and since the plaintiff did not meet the presumption judgment must go to the defendant. In other words, there was a presumption that the drawer had checked out the full amount. Colonial Lumber Co. v. Andelusia Nat. Bank, 136 Miss. 566, 103 So. 343, not citing the 

N. I. L.

This section is inapplicable to an indorsee who takes a note to Collateral indemnify himself against liability to a third person as surety for the indorsee in another transaction, and receives notice of the indorser's fraud on the maker after the indorsement but before any loss is actually incurred. He retains a lien on the note to

§ 592 

Collateral the extent of any such subsequent loss. Sec. 54 applies only where the obligation incurred by the indorsee is such that, on discovering the infirmity in the instrument, he is relieved from liabilty to make any further payment. Griswold v. Morrison, 53 Cal. App. 93, 200 Pac. 62.

Credit transactions A note taken as collateral for an antecedent debt is not affected by this section. The relation of the holder to the paper is then ordinarily fixed at the time of delivery. But if it was taken by the plaintiff bank in payment for such a debt, notice of infirmities received after delivery and agreement to apply the note upon the debt but before the credits were made upon the books of the bank prevented the bank from being a holder in due course. American Nat. Bank v. Kerley, 109 Oreg. 155, 220 

Pac. 116, 32 A. L. R. 262.

Where the holder took a note from the payee in satisfaction of a pre-existing debt, in good faith, for $5,000.00 it was held that he was a holder in due course to the extent of the satisfied debt, although he later received notice of infirmity. Haschenberger v. Dennis, 118 Neb. 411, 225 N. W. 25, and note 63 A. 

L. R. 493.

Where the plaintiff took the note in suit as security for a loan of $500.00 and then purchased it after learning that the maker was going to sue the payee for failure of consideration in the transaction out of which it arose, it was held that $500.00 was the limit of recovery. Cockrill v. First Nat. Bank, 208 Ky. 

755, 271 S. W. 1054. 

The plaintiff bank bought a note and deposited the amount thereof to the credit of the seller. Held, the bank was a holder in due course only to the extent that the seller had drawn out the deposit before the bank acquired notice of defenses to the note. State v. Emery, 73 Okla. 36, 174 Pac. 770, 6 A. L. R. 234;

The bank subsequently received notice of the maker's defenses and afterwards allowed the payee to withdraw the deposit. 

Held, the bank was not a holder in due course. Callahan v. 

Stewart Land Co., 113 Kan. 577, 215 Pac. 831. 

When a forged check was deposited by the payee in the defendant bank which paid the payee part in cash and deposited the ba to his credit, held, the drawee bank could recover from the defendant the undrawn balance. First State Bank & 

T. Co. v. First Nat. Bank, 314 Ill. 269, 145 N. E. 382.

A bill of exchange was sold to the plaintiff bank by the X bank, which debited the amount against the deposit kept by the plaintiff bank in the X bank. The plaintiff was held a purchaser for value, entitled to recover from the acceptor. Farmers and Merchants Bank v. Nissen (S. D.), 190 N. W. 1014.

actions A draft drawn by the defendant for $2,000, payable to a bank, Credit transwas sent by the payee bank to its St. Paul correspondent, the plaintiff bank, for collection together with other items. The plaintiff bank credited the payee bank with the total of these items before collection was made. If the draft had not been so credited, the payee's account with the plaintiff would have been overdrawn to the extent of nearly $1,800. Held, the plaintiff was to that extent a purchaser for value free from the defense of failure of consideration. St. Paul State Bank v. Rippe Grain & Milling Co., 160 

Minn. 102, 199 N. W. 519.

Where a bank discounted a note and placed the proceeds to the credit of the depositor, quaere whether the mere fact that the note was not paid when due is such notice of defect of title of the depositor as to make the subsequent payment of the balance of the proceeds a wrongful payment. Albany County 

Bank v. People's Ice Co., 92 App. Div. 47, 86 N. Y. Supp. 773.

A bank discounted notes for the payee by placing the amount to the credit of his account. The evidence did not show when the account was drawn upon or exhausted, whether before or after maturity or notice to the bank of fraud upon the maker. 

Held, the bank did not sustain the burden of proof that it was a holder for value to any extent. Central Sav. Bank v. Stotter, 207 Mich. 329, 174 N. W. 142. After a second trial a verdict was ordered entered for the plaintiff because the undisputed evidence showed that the payee's account was exhausted after the deposit, and before maturity or notice of fraud. Central 

Sav. Bank & Trust Co. v. Wachman, 221 Mich. 512, 191 N. W. 5.

At common law in some jurisdictions the bank could recover, not only the amount paid before maturity, but also the amount paid after it, if the bank had no actual notice of the defect in the depositor's title. Bancroft v. McKnight, 11 Richardson L. 663; 

Spering's Appeal, 10 Barr 235. But Michigan was probably contra. Drovers Nat. Bank v. Blue, 110 Mich. 31, 64 Am. St.

Rep. 327. Professor Brannan stated in the third edition that there should be no doubt of the same result under the  

The case in the preceding paragraph is, in its first stage, opposed to his position; but the cases holding mere credit is value amply support him.

To deny complete recovery to the bank is somewhat harsh. 

Its payment of money after maturity is made in due course of business without actual notice of any defense rendering it inequitable to honor the depositor's checks. And the passage of maturity does not in this case naturally put the bank on inquiry, for unlike cases of taking after maturity it does not indicate the possible existence of some defense to account for non-payment of the instrument when due, since the bank here knows that non-payment is due to its own delay in collection, which involves nothing unconscientious.

§ 594 

 Credit transactions On the other hand, this same reasoning would protect an innocent transferee who bought and received the instrument before maturity but got his indorsement after maturity; yet he is subject to defenses both under sec. 49 and at common law. 

Lyon v. First Nat. Bank, 85 Fed. 120; sec. 1 Ames, Cases on 

Bills and Notes, 345. Cf. Watkins v. Maule, 2 Jac. & W. 237, 244 and note, accommodation. It is also arguable in support of the Michigan view that "notice" in sec. 54 includes constructive notice from the passage of maturity. Under this view, an innocent purchaser must do everything in his power to perfect his title, i. e., pay the complete price and secure the indorsement, before maturity. If the deposited instrument is dishonored at maturity, the bank is protected under sec. 54 as to past payments of depositor's checks, and should refuse to honor his subsequent checks drawn against the deposit, which as a commercial matter is almost impossible.

Where the plaintiff purchased three notes before maturity in good faith and without notice of a defense of fraud, and gave his indorser three checks for one-half the face value of the notes, retaining the other half as security for the payment of the notes, in an action against the maker on one of the notes, plaintiff is entitled to recover one-half its face value. Rosenbaum v. Roth, 164 App. Div. 617, 150 N. Y. Supp. 396.

A certificate of deposit for $2,000 was pledged by the payee to the plaintiff to secure a loan of $550. After learning that the certificate had been obtained from the maker by the payee's fraud, the plaintiff sold it at public auction, the loan to the pledgeor being unpaid, and itself became the purchaser. Held, the plaintiff could not recover from the maker of the certificate more than the amount of the loan to the payee. Corinth Bank & 

Trust Co. v. Security Nat. Bank, 148 Tenn. 136, 252 S. W. 1001.

The defendant indorsed a note on condition that it should not be negotiated until another indorser had been procured. The maker nevertheless negotiated it to the plaintiff who paid part in cash, part by a negotiable draft purchased from a bank by plaintiff, and retained part of the consideration. Subsequently the defendant notified the plaintiff's agent that the note had been negotiated in violation of the condition. Held, that the plaintiff can not recover subsequent payments on the note, but can only recover the amount of the cash paid to the maker and the amount paid for the draft. The draft being out of his control, plaintiff was not bound to stop payment on it. The violation of the condition was a good defense against any but a holder in due course. 

Notice to the agent was notice to the principal. But knowledge that the maker was financially embarrassed was not sufficient to put the purchaser on inquiry as to the indorsement.  Baruch v. Buckley, 167 App. Div. 113, 151 N. Y. 

Supp. 853.

8 54 

actions Plaintiff in good faith gave his negotiable check in payment Credit transfor a note made by defendant. Before the check had been paid, plaintiff was notified of an infirmity in the note. The check was subsequently presented and paid. Held, that plaintiff was a holder in due course, that he was not bound to stop payment of the check and was entitled to recover the amount of the note. 

Miller v. Marks, 46 Utah 257, 148 Pac. 412.

When the indorsee of a negotiable note gave a non-negotiable note in part payment thereof, this did not constitute value except in so far as the non-negotiable note was paid before the maker thereof received notice that the negotiable note was based on illegal consideration. Merely starting suit on the negotiable note did not constitute such notice, when the illegal aspect of the negotiable note was not raised until during the trial. Ayub v. 

Saloman (Tex. Civ. App.), 252 S. W. 291. 

See the interesting adverse criticism of this case in a note in 

33 Yale L. J. 628 on "Value in the transfer of negotiable instruments."'

The writer contends that the person who has given a non-negotiable instrument, like the bank which has credited the depositor's account, has assumed an obligation which he must normally as a business matter carry out, and that it is unfair to lige him or the bank to determine at his peril the fact of defect of title in the negotiable instrument at the moment when he is called upon to perform the non-negotiable obligation which he has assumed. Although he has been notified of the alleged equity against the instrument, it may eventually prove to be unfounded, after the dishonor of the obligation has injuriously affected the business reputation of the bank or other obligor. 

In First Nat. Bank v. Buffalo Brewing Co., 154 N. Y. Supp. 

765, bonds, with interest coupons attached, were assigned to plaintiff (whether by indorsement or not does not appear) as collateral security for a debt, and it was arranged that plaintif should collect the proceeds of the coupons, as they matured, and apply the moneys to the debt. The court said that the plaintiff was a holder in due course of such coupons only as were applied to the debt before any notice of a defect in the title thereto was brought home to the plaintiff. It is submitted that if the bonds were negotiable, and payable to bearer or indorsed, and were pledged for a debt, the plaintiff at once became a holder in due course of the bonds and all the coupons to the extent necessary to pay the debt, and his title was not affected by any subsequent notice of a defect. If notice before the application of the proceeds of a coupon would impair plaintiff's title to the coupon, in like manner, notice before the maturity and application of the principle of the bond would impair the plaintiff's title to the bond. Such a rule would make pledges of negotiable instruments of doubtful value as security.

Credit A bank took a draft from X, who was indebted to it, surrendering his evidences of indebtedness. When the bank learned that the draft had been obtained by fraud, it repossessed itself of all that it had surrendered and took a chattel mortgage from X to secure the old indebtedness, which recited that when the draft was collected the proceeds should be applied to the payment of X's indebtedness. Held, the bank could not recover from the drawer. It had not parted irrecoverably with anything of value before it learned of the infirmity. First Nat. Bank v. 

Lyons Exch. Bank, 100 Kan. 194, 164 Pac. 137. Sec. 54 does not seem applicable.

Sec. 55. When Title Defective. 

The title of a person who negotiates an instrument is defective within the meaning of this act when he obtained the instrument, or any signature thereto,' by fraud, duress, or force and fear, or other unlawful means, or for an illegal consideration, or when he negotiates it in breach of faith, or under such circumstances as amount to a fraud.

On the meaning of "defective" title, see Alcock v. Smith "infirmity" [1892], 1 Ch. 238, and Chalmers, Bills of Exchange (9th ed.), "defenses" 111, in which the draftsman of the B. E. A. says that "defect of title" was used to mean "equity attaching to the bill" since "equity" was a term unknown in the law of Scotland, to which the B. E. A. extends. Inasmuch as this reason has no force in this country, it is regrettable that sees. 52(4), 55, 56, 57, 59, of the  follow the B. E. A. in using a phrase whose meaning was not established by common law decisions, instead of speaking of equities and equitable defenses, which were terms familiar to our courts and text writers.

ENGLAND 

X owed plaintiff. In order to provide funds to pay the debt, defendant at X's request drew a check payable to X or order, which X was to pay into his bank to meet his check for the same amount to plaintiff. X indorsed the defendant's check, paid it into his bank and gave his own check to plaintiff. Defendant changed his mind and stopped his check, whereupon X stopped his check and indorsed and delivered defendant's check to plaintiff who had notice of its dishonor. Held, that as the check was an accommodation bill and plaintiff, even assuming that he gave consideration for it, not being a holder in due course, since he took the check with notice that it had been dishonored, took it subject to any defect of title at the time of dishonor, and as X had negotiated it to plaintiff in breach of faith, there was a defect of title attaching to it and the plaintiff could not recover. Hornby v. McLaren (C. A., March 31, 1908), 24 T. L. 

Rep. 494.

An overdue bill indorsed in blank was sold in Norway on a judicial proceeding against one of several joint owners of the bill. By the laws of Norway the purchaser acquired a good title as against the equity of the other joint owners. Held, that although the bill was drawn and payable in England, sec. 36(2), see infra, Appendix I of the Bills of Exchange Act was not applicable and the purchaser was entitled to the bill. Alcock v. Smith [1892], 1 Ch. 238. 

In this case Lindley, J. (p. 263), said that "defect of title' is a phrase introduced into the Bills of Exchange Act in lieu of the old expression 'subject to equities,' which is an expression not adopted, because the Act applies to Scotland as well as to England, and 'subject to equities' is an expression not known to Scotch law."

§ 604 

 Duress 

A negotiable instrument obtained by duress is not void but only voidable and is valid in the hands of a holder in due course. 

State v. Wegener, 180 Ia. 102, 162 N. W. 1040.

This was the weight of authority at common law, but some cases held duress a real defense, Loomis v. Ruck, 56 N. Y. 462; 

Barry v. Equitable L. Ins. Soc. 59 N. Y. 587; see Fairbanks v. 

Snow, 145 Mass. 153; 8 Corpus Juris 762, and such was Daniel's view. Daniel Negotiable Instruments (6th ed.), secs. 809, 857, 858. The question is clearly settled in favor of the equitable view by the  with the possible exceptions of signing under direct physical compulsion, which is discussed, infra, p. 623. 

The question, what acts are sufficient to constitute duress, is discussed by Roscoe Pound, 28 Harv. L. Rev. 358 and note. The addition of the words "force and fear" in sec. 55 strengthens his view that any acts which in fact overcome the signer's will are a defense, even though they would not have been sufficient under the older common law decisions.

In an action upon a note payable to the plaintiff hotel company an answer alleging an agreement that the defendant was not to be personally liable for his bill, which was to be paid by his employer, and that the defendant executed the note in payment of his bill when the hotel refused to permit him to remove his personal belongings otherwise, raised a substantial issue of duress.
