Illegality 

The payee sued on note, one of a series given because the payee threatened to prosecute the maker's brother-in-law for embezzlement unless the maker gave his notes for the amount of the indebtedness. The maker set up these facts as constituting duress, and counterclaimed for the recovery of payments already made on other notes of the series. The sufficiency of the counterclaim was certified, but not the adequacy of the answer considered as a defense to this note. Held, the counterclaim was invalid. The law will not interfere to aid either of the parties who have combined to stifle a charge of crime, even if the accused is innocent and no prosecution has been started.  Union Exch. Nat. Bank v. Joseph, 231 N. Y. 250, 131 N. E. 905, 17 A. L. R. 323, affg. 194 App. Div. 295, 185 N. Y. 

Supp. 403. See note, 17 A. L. R. 325, on the effect of innocence upon contracts made to suppress a criminal prosecution. 

The execution of a note by plaintiff to a bank under threat of prosecution of her brother for embezzlement and to involve her, was held to amount to duress entitling plaintiff to secure cancellation of the note. The N. I. L. was not cited. Carek v. Schmidt, 126 Neb. 591, 253 N. W. 864. 

Where the holder purchased an instrument with knowledge that it was given under threats to prosecute the maker's son for forgery of maker's name on the note which it replaced, the holder can not recover from the maker. Guardian Trust Co. v. 

Meyer (C. C. A.), 19 F. (2d) 186.

A person who acquires a note by indorsement of part thereof gets title by "unlawful means" within this section, since the transfer is in contravention of statutory provisions of the N. 

I. L. Edgar v. Haines, 109 Ohio 159, 141 N. E. 837, 38 A. L. R. 

795. Sed quaere.

When a note was given partly for illegal consideration and partly for lawful consideration, the entire note was unenforceable. The N. I. L. was not cited. Johnson v. McMillion, 178 Ky. 

707, 199 S. W. 1070, L. R. A. 1918C, 244, with note on "Right to recover money lent for use in an illegal transaction." Webb v. J. R. Lowe & Co., 215 Ala. 552, 112 So. 138, not citing the 

N. I. L.; De Borde v. Moore, 211 Ky. 396, 277 S. W. 461, not citing the N. I. L. Contra, a note given in part for an illegal consideration is divisible into its legal and illegal parts. The 

N. I. L. was not cited. Greene v. Atwood, 106 Wash. 416, 180 

Pac. 399.

Sawdust Co., 240 Mich. 549, 215 N. W. 364; Licensed Retail

Negotiation in violation of a statute is no defense against the innocent purchaser. Stevens v. Pierce, 109 Okla. 106, 235 Pac.

In an action by the payee against the maker the note was given in settlement of a fine imposed upon one Lloyd, who was convicted in the recorder's court for a violation of a city ordinance, and who was discharged from custody upon delivery of said note to the city. In Quiggle v. Herman, 131 Wis. 379, 111 N. I. L. was not considered. 

In Sampson v. Ward, 147 Wis. 48, 132 N. W. 629, plaintiff sold land to X and took in part payment a note made by defendant to one Y upon the sale of a stallion, but the note did not state the consideration as required by statute. The note was indorsed by Y and by X. At the time plaintiff took the note he had no notice of the consideration. Subsequently X paid the balance due for the land and received his deed from plaintiff. 

Held, that the note was not void as to a holder in due course, that plaintiff was such a holder even though he received notice of the consideration before Y paid the unpaid balance and received his deed. 

In Benton v. Sikyta, 84 Neb. 808, 122 N. W. 1057, 24 L. R. A. McCabe v. Williams, 45 N. D. 330, 177 N. W. 378.

A corporation which gave a note in payment of a subscription to stock in the payee corporation can not set up the defense of ultra vires against an indorsee for value who knew of the consideration. The court said that notice of the consideration did not constitute notice of its illegality, and even if the indorsee knew that the defendant's charter did not give it power to subscribe to stock in another corporation, the defense would not be available in litigation where the rights of the public were not involved. Although a statute requiring a subscriber for corporate stock to pay 10 per cent. in cash was violated when he gave a note for his subscription, the note is nevertheless enforceable in the hands of an indorsee with knowledge of the purpose for which it was given, at least if he paid a price amounting to 10 per cent. of the subscription. for gambling

Plaintiff may recover against the drawer of a check given to Indorsements the payee for salary and which the plaintiff cashed for one to consideration whom it had been indorsed by the payee for a gambling consideration, plaintiff having no notice of such illegality. The

A draft payable to the plaintiff was indorsed by him in a gambling transaction and came into the hands of a holder in due course who was paid by the defendant drawer despite the plaintiff's countermand. Held, the drawer was not liable to the payee. The plaintiff lost title to the draft, and since the holder in due course could have recovered from the defendant regardless of the illegality and failure of consideration, the defendant was justified in paying him. The case did not fall within 

Criminal Code, c. 38, sec. 131, providing that all promises, agreements, conveyances, etc., made for å gaming consideration should be void and of no effect, or sec. 136 providing that no assignment of any bills, notes, etc., should affect the defense of the person executing the same for a gaming consideration. Porter v. First 

Nat. Bank, 212 Ill. App. 250. Before the N. I. L. the contrary result was reached in Illinois and the Criminal Code sections were held to apply in similar cases. Thomas v. First Nat. Bank, 213 Ill. 261, 72 N. E. 801; Commercial Nat. Bank v. Spaids, 8 

Brad. 493 (Ill.).

Defendant bank paid its cashier's check to an indorsee of the payee after notice that the indorsement had been made in an unlawful gambling transaction. Held, that the bank was liable over again to the payee, although the statute against gambling did not in express terms declare gambling contracts void. Drinkall v. Movius State Bank, 11 N. D. 10, 88 N. W. 724. On the effect of a statute which does so declare, see infra, p. 615 ff.

Usury The title of the payee of a note is defective where the only consideration is accrued interest on a loan previously made at an unlawful rate of interest. Keene v. Behan, 40 Wash. 505, 82 

Pac. 884.

A note made and payable in North Dakota is governed by the usury law of that state, though secured by mortgage on Minnesota lands and sued on there. Usury was found to exist. 

 Patterson v. Wyman, 142 Minn. 70, 170 N. W. 128.

A note executed in Texas to a Kansas payee and payable in Kansas is governed by Kansas usury law, although secured by a mortgage in Texas land. The  was not cited. Smith v. 

Western & Southern Life Ins. Co., 87 F. (2d) 839 (C. C. A. 

5th).

On waiver of usury by renewal, see infra, p. 628. On usury as a real defense, see infra, p. 616.

Where the statute provided that if usurious interest was paid the debtor was allowed to recover double the amount paid it was held that such a penalty did not apply to a holder in due course where the illegal interest was collected by the usurious payee who happened to also be the holder's agent. Fry v. 

Knouse, 142 Wash. 500, 253 Pac. 802. 

Where the usury statute (such as the one in Mississippi) does not in express words denounce the contract as void but provides certain penalties and forfeitures for its violation, the defense of usury is not available against an innocent holder for value before maturity. Allen v. Grenada Bank, 155 Miss. 91, 124 So. 69.

The North Carolina usury statute providing for the forfeiture of the entire interest operates against a holder in due course. 

Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond v. Jones, 205 N. C. 648, 172 

S. E. 185, 8 U. of Cin. L. Rev. 207.

The right of a holder in due course to recover on an instrument can not be defeated by usury laws unless the law makes the instrument absolutely void. Boston Mut. Life Ins. Co. v. 

Newton, 174 Ark. 547, 297 S. W. 1035. Accord, Whipp v. 

Glueck, 58 F. (2d) 523 (App. D. C.). 

Where the statute makes a usurious contract void, a holder in due course takes subject to the defense. The N. I. L. was not cited. Dallas Trust & Savings Bank v. Brashear (Tex. 

Com. App.), 65 S. W. (2d) 288; Ward v. Pace (Tex. Civ. App.), 73 S. W. (2d) 959, not citing the N. I. L. 

Where a statute declares the interest void for usury, the holder in due course may, nevertheless, recover the principal and interest in full. Brown v. Guaranty Mortg. Co. of California, 220 Cal. 532, 31 P. (2d) 788. 

Where the statute provides that the maker shall never "in any case in law or equity be required to pay more than the principal sum borrowed," the holder in due course can recover

§ 55 

only the principal. McCormick v. Fallier, 223 Ala. 80, 134 So. Usury 471. 

A holder in due course is expressly protected by statute in 

Kansas.  Smith v. Western & South ern Life Ins. Co., 87 F. (2d) 839 (C. C. A. 5th).

The transfer of a negotiable instrument by a holder at a discount greater than legal interest is not usurious, although the transferor indorsed it. Bernheimer v. Gray, 201 Ala. 462, 78 

So. 840; Van Noy v. Goldberg (Cal. App.), 277 Pac. 539; Peo ples Bank & T. Co. v. Fenwick Sanitarium, 130 La. 723, 58 So. 

523, 43 L. R. A. (N.S.) 211, Ann. Cas. 1913C, 1322, with notes; 

Dobbs v. Coleman Lumber Co., 102 N. J. Law 560, 134 Atl. 296;

Victoria Finance Corp. v. Coleman Lumber Co. (N. J. Law), 134 Atl. 297, not citing the  Coast Finance Corp. v. 

Powers Furniture Co., 105 Oreg. 339, 209 Pac. 614, 24 A. L. R.

If an indorsement is not a true sale, but a collusive transaction planned at the time of the issue of the note, it may be considered usurious. The N. I. L. was not cited. Quinn v. Van 

Raalte, 276 Mo. 71, 205 S. W. 59.

An acceleration clause providing that in case of default in the payment of any of a series of notes secured by a mortgage the entire sum was to become due at the election of the holder is not a usurious contract. N. I. L. not cited. Smith v. Western 

& Southern Life Ins. Co., 87 F. (2d) 839 (C. C. A. 5th). 

For a general discussion of the various types of usury laws see Weinstein, "When a Note Represents an Usurious Contract in Louisiana," 5 Tulane L. Rev. 211, 218 ff. See also Beutel, 

"The Interpretation of the N. I. L. and Statutes Declaring Instruments Void," 83 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 744. 

The defendant, desiring to raise money, executed a note to the order of her agent for $2,100, and delivered it to him with directions to sell it. He procured the defendant to indorse it and sold it to the plaintiff for $1,850. Held, that the usury laws. have not been repealed by the Negotiable Instruments Law and that the transaction constituted a usurious loan which avoided the note even in the hands of a holder in due course. Sabine v. Paine, supra, did not modify the established principle that usury was a personal defense not available to a stranger to the instrument; but the brother of a maker of a note, who voluntarily paid it by check, was not a stranger and could set up the usury on the note as a defense to liability on the check. He was analogous to an accommodation maker, who can set up usury. Levy v. Hallager, 119 Misc. Rep. 695, 197 

N. Y. Supp. 257.

When the usurious lender is a bank, usury is only an equitable defense in New York with respect to the principal of the instrument. Although under N. Y. Laws 1837, c. 430, sec. 1, all usurious securities are void, the National Banking Act provides that a national bank knowingly charging a usurious rate on a loan or discount shall forfeit all interest, but does not make the instrument void, and N. Y. Laws 1900, c. 310, and N. Y. Laws 

1922, c. 623, places state and private banks on a parity with national banks as to usury. A state bank bona fide in due course and for value discounted a note which was void for usury as between the original parties. Held, that the bank can recover on the note. Schlesinger v. Gilhooly, 189 N. Y. 1, 81 N. E. 619; 

Weaver Hdwe. Co. v. Solomovitz, 235 N. Y. 321, 139 N. E. 353, accord. This section of the banking law marks the single exception to the real defense rule of Sabine v. Paine, supra. Weisman v. Naitove, 125 Misc. 647, 211 N. Y. Supp. 740.

But if the bank had knowledge that the note was usurious as between the original parties, it can not recover, Laws 1900, c. 310, having no application in such a case. Schlesinger v. Lehmaier, 191 N. Y. 69, 83 N. E. 657, 16 L. R. A. (N.S.) 626. 

In an action by the maker against the payee to enjoin the payee from transferring the unmatured notes on the ground that they were tainted with usury, it was held that the injunction should issue because the notes if negotiated to a National bank could be collected under sec. 114 of the Banking Law, Laws of 1922, c. 623 and U. S. Rev. St. sec. 5197. Weisman v. 

Naitove, 125 Misc. Reps. 647, 211 N. Y. Supp. 740. 

In an action by the payee against the makers of a renewal note the original note was made and made payable in New York, where usury renders the entire note void and all renewals void. 

The renewal was made in New Jersey and mailed from New Jersey to New York where it was made payable. In New Jersey a note representing usurious interest is void only to the extent of the usury. It was held that forbearance to sue on an honestly asserted claim was sufficient consideration to support the renewal, so the question of whether the parties intended the New Jersey law to govern was properly submitted to the jury. The

§ 55 jury's finding for the plaintiff either showed that the New Jersey law was intended to govern, or that there was no usury, which, in either case, is sufficient to support a verdict for the plaintiff. Joffe v. Bonn (U. S. C. C. A.), 14 F. (2d) 50. The 

 was not cited.

For a discussion of the effect of the usury laws and especially for the condition of the law in New York, see Beutel, "The 

Interpretation of the N. I. L. and Statutes Declaring Instru ments Void," 83 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 744, 762.

The problem of defenses on negotiable instruments due to illegality is largely one of reconciliation of conflicting statutes. der statutes which do not clare instru- expressly de- ments void

under statutes

Illegality Each case depends upon the wording of the particular statute making the involved, as compared with the  In this respect it void should be noted that sec. 55 makes not only "illegal consideration" but also any "other unlawful means" of obtaining the instrument a defect of title which is not, under sec. 57, available against a holder in due course. It is hard to see how the framers of the act could have stated more broadly an intention to include all forms of illegality within sec. 55. It has been the almost uniform holding of all courts, as indicated by the cases above, that the holder in due course cuts off all defenses of illegality except those where the statute made the instrument "void." In these situations there is a split of authority, some courts holding that the instrument being void ab initio by statute can not be given life by the N. I. L. Such an argument overlooks the fundamental purpose of the N. I. L., which is to give a holder in due course all the rights which appear on the face of the instrument and invalidity in inception is often no defense; see secs. 14 and 16.

It is submitted that a proper result can be had in these cases only by attempting to reconcile both the words and purposes of both the N. I. L. and the particular statute of illegality, if this fails then the N. I. L. should be broadly construed in favor of the holder, and the particular statute being penal should be narrowly construed. Where there is an innocent holder suing a party to the illegality it seems that the equities are all in favor of the holder who is not a party to the wrongful act, and he should be allowed to recover, unless the statute plainly indicates the intent of the legislature to make the instrument illegal in its inception void in the hands of a holder in due course.

The defendant maker's defense that notes in suit were issued for stock in a corporation in violation of a statute which made all obligations of the corporation so issued void, was held invalid against a holder in due course. Grange Nat. Bank of McKean 

County v. Collman, 103 Pa. Super. 235, 158 Atl. 195.

Under the Blue Sky Laws the courts have usually held that statutes making the instrument "void" are not effective against holders in due course. McGregor v. Lamont, 223 Ill. App. 451, not citing the N. I. L.; Fentress v. City Nat. Bank, 172 Ark.

defenses Real Real defenses. At common law the distinction was well established between real or legal defenses, which prevailed against a holder in due course, and personal or equitable defenses, which were cut off by a transfer to such a holder. See 

2 Ames, Cases on Bills and Notes, 811, 812. The N. I. L. makes no mention of this distinction. Some former real defenses are covered by specific sections, e. g., forgery by sec. 23, discharge, now a personal defense, cancellation, etc., by secs. 119-123, and

§ 55 defenses alteration by secs. 124, 125. Want of delivery at the inception Real of the instrument, which was a real defense in some states at common law, has been made an equitable defense by sec. 16, except for incomplete instruments, which fall under sec. 15. 

But other real defenses are either omitted from consideration or else fall within the terms of secs. 55 and 57 and hence have become equitable defenses under the Act. 

It is true that none of the common law real defenses are clearly specified in sec. 55, but "fraud" and negotiation "under such circumstances as amount to fraud" seem to include fraud in the factum, and "duress, or force and fear" a signature under physical pressure, both real defenses at common law, while "other unlawful means or for an illegal consideration" may include forms of illegality which statutes before the Act made defenses against a holder in due course. On the other hand, it may be argued that the limitation of these phrases to mean only those forms of fraud, duress, and illegality which were previously equities is favored by the use of these phrases in sec. 55 in a definition of "defective" title, which probably signifies title "subject to equities." It has been suggested that a real defense is not a defect of title, but no title at all. 

These arguments, however, do not meet the provision in sec. 

57, that a holder in due course is free, not only from any defect of title, but also from "defenses," a word sufficiently broad to include real defenses included in a broad interpretation of sec. 

55 not elsewhere covered by the , especially as sec. 57 deliberately failed to follow the definite wording of the B. E. 

A., "free from mere personal defenses.' For the discussion of real defenses under the B. E. A. see J. L. Falconbridge (1923), 4 D. L. R. 4, and see the discussion of defects of title defenses and infirmities under sec. 52(4), supra. See also Green, "Real

Defenses and the N. I. L., 9 Tulane L. Rev. 78. 

Many of the decisions under the N. I. L. construe sec. 57 so as to exclude common law and statutory real defenses not otherwise covered in the Act and leave them available against a holder in due course. 

1. Incapacity. The N. I. L. has not incorporated the provi- Incapacity sion of the B. E. A., sec. 22, see infra, Appendix 1, making capacity to incur liability as a party to a negotiable instrument coextensive with capacity to contract generally. Similar provisions have been inserted in later Uniform Acts. See U. S. A. sec. 2; U. S. T. A. sec. 2. Secs. 60 to 62 and 65(3) also indicate that capacity remains a real defense, and the result under the other uniform acts will doubtless follow under the N. I. L., just as if such an express provision were inserted. Sec. 196 applies, if the law of persons is part of the law merchant. As to capacity to pass title by indorsement see sec. 22 and cases there cited.

Infants

Corporations Married women

Infants are affected by sec. 22, but this relates merely to the infant's indorsement or assignment as a transfer of the instrument, and not to the liability of the infant who indorses or otherwise places his signature upon a negotiable instrument. 

As on contracts generally, his obligation seems revocable, even against a holder in due course. See 1 Williston on Contracts, c. VIII; In re Soltykoff, under sec. 22, and cases there cited on the question of capacity to convey title. 

An infant who fraudulently represented himself to be of full age when he made promissory notes payable to the plaintiff was held estopped to set up infancy.  Klinck v. Reeder, 107 Neb. 342, 185 N. W. 1000.

An infant is liable in an action upon a note given in settlement of a tort for which he was liable, so long as the consideration for the note is open to inquiry. There is no presumption that the consideration for an infant's note was lawful. The 

 was not cited. Swoboda v. Nowak, 213 Mo. App. 452, 255 S. W. 1079. The decision is questionable. By the better view an infant giving a note for necessaries is liable, not on the note, but in quasi-contract for the actual value of the necessaries. So here, the infant should be liable only in tort, the note being merely evidence as an admission. See the note in 

37 Harv. L. Rev. 1133.

Corporations are similarly affected by sec. 22, but the Act does not otherwise apply to instruments executed by them outside the scope of their corporate powers, and common law principles must determine whether the defense of ultra vires is legal or equitable or wholly unavailable to the corporation. 

Numerous cases will be found under sec. 22, and under other sections. See the General Index under Corporations. 

A drainage district, created for the purpose of building levees, etc., is incapable of making a note for payment of lobbying the contract, and such a note cannot be enforced against the drainage district by a holder. Planters' Bank of Clarksdale v.

Yazoo Coldwater Drainage District (Miss.), 126 So. 9. 

A municipal corporation in absence of special authorization cannot bind itself on a note to promote a silk mill as a private enterprise. Bolton v. Wharton, 163 S. C. 242, 161 S. E. 454, 86 A. L. R. 1101, with note on estoppel in such cases.

Married women have been given contractual capacity by statutes, 1 Williston, ibid, sec. 268, but in some states they may not contract with their husbands or may not become sureties for them. See the General Index under Married Women for additional cases construing this limited statutory incapacity.

Signing under physical pressure. In Fairbanks v. Snow, Physical 

145 Mass. 153, Holmes, J., in holding duress by threats an equitable defense, said, "No doubt, if the defendant's hand had been forcibly taken and compelled to hold the pen and write her name, and the note had been carried off and delivered, the signature and delivery would not have been her acts; and no contract would have been made, whether the plaintiff knew the facts or not."

This dictum is no longer law under the N. I. L. if such conduct is "duress" within sec. 55; but it is arguable that this is like forgery and is more than duress, which should be construed to apply to cases where the defendant himself moves the pen under coercion through such external facts as imprisonment or fear of injury to life and limb or less serious pressure which actually overcomes his will. If so, such direct physical compulsion might constitute a real defense even under the Act. But even so it seems that negotiation of such an instrument would be "under such circumstances as amounts to fraud" and still a holder in due course should be protected. the factum 3. Fraud in the factum. At common law a real defense was Fraud in held in most jurisdictions to exist in those cases in which a person, without negligence, has signed an instrument, which was, in fact, a negotiable instrument, but was deceived as to the character of the instrument and without knowledge of it. 

In such cases, there is no contract because there was no consenting mind, but the signer may be estopped by negligence to deny knowledge of the character of the instrument which he has signed. If he was not negligent he is not liable. See Williston, 14 Ill. L. Rev. 525. Such fraud was distinguished from "fraud in the inducement," where the signer was led by deception to execute what he knew to be a negotiable instrument. 

The subject is discussed, with an exhaustive collection of common law cases, in an article by Professor W. E. Britton, "Fraud in the Inception of Bills and Notes," 9 Corn. L. Q. 138.

§ 624 

Fraud in the factum 

In Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Illinois (sec. 57) the  or other legislation expressly makes fraud in the factum a real defense, supra, pp. 30 to 32. The Uniform Act does not cover the question in so many words. It is possible, however, that such conduct is "fraud" within sec. 55 and hence causes merely a "defective" title, or that it is one of the "defenses" under sec. 57. It might also be assimilated to want of delivery, which was made an equitable defense by sec. 16. Either possibility would change the common law and protect a holder in due course. In further support of this position it should be noted that the other real defenses are covered by the act and a broad interpretation of sec. 55, especially the last clause "under such circumstances as amount to fraud" certainly includes all kinds of fraud in factum. Since this is so it is hard to believe that the framers overlooked this particular defense. The equities are all in favor of such an interpretation, since the defrauded party really caused the situation and should be the one to suffer. Britton, 9 Corn. L. Q. 156, discusses the effect of the N. I. L., and concludes that it admits of either the real or equitable defense view. The small amount of litigation under the Act may per haps be due to a decline in this type of rural swindling, which recalls the money-making devices of the King and the Duke in "Huck Finn." Britton noted a steadily decreasing number of cases since 1890, op. cit., 140.

Under the old common law view "fraud" in sec. 55 would be limited to fraud in the inducement, and "defenses" in sec. 57 restricted to defenses which were equitable at common law, while fraud in the factum would continue to be a real defense analogous to forgery under sec. 23. Such is the result of a number of the cases which have arisen since the N. I. L., most of which do not cite the act, but there is a strong line of well reasoned cases contra.

Fraud in factum in its essence is really mistake, and it has been held in South Carolina that mistake is no defense against a holder in due course. Southern Bank & Trust Co. v. Sumpter 

Pine Co., 151 S. C. 274, 148 S. E. 887.

In England it was held, in the case of Lewis v. Clay, 67 

L. J. Q. B. (N.S.) 224, that the case of Foster v. MacKinnon,

L. R. 4 C. P. 704, is still law under the provisions of the Bills of Exchange Act, which are in this respect substantially the same as the N. I. L. except for the insertion of "mere personal" before "defenses" in the section corresponding to the N. I. L. sec. 57. The court said that "the use to which the defendant's signature was applied was in substance and effect forgery," and that it was as if he had written his name for an autograph collector or in an album, when he was led to sign a note supposing that he was witnessing a deed. However, the decision was rested partly on the ground that the plaintiff payee was not a holder in due course.

Sec. 56. What Constitutes Notice of Defect. 

To constitute notice of an infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating the same, the person to whom it is negotiated must have had actual knowledge of the infirmity or defect, or knowledge of such facts that his action in taking the instrument amounted to bad faith.¹

Failure to charge the jury that knowledge of such facts that his action in taking the instrument amounted to bad faith would preclude one from being a holder in due course was held a reversible error. Merchants' & Miners' Bank v. Gaujot, 102 W. 

Va. 643, 136 S. E. 199; Charles H. Fuller Co. v. St. Louis Wholesale Drug Co., 219 Mo. App. 519, 282 S. W. 535.

An instruction to the jury which used only the words of this section was held sufficient instruction on the question of bad faith. Title Guaranty Co. v. Barone, 319 Pa. 499, 181 Atl. 765. 

It is not material that an indorsee's denial that the instrument was obtained by fraud was insufficient where he had suffieiently denied knowledge or notice of the fraud. Bothwell v. 

Corum, 135 Ky. 766, 123 S. W. 291.

The question of good faith is one of fact for the jury. Winter v. Hutchins, 20 Ida. 749, 119 Pac. 883; Seaside Nat. Bank v. 

Allen, 35 Ariz. 302, 277 Pac. 68; Sweet v. Security Sav. Bank of Perry, 200 Ia. 895, 205 N. W. 470; McCreary v. Stevens (Miss.), 126 So. 4; Stevens v. Wey, 139 Okla. 210, 281 Pac. 780.

Where the testimony of the plaintiff's bona fides is undisputed, it is the duty of the court so to charge the jury; and that question should not be submitted to them. Van Slyke v. Rooks, 181 Mich. 88, 147 N. W. 579; Security Finance Co. v. Sharpe, 152 Miss. 286, 119 So. 829; Liberty Nat. Bank of Pawkuska v. 

Kendall, 113 Okla. 140, 240 Pac. 72; Commercial Credit Co. v. 

Nissen (S. D.), 231 N. W. 534.

The evidence being positive, certain and in no way contradicted, that plaintiff paid value in the usual course of business, bona fide and without notice, a verdict of the jury and judgment of the lower court thereon in favor of the defendant was reversed by the Supreme Court. Southwest Nat. Bank v. Baker, 23 Ida. 428, 130 Pac. 799.

But where there is any evidence which tends to show bad faith on the part of the plaintiff the case must be submitted to the jury. John C. Boehm Co. v. Commonwealth Banking & 

Trust Co., 119 Ohio St. 516, 164 N. E. 751.

The question whether the facts have any fair tendency to show bad faith is one of fact and not of law, especially where the evidence of fraud is sufficient to put the burden of showing good faith on the indorsee. McNight v. Parsons, 136 Ia. 390, 113 N. W. 858, 22 L. R. A. (N.S.) 718, 15 Ann. Cas. 665, 125 

Am. St. Rep. 265; Cedar Point State Bank v. Youtz, 200 Ia. 86, 204 N. W. 233.

§ 56 

In order to direct a verdict for the holder of a note procured Procedure by fraud of the transferor, there must be a showing so conclusive that fair-minded men could draw no other inference than that the holder acquired the note without knowledge of the fraud practiced on the maker, and also without knowledge of such facts, as that if taken as true, the holder must have acted in bad faith. German-American Nat. Bank v. Kelley, 183 Ia. 269, 166 

N. W. 1053.

Where good faith of an indorsee is an issue a verdict should only be directed for the plaintiff when the evidence offered by him is uncontradicted, his witnesses stand unimpeached directly or circumstantially, and no reasonable or fair inferences tending to prove bad faith can be drawn by reasonable men from the circumstances surrounding the purchase of the instrument. 

Commercial Savings Bank v. Colthurst, 195 Ia. 1032, 188 N. W. 

844, 191 N. W. 787.

There must be evidence of the plaintiff's bad faith, not merely a disbelief by the jury of the plaintiff's evidence of good faith. 

Downs v. Horton, 287 Mo. 414, 230 S. W. 103, affirming 209 

S. W. 595.

Where there is no evidence of the holder's bad faith, other than the fact that he knew that the payee was doing business under a fictitious corporate name, the jury is not justified in finding that the holder took in bad faith. Judgment for the defendant maker based on such a verdict was reversed and remanded. Wakern v. Schneider, 192 Wis. 528, 213 N. W. 328.

The quantum of proof required to show good faith on the part of the holder of negotiable paper is not different in a suit in equity than in an action at law. Hess v. Ia. Bankers Mtge. 

Co., 198 Ia. 1365, 201 N. W. 91.

The maker of a note brought replevin against the indorsee, to whom it had been negotiated by the payee in breach of faith. 

Held, he could not recover, because he failed to produce evidence showing that the defendant indorsee had notice and because the maker was not entitled to possession of the note since the defendant would then be deprived of the opportunity to hold indorsers. Farr v. Farmers Bank (Mo. App.), 228 S. W. 1073.

The maker should have sued in equity for cancellation of his signature, and left the possession of the note in the indorsee, who could then resort to action against the indorsers, as in 

Huston v. Roosa, 43 Ind. 517.

This section has changed the former law of South Dakota under which negligence constituted notice. That a note was accompanied by a mortgage did not put the pledgee on inquiry that the pledgeor was an agent acting in violation of his authority. One judge dissented on the ground that the case was governed by the law of non-negotiable mortgages and not by that of negotiable instruments. Gold Bros. Sec. Co. v. Fidelity 

Trust Co. (S. D.), 195 N. W. 830. Accord as to the change in South Dakota law, Oschenreiter v. Block, 42 S. D. 151, 173 

N. W. 736, 6 A. L. R. 456; Orient State Bank v. Zemlicka, 49

The facts that the plaintiff purchased the notes in suit at a down payment of sixty-five percent from a company of whose assets they constituted about seventy-five percent, and that the plaintiff thoroughly investigated everything except calling on the maker, was held sufficient evidence of bad faith to go to a jury and to support a verdict for a defrauded maker. Silver 

Discount Corporation v. Blair, 106 Vt. 11, 168 Atl. 917; but cf., Windell v. Steinhaff, 211 Ia. 999, 234 N. W. 795.

This section has changed the previous Tennessee law allow ing constructive notice. That the plaintiff took a certificate of deposit for $2,000 as collateral for a loan of $550 to an unshaven man in overalls did not constitute notice that the certificate was obtained by him from the maker by fraud, so as to bar the pledgee's recovery from the maker, especially when the maker showed even less diligence in issuing the certificate of deposit to

This section has changed the previous common-law rule in Vermont that a negligent purchaser was not a holder in due course. Howard Nat. Bank v. Wilson, 96 Vt. 438, 120 Atl. 889. 

Good faith in the purchase of a negotiable note does not require the purchaser to make inquiries as to the purpose for which it was given or the existence of possible defenses. faith is imputed only from knowledge of defenses and mere knowledge of suspicious circumstances will not defeat a recovery. 

American Nat. Bank v. Lundy, 21 N. D. 167, 129 N. W. 99.

Semble, an indorsee is under no duty to inquire how his indorser got the note. Atkins v. Brown (Mo. App.), 208 S. W. 502. 

Where the holder "exhausted all reasonable sources of information except applying to the acceptor himself" and found nothing wrong, he is in good faith. Sonabend v. Charron, 86 

N. H. 386, 169 Atl. 589.

The payee of series of notes by the same maker, some of them overdue, transferred them as collateral for a pre-existing open account to a brother-in-law, after the maker had been garnished by a creditor of the payee. The transferee had no notice of the garnishment of the notes, but took them without previous correspondence with the transferor or inquiry into the solvency of the maker. Held, judgment that the transferee took with notice reversed, except as to the past due note. Guaranty Security Co. v. Coad, 114 Wash. 156, 195 Pac. 22, rehearing denied, 197 Pac. 326. 

But if the purchaser does in fact suspect and fails to make investigation lest it disclose a defense, he is not a purchaser in good faith. Walters v. Rock (N. D.), 115 N. W. 511; Iowa 

Nat. Bank v. Carter, 144 Ia. 715, 123 N. W. 237; Starwaggi v. 

Ludden, 116 Oreg. 119, 240 Pac. 432. Contra, Youle v. Fosha, 76 

Kan. 20, 90 Pac. 1090, semble. 

In Scandinavian Bank v. Johnston, 63 Wash. 187, 115

Pac. 102, the court said, obiter, that it is well established that "mere suspicion of an infirmity is insufficient to put the indorsee upon inquiry or to show that he is not a holder in good faith.”

If the court meant to say that, although the plaintiff himself actually suspected that, there was an infirmity and made no inquiry, he could yet be a holder in good faith, it is submitted that this is erroneous, and that no case has been found which so decides, although similar language is used in some cases. Confusion often arises from the fact that the distinction is not always clearly expressed, although probably intended, between suspicious circumstances and a suspicious purchaser.

X, a bank cashier, held as trustee a note and mortgage belonging to plaintiff. Defendant, knowing that X was in danger

§ 640 

negligence Suspicious of prosecution by the bank for embezzlement and that he was stances and financially embarrassed, advanced to X the amount stolen and received as security the note and mortgage without actual knowledge of X's defective title. Held, that knowledge of these facts should have put defendant on inquiry and that failure to inquire amounted to commercial bad faith, something more than mere negligence. Bergheim v. McRae, 190 Minn. 571, 252 N. W. 833. "Mere lack of notice is not sufficient; good faith implies honest intent. It is consistent with negligence, even gross negli gence. A blundering fool may therefore be found to have acted in good faith, though under like circumstances a shrewd business man might be deemed to have acted in bad faith." Schintz v. American Trust & Sav. Bank, 152 Ill. App. 76.

The existence of suspicious circumstances does not necessarily spell bad faith. Negligence is not a synonym for bad faith, and failure to make inquiries does not compel a finding of bad faith; yet as the question is one of honesty and good faith it is competent to show these facts and it then becomes the province of the jury to say whether the person taking the instrument was guilty of bad faith. Everding v. Toft, 82 Oreg. 1, 160 Pac. 

1160; Commercial Nat. Bank of Muskogee v. Ahrens, 117 Okla. 

65, 245 Pac. 557; Snell Nat. Bank of Winter Haven v. Janney, 219 Ala. 306, 122 So. 362. Accord, St. Pasteur v. Wilson, 144 

Ark. 642, 218 S. W. 843; Voss v. Smith, 98 Okla. 90, 224 Pac. 

328; Boone Nat. Bank v. Evans (Ia.), 213 N. W. 786, not citing the ; Fenner v. American Surety Co. of New York (Tex.

Taft, 123 Tex. 388, 71 S. W. (2d) 1090.

Where a pledgee took notes as security from the payee knowing that he was financially embarrassed at the time the notes were issued to him and that he dominated the affairs of the corporate maker, it was held that failure on his part to make further inquiry would not justify an imputation of bad faith, particularly in view of the fact that an inquiry would not have disclosed the fraud alleged as defense. Cohen v. Superior Oil 

Corp. (Okla.), 71 P. (2d) 626.

It is error to instruct that "if circumstances were such as to put a person of ordinary prudence upon inquiry" the holder is not a holder in due course. Fenner v. American Surety Co. of New York (Tex. Civ. App.), 97 S. W. 741.

In order to show that the defendant had "knowledge of such facts that his action in taking the instrument amounted to bad faith," it is not necessary to prove that the defendant knew the exact fraud that was practiced upon the plaintiff by the defendant's assignor, it being sufficient to show that the defendant had notice that there was something wrong about his assignor's acquisition of title, although he did not have notice of the particular wrong that was committed. Paika v. Perry, 225 Mass. 563, 114 

N. E. 830.

A fraudulent payee of a series of negotiable certificates of Suspicious deposit presented $50,000.00 worth of them to the plaintiff and negligence bank. The bank wired the defendant bank "did you issue for value?" A letter and telegram signed by the cashier, a party to the fraud, who also signed the certificates, said in reply "certificates issued and will be paid at maturity." No other suspicious circumstances appeared except that the bank subsequently made other inquiries that disclosed no fraud. It was held that on this evidence the lower court properly held that the plaintiff did not meet the burden of proof that it was a holder in good faith. International Bank v. Peoples Bank of 

Keyser, 103 W. Va. 597, 138 S. E. 745.

On the same facts as the above case, with the exception that the certificate was taken in payment of a worthless check the lower court was affirmed in holding that the plaintiff took in bad faith. Bethlehem Const. Co. v. Peoples Bank of Keyser, 104 

W. Va. 67, 138 S. E. 748; see also Merchants' Bank & Trust 

Co. v. Peoples Bank of Keyser, 99 W. Va. 544, 130 S. E. 142.

It is submitted that all these cases take an improper view of the requisites of notice and bad faith under sec. 56 and are contrary to the great weight of authority. The Federal District Court (N. D. W. Va.) properly refused to follow them in International

Finance Corporation v. Peoples Bank of Keyser, 27 F. (2d) 

523, 526, affd. 30 F. (2d) 46, certiorari denied 279 U. S. 858, 49 Sup. Ct. 352, 73 L. Ed. 999.

It is sufficient that the buyer of a note had notice or knowledge that the note was in some way tainted with fraud. It is not necessary that he should know the particulars or even the nature of the fraud, since all that is required is knowledge of such facts that his action in taking the note amounted to bad faith. Ozark Motor Co. v. Horton (Mo. App.), 196 S. W. 395. 

Accord, Davis v. First Nat. Bank, 26 Ariz. 621, 229 Pac. 391.

It is in harmony with the statute to charge that "the circumstances must be such as to show wilful neglect or such gross carelessness as fairly tend to the conclusion of bad faith. 

Farmers & Merchants Bk. v. Shaffer (Ia.), 147 N. W. 851. Sed quaere. "Wilful neglect" may possibly imply that the purchaser suspected and wilfully neglected to inquire. But "gross carelessness" alone should not be held to tend to the conclusion of bad faith.

The Supreme Court of Alabama seems to hold that although an indorsee takes without actual knowledge of defenses, yet if he has knowledge of facts which if pursued would have led to actual knowledge, he is chargeable with such knowledge. Elmore 

Co. Bank v. Avant, 189 Ala. 418, 66 So. 509. Sed quaere, as this seems to adopt the test of the reasonably prudent man and not that of actual good faith?

Liberty bonds stolen from the plaintiff were brought by the thief, a boy fifteen years old, less than five feet tall, immature

§ cos 56 

circum- negligence

Suspicious in appearance and bearing on his face the stamp of a degenerate, stances and to the defendants' clerk for sale. The boy stated that they belonged to his mother. The defendants paid the boy for the bonds without any further inquiry. Held, the plaintiff could recover the value of the bonds. The term "bad faith" does not necessarily involve furtive motives, but means bad faith in a commercial sense. The manner in which the defendants conducted their Liberty Loan department provided an easy way for thieves to dispose of their plunder. It was a case of "no questions asked." Although gross negligence does not of itself constitute bad faith, it is evidence from which bad faith may be inferred. The circumstances thrust the duty upon the defendants to make further inquiries and they had no right to shut their eyes deliberately to obvious facts. Morris v. Muir, 111

Misc. Rep. 739, 181 N. Y. Supp. 913, affd. in memo., 191 App. 

Div. 947, 181 N. Y. Supp. 945. The case goes far in making negligence a test of bad faith. 

In Park v. Brandt, 20 Ida. 660, 119 Pac. 877, it was held that a charge that "as matter of law wilful ignorance of facts is as much evidence of bad faith as actual knowledge of the same" was erroneous. A purchaser is not bound to investigate fully all the facts in relation to the execution of a note. The court, however, in this case, and also in Park v. Johnson, 20 Ida. 

548, 119 Pac. 52, and in Vaughan v. Johnson, 20 Ida. 669, 119 

Pac. 879, 37 L. R. A. (N.S.) 816, erroneously said that the purchaser is required to exercise such care as an ordinarily prudent man would under the circumstances. But the same court in 

Winter v. Nobs, 19 Ida. 18, 112 Pac. 525, Ann. Cas. 1912C, 302, said that though the purchaser "may have been negligent in taking the paper, and omitted precautions which a prudent man would have taken, nevertheless, unless he acted mala fide, his title according to settled doctrines will prevail." 

In Burdell v. Nereson, 28 Ida. 129, 152 Pac. 576, the court said that it had gone to the very limit, meaning, apparently, in favor of defendants in this class of cases (a stallion note fraud), in Winter v. Nobs, Vaughan v. Johnson, and Vaughan v. Brandt. 

And in First Nat. Bank v. Pond, 39 Ida. 770, 230 Pac. 344, the court said that the indorsee's right must be judged "by the simple test of honesty and good faith, and not by speculative issues as to diligence or negligence." See also Butte Machinery 

Co. v. Jeppesen, 41 Ida. 642, 241 Pac. 36.

A finding that the plaintiff indorsee had notice of the acceptor's defense of failure of consideration was supported by evidence that the payee, a novelty company, had been engaged in this business for many years, and had been selling acceptances received for the same worthless stuff to the plaintiff and others for fifteen years; that the plaintiff had bought about forty sets of these acceptances amounting to over $5,000 the year before; that these particular acceptances were not protested when the defendant refused to pay them, and no effort was afterward made to collect them from the payee indorser.  Metropolitan Discount Co. v. Flippo, 163 Ark. 331, 260 S. W. 32. See Nevada Laws 1913 c. 89 which make habitual purchase by persons other than banks prima facie evidence of notice. 

Mere acquaintance with the transferor and previous operations with him in similar deals is not in itself sufficient grounds on which to predicate bad faith. Harpas v. Bandler, 223 App. 

Div. 306, 228 N. Y. Supp. 241.

Refusal of the transferor to indorse is not evidence of the holder's bad faith. Continental Nat. Bank of Salt Lake City v. 

Cole, 51 Ida. 140, 3 P. (2d) 1103.

When a note, which was one of several obtained by a swindler and made out on forms furnished by the plaintiff bank, was bought by the bank from him after banking hours at a discount of fifteen per cent., although the sum was due in six months, and the swindler was a stranger to the bank when he began obtaining notes in the locality, there was evidence of notice to sustain a verdict for the maker. Platte Valley State Bank v. 

Burge, 73 Colo. 296, 215 Pac. 149.

The defendant was induced by the same fraud as in Stevens v. Pearson, supra, p. 31, to sign a note payable to the same payee, which was transferred to the same indorsee, the plaintiff. The plaintiff was an attorney, who had taken many thousands of dollars of paper from the fraudulent payee, and knew there was litigation over collection of some of the payee's paper. 

The note bore evidence of being detached from some other paper. 

Held, a verdict was properly directed for the defendant. The

Buffalo Porcelain Enameling Corp. v. Paramount Service

The maker was induced by fraud and misrepresentations on the part of M to give notes for the purchase price of land. 

These notes were payable to M. Co. originally. President of 

M. Co. tried to sell them to the plaintiff. Plaintiff refused to buy, knowing of the unscrupulous nature of M, and the kind of deal for which the notes were given, and refused to have anything to do with the notes as long as M's name was connected therewith. M then had the maker make new notes with the plaintiff's name substituted as payee. These the plaintiff purchased at a $1,000.00 discount. In a suit by the payee it was held that the payee had such knowledge as amounted to bad faith in taking the notes, and therefore he cannot recover. Mutual Inv. Co. v. Shull (C. C. A. 4th) 28 F. (2d) 830.

In an action by an indorsee against the maker it was held, that evidence that the plaintiff knew that there were charges of crookedness in business transactions against his transferor, was not competent. The N. I. L. was not cited. Setzer v. Deel, 135 

N. C. 428, 47 S. E. 466. Such evidence is not of itself sufficient to put an otherwise bona fide purchaser on notice of fraud. 

Vaughan v. Brandt, 21 Ida. 628, 123 Pac. 591; Standard Ac ceptance Corporation v. Chapin, 277 Mass. 278, 178 N. E. 538, 6 U. of Cin. L. Rev. 240. 

W negotiated worthless checks to a bank through collusion with its bookkeeper. A surety company, which had agreed to reimburse the bank, in seeking to recoup its loss took from Wa note made by the defendant, who had a defense against W. 

Held, the surety company's knowledge of W's fraud upon the bank did not in itself make the issue of notice a question for the jury, so that a verdict was properly directed for the company. American Surety Co. v. Palmer, 211 App. Div. 33, 206 

N. Y. Supp. 817, reversed on another point in 240 N. Y. 63, 147 N. E. 359. The ruling of the Appellate Division on notice is adversely criticized in 10 Corn. L. Q. 356.

In an action by the indorsee bank against the maker, it was evidence of the transferor's fraud that the bank had bought another note made by one of its directors payable to the same transferor, which had been returned on account of its fraud. 

One judge dissented. Bank of Varina v. Sherron, 186 N. C. 

297, 119 S. E. 497.

§ 56  

In a suit for conversion of bonds wrongfully sold by the plaintiff's broker, where the purchasing partner in the defendant's firm had previously been an employee of a wrongdoing brokerage firm and knew that they were in the habit of fraudulently converting their customers' bonds, and had himself previously benefited by such conversions, it was held that on such evidence the jury was justified in finding that the defendant did not purchase the plaintiff's bonds in good faith. Kittredge v. 

Grannis, 244 N. Y. 168, 155 N. E. 88, affirming 215 App. Div. 

486, 214 N. Y. Supp. 33.

Knowledge that the consideration for a former note the plaintiff had purchased from the same payee had failed was held not sufficient to impute bad faith in taking the note in suit. Jewett v. Geiger, Geiger v. Jewett, 263 Mass. 525, 161 N. 

E. 812. 

In the same situation where the additional fact appeared that the plaintiff purchased at a large discount it was held that the jury was justified in finding bad faith. Security Finance. 

Co. v. Ozark Hardware Co., 172 Ark. 562, 289 S. W. 761.

Knowledge of absence of consideration is a sufficient fact to go to the jury on question of bad faith. Renfrow v. Kramer, 341 Ill. 398, 173 N. E. 390, but see cases under section 29 on possibility of one with knowledge of accommodation being a holder in due course.

Where the plaintiff, a discount company, had previously purchased notes from the payee corporation, a number of which had gone to suit on a defense of fraud, which was sustained in only part of the previous cases, it was held that in absence of evidence of bad faith the court properly directed a verdict for the plaintiff. Lamar v. Security Finance Co. (Miss.), 112 So. 577. 

When a note subject to defenses as between maker and payee is indorsed to a person not in the business of buying commercial paper, who has known for several weeks that the note was on sale and that the maker is possessed of ample property to pay it, but buys the note for less than one-third of its face value after inquiring of his attorney whether he would be free from defenses, when the payee who is selling the note writes "without recourse" over his indorsement at the last moment before delivery to the indorsee, and the latter subsequently states that his purchase was risk, there is evidence for the jury that the indorsee took with notice of defenses. Underwood v. Leichtman, 188 Ia. 794, 176 N. W. 683.

It was held that the purchase of the instruments in question by holder's agent without ordinary inquiry into the facts of the case and at a discount, was not sufficient evidence of bad faith to charge the purchaser with notice of violation of the blue sky laws, and failure of consideration. National Bank of Republic v. Beckstead, 68 Utah 421, 250 Pac. 1033. This case expressly

The purchaser of a note secured by a mortgage is not put upon inquiry as to want of consideration from the fact that the property was not worth the face of the note, or that the note was indorsed by a trustee of the payee who had authority to indorse. Barker v. Sartori, 66 Wash. 260, 119 Pac. 611.

Plaintiff paid only one-half its face for a note made payable at a place in Alaska, which was inaccessible for half the year. 

There was no evidence of lack of good faith. Held, no error to direct a judgment for plaintiff, although the maker had a good defense against the payee. McNamara v. Jose, 28 Wash. 461, 68

Where the evidence showed that the plaintiff bought trade acceptances showing on their face that they were taken for a sale of goods, at a twenty per cent discount to cover expenses of collection, and took credit insurance without investigating the transaction, it was held that a directed verdict for the plaintiff was error, his good faith should have been submitted to the jury. Land Finance Corporation v. Sherwin Electric Co., 101 

Vt. 114, 141 Atl. 598.

That a noninterest-bearing note was purchased by a bank when money was much in demand, was a fact which might be considered by the jury on the issue of good faith, and it was error to direct a verdict for the bank.  State Bank v. Sukut, 48 N. D. 987, 187 N. W. 960.

The fact that plaintiff paid only $2,100 or $2,300 for a note for $2,500 does not raise a presumption of knowledge of an infirmity in the note. Miller v. Marks, 46 Utah 257, 148 Pac. 412.

The purchase of a $650 note for $550 to be paid on the installment plan did not constitute notice of defenses. Inadequacy of price is evidence of bad faith, but does not charge the purchaser with notice unless the consideration is grossly inadequate. Negotiable paper may be sold like any other chattel and be transferred at a discount greater than the legal rate of interest. 

Spires v. Jones, 212 Ala. 117, 101 So. 753.

The fact that the plaintiff paid only $100 for a note for $300 is not of itself sufficient to prevent him from being a holder in due course, in the absence of evidence that he had knowledge of fraud in the procurement of the note. Ham v. Merritt, 150 Ky. 

11, 149 S. W. 1131. Nor does the mere fact that the plaintiff who bought at a discount of twenty-five per cent. had bought many notes from the payee at the same discount. 

Pratt v. 

Rounds, 160 Ky. 358, 169 S. W. 848.

When the alleged purchaser of a note was related to an officer of the payee corporation, and was a person of no apparent large means who had never bought a note before and did not know the maker, the question of his good faith should have been submitted to the jury, although his testimony was uncontradicted. 

The N. I. L. was not cited. Breakstone v. Wolfinger, etc., Bldg. 

Co., 172 N. Y. Supp. 158.

It is not within the apparent scope of the authority of the president and general manager of a corporation to pay an extraordinary rate of interest (130 per cent. per annum) for a loan, and the person with whom the contract is made is put upon inquiry. A draft, although payable to the order of the bank forwarding it for collection and credit, taken in connection with the bills of lading attached, bearing on its face unmistakable evidence that it was for the purchase price of cotton sold by the drawer to the drawee, together with specific instructions to "credit our account only when paid," was held sufficient to put the collecting bank on notice that the forwarding bank was not the owner of the draft, and, hence, precluded the collecting bank from being a holder in due course. Before the plaintiff purchased the note in suit it called another bank and inquired as to whether the maker was responsible. The fact that the plaintiff bank knew that a draft by the payee bank on correspondent bank had been dishonored the day before the indorsement of the in rument in suit, was held not sufficient evidence to constitute notice that the payee bank had committed an act of bankruptcy. Merced Security Sav. Bank v. Bent Bros., Inc., 207 Cal. 652, 279 Pac. 765.

Where a corporation has general authority to issue negotiable notes, a note issued by it for ultra vires purposes, e. g., for purchase of stock in another corporation, is not enforceable by the payee, but is good in the hands of a holder in due course. Jefferson Bank v. Chapman-White-Lyons Co., 122 Tenn. 415, 123 

S. W. 641.

A note made by the defendant to a railroad company was indorsed by the latter to the plaintiff, to secure his claim against a realty company. Held, whether or not the railroad acted within its corporate power in securing the debt of another corporation, the plaintiff was not subject to the maker's defense of fraud. The plaintiff was under no duty to anyone to investigate the circumstances and decide at his peril whether the railroad was transgressing the limit of its power. The state alone could object to that. Bad faith in fact was necessary to constitute notice. Failure to use ordinary diligence in following up suggestive facts, or facts arousing suspicion, was not sufficient. The expression found in the old law of Bills and 

Notes, "usual course of business," is not found in sec. 56. The plaintiff was not intentionally colluding in the misappropriation of corporate assets. Gigoux v. Moore, 105 Kan. 361, 184 Pac. 

637 (construing Colo. and Kan. Acts). 

The payee of a note was a foreign corporation which had not registered under the New Hampshire statute, which provides that failure to comply should not affect the validity of a contract made by the corporation, but it could not maintain an action on the contract in the New Hampshire courts until compliance. Held, the indorsee of the note was also barred from suit against the maker if he took with notice of the noncompliance, and the burden of proving want of notice was on the plaintiff. Ensign v. Christiansen, 79 N. H. 353, 109 Atl. 857. 

See the note in 91 Cent. L. J. 50, "Knowledge that payee is a foreign corporation as putting indorsee on inquiry," and other cases under sec. 60.

In violation of Neb. Rev. Stat. 1913, sec. 3291, making it unlawful for an insurance company or agent to dispose of a promissory note received in payment of a premium prior to the delivery of the policy, an agent sold and indorsed such a note to a bank, which knew the facts. The maker did not receive notice that his application for hail insurance had been accepted until after his crops were harvested. Held, the bank can not recover from the maker. Its participation in the unlawful transaction made it not an innocent purchaser. Stockmen's State 

Bank v. Fisher, 106 Neb. 525, 184 N. W. 55.

The shipper of goods drew drafts on the buyer and transferred them with bills of lading to a bank. An agreement for the sale of land provided that on default by the purchaser, the vendor might rescind the agreement and resume possession. § 660 

A dealer in advertising specialties furnished a merchant with a scheme for a piano contest among his customers, and agreed to deliver a piano which would serve as a prize. The merchant gave negotiable promissory notes to the advertiser, who sent an order for the piano to a manufacturer, who had shipped several pianos to merchants on the advertiser's account for similar contests and had received from him notes of merchants in payment. As a considerable sum due for former pianos was unpaid, the manufacturer did not ship any piano to the maker of the notes, but a few days later, these notes were transferred to the manufacturer who credited them on the advertiser's general account as cash. The manufacturer had no actual notice of the terms of the contract between the maker and the payee, but knew in general that the payee was engaged in the piano contest business. The manufacturer sued the merchant, who set up want of good faith. A verdict was directed for the plaintiff. Held, there was evidence to go to the jury on this point. 

The relation between the order for the piano to be shipped to the defendant, and the notes of the defendant would sustain a finding that it became the duty of the plaintiff to inquire as to the real situation between the defendant and the payee. 

Although knowledge of an executory contract does not in itself put an indorsee on inquiry of a possible breach, this indorsee knew additional facts from which the inference could fairly be drawn that the plaintiff had knowledge of a breach. Kelso & Co. v. Ellis, 224 N. Y. 528, 121 N. E. 364, discussed in 33 Harv. 

L. Rev. 273, 19 Col. L. Rev. 222.

When the indorsee knew that the executory contract between the maker and payee could not be performed because of the payee's insolvency, he can not recover from the maker. The 

 was not cited. Allen Cty. State Bank v. Central Stone 

Co., 205 Mo. App. 588, 226 S. W. 665.

When the plaintiff indorsee knew that notes were held by the payee as agent of the makers on condition, it was the plaintiff's duty to make sure that the conditions had been performed. 

McClellan v. Morris, 71 Colo. 304, 206 Pac. 375.

Where a note was secured by a mortgage showing that the transaction was usurious it was held that a purchaser of the note and mortgage was charged with notice of the usury. Deming Inv. Co. v. Clark (Tex. Civ. App.), 89 S. W. (2d) 853.

Extension slips executed and signed by plaintiff as holder and attached to the notes did not serve as notice to the defendant of the fraud committed by the holder's agent in transferring the notes to defendant as security for his own debt where the only indorsement was one in blank. Ragan v. Wardell, 91 F. (2d) 253 (App. D. C.).

The facts that the purchaser saw a signed statement by the makers of a note that it was for full consideration, and that they paid the payees the full face value thereof so as to appear

§ 56 

! that the payee apparently made no profit was held no notice of usury. Guaranty Inv. & Loan Co. v. Stevens, 161 Miss. 473, 137 So. 335.

Cases on the effect of memoranda on the instrument of executory contracts, etc., are collected, supra, pp. 656-658. 

The knowledge afforded by mere indorsements of partial payments on a negotiable note as of the date of its issue, does not make the purchase of the note "amount to bad faith."

Bland v. Fidelity Trust Co., 71 Fla. 499, 71 So. 630. 

It was error to direct a verdict that the plaintiff was not a holder in due course because the evidence showed that revenue stamps were placed on the note at the time of the transfer to it or because the note was payable to the maker and indorsed by him. Ranchmens Trust Co. v. Gill, 113 Kan. 261, 214 Pac. 413. 

Where A deposited a check containing an unqualified indorsement in B bank for collection, it was held that C bank, to whom it was sent for collection, took without notice of A's interest. Deitrick v. MacCarthy, 13 F. Supp. 850 (D. C. D. 

Mass.).

The mere failure to cancel revenue stamps as required by law does not affect the good faith of a purchaser of a note. 

Semble, failure to affix such stamps is evidence of bad faith. 

Farmers Sav. Bank v. Neel, 193 Ia. 685, 187 N. W. 555, 21

A. L. R. 1116. But in view of later Iowa cases discussed sub sec. 52-1, it is doubtful if this dictum is now law in Iowa. See other cases on revenue stamps there collected.

A note payable "to the order of myself" and indorsed by the maker, while not in the ordinary form, does not put a purchaser on inquiry, and it is immaterial that the plaintiff made no inquiry, though only a few miles distant from the maker with telephone communication at hand. Oschenreiter v. Block, 42 

S. D. 151, 173 N. W. 734, 6 A. L. R. 456, with annotation on good faith as affected by the fact that a note is payable to the maker, see also sec. 184, where other cases are cited. 

The maturity of a note was mistakenly dated a year too soon but was correctly stated in the accompanying mortgage. Held, a purchaser of the note and mortgage who knew of the discrepancy in dates had notice of the mistake, which could be reformed so as to prevent suit before the correct date. Naylor v. Lovell, 109 Wash. 409, 186 Pac. 855.

The purchaser of a check was not put on inquiry by two very small red marks beside the signature, placed there at the drawer's request by an official of the bank as notice to the cashier not to pay the check without hearing further from the drawer.

An indorsee took a note calling for "six hundred dollars" ment itself with a marginal notation of "$500.00," and with knowledge the instru- and understanding that the note was only for $500.00, and sued thereon for $500.00. It was held that these facts did not constitute bad faith or put him on notice of fraud. Sed quaere if the instrument was complete and regular on its face under sec. 

52-1 Sandifer v. Stephens, 8 La. App. 546. 

An indorsement waiving presentment and notice and guaranteeing payment by the indorser, was not evidence to support the finding of bad faith in the indorsee. The court also discussed the indorsee's knowledge of specific facts connected with the payee and the note, and held that this was improperly admitted to establish bad faith. Peoples State Bank v. Penello, 59 Cal. App. 174, 210 Pac. 432, 67 Cal. App. 103, 227 Pac. 190. 

Indorsements without recourse do not constitute notice or effect bad faith; see cases cited under sec. 38. Worth Sav. Bank v. Foster, 175 Minn. 293, 221 N. W. 12.  

The plaintiff payee indorsed a note in blank, pledged it, and later got it back on repaying the debt. Subsequently he sold the note to M, placing an inch below his name the unsigned rubberstamp indorsement, "Pay to the order of without re- course -." M sold the note to the defendant, after indorsing his own name immediately below the plaintiff's and above the rubber stamp. The trial court held that M had no recourse against the plaintiff because he had taken the note with that understanding, but that the defendant was a holder in due course to whom the plaintiff was liable on an unqualified indorsement. Held, judgment dismissing action to reform the indorsement affirmed. The rubber stamp indorsement did not constitute notice to the defendant. Kolmitz v. Jansen, 130 Wash. 308, 226 Pac. 1023, 34 A. L. R. 1369, with note.

The fact that a negotiable note shows by perforation on its edge that it was detached from a larger contract does not affect the purchaser's good faith or charge him with notice of the provisions of the contract. Crane v. Guaranty Finance Corp., 

141 Miss. 692, 105 So. 485, 11 St. Louis L. Rev. 48, 26 Colum. L. 

Rev. 478. See also detachment cases sec. 124.

Obvious alterations of an instrument constitute notice. 

Mechanics Am. Nat. Bank v. Helmbacher, 199 Mo. App. 173, 201 S. W. 383, certiorari denied in State, ex rel., Bank v. Sturgis, 276 Mo. 559, 208 S. W. 458.

In an action against the drawer, held, that the bona fide purchaser for value from the payee of a check is none the less a holder in due course because of the erasure of an indorsement of a subsequent party of which a plausible explanation was given at the time of plaintiff's purchase. Goetting v. Day, 87 N. Y. 

Supp. 510,

§ 56 

The fact that a check was payable to a person in his fictitious trade name was held not a suspicious circumstance to convey notice to one who took it in exchange for a personal debt and cash. Cook v. Derewicz, 102 Pa. Super. Ct. 565, 157 Atl. 360, 6 Temple L. Rev. 425. 

The fact that the maker presents to a bank for discount a note indorsed in blank by the payee does not constitute notice of wrongful possession by the maker. Mass. Nat. Bank v. Snow, 187 Mass. 159, 72 N. E. 959.

Where the collecting bank received for collection and credit a check unrestrictedly indorsed by both the payee and the forwarding bank, it took without notice that the forwarding bank was the payee's agent for collection.  

Ruden v. Agricultural Finance Corporation, 60 S. D. 493, 244 

N. W. 919. 

Municipal bonds payable to bearer are negotiable instruments. The fact that the mayor of a municipality had signed, as mayor, negotiable municipal bonds, which he wrongfully appropriated and pledged to secure a loan to himself, is not sufficient to charge the pledgee, who had no knowledge of the pledgeor's lack of authority, with notice of the pledgeor's defect of title. Borough of Montvale v. Peoples Bank, 74 N. 

J. Law 464, 67 Atl. 67. The same result was reached as to a pledge of corporate bonds by an officer of the issuing corporation. 

Nickey Bros. v. Lonsdale Mfg. Co., 149 Tenn. 1, 257 S. W. 403, 31 A. L. R. 1383.

Fiduciaries 

The Uniform Fiduciaries Act which has been adopted in Uniform fifteen states, see 9 U. L. A. Supp., materially affects the ques- Act tions involved in the following cases of instruments drawn by or payable to trustees, agents, partners, officers or corporations, etc. 

A different statute in Missouri is cited, infra, p. 672. 

A certificate of deposit payable to "A, trustee," or to "A, trustee of B," gives actual notice that it represents a trust fund, and an indorsee is bound to inquire as to the right of the trustee to dispose of it. Ford v. Brown, 114 Tenn. 467, 88 S. W. 1036; 

Barry v. Hensley, 170 Tenn. 598, 98 S. W. (2d) 102.

But he is not bound to inquire into the maker's defenses against the payee-trustee. Long v. City Nat. Bank of Commerce (Tex. Civ. App.), 256 S. W. 1006, noted in 24 Colum. L. Rev. 

538. One judge dissented. The majority also held that the indorsement of the names of the three trustees by one of them as agent did not constitute notice of the maker's defenses. 

The word "trustee" after the name of the payee, puts the purchaser upon notice as to the trustee's authority to sell and re-

The word "trustee" after the payee's name does not impute bad faith to his indorsee or charge him with defenses arising from other sources. W. J. Howey v. Cole, Special Deputy Com missioner of Finance of the State of Missouri, 222 Mo. App. 

1200, 4 S. W. (2d) 861, 7 Tex. L. Rev. 175; see also same case, 269 S. W. 955. 

The fact that a trustee deposits a check payable to him as trustee to his personal account, at a bank where he has no account as trustee, gives the bank no reason to believe that he is acting dishonestly, and the bank is not liable to the cestui though the trustee fails to account for the proceeds of the check. Batchelder v. Central Nat. Bank, 188 Mass. 25, 73 N. E. 1024; U. S. Fidelity & G. Co. v. Home Bank, 77 W. Va. 665, 88 S. E. 109; Miami 

County Bank v. State, 61 Ind. App. 360, 112 N. E. 40; Bischoff v. 

Yorkville Bank, 218 N. Y. 106, 112 N. E. 759, L. R. A. 1916F, 1059. See also Allen v. Puritan Trust Co., 211 Mass. 409, 97 

N. E. 916, L. R. A. 1915C, 518; Allen v. Fourth Nat. Bank, 224 

Mass. 239, 112 N. E. 650. The N. I. L. was not cited in the foregoing cases. Kendall v. Fidelity Trust Co., 230 Mass. 238, 119 N. E. 861..

Where notes payable to bearer and held by X as trustee for his mother-in-law showed on their face that X was the trustee in the deed of trust securing their payment, whether the bank who took the notes as security for X's personal indebtedness was a bona fide transferee was held a jury question, when in addition the bank knew that X habitually acted as trustee for his mother-in-law and that he was financially embarrassed. 

Sawyer v. National Bank of Commerce of Norfolk, 166 Va. 439, 186 S. E. 1. 

Where a note was payable to "X, trustee" and the holder took it in part payment of a personal debt and cash, the court said the holder was charged with notice of the provisions of the trust. Owens v. Nagel, 334 Ill. 96, 165 N. E. 165. Sed quaere?

The statement seems contra to the weight of authority and was unnecessary to the decision, as the lower court clearly erred in refusing to admit evidence of defect of title and in directing a verdict after the plaintiff gave no evidence of good faith. The most that can be said for the position of the court is that under the circumstances of the case there might be evidence for the

§ 56 

jury on the question of the plaintiff's good faith. The question of the effect of the term "trustee" as notice in a similar case was properly disposed of in Meyer Milling Co. v. Strohfeld, 222 

Mo. App. 1194, 4 S. W. (2d) 864; see also 20 S. W. (2d) 963, 964. 

A trustee under a trust deed securing bonds pledged them as security for his own pre-existing debt with the plaintiff who knew he was trustee but not that he was acting in breach of trust. Held, the plaintiff was in good faith. Marine Nat. Exchange Bank of Milwaukee v. Kallzimmers Mfg. Co., 293 U. S. 

357, 79 L. Ed. 427, 55 S. C. 226. The court considered itself bound by Pollard v. Tobin, 211 Wis. 405, 247 N. W. 453, where the same trustee was engaged in similar defaults. 

A receiver of a bank is not a holder in due course of paper Receivers formerly owned by the bank. Young v. Victory, 112 Fla. 66, 150 So. 624.

X, a trustee in bankruptcy for Y, opened an account with the defendant in the name of "X, trustee." Checks were deposited in this account, usually payable to the order of "X" or "X, trustee," and indorsed "X, trustee." One was payable to the order of "X, trustee in bankruptcy for Y, bankrupt,' and similarly indorsed. Withdrawals from the account were made by checks most of which were countersigned by the clerk of the U. S. District Court, usually with "In re Y" on the face. 

Other checks were drawn by X to his own order without countersignature, and some were deposited in the individual account of X with the defendant. These were misappropriations of the trust funds. The defendant received no benefit from these wrongful deposits, and had no actual notice of the United States 

Supreme Court General Order in Bankruptcy requiring checks drawn on such an account to be countersigned by a judge, referee, or clerk of court. The defendant bank was held liable to a surety company, which had reimbursed the estate for the misappropriations. The defendant was chargeable with notice of the bankruptcy, and of countersignatures which were formal notice of the provisions of trust. Fidelity & Deposit Co. of Mary land v. Queens County Trust Co., 226 N. Y. 225, 123 N. E. 370, reargument denied, 226 N. Y. 711, 123 N. E. 864.

When a check payable to “E, Trustee" was deposited in the defendant bank to the account of "E, special," held, the defendant did not have notice of the misappropriation of trust funds. The rule of Ward v. City Trust Co., 192 N. Y. 61, 84

N. E. 585, and other cases of instruments payable to a corporation does not apply since here the instrument was collected according to its tenor for the account of the very person who is named as payee. "The transactions of banking in a great financial center are not to be clogged and their pace slackened by

The plaintiff drew a check payable to the order of the defendant brokers and delivered it to his agent M, so that the defendants could use the money for investment on behalf of the plaintiff. Levy, 186 App. Div. 767, 174 N. Y. 

Supp. 828, affg. 170 N. Y. Supp. 930. 

Underhill Moore, in his article, "The Right of the Remitter of a Bill or Note," 20 Colum. L. Rev. 749, 759, while recognizing that the payee can be a holder in due course if without notice, points out that it is not business practice for checks of individuals or corporations, except bankers or banks, to be drawn payable to the order of a person other than the purchaser or creditor who first acquires them from the bank for value. Personal checks are not ordinarily purchased by third persons to be remitted by them to the payee. Consequently a third person offering a check to the payee commonly is, and always offers the appearance of being, agent for the drawer, and the form of the check therefore puts the payee on inquiry as to the scope of the agency of the possessor. See also, the note in 19 Colum. L. Rev. 339.

Walker v. Bartlesville State Bank, 91 Okla. 231, 216 Pac. 928. The treasurer of a corporation drew checks as treasurer payable to his own order, and indorsed them to his individual creditor in payment of a debt. Fillebrown v. Hayward, 190 Mass. 472, 77 N. E. 45. 

In Gilman v. F. O. Bailey Carriage Co., 125 Mo. 108, 131

But where a treasurer drew checks, as treasurer, payable directly to his creditor, the transaction showed on its face an

§ 56 

appropriation of corporate money to pay the individual debt of the treasurer, and the transaction was bad, unless shown to be good, and the creditor's rights depended on whether the transaction was good, and the question of good faith did not arise. 

Johnson & Kettell Co. v. Longley Luncheon Co., 207 Mass. 52, 92 N. W. 1035.

On the other hand, when the defendant seller of goods at the request of the individual buyer sent a messenger to an individual to get the money for payment, and he returned with a check payable to the defendant, signed by a corporation through its president, in return for which the goods were delivered, the defendant was a holder in due course as against the corporation and did not have notice that the check was an unauthorized use of corporate funds to pay the debts of an officer other than the president. The preceding case was distinguished. 

McLaughlin v. Paine Furniture Co., 245 Mass. 377, 139 N. E.

542.

A bank bought a note from the payee, a manufacturing company. The president of the bank was a director of the company. 

The company took the note on an agreement with the maker that it should be renewed until the goods for which it was given were sold. The president of the bank had been asked if the bank would discount notes for the company, if taken for goods sold to responsible parties, but it did not appear that he had any knowledge of the agreement as to renewal, and such knowledge could not fairly be inferred from the surrounding circumstances. 

Held, that a finding that the bank had no notice of the infirmity in the note was not erroneous. First Nat. Bank v. Fairfield Auto 

Co., 91 Conn. 260, 99 Atl. 577.

A corporation owning notes of the face value of $10,000 and interest, gave them to its vice-president to sell. He told his creditor, the defendant, that he was authorized to sell at a price which would net the corporation $9,000, and was to have the excess for his commission, which he would apply on his indebtedness. The defendant bought the notes for more than $10,000, and applied the excess over $9,000 on the vice-president's debt. He paid $9,000 to the corporation but did not inform it about the transaction respecting the excess. The defendant collected the notes. Held, it was not liable to the corporation for the excess. The  was not cited. Widlar v. Federal L. Ins. Co., 215 Ill. App. 5.
