§ 56 corporation. Sec. 56 was not cited. Lebo State Bank v. Booth, 111 Kan. 222, 206 Pac. 743.

The treasurer of a town has no power to indorse a check payable to the order of the town except for deposit for collection to the account of the town. Therefore his indorsement of such a check to a third person, who deposited it in defendant bank, is notice to the bank of defect in the title of the depositor. Fillebrown v. Hayward, 190 Mass. 472, 77 N. E. 45, distinguished, because there the treasurer was treasurer of a private corporation.  Franklin Sav. Bank v. International Trust Co., 215 Mass. 231, 102 N. E. 363.

A note forged by the treasurer of a town in the name of the town, as maker, was made payable at defendant bank, where the town had a deposit. The bank paid the note in good faith on the verbal order of the treasurer with the proceeds of a check by a third person, which was payable to the order of the town and indorsed by the treasurer to the bank. Held, that the bank, not being a purchaser of the note, was not put upon inquiry, and was not liable to the town. The  was not cited. City of 

Newburyport v. First Nat. Bank, 216 Mass. 304, 103 N. E. 782.

A bank, which received and credited to the account of a depositor a check payable to the treasurer of a town and indorsed by him as treasurer, is chargeable with notice that the check was the property of the town, and that the treasurer had no authority to indorse the check for circulation, but only for deposit and collection for the account of the town. The N. I. L. was not cited.

Where defendant bank accepted as deposits in X's personal account drafts drawn payable to X as treasurer of plaintiff corporation knowing that they were corporate property and honored his withdrawals as treasurer without actual knowledge of his embezzlement, it was held that defendant had acted in good faith and was not charged with knowledge of the embezzlement particularly in view of the fact that the corporation had made no complaint about such transactions over a period of six years. 

Quanah, Acme & Pacific Ry: Co. v. Wichita State Bank & Trust 

Co., affd., 127 Tex. 407, 93 S. W. (2d) 701, 106 A. L. R. 821 with note.

X sold his business, but not the credits, to the plaintiff corporation of which he became vice-president and general manager.

RIGHTS OF § 56 THE HOLDER 

A note payable to a bank and delivered by the maker to the cashier was indorsed to the president for value before maturity without actual notice of defenses. Held, the president could not recover from the maker. By virtue of his office, he was chargeable with notice that the note was without consideration and a fictitious purported asset upon the books of the bank in violation of the banking laws. Two judges dissented. McCarthy v. Kepreta, 24 N. D. 395, 139 N. W. 992, Ann. Cas. 1915A, 834, 48 L. R. A. (N.S.) 65, with note, "Is officer or employee of corporation chargeable with its knowledge of infirmities in commercial paper purchased from it?" Accord, Denver Suburban 

H. & W. Co. v. Fugate, 63 Colo. 423, 168 Pac. 33; McFerson v. 

Bristol, 73 Colo. 214, 214 Pac. 395; Reiter v. Pollard, 75 Colo. 

203, 225 Pac. 222; Hughett v. Shain, 253 Ky. 330, 69 S. W. (2d) 688, not citing the ; Hardin v. Dale, 45 Okla. 694, 146 Pac. 717, L. R. A. 1915D, 1099, with note; Duncan v. Carson, 127 Va. 306, 103 S. E. 665.

Contra, an officer of a corporation purchasing a note from it is not affected with notice of the maker's defenses received by other officers of the corporation. Sec. 56 was not cited. Pitman v. Walker, 187 Cal. 667, 203 Pac. 739. Accord, Dodo v. Stocker, 74 Colo. 95, 219 Pac. 222, approved in 8 Minn. Law Rev. 336; 

72 Univ. Pa. Law Rev. 317.

In a suit by a director-payee against a corporation-maker on a note given to him to reimburse him for money expended after the defendant's property had been leased to another corporation, it was held that plaintiff as a director of the corporation was chargeable with notice of the fact that the note was without consideration. Sumner Coal-Mining Co. v. Pleasant, 127 Okla. 174, 259 Pac. 1055. The N. I. L. was not cited and the case is clearly wrong on point of notice. The case probably should be rested on the proposition that the payee is not a holder in due course in Oklahoma, which is also erroneous; see cases under sec. 52. 

The fact that the holder is an officer of a corporation for whose stock the instrument in question was given, under false representations as to its value by agents of the corporation, does not charge the holder with bad faith even though he may have known the condition of the corporation and of the sale of stock in question. Ingold v. Daly Bank & Trust Co. of Anaconda (Cal. App.), 281 Pac. 1075.

A purchaser of a note from a corporation in which he is a stockholder is not put on notice as to the methods by which the corporation acquired the note. Sec. 56 was not cited. Murphy v. Estle, 75 Okla. 75, 182 Pac. 83.

Where the note was obtained through fraud, and the present holder was found to be connected with the payee corporation and was a medium for collection, it was held that he is not a holder in due course. McCurdy v. Stevens, 30 Ohio App. 545, 165 N. E. 855.

§ 684 

 Sec. 57. Rights of Holder in Due Course. 

A holder in due course holds the instrument free from any defect of title of prior parties, and free from¹ defenses available to prior parties among themselves, and may enforce payment of the instrument for the full amount thereof against all parties liable thereon. 

Cross Reference: §§ 16. 28, 51, 52, 55, 88, 119, 120, 124, 182, 191, 5, 13 to 15, 23, 50, 54, 60 to 62, 65(3), 66, 71, 85, 89, 121, 122, 179.

ANNOTATIONS 

The meaning of "defect of title" and "defenses," and the effect of this section on real defenses, are discussed under secs. 52(4) and 55. "For the full This section changes the law of Tennessee and under it a amount' holder in due course may recover the full amount of the instrument, not merely the amount paid for it. Jefferson Bank v. 

Chapman-White-Lyons Co., 122 Tenn. 415, 123 S. W. 641. 

The purchase of a negotiable promissory note at a heavy discount (two-thirds of the face value) is not of itself enough to prevent the buyer from being a holder in due course and recovering the full amount. Lassas v. McCarty, 47 Oreg. 474, 84 Pac. 

76. See also, McNamara v. Jose, 28 Wash. 461, 68 Pac. 903; 

Enslen v. Mechanics & Metals Nat. Bank, 255 Fed. 527, 166 C. 

C. A. 595, certiorari denied, 249 U. S. 617, 39 S. Ct. 391 (Ala.), and other cases under sec. 56.

In the hands of a holder in due course, a note is not subject to set offs or compensation between the maker and the payee. Hibernia Bank and Trust Co. v. Champagne, 8 La. App. 

664; Thompson v. Crow, 3 La. App. 158; Federal Reserve Bank of Boston v. Gray-United Stoves, 290 Mass. 77, 194 N. E. 709.

In a suit by a holder in due course on one of a series of notes constituting a lien on property, after cancellation of the balance of the series for fraud, it was held that he was entitled to payment of the full face value of the note out of the proceeds of the property on foreclosure sale and not in the ratio which such note bore to the whole amount of the series. Pearson v. Scott, 168 Ark. 6, 269 S. W. 370. 

The plaintiff indorsed a note after delivery by the maker, and was obliged to take it up, but paid less than face value. 

Held, he may recover the full amount from the maker, and is not barred by fraud on the maker of which he had no knowledge. The  was not cited. Adolphus v. Kendall, 205

Ill. App. 316. It does not appear whether the plaintiff indorsed for the accommodation of the payee or was a former holder.

2 The words "for the full amount thereof" are omitted in the English 

Act. B. E. A. s. 38 (2).

The fact that a pledgee sold the collateral in violation of law does not prevent the innocent purchaser from becoming a holder in due course, and from recovering in full thereon. Stevens v. Pierce, 109 Okla. 106, 235 Pac. 174. decisions a holder 

In Conqueror Trust Co. v. Bayless Drug Co., 75 Okla. 288, Miscellaneous 

183 Pac. 419, S. C. sec. 56, the court refused to subscribe to the protecting view that the telephone, telegraph and other means of rapid communication had deprived the rules of the law merchant of their usefulness, and held that a purchaser before maturity was not under obligation to communicate with the maker before taking the instrument. 

If the maker of notes negligently allowed them to get into circulation, he was estopped to deny a valid delivery in a suit by a holder in due course. Semble, a negotiable promissory note has no legal inception or valid existence until it has been deliv ered according to the intent of the parties. Cannon v. Dillehay, 17 Ala. App. 294, 84 So. 549. In view of the express language of sec. 16, negligence seems immaterial.

Where a bank issues a cashier's check to the payee, and a creditor of the payee attempts to garnishee the amount, a holder in due course is entitled to payment as against the garnisheeing creditor. Causey v. Eiland (Ark.), 1 S. W. (2d) 1008.

The fact that an indorser's signature was placed on the instrument by mistake is no defense against a holder in due course. 

Southern Bank & Trust Co. v. Sumter Pine Co., 151 S. C. 274, 148 S. E. 887.

A holder in due course is not affected by subsequent knowledge of defenses. Gibson v. First Nat. Bank, 196 Ky. 119, 244 

S. W. 290; not citing the ; Commercial Nat. Bank v.

Employers' Liability Assur. Corp. v. Greenfield, 316 Pa. 477, 

175 Atl. 403.

The fact that a bank, which is a holder in due course of a check, obtained by the payee by fraud, sues the drawer alone and not the payee-indorser is not evidence that the bank is no longer the holder, but is suing for the benefit of the indorser. Choteau 

Trust & Banking Co. v. Smith, 133 Ky. 418, 118 S. W. 279.

A trading partnership is liable on negotiable paper executed by the managing partner for accommodation when this fact does not appear on the face of the paper, and it is in the hands of a holder in due course. The N. I. L. was not cited. Power 

Grocery Co. v. Hinton, 187 Ky. 171, 218 S. W. 1013. 

When a broker by fraud obtained property and a negotiable note from his principal to be exchanged for other property, and transferred the note to a holder in due course, it was error to order the return of the note to the principal, but the broker was ordered to repay his principal the amount of the note or to

Several notes received from the buyer of a chattel were indorsed by the payee to the defendant, a holder in due course. 

One note had already been paid to the payee. After the buyer had paid two notes to the defendant, he agreed with the payee for a rescission of the sale, without any consent by the defendant, and returned the chattel to the payee. Citizens Nat. Bank v.

After the negotiation to a holder in due course of notes secured by a grantor's lien, the grantor-payee brought a suit in equity against the grantee-maker to enforce the lien, not joining the indorsee, and obtained a decree fixing the amount of the lien. The grantee-maker, who had no notice of the negotiation, paid almost all the amount due on the notes to the grantorpayee. Held, these payments and the decree constituted no defense to a subsequent equity suit brought by the holder in due course against the grantee-maker to enforce the grantor's lien. 

The holder in due course of the notes could enforce the lien free from equities. It was also held that the purchaser of one note after maturity was subject to the defense of the decree and payment. Morgan v. Farmington Coal & Coke Co., 97 W. Va. 83, 124 S. E. 591. For adverse criticism of the holding as to the purchaser of the overdue note, see under sec. 58.

Sec. 58. When Subject to Original Defenses. 

In the hands of any holder other than a holder in due course, a negotiable instrument is subject to the same defenses as if it were non-negotiable.' But a holder² who derives his title through a holder in due course, and who is not himself a party to any fraud or illegality affecting the instrument, has all the rights of such former holder in respect to all parties prior to the latter.

G purchased an undivided one-fifth of land, which was held as security for a note under a deed of trust, assuming and agreeing to pay one-fifth of the note. Subsequently G purchased the note, which was indorsed by the payee to the plaintiff, G's wife, as a gift to her from her husband. A third person subsequently bought four-fifths of the land and paid four-fifths of the amount of the note to G, but did not get the note. Held, that the plaintiff can not recover from the makers on the note. Greer v. Orchards, 175 Mo. App. 494, 161 S. W. 875. It is submitted that the decision is erroneous, at all events, as to four-fifths of the amount of the note. For there was no equity existing against the note at the time the plaintiff took it. If the payee or other holder of a note indorses it as a gift to another and there is no equity against the donor, the donee will not be affected by equities subsequently arising, such as payment, between the maker and the donor. 

Milnes v. Dawson, 5 Exch. 948; First Nat. Bk. v. Wood, 128 N. Y. 

35, 27 N. E. 1020. And this case is even stronger in favor of the plaintiff, because the note was never held by the husband but was indorsed directly to the wife by the payee, against whom there was no equity. If it had been shown that the wife really held the note and was suing as agent for her husband, the case would be different, but this was not done. 

Only defenses existing at the time of its transfer affect a promissory note, although it was not indorsed by the payee.

Therefore, where a note was given for advances to be made subsequently, failure of the payee to make the advances will not prevent recovery by the assignee. Marling v. Fitzgerald, 138 Wis. 93, 120 N. W. 388. See note criticising this case, supra, sec. 49.

Sec. 58 was not cited. Cosmopolitan Trust Co. v. Leonard Watch Co., 249 

Mass. 14, 143 N. E. 827.

It was held that the defense of payment was good. 

Sacks v. Sherman, 105 Conn. 73, 134 Atl. 240; Hibbard v. Collins, 127 Me. 383, 143 Atl. 600.

The purchaser of an overdue note secured by a grantor's lien sued the grantee maker to enforce the lien. Held, the plaintiff was subject to the defense that after the negotiation, the grantor payee in a suit to which the indorsee was not a party, had obtained a decree against the grantee maker for discharge of the lien, and had been paid by the maker. Morgan v. Farmington 

Coal & Coke Co., 97 W. Va. 83, 124 S. E. 591.

The holding on this point, which was a minor feature of the case and not discussed by the court, is contrary to the correct rule that even an indorsee after maturity is subject only to equities existing at the time of his purchase. It is arguable, however, that the result of the case necessarily follows from the language of sec. 58, which was cited by the court; for the assignee of a non-negotiable instrument is subject to the defense of payment by the maker to the assignor prior to knowledge by the maker of the assignment, and sec. 58 declares in effect that the purchaser of an overdue negotiable instrument is subject to the same defenses as if it were non-negotiable. 

On the question what defenses can be set up on non-negotiable instruments, see Machen v. Cape Girardeau, etc., Ry. Co. (Mo. App.), 242 S. W. 131, not citing the N. I. L.

The maker of a negotiable promissory note made payments on fenses against account thereof after maturity to the holder, an indorsee from party the payee. Thereafter the holder transferred the note to plainintermediate -Set-offs and counterclaims tiff, who paid value, bona fide, and without notice of the payments, which had not been indorsed on the note. Held, that the rule that a purchaser after maturity takes subject to equities. between the original parties has no application to equities affecting intermediate holders or indorsers, and that plaintiff could hold the maker. The N. I. L. was not cited. Reardon v. Cockrell, 54 Wash. 400, 103 Pac. 457, 50 L. R. A. (N.S.) 87.

It is submitted that this case is wrong. Payment to a holder after maturity is an equity which attaches to the instrument itself and travels with it into any hands, the instrument being then subject to the same defenses as if it were non-negotiable (sec. 58). The court was evidently thinking of set-offs and other defenses arising out of collateral matters as to which there was a conflict of authority, some courts holding that all such defenses travel with the instrument after maturity, whether between the original parties or between intermediate parties and the maker, other courts holding that only such defenses of the maker against the payee travel with the instrument. 1 

Ames, Cases Bills & Notes, 759 n. See criticism of this case, Chafee, Rights in Overdue Paper, 31 Harvard Law Rev. 1123, n. 56. 

So also an agreement to set off a bank deposit against an indorser's liability on a note is good against a purchaser after maturity. Amite Bank & Trust Co. v. Standard Box & Veneer 

Co., 177 La. 954, 149 So. 532.

The word "defenses" used in this section was held sufficiently broad to cover set-offs especially where notes transferred after maturity were subject to set-offs before the passage of the N. I. L. 

Smith v. Fulton, 51 Ohio App. 12, 199 N. E. 219, 10 U. of

Cin. L. Rev. 326. Contra, Stegal v. Union Bank & Federal 

Trust Co., 163 Va. 417, 176 S. E. 438, 95 A. L. R. 582, where the court in an exhaustive opinion cited the history of set-off and the Commissioners' notes to the effect that this subject was

purposely omitted from the Act, and left to the conflicting rules -Set-offs under the various statutes. "Defenses" in this section also includes statutory set-offs and a purchaser after maturity is subject to such set-offs as in cases of non-negotiable paper even though such was not the law before the Act. Litcher v. North City Trust Co., 111 Pa. Super Ct. 1,

In Justice v. Stonecipher, 267 Ill. 448, 108 N. E. 722, the Overdue plaintiff intrusted negotiable notes, made by third parties, pay- claims of able to plaintiff and indorsed in blank to one S for safe keeping. and patent 

S, without authority, pledged the notes after maturity to defend- equities ant to secure a loan to S made by defendant in good faith and without notice of plaintiff's rights. Plaintiff sued defendant for an accounting and for general relief. Held, on the authority of Young Men's Christian Assn., etc., Co. v. Rockford Nat. Bank, 179 Ill. 599, 54 N. E. 297, 46 L. R. The case cited as authority was upon an instrument made before the Negotiable Instruments Law was adopted in the state, as was also the similar case of Gardiner v. 

Beacon Trust Co., 190 Mass. 27, 76 N. E. 455, 2 L. R. A. (N.S.) 

767, in which the same result was reached. But the principal case being upon an instrument made after the adoption of the Negotiable Instruments Law, it became necessary to consider the effect of the act upon this question as to which there had previously been a conflict of authority. The Illinois court held that under sec. 59 the purchaser from one having defective title, had only the burden of bringing himself within the provision of the fourth clause of sec. 52, defining a holder in due course, that is, that he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating it, thus ignoring the requirement of the second clause of sec. 52 that the purchaser should become a holder before the instrument was overdue. 

The title of S was certainly defective because he negotiated the instrument in breach of faith (sec. 55). Sec. 59 then made it necessary for the purchaser from S to show that he was a holder in due course, and to do this he must bring himself within the definition in sec. 52, and that he could not do, because he did not take before maturity. If the purchaser in such a case could hold the instrument, it must be on some principle of estoppel, in spite of the fact that he was not a holder in due course, and it is just the conflict on this question which the provisions of the act seem intended to abrogate. The only alternative seems to be to treat secs. 52 to 59 inclusive as intending to apply only to defenses to obligations on the instrument, whether of parties primarily or secondarily liable, leaving the cases of equitable claims to ownership of the instrument to be dealt with as omitted cases, under sec. 196, that is in accordance with the law merchant of the respective states, in which case the former conflict would continue. W. 504. paper- claims of Latent equities In an action in equity to establish priority of a lien and to enjoin foreclosure of a deed of trust of a prior date, the bank held a note of the payee secured by a deed of trust as collateral security for a note by the payee to the bank. It was agreed between the bank and the payee that the maker of the note should make a note with the bank named as payee, and execute a new deed of trust in satisfaction of the original note. This was done and the old note and deed of trust were delivered up to the payee, the bank, however, negligently failing to mark the old note and deed of trust paid. After maturity the payee negotiated the old note and deed of trust to a holder, a purchaser for value, who brought suit to foreclose thereon. It was held that the note which the bank surrendered to the payee, although overdue, was negotiable, and it seems to be the settled rule that the assignee of overdue negotiable paper takes it with notice of all the equities or defenses which the maker may have, but he does not take it with notice of the secret equities of third parties, or those arising out of collateral transactions. Wilkinson v. Lore, Superintendent of Banks, 149 Miss. 523, 115 So. 707. 

Warrants issued by a city and payable to the order of a payee were presented by them to the city treasurer who indorsed them "Not paid for lack of funds." The warrants were later indorsed in blank by the payees and transferred to a bank which deposited them with the city treasurer as indemnity against loss of city funds deposited in the bank. After the bank failed, the city delivered the warrants for use during litigation against it

§ 58 to an attorney, who pledged them to the defendant as collateral Latent equities for his own debt. Held, the city could not recover possession of the warrants from the defendant. Such a warrant is a negotiable instrument for purposes involving its title, although it differs from negotiable paper in one respect, that it is open to any defense which might have been made to the claim upon which it is founded.  Marcus v. Offner, 103

If in the case of Bank of Willard v. Pennsylvania, etc., Brick

An equity intervening after a bona fide purchase will affect a subsequent transferee after maturity.

But the court stated that the plaintiff "having taken the note after it became due, although from one to whom it had been indorsed before maturity, occupies no better position than if it had taken the note at the time it did from the payee," and, "A transferee from a prior transferee occupies no safer position than does a transferee from the original payee. The controlling fact always is whether the note was due at the time it was transferred, and not the relation of the transferrer to it." This language is too broad and does not represent the law. It has long been the common law that one who takes from a holder in due course takes the rights of such holder in due course, except in the case of a transfer to a party to any fraud or illegality affecting the instrument, as provided in sec. 58. And sees. 58 and 59 of the Negotiable Instruments Law confirm the right of a holder, though not himself entitled to be regarded as a holder in due course, to rely upon the rights of a holder in due

§ 58 course through whom he claims title. He gets at least the title of his transferrer and, if this is not defective, neither is that of the purchaser after maturity.

If the court had interpolated the words "and to whom it had been paid" after the words "indorsed before maturity" in the first of the statements quoted above and had omitted the second statement altogether, the whole discussion would have been less liable to misconstruction. An amendment to sec. 58 has been suggested in order to make certain that a purchaser with notice should not be able to cure a defect in his title by the procedure above described. It is argued, however, that a party taking with notice, although not the payee, becomes a party to the fraud or illegality by taking it with notice, and still more so when he transfers it, and that, therefore, he can not recover on the instrument upon re-acquiring from a holder in due course. And this position seems to be supported by Berenson v. Conant, 214 Mass. 129, 101 N. E. 60, and Bank of Meno v. Coulter, 94 Okla. 213, 221 Pac. 495; and Comstock v. Buckley, 141 Wis. 228, 124 N. W. 414.

But sec. 121 would not affect a party who reacquires an instrument after a transfer by indorsement without recourse or by delivery of an instrument payable to bearer.

To the preceding argument by Professor Brannan, the following may be added. A taker with notice of fraud does not by that fact alone become "a party to the fraud," for such a view would deny protection to one who buys, with notice of the fraud, from a holder in due course. But the holder with notice in Horan v. Mason became "a party to the fraud" when he sold the instrument to a holder in due course and thus cut off the defense of fraud. That such conduct is a tort to the victim of the fraud is shown by the note in 27 L. R. A. 519. Having become a party to the fraud by this transfer, he can not afterwards take back the instrument from the holder in due course and enforce it free of the defense of fraud. It should also be noted that under sec. 55 such a negotiation amounts to fraud. 

Professor Brannan also overlooked sec. 50, which provides that upon reacquisition a holder acquires no rights against intervening parties to whom he was liable. It also seems to follow that he would acquire no rights from them.

The payee acquired three notes by fraud from the defendant maker, indorsed them in blank, and sold them to the plaintiff, who transferred them to a holder in due course. After maturity of two notes, the holder in due course indorsed them all without recourse to the plaintiff. The trial judge instructed the jury that if the plaintiff held the notes by indorsement for value from a bona fide holder, he was entitled to recover unless the defendant had satisfied them by the greater weight of the evidence that the plaintiff was a participant in the fraudulent conduct by which the notes were secured. The jury found for the defendant.

The plaintiff employed K to purchase land, and gave K the purchase price, which K paid to the vendor, who conveyed title to M, a "straw man" acting for K. Without the plaintiff's knowledge, K caused M to execute a note for $4,000, secured by a deed of trust on the land, which K delivered to the payee for value and retained the proceeds. The "straw man" subsequently conveyed the land to the plaintiff. At maturity of the note, K procured an extension and at the expiration of the extension paid the full amount to the payee who indorsed the note in blank and delievered it with the deed of trust to K. The defendant bank, without notice of the fraud, took the note and deed of trust from K as collateral for his individual debt. Held, the note and deed of trust should be cancelled. Since K was a party to the original fraud, the note when reacquired by him was affected by the same infirmity which made it unenforceable by him in the first place, and the defendant bank having acquired the note after maturity was not a holder in due course but was subject to the same defenses as if the note had been non-negotiable. To the argument that K was a purchaser from the original holder in due course," whose title therefore passed to the defendant, the court replied that the transaction of reacquisition was a payment and not a purchase. Since the note was signed by the straw man for K's accommodation, it was paid by an accommodated party, and therefore discharged under sec. 119(2). Payment is a good defense against the defendant bank, which was not a holder in due course. Hoeley v. South 

Side Bank, 280 Mo. 336, 217 S. W. 504.

Sec. 59. Who Deemed Holder in Due Course. 

Every holder is deemed prima facie to be a holder in due course; but when it is shown that the title of any person who has negotiated the instrument was defective, the burden is on the holder to prove that he or some person under whom he claims acquired the title as holder in due course.' But the last mentioned rule does not apply in favor of a party who became bound on the instrument prior to the acquisition of such defective title.²

ANNOTATIONS 

This section is declaratory of the common law. The Negotiable 

Instrument Act is in the main a codification of the common-law rules. Where it lays down a new rule it controls; but where its language is consistent with the rule previously recognized, it should be construed as simply declaratory of the law as it was before the adoption of the Act. Campbell v. Fourth Nat. Bank, 137 Ky. 555, 126 S. W. 114.

This section applies to an accommodation note obtained from the accommodating party by fraudulent representations of the payee. Kennedy v. Spilka, 72 Misc. Rep. 89, 129 N. Y. Supp.

In Stannard v. Orleans Flour Co., 93 Neb. 389, 140 N. W. 

636, it was held, not citing the , that where there is no allegation in the pleadings that plaintiff is an innocent purchaser, and purchased the note without notice of an equity against his transferor, and there is no evidence tending to support such a contention, the plaintiff's claim must be considered as if owned and held by his transferor. This holding is, of course, erroneous both at common law and under the statute which clothes the holder with the presumption that he is a holder in due course, so that it is not incumbent upon him to so allege. It is only when there is an allegation and proof of an equity, that plaintiff is put upon proof that he paid value bona fide and without notice.

An allegation in a petition that the plaintiff was a holder and owner of a note indorsed to the plaintiff, or order, is sufficient. 

Welker v. Hayes (Mo. App.), 22 S. W. (2d) 1052; Johannsen v. Klipstein (Calif. App.), 284 Pac. 1047.

In an action by the indorsee against the maker it is not necessary for the plaintiff to aver that his transferor was a holder in due course. Putnam v. Ensign Oil Co., 272 Pa. 301. 

116 Atl. 285.

In an action by an indorsee, the allegation in the complaint that the plaintiff was the owner of the note was sufficient after verdict, without alleging title by indorsement and before matur ity, when a copy of the note was attached to the complaint 

Berghoff v. Cummings, 225 Ill. App. 1. 

A complaint by an indorsee against a maker alleging indorse ment and delivery to the plaintiff imports that this was done before maturity and for value, so that an allegation that the plaintiff is a holder in due course is unnecessary; and a denial by the defendant of the indorsement and delivery also denies the implied holding in due course, and allows the defendant to set up lack of consideration although not affirmatively pleaded. 

Bank of Coney Is. v. Weinberg, 190 N. Y. Supp. 203.

The defense of fraud must be both pleaded and proved. It can not be proved under a bare allegation of no consideration. 

German-American Bank v. Barnes (Mo. App.), 185 S. W. 1194; 

Brown v. Kevorkian, 21 Ala. App. 252, 107 So. 228, not citing the N. I. L.; Bass Furniture & Carpet Co. v. Finley, 129 Okla. 

40, 263 Pac. 130, not citing the N. I. L.

A mere allegation that there were fraudulent misrepresentations is not enough. The defendant must set up the facts upon

which he bases his conclusions. Security Nat. Bank of Fargo V. Pleading

The presumption that the holder of a note is a holder in due course, is not rebutted by a denial in the answer of the owner ship of the plaintiff. Gulf States Steel Co. v. Ford, 173 N. C. 

195, 91 S. E. 844.

The presumption that a holder is in due course is not met by allegations in the pleading denying the plaintiff's ownership or the essentials of holding in due course; but such allegations must be supported by proof. Waszkowski v. Beatrous, 9 La.

Contra. Where it was alleged that payee's title is defective it was held that the burden is on the holder to prove that he or some person under whom he claims acquired title as a holder in due course. Eichinger v. Zimmerlein, 243 N. Y. Supp. 155.

The case cites sec. 59 but is clearly wrong. If a mere allegation in the pleadings can deprive the holder of the benefit of the presumption, it is practically worthless. The section requires that the defect of title must be "shown." This clearly indicates that evidence must be introduced, mere allegation is not sufficient.

On a plea of nil debet by the maker, and a plea that the plaintiff was not "a holder for value in due course and before maturity of note," it is sufficient for a prima facie case for the plaintiff to give evidence of the making of the note and the indorsement. Holdsworth v. Anderson Drug Co., 118 Va. 

359, 87 S. E. 565.

In an action by an indorsee against the maker, where the defendant admits that the note was made for a valuable consideration, but denies, on information and belief, the indorsements, it was sufficient for the plaintiff to introduce the note in evidence with the indorsements thereon. Beck v. Maller, 131 App. Div. 243, 115 N. Y. Supp. 596.

Where the maker did not deny the allegations of the complaint that the payee, before maturity, indorsed, assigned and delivered the note to plaintiff for value, an allegation, coupled with a defense of failure of consideration, denying that plaintiff was an innocent purchaser for value, raises no issue, because the fact intended to be disputed was already admitted by the failure to traverse the allegations of the complaint. Brown v. 

Feldwert, 46 Oreg. 363, 80 Pac. 414.

In an action by the maker of a note against the payee and indorsee to cancel the note on the ground of fraud, the complaint was held not to be defective for failure to state that the indorsee was a party to the alleged fraud or had notice thereof.

A petition in a suit for conversion alleging that defendant bank accepted X's deposits of bills of exchange payable to X as treasurer of plaintiff corporation in his personal account knowing that they were corporate property, permitted withdrawals by X who misappropriated the funds, and that defendant was thereby charged with knowledge of the theft, was held demurrable notwithstanding sec. 59 on the ground that as a matter of law no knowledge or bad faith could be imputed to defendant on the allegations, and burden was on plaintiff to affirmatively prove such bad faith. The burden put upon the plaintiff involves something more than the mere presumption arising from an indorsement regular in form. O'Connor v. Kleiman, 143 Ia. 435, 121 N. W. 1088. 

This section does not change the common law rule that the holder must prove the indorsement of the payee to come within this presumption. Van Syckel v. Egg Harbor Coal & Lumber 

Co., 109 N. J. Law 604, 162 Atl. 627. Sed quaere. 

Ordinarily a note makes out a prima facie case for the holder of it, but this rule does not apply where the signature of the note has been cut off. The burden of proof in such case is on the holder. Pooley v. Hunt Oil Co., 216 Ky. 139, 287 S. W. 555. 

In an action on a note the introduction of the note in evidence by plaintiff as holder makes a prima facie case for him so that a motion to strike is properly denied. Cox v. Parsons, 165

Where a defective title in the transferor was shown, the holder bank placed its bookkeeper on the stand, who testified that the record was regular but he knew nothing of the conditions under which the bank acquired the instrument. Held, the bank failed to meet the burden. Taylor v. Goodrich Tire & Rubber Co. (Tenn.), 98 S. W. (2d) 1094.

In an action against the drawer of a check, the indorsee need not show as part of its case consideration as between it and the payee. Irving Trust Co. v. Horowitz, 185 N. Y. Supp. 370.

The plaintiff was allowed to open the case, and offered evidence that the bank made the loan at the request of an officer of the X Co., who was also president of the bank. The loan was granted by the cashier of the bank, who had no knowledge of the transaction between the X Co. and the maker. At their request the proceeds of the loan were paid to the X Co. The maker attempted to show that the note was given as part of a gambling transaction between him and the X Co., but the court ruled that he must connect the bank with this transaction or adduce evidence of its bad faith before showing that the transaction was illegal. Held, these rulings were correct. The maker of notes obtained by fraud paid interest and part of the principal before maturity to the indorsees then holding the notes, and said they were good and would be paid at maturity. These holders indorsed the notes after maturity to the plaintiff. At the trial the maker set up the fraud, but the plaintiff offered no evidence that the prior holders were bona fide. 

Held, (1) these payments and statements did not estop the maker to set up the fraud, since the holders did not change their position because of his conduct and the plaintiff did not know of it in buying the notes; (2) they were not a waiver of his defense, for waiver is the voluntary or intentional abandonment of a known right, and there was no evidence that the maker knew that the holders were not bona fide. Semble, the maker was not estopped by negligence in believing the payee's fraudulent statements. Semble, the burden was on the plaintiff to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the prior indorsees acquired the note in due course. Ford v. Ott, 186 Ia. 820, 173 N.

A verdict for the defendant should not be directed where there is evidence of the indorsee's good faith.  Cosmopolitan Bank v. Sommervold, 155 Minn. 492, 191 N. W. 1000.

And a verdict should be directed for the plaintiff where all the facts are shown and are undisputed, and the transaction discloses nothing which would justify an inference of bad faith. 

Goedhard v. Folstad, 156 Minn. 453, 195 N. W. 281, semble, Traders' Security Co. v. Oney, 228 Ky. 182, 14 S. W. (2d) 752; 

Still v. Stevens (Tex. Civ. App.), 13 S. W. (2d) 956. In the following cases it was held that a verdict for the indorsee was properly directed or should have been directed. White v. Mc-

Although the plaintiff may offer testimony direct and positive to the effect that he is a holder in due course, the facts and circumstances surrounding the transaction may be such as to leave the question one for the jury. Second Nat. Bank v. Scanlon, 196 

Ia. 1305, 196 N. W. 65.

Where there is a conflict of evidence as to whether the plain- Directed tiff is a holder in due course, the question is properly submitted to the jury. Ginsburg v. McBride, 248 Mich. 221, 226 N. W. 873. verdicts, instructions, etc.

Where plaintiff proved ownership and rested, and the defendant offered evidence of fraud and notice, which officers of the plaintiff corporation contradicted, it was held an error to direct verdict for the defendant. Grimes Savings Bank v. Mc- 

Harg, 204 Ia. 322, 213 N. W. 798.

When a $5,000 note was purchased for $3,000 outside the ordinary course of business, it is error to direct a verdict for the indorsee.  Weiss v. Goldberger, 209 App. Div. 615, 205 N. Y. Supp. 1, app. dismissed, 239 N. Y. 

509, 147 N. E. 173.

Where an indorsee purchased notes from the fraudulent payee at a discount of ten per cent. and gave in return other paper maturing at a later date, the indorsee's bad faith was a question for the jury. Mechanics Savings Bank v. Feeney, 79 N. H. 267, 108 Atl. 295.

Where the plaintiff has the burden of proving that he is a holder in due course, he is not entitled to a verdict as a matter of law, even though the testimony of his witnesses warrants such a finding. The jury was not bound to believe their testimony, although uncontradicted. Phillips v. Eldridge, 221 Mass. 

103, 108 N. E. 909.

When evidence as to the holder's knowledge was not made out as part of his case, but was drawn out on cross-examination of his witness by the defendant, the burden of coming forward with evidence was not sustained. Lambert v. Smith, 53 Okla. 

606, 157 Pac. 909, 18 A. L. R. 1.

Where there was evidence that the payee obtained notes by fraud, the indorsee, a bank, did not necessarily sustain the burden of proof placed upon it by this section, although its president testified the notes were bought without notice and was not directly contradicted by any witness. His credibility was a question for the jury. Nat. City Bank v. Kirk (Ind. App.), 134 N. E. 772. See 1 Ind. L. J. 49.

Where the plaintiff was the only witness as to his being a holder in due course, and his testimony is of such character that reasonable men might differ upon the issue, it is not error to deny a motion to direct a verdict for plaintiff and a motion for judgment, notwithstanding the verdict. The  was not cited. Rohweder v. Titus, 85 Wash. 441, 148 Pac. 583; 

Woodsmall v. Myers, 87 Ind. App. 69, 158 N. E. 646, 2 Ind. 

L. J. 667.

But although the burden is on the plaintiff to show that he was a holder in due course, the question may be withdrawn from the jury and determined as a matter of law when the evidence is clear and convincing, and of such nature that reasonable minds can draw but one conclusion therefrom. Mc-

Although the jury is the judge of the evidence, yet where there was no conflict in the evidence as to plaintiff's good faith, and nothing to indicate that the witness for plaintiff was testifying falsely, a verdict for defendant was set aside. Southwest Nat. Bank v. Lindsley, 29 Ida. 343, 158 Pac. 1082.

A verdict may be directed for the indorsee in a suit against the maker, when there is no rational inference of bad faith. 

The indorsee's failure to make inquiries of the bank at which the note was payable, if not deliberate, does not constitute such evidence. Edelen v. First Nat. Bank, 139 Md. 413, 115 Atl. 

599. 

In an action by plaintiff bank against an indorser, who claimed that the note was procured from him by the fraud of the maker, the only witness as to the bona fides of the bank was its cashier. It was held error not to permit the case to go to the jury to pass on the credibility of the cashier, although his testimony had not been contradicted. Second Nat. Bank v. Hoffman, 229 Pa. 429, 78 Atl. 1002. But after the second trial of the same case it was held that when it was shown by the testimony of the cashier, by that of the maker called as a witness and by the admission of the defendant, that the bank had no knowledge of the fraud, it was error to submit the question of the bank's knowledge to the jury. Second Nat. Bank v. Hoffman, 233 Pa. 390, 82 Atl. 463. See the discussion of these cases in McKinley v. Wainstein, 74 Pa. Super. Ct. 482.

Plaintiff paid to defendant a note to which plaintiff's signature as maker was forged, mistaking it for a genuine note of like amount which he had made. Plaintiff sued defendant to recover back the money and was nonsuited. Held, error, that the rule is the same as in the case of a payment by the drawee of a bill to which the name of the drawer is forged, and that plaintiff could not recover if defendant was a holder in due course. But the burden upon this point was on the defendant under secs. 

55-59, , and the question should therefore have been submitted to the jury. Jones v. Miners & Merchants Bank, 144 

Mo. App. 428, 128 S. W. 829.

Where the defendant does not offer any objection to the indorsements, no proof is necessary, other than the introduction of the note with the indorsements thereon. Williams v. Schmeltz (Mo. App.), 14 S. W. (2d) 966.

 Establishment of defenses An instruction to the jury that assumes that the burden rests on the plaintiff to prove himself a holder in due course, is erroneous, unless qualified by instruction that such burden is not imposed on the plaintiff until the defendant has shown that the note was negotiated in fraud of him. Crosby v. Reynolds, 196 Fed. 640, 116 C. C. A. 314. It is also erroneous if the defendant has failed to establish his defense of fraud. Boone

The view of the numerous preceding cases is adopted in 

Wyoming in Glendo State Bank v. Abbott, 30 Wyo. 98, 216 

Pac. 700, 34 A. L. R. 294, with note, which also holds that the burden of coming forward with evidence of all the requirements of holding in due course is on the indorsee, and contains an able classification of the authorities into three different groups. 

The cases in two groups consider that the burden as to notice is different from that as to value. 

The statute upon proof of fraud, etc., casts on the holder, not merely the duty of going forward, but the burden of establishing that he or someone under whom he claims, acquired the title as a holder in due course. The burden of proof remains on the holder and does not shift, though the burden of proceeding may shift even though the defendant introduces no evidence to contradict the plaintiff, since on this point the defendant is entitled to have the case submitted to a jury. Leavitt v. Thurston, 38 Utah 351, 113 Pac. 77.

Where the plaintiff shows that he took the instrument in good faith and for value and without notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of his transferor and the defendant failed to show the contrary it was proper peremptorily to instruct the jury to find for the plaintiff. Asbury v. Taube, 151 Ky. 142, 151 S. W. 372; Meyer Milling Co. v. Strohfeld (Mo. App.), 20 S. W. (2d) 963.

When a note was shown to have been taken by the payee in consideration for a fraudulent voting contest, the burden was on the indorsee to establish by preponderance of the evidence that he was a holder in due course. Harrison v. Perry, 184 Ky. 

722, 212 S. W. 911.

A folded sheet of paper contained a written contract on the first page and four partly blank forms for notes printed on the second page. No perforated lines divided the pages or separated the notes from each other. The defendant signed the contract and the notes at the same time, upon the understanding that they constituted and would remain a single instrument and that the notes would not be used by the payee until it had performed its part of the contract. The payee, without performing, detached the notes and discounted them with the plaintiff bank more than one thousand miles away from the defendant, the bank at the same time purchasing other paper aggregating $13,000 which had been given the payee upon similar transactions by makers residing in various parts of the country. The plaintiff knew the nature of the payee's business. Held, the negotiation of the notes in breach of faith made it incumbent upon the plaintiff to establish the payment of value and good faith. 

Security Bank & Trust Co. v. Dery, 194 App. Div. 572, 185 N. 

Y. Supp. 476.

In an action by the indorsee of a note, evidence that the note had been signed in blank by the maker and stolen and filled out, should not have been excluded by the trial court as not binding on the plaintiff. It showed a defect of title which would impose on the plaintiff the burden to show that he or a predecessor took in due course. Karten v. Tabachnik, 192 N. Y. Supp. 335. The defense, if proved, would prevent recovery even by a holder in due course, under sec. 15.

Fraud by the payee of a note in persuading the maker to accept worthless bonds in exchange for the note was a defect of title, which obliged an indorsee to prove good faith by a fair preponderance of the evidence. The maker was not estopped by accepting worthless stock in a subsequent reorganization under the belief that the indorsee was bona fide. Also since the indorsee bank took the note as collateral for a loan which it held on deposit to the payee's credit and which was not shown to have been checked out, the bank was not proved to be a holder for value. First Nat. Bank v. Denfeld, 143 Minn. 281, 173 N. W.

The langauge of sec. 59 of the Negotiable Instruments Law is quite different from the English section, but under sec. 59 the same result seems to be reached, although for different reasons. The section does not purport to shift the burden of proof when the payee's title is defective. It is only when it is "shown that the title of any person who has negotiated the instrument is defective" that the burden of proof shifts to the holder. But it is a rare case in which the person who negotiates the instrument to the payee is other than the party making the instrument and of course his title to his own obligation can not be defective. "But the last-mentioned rule does not apply in favor of a party who became bound on the instrument prior to the acquisition of such defective title"

In Kinney v. Kruse, A, who held possession of a note for the payee, fraudulently transferred it. This was held to be no defense in a suit by the holder against the maker and not to change the burden of proof so as to require the plaintiff to show that he was a bona fide holder for value. The fraud in putting the note in circulation which will operate as a defense or change the burden of proof, must be a fraud against the defendant. The 

Supreme Court of Connecticut, while holding that this case is opposed to the strong current of authority, cited no cases except 

Fulton Bank v. Phenix Bank, 1 Hall (Superior Court of New 

York) 562, which case, in turn, cited no authority upon the point except an earlier case of Talman v. Gibson in the same volume p. 308. In this case, no cases were cited on the point except 

Solomons v. Bank of England, 13 East, 135, and Rees v. Marquis of Headfort, 2 Campbell, 574. In the first of these cases it appeared that the defrauded owner of the instrument had given notice to the maker not to pay, and in the second case, which was an action against the acceptor of a bill of exchange, it appeared that the drawer, called as a witness, testified that he had been tricked out of the bill by fraud, whereupon it was held that the plaintiff was bound to prove what consideration he gave. The truth is, that this question is rather one of substantive law than of the burden of proof, that is, whether a defendant, who has no defense of his own, can set up collateral equities existing in favor of other persons. It is submitted that, by the great weight of authority, he can not do so, unless he has been notified by the rightful owner of the instrument not to pay the same to the holder. This exception, even, is an exercise of equitable jurisdiction by a court of law. The proper remedy for the defendant in such a case is either to file a bill of interpleader, bringing in the third party, who claims an equity, or where the procedure in the jurisdiction permits it, to make such third person a party to the action at law. If notice has been given

§ 59 

by the defrauded owner of an instrument not to pay, the court of law may well permit the rights of such defrauded owner to be set up by the defendant by analogy to a case of bailment. 

A bailee is ordinarily estopped to dispute the title of his bailor and to set up the right of a third person, but where a person, claiming to be the owner of the property, serves notice on the bailee, he may defend an action by the bailor, it being held that in such case the defendant may set up the jus tertii in answer to the action. "The bailee can set up the title of another only if he defends upon the right and title and by the authority of that person. "Biddle v. Bond, 6 B. & S. 225.

Sec. 59, it is submitted, does not present a satisfactory way of dealing with the question. The first part of the section requires that when it is shown that the title of any person who has negotiated the instrument was defective, the burden is on the holder to show that he or some person under whom he claims, acquired the title as a holder in due course, which included, under sec. 52(4), the requirement that at the time it was negotiated to him he had no notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating it. From this the inference seems necessary that, if he had notice, even of an equity in favor of a former holder, he could not recover against any party to the instrument—a result, it is submitted, contrary to the authorities. In order to prevent this result the last clause of sec. 59 was inserted, but it is insufficient for the purpose since it implies that, if the defendant successfully sustains the burden of showing that the plaintiff is not a holder in due course, the action must fail, whether the equity against his ownership is in favor of the defendant or of a third person. 

The question is one of substantive law and not merely of rules of evidence and it is to be regretted that a section regulating the burden of proof should be so drawn as to involve this question in uncertainty.

A possible interpretation of this last sentence is, that it codifies the cases holding that failure of consideration does not shift the burden of proof. This is a defense arising after the maker became bound upon the instrument. This view is further supported by the fact that negotiation with knowledge of such failure creates a defective title within sec. 55. See cases cited at the end of this section. It is significant, however, that no such interpretation was in the mind of the draftsman of the 

 Consequently, the last sentence of sec. 59 probably applies also to the burden of proof of defenses of fraud, etc., in a 

Prouty v. Roberts situation in jurisdictions where that case is not followed and the fraud of the payee can be set up at law. 

On the other hand, in jurisdictions where Prouty v. Roberts was followed at common law, the defense could not be set up so that no question of the burden of proof arose. In such jurisdictions, this substantive rule as to defenses can hardly be alproof when

A Liberty bond payable to bearer was found in a post office building in Colorado by an employee and forwarded to the Treasury Department. The former owner could not be discovered. The Attorney General ruled that the finder was not entitled to the return of the bond. The ruling is based on an absence of property in the finder, and not on the fact that the bond was found on government property. The opinion states that the maker of a negotiable instrument is not protected if he pays with notice that the person presenting has no right to receive payment, citing Chappelear v. Martin, 45 Oh. St. 126; 

Wheeler v. Guild, 20 Pick. 545, 552; The Emblem, 2 Ware 67, 8 Fed. Cas. No. 4434. Even if it be conceded that the finder would have been entitled to retain possession as against every one but the true owner and to receive payment of principal and interest if the government had had no notice that he was not the true owner, under existing conditions he is not entitled to either principal or interest, and the Treasury is not justified in returning the bond and giving him an opportunity to sell it to a bona fide purchaser who would be entitled to payment. The 

Treasury should, therefore, hold the bond until claimed by the true owner.  Anonymous, 32 Ops. 

Atty. Gen. 80.

§ 59  

Sed quaere. The finder is a "holder" within the definition of sec. 191, and so has legal title to the bond, subject only to the equitable claim of the loser, if he should be discovered. 

Even if the government be allowed to set up the loser's equity despite Prouty v. Roberts and other cases cited, supra, p. 742, the defense, like the equity, should be contingent on the loser's appearance. The finder was not a wrongdoer like the plaintiff in Parsons v. Utica Cement Co., supra, and consequently should not have been denied recovery in toto. Like the finder of a chattel, he was the owner of the bond as against all the world except the loser. As between the finder and the government, the latter was only entitled to protect itself against liability to make a second payment, and to insist that the rights of the loser be sufficiently safeguarded. The Liberty Bond should have been returned to the finder upon his furnishing an indemnification bond with sufficient sureties, to repay its value to the loser if he should appear. The ruling enabled the government to avoid paying the bond to anybody, since the loser will probably never be discovered.

The payee of a note indorsed it to a corporation, of which he was a director. In a suit by the indorsee the maker set up failure of consideration as between himself and the payee. The indorsee merely proved its prima facie case and offered no evidence of purchase for value without notice. Held, maker not liable.

Although knowledge of the defense by one director was not notice to the corporation, when the maker offered evidence of a defense the indorsee's prima facie case was no longer sufficient, but was required to be supplemented by evidence showing that the indorsee was a holder in due course. First Nat. Bank v. Carroll, 46 N. D. 62, 179 N. W. 664.

 ARTICLE V LIABILITIES OF PARTIES Sec. 60. Liability of Maker. 

The maker of a negotiable instrument by making it engages that he will pay it according to its tenor, and admits the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse.¹

Sec. 61. Liability of Drawer. 

The drawer by drawing the instrument admits the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse;¹ and engages that on due presentment the instrument will be accepted or paid, or both, according to its tenor, and that if it be dishonored, and the necessary proceedings on dishonor be duly taken, he will pay the amount thereof to the holder, or to any subsequent indorser who may be compelled to pay it. But the drawer may insert in the instrument an express stipulation negativing or limiting his own liability to the holder.

Where a check is given for a valuable consideration, the drawer is the principal debtor, and in the event of no funds in the bank to pay the check, he becomes absolutely liable. this obligation survives the death of the drawer.  Baxter v. Brandenburg, 137 Minn. 259, 163

N. W. 516. 

In a suit by an indorsee where the payee of a cashier's check was insane, the drawer bank deposited the fund in court and the plaintiff-indorsee failed to sue the bank on its remedy under sec. 61, it was held that payment into court discharged the drawer bank's liability. Hellman Commercial Trust & Savings 

Bank v. Alden (Cal. App.), 268 Pac. 688, affirmed on grounds of waiver of rights as to the issuing bank, 206 Cal. 592, 275 Pac. 794. 

If a check is a gift to the payee, the drawer's promise that it will be paid is unenforceable by the payee, but if delivered for a consideration it is enforceable against the drawer's executors although payment has been countermanded by his death. 

A check is a memorandum of a contract under the Maine statute of frauds, which does not require the consideration to be stated in the writing. Guild v. Eastern Trust & Banking Co., 122 Me. 

514, 121 Atl. 13.

The giving of a check is a representation that the drawer has money or credit with the bank and is sufficient to make the drawer guilty of obtaining money under false pretenses if the drawer has no money in the bank or credit with it and intends to defraud. State v. Hammelsy, 52 Oreg. 156, 96 Pac. 865, 17

L. R. A. (N.S.) 244.

§ 760 

Drawer's liability The payee of a check deposited it for collection in a bank and it was eventually presented by a Federal Reserve Bank to the drawee bank which marked it paid, charged the drawer's account, and issued a sight draft for the amount in favor of the Federal Reserve Bank. The bank failed and the draft was dishonored. Held, the drawer of the check was discharged by the draft, which was negligently accepted in payment by the plaintiff's agent. Friends' In Need Society of Bell County v. Peterson (Tex. Civ. App.), 9 S. W. (2d) 1110; Loland v. 

Nelson, 139 Öreg. 581, 8 P. (2d) 82. Semble, the plaintiff has an action against its agent, the Federal Reserve Bank. Jensen v. Laurel Meat Co., 71 Mont. 582, 230 Pac. 1081. See the note on various aspects of this decision in 1 Wash. L. Rev. 67. 

See also cases under sec. 156 infra.

So also the acceptance of a bank draft in payment of the check sent in for collection discharges the drawer, even if no negligence is shown. Odle v. Barnes (Tex. Civ. App.), 2 S. W. (2d) 577, certified question answered, 299 S. W. 636, 6 Tex. L. 

Rev. 529. 

Subsequently, Montana Laws, 1925, c. 65, has amended the state banking law, so that an instrument may be sent for collection to the drawee and a check or draft of the drawee may be taken in payment; and the failure of the collecting bank to account for the proceeds of payment because of insolvency or otherwise shall not render the forwarding bank liable to the depositor or discharge the drawer's liability to the holder, if due diligence has been exercised by the holder and if the drawer has been notified by the drawee bank through deposit tickets, etc., that his account has been accepted pursuant to these provisions. See also other bank collection codes, supra, p. 24.

Sec. 62. Liability of Acceptor. 

The acceptor by accepting the instrument engages that he will pay it according to the tenor of his acceptance; and admits,- (1) The existence of the drawer, the genuineness of his signature, and his capacity and authority to draw the instrument, and (2) The existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse.¹

Although the bill was made since the Negotiable Instruments Law was adopted in North Dakota, no reference whatever is made to the statute, either by counsel or the court, and naturally none of the cases above cited construing sec. 62 were reviewed, since they had not been decided at that time. vania 2 In Pennsylvania a statute passed in 1849 abrogated the rule Pennsylof Price v. Neal and permitted the drawee of a forged negotiable instrument to recover money paid thereon. The learned writer, already quoted, expressed the opinion that this statute had been repealed by sec. 62 and said, "It is inconceivable that any legislature should intend that a paying drawee can recover back money paid to a holder on a forgery of the drawer's name and yet be liable on his acceptance to that holder if sued thereon. 

He would be compelled to pay and instantly permitted to recover what he had paid. Facts constituting no defense would yet grotesquely constitute a cause of action." But the Pennsylvania courts, in cases arising since this opinion was expressed, have held that the Act of 1849 was not repealed and that the drawee who has paid a forged negotiable instrument may recover from the holder. Union Nat. Bank v. Franklin Nat. Bank, 249 Pa. 

375, 94 Atl. 1080; Colonial Trust Co. v. National Bank of Western Pennsylvania, 50 Pa. Super. Ct. 510. In these cases the courts argued that since by sec. 132 an acceptance must be in writing and the instruments were therefore not accepted, sec. 

62 has no application to the case of a payment by a drawee of an unaccepted bill. As has been seen, however, the courts in other states have not limited the operation of sec. 62 to the case of an accepted bill, but have reasoned that, "A payment of a bill is more than an acceptance, for the one is an obligation to pay, the other a discharge of the indebtedness represented by such bill. If the one concludes the drawee it is inconceivable why the other would not," Nat. Bank of Rolla v. First Nat. Bank of 

Salem, 141 Mo. App. 719, 125 S. W. 513; or that, "The payment

Grove, 59 Oreg. 388, 117 Pac. 293.

The only way to avoid the grotesque conclusion described by Professor Hening seems to be to hold that where the forged bill is accepted, the acceptor is liable, and that where the payment is after an acceptance, the acceptor can not recover back. But where payment has been made without acceptance, the right of the drawee to recover will depend on the rules of the law merchant under sec. 196, or the statutory law of the state, if any. 

But, of course, this is fatal to uniformity.

In Union Nat. Bank v. Franklin Nat. Bank, supra, the swindler deposited the check in the United States Nat. Bank, which paid value to him and forwarded the check to the Franklin Nat. Bank for collection; the Franklin Bank was obliged to refund to the drawee bank the amount collected. In the later case of United States Nat. Bank v. Union Nat. Bank, 268 Pa. 

147, 110 Atl. 792, the bank of deposit sued the drawee bank to recover the sum which the drawee had secured from the Franklin Bank, alleging that the drawee had been negligent in not discovering the forgery and notifying the Franklin Bank or the plaintiff, so that they would not change their position for the worst. Recovery was denied on the ground that the matter was res judicata because of the previous decision. The court said that negligence could have been raised as a defense by the agent bank when it was sued by the drawee, and could not now be raised by the principal bank. A note in 30 Yale Law Journal 

296 points out that the Pennsylvania cases are fatal to uniformity under sec. 62.

In a later case, with facts similar to Union Nat. Bank v. 

Franklin Nat. Bank, supra, the negligence of the drawee bank was held to bar its recovery from the collecting bank of the amount paid on forged checks. The burden was on the plaintiff to show that its negligence caused no loss.  Union Nat. Bank v. Farmers & Mechanics Nat. 

Bank, 271 Pa. 107, 114 Atl. 506, 16 A. L. R. 1120, noted in 70

U. Pa. L. Rev. 125. 

Under the Pennsylvania statute it was held that a person who indorsed a check, in order to identify a holder who was unknown to the paying teller, was liable to the bank when the drawer's signature had been found to be forged. Judge v. West

Phila. Title & T. Co., 68 Pa. Sup. Ct. 310. The decision seems erroneous. The defendant was not liable as an indorser, as the court says, since he did not sign for the purpose of transferring title to the drawee. The indorsement was not even a receipt by the person to whom the money was paid, but merely an agreement that the person in possession of the check was its lawful

§ 62 

owner. Compare Schmitt v. Mellon Nat. Bank, 67 Pa. Super.

Ct. 453, which held that the payee of a check fraudulently issued by the drawer's agent was not liable, because of its indorsement, to return the proceeds to the certifying bank. Dakota

In South Dakota the rule of Price v. Neal had been repudiated South before the adoption of the Negotiable Instruments Law in that state. In the earliest case to arise under the act, the Supreme 

Court at first adhered to its own rulings, by a course of reasoning difficult to follow and impossible to agree with, but on rehearing the court modified its position and based the decision on the special facts of the case. First Nat. Bank v. Brule Nat. Bank, 38 S. D. 396, 41 S. D. 87, 161 N. W. 616, 168 N. W. 1054, 12 

A. L. R. 1079, with note, "Right of drawee of forged check or draft to recover money paid thereon." In this case, Kost, a laborer, made deposits in the plaintiff bank, which were entered in the usual pass-book delivered to him. Kost was identified by his foreman, and said he could not write. Some weeks later, two impostors came to the cashier of the defendant bank in another town with Kost's pass-book. One introduced himself as Kost's foreman and said the other was Kost, who wished to cash a check on his own bank. The cashier refused, but said he would take the check for collection and pay over the proceeds when it was paid by Kost's bank. A check was drawn payable to the defendant for the amount in the pass-book, and signed by the supposed Kost with his mark, which the cashier witnessed. The check was collected through a clearance bank from the plaintiff drawee, and the proceeds paid to the supposed Kost. The check bore the indorsement in blank of the defendant bank with the word "Paid" and the date, though no payment had been made.

This was followed by the indorsement of the clearance bank "to any bank or banker." The real Kost later recovered the amount of his deposits from the drawee bank, which sued the collecting bank. In both opinions the drawee was held entitled to recover, but for different reasons. 

In its first opinion, 38 S. D. 396, 161 N. W. 616, the court held that the payee bank by its unrestricted indorsement warranted to the drawee the genuineness of the drawer's signature. 

It reached this result by asserting that since by sec. 65 every person negotiating an instrument by delivery or by qualified indorsement, warrants that the instrument is genuine and in all respects what it purports to be, and since sec. 30 declares that an instrument is negotiated when it is transferred from one person to another in such manner as to constitute the transferee a holder thereof, the holder warrants the genuineness of a draft to the drawee who pays it. It is a novel construction of these sections that under them a holder negotiates a bill or check when he surrenders it to the drawee upon payment, and that the drawee "by making payment" becomes a holder. The defini-

§ 768 

 Dakota 

South tion of "holder" in sec. 191 is made with reference to live instruments, not those which have been discharged by payment. 

The drawee, who has paid the instruments, is not "the payee or indorsee of a bill or note," although he is in possession of it and therefore does not become a holder. But even on the court's own construction of secs., 65 and 66, the judgment was wrong.

The court said that under sec. 66 the warranty of the negotiator runs only to holders in due course and that the drawee "is not and can not become a holder in due course, " but that under sec. 65 he becomes a holder to whom the negotiator warrants the genuineness of the instrument. But sec. 65 applies only to a person negotiating an instrument by delivery or by a qualified indorsement, whereas, in the case under consideration, the holder, who presented it for payment and who received payment, indorsed without qualification, and his liability was therefore defined by sec. 66, according to which, the court said the drawee could not recover back the money.

The court in this case also took the view that sec. 188 (186, South Dakota Act), by which the drawer and indorsers are discharged when the holder procures a check to be certified, excludes the application of sec. 62 to checks and that therefore the admissions specified in sec. 62 have no application to checks. According to this reasoning a bank, which accepts or certifies a check, not only does not admit the existence of the drawer of the check, whether genuine or forged, or his capacity or authority to draw, but does not even admit the existence of the payee and his then capacity to indorse. Sec. 185 provides "except as herein otherwise provided, the provisions of this act applicable to a bill of exchange, payable on demand, apply to a check," and there is nothing in any of the other sections relating to checks, which prevent the application of sec. 62 to them. Sec. 188 has no bearing whatever on the effect of presentment for payment and payment of a check. It applies only where a holder of a check, instead of presenting it for payment, chooses to have it accepted or certified. The third edition of this book, p. 232, contains an analysis of the precedents upon which the court relied in this first opinion.

This first opinion illustrates the occasional inclination of courts to construe the  so as to retain the former law of the state regardless of the value of national uniformity. 

On rehearing, 41 S. D. 87, 168 N. W. 1054, the court in an admirable opinion approved the doctrine of Price v. Neal. It frankly corrected its error in applying sec. 65; the indorser's warranty extends only to transferees of title, and the drawee is not such; "the last holder's indorsement does not transfer the check, but converts what was a check into a voucher." The drawee's inability to recover from a holder without fault was not based by the court on sec. 62, since "accepting" was thought not to include paying, but on the exigencies of business, which

§ 62 

demand that the ordinary right to recover money paid under South Dakota mistake of fact should not apply to negotiable paper. "When a holder of a bill of exchange uses all due care in the taking of bill or check and the drawee thereafter pays same, the transaction is absolutely closed-modern business could not be done. on any other basis."

The doctrine of Price v. Neal did not apply here, however, because the defendant did not use ordinary business prudence. 

It took the check from a stranger without any identification except from another stranger; the cashier by witnessing his mark vouched for the signature of the drawer; it further threw the drawee off guard by marking the check paid. On the facts the payment to the swindler after the drawee honored the check is not such a change of position as will bar recovery. Semble, the defendant might not be liable if it had indorsed for "collection."

South Dakota has since gone farther in following Price v. 

Neal. In Minnehaha Nat. Bank of Sioux Falls v. Pence Pharmaey, 42 S. D. 525, 176 N. W. 37, a forged check indorsed by the payee and transferred for value to the defendant was collected by the defendant from the drawee bank through the clearing house. The check also bore the indorsement of the defendant. The drawee bank was denied recovery. The court distinguished First Nat. Bank v. Brule Nat. Bank, supra, on the ground of negligence, which was not present in the case at bar. The court said that the indorsement by the transferee was not for the purpose of transferring title or in the course of negotiation, but for the purpose of receipting for the proceeds thereof. This result is in accord with Price v. Neal, but it is doubtful whether South Dakota is yet in complete agreement with that case, since one judge concurred in the result only, without opinion, and the opinion itself suggests that if the payee had collected the check he might be held liable to the drawee bank.

Section 62 is a re-enactment of sec. 54 in the English Bills of 

Exchange Act. It has been sharply criticized by a learned writer, because, although it is, in truth, declaratory of the common law of England, it does not in terms recognize any of the equitable exceptions, e. g., negligence of the holder, in taking the instrument, which have generally been recognized in this country. Where the collecting bank has been paid by the drawee bank on the drawer's forged signature and has given credit which has not been drawn upon, the drawee may recover. American 

Surety Co. of New York v. Industrial Sav. Bank, 242 Mich. 

581, 219 N. W. 689, 27 Mich. L. Rev. 100.

In a suit by a drawee bank to recover from an indorsee bank the amount paid on the drawer's forged check, where the defendant had paid part in cash and given credit for the balance, it was held that the amount of unchecked credit remaining could be recovered. First State Bank & Trust Co. v. First Nat. Bank of Canton, 314 Ill. 269, 145 N. E. 382, 38 Harv. L. Rev. 680, 99 

Cent. L. J. 2. The court drew an analogy from sec. 54.

In First State Bank & T. Co. v. First Nat. Bank, 314 Ill. 

269, 145 N. E. 382, the defendant bank negligently took a forged check from the payee, paying part in cash and placing the balance to his credit. The drawee bank, after paying the check, recovered the undrawn balance from the defendant bank, but as to the amount paid by the defendant, the court held that the defendant was not liable, because its negligence was offset by that of the drawee bank in not notifying the defendant of the forgery until over three months after payment. The drawee's delay was due to that of the drawer in not discovering the forgery for over two months after vouchers were returned. Sec. 

62 was not cited. First State Bank & T. Co. v. First Nat. Bank, 314 Ill. 269, 145 N. E. 382, affg. 234 Ill. App. 39.

Where the defendant was negligent in cashing a check upon which the drawer's signature was forged, it was held that the drawee could recover the amount paid. Louisa Nat. Bank v. 

Kentucky Nat. Bank, 239 Ky. 302, 39 S. W. (2d) 497, 17 

St. Louis L. Rev. 273, 26 Ill. L. Rev. 818, 30 Mich. L. Rev. 456.

If the delay was due to the drawer, the drawee bank would not seem negligent, but it could doubtless charge this portion

§ 62 of the check to the drawer because of his negligence, so that the holding on this point is just, though somewhat inconsistent with American Exch. Nat. Bank v. Yorkville Bank, 122 Misc. Rep. 

116, 204 N. Y. Supp. 621, stated under sec. 23, which held that the drawer's delay was immaterial in an action between the collecting bank and the drawee bank. 

A note on the Illinois case in 38 Harv. L. Rev. 680 considers that the negligence of the presenting bank should be immaterial in a Price v. Neal situation so long as it took in good faith, because of the terms of sec. 56. However, sec. 56 is concerned with the requirements of a holder in due course who can enforce the instrument free from defects of title; whereas the decision just discussed involved a forgery, which is not a defect of title, and the enforcement, not of the instrument, but of a quasicontractual liability. Since even a holder in due course can not enforce a forged instrument, he should not necessarily be able to retain a payment made on such an instrument. He must show a greater claim to protection than the ordinary policy favoring free circulation of a commercial instrument which protects negligent purchasers of genuine paper. He must show a meritoriousness greater than that of the ordinary holder in due course in order to make the equities equal as between himself and the drawee bank. Or, to put the matter in another way, the policy which throws on the drawee bank the duty of ascertaining the genuineness of the drawer's signature should not operate in favor of a purchaser who could have ascertained the forgery by the exercise of due care. 

A note in 20 Ill. Law Rev. 160, by L. M. Greeley, considers that there was no negligence on either side in the Illinois case. 

He contends that a bank cashing a check owes no duty of care to other persons to identify the person with whom it deals, and that delay in discovering a forgery is immaterial in forged indorsement cases although there is a duty to report the forgery promptly after discovery.

So also in Bank v. Wood County (Tex. App.), 294 S. W. 

324, affd. (Com. of App.), 299 S. W. 856, it was held that payment was not acceptance, and, therefore, sec. 62 was not an absolute bar to recovery by the drawee after payment when there was negligence on the part of the cashing bank. 

On negligence of the drawer in not examining his vouchers or reporting the discovery of a forgery, see under sec. 23, supra, p. 336 ff; Woodward, 24 Colum. L. Rev. 463, 470.
