X, an employee of the defendant bank, forged a check on the plaintiff bank in the name of a depositor therein, and sent it through the clearing house for collection. Through the collusion of an employee of the plaintiff bank, the clearing house transaction was completed without discovery until some time afterwards, after the expiration of the period allowed by clearing house rules for the return of invalid checks. The forger applied the proceeds of the check toward paying back his peculations from the defendant bank. Neither the peculations nor the repayment were known to any other officer of the bank. Held, the defendant bank must return the amount of the check. The situation is just as if payment had been made at the plaintiff's counter in the ordinary way. Neither Price v. Neal nor the N. I. L. was cited. Metropolitan Trust Co. v. Federal Trust Co., 232 Mass. 

363, 122 N. E. 413.

The decision may be reconciled with Price v. Neal on the ground that the defendant bank was not a purchaser for value of the check or-under Massachusetts decisions-of the money. 

While the money was used to pay an antecedent debt owed by X to the defendant, this debt was unknown to anybody in the bank except X, and such a secret repayment of undiscovered peculations had been held in prior Massachusetts cases not to be value. On this question, see London & County Banking Co. v. London, etc., Bank, under sec. 59, supra, p. 744, and the other authorities there cited.

This leaves untouched the question whether an acceptor of a raised, but otherwise genuine instrument, is liable thereon. 

It is difficult to see how he can escape liability if any meaning is to be given to the words "engages that he will pay according to the tenor of his acceptance. The tenor of the acceptance is determined by the terms of the bill as it is when the drawee accepts and that is a bill for the raised amount. That is the bill he accepted and no other, and according to its tenor he has engaged that he will pay it. 

Where the drawer and drawee are the same person, the drawee can not recover money paid under mistake to an innocent indorser on a raised check. United States v. National Exchange Bank, 270 U. S. 527, 46 Sup. Ct. 388.

A bill of exchange drawn by the United States upon itself was fraudulently raised by someone and indorsed by the payee to a bank, which collected it through the defendant bank from the United States. Held, the United States could not recover the amount paid. It was like one paying paper on which his own signature has been forged. Since the plaintiff was both drawer and drawee, it was not necessary to decide whether sec. 62 had changed the common law view that a drawee could recover the amount of a raised check from the recipient of payment. A swindler stole a check drawn on the plaintiff bank from the mails, raised the amount, substituted the defendant's name as payee, and offered it to the defendant in payment for jewelry. 

The defendant took the check to the plaintiff bank and was informed that it was good. After receiving from the plaintiff a cashier's check for the amount of his check, he delivered the jewelry to the swindler. The amount of the raised check was charged by the plaintiff to the drawer's account but subsequently refunded. Held, the defendant must refund to the plaintiff bank the amount received. The plaintiff, in stating that the check was good and paying it, thereby admitted the genuineness of the drawer's signature and the sufficiency of funds on deposit to cover the amount named in the check, but did not guarantee the identity of the payee, nor the correctness of the amount. The defendant either was guilty of bad faith, or represented by presenting the check that the amount and name of the payee were genuine and was liable to refund the money received through mutual mistake.

L drew a check on the plaintiff bank payable to his client, James Glen, but mailed it by mistake to the client's son of the same name at another address. After obtaining certification the son indorsed the check in the defendant bank, which collected it from the plaintiff. In an action by the drawee, which alleged that it had accepted the check and thereby become liable to pay its amount to the father, held, a verdict should have been directed for the defendant collecting bank, because the plaintiff did not become liable as acceptor. Since the intended payee never received the check he acquired no rights against the plaintiff before or after the purported acceptance, which was not known to or requested by him and therefore did not discharge the drawer or otherwise alter the rights of the parties. Semble, if the allegations of acceptance were stricken from the declaration, it would show a cause of action in the drawer against the defendant based on payment, which is entirely different from acceptance since not in writing, but the defenses would be different from those in the cause of action set forth. The court did not decide whether the trial court erred in excluding evidence of the drawer's negligence in mailing the check to the wrong person.

A draft on the plaintiff bank was purchased from the drawer certification bank by A and mailed to the payee, A's creditor. It was stolen from the mails by one Manning, who erased the payee's name,

§ 62 

substituted his own, indorsed the draft in blank, and offered it to B, an innocent storekeeper, in payment for goods which Manning wished to buy. With his consent B took the draft to the plaintiff drawee bank and had it certified. B then furnished the goods to Manning and the balance of the amount of the draft in cash, retained the draft, and after indorsing deposited it in the defendant bank, which collected it from the plaintiff certifying bank. When the alteration was discovered, the certifying bank voluntarily credited the drawer's account, and sued the collecting bank. Held, no recovery. Under sec. 62 the certifying bank was bound to pay "according to the tenor of its acceptance," which ran to the order of Manning, and it warranted the capacity to indorse of Manning, the payee in the draft at the time of acceptance. Nat. City Bank v. Bank of the

An interesting fact from a banker's point of view is not furnished by the opinions. The draft was really a cashier's check, and a bank drawing such a check is accustomed to send a letter of advice to the drawee bank, giving a description of the check. The opinions do not state whether such a letter was sent in this case. If so, the plaintiff would seem negligent in certifying a check which differed from the letter of advice. 

However, the fact can have no legal importance as the case arose, inasmuch as it was tried upon a stipulation of facts, which specified (219 Ill. App. 346) that neither party was negligent in failing to know of the alteration.

The case is, therefore, a heavy blow at the view that a certifying bank does not guarantee the body of the instrument, but only the genuineness of the drawer's signature and the sufficiency of his deposit.

The decision seems commercially desirable since it strengthens the security of certified checks, so extensively used as a substitute for cash. The risk which it throws on the drawee bank can be shifted to the business world at large by forgery insurance, which is more conveniently taken out by banks that by bona fide purchasers of certified checks like the storekeeper in the principal case.

It will be observed that the case makes probable a similar decision in favor of the purchaser even if the certified check had not been paid, since the court relies on the obligations involved in certification; and on the other hand that it does not determine the effect of payment of an altered check, which has not been certified.

The same result was reached on almost identical facts in 

Wells Fargo Bank v. Bank of Italy (Cal. 1930), 292 Pac. 281, affd., 214 Cal. 156, 4 P. (2d) 781, 79 U. of Pa. L. Rev. 492, 19 

Calif. L. Rev. 210, 29 Mich. L. Rev. 503, 4 So. Calif. L. Rev. 238, 50 Yale L. It was held that the drawee could not recover. The result is approved in an able note, 26 Ill. L. Rev. 697, and criticized in 31 Mich. L. Rev. 408, 9 N. Y. U. L. Q. 475. 

Contra to the Illinois case is Interstate Trust Co. v. U. S. 

Nat. Bank, 67 Colo. 6, 185 Pac. 260, involving a somewhat similar fraud, but not citing sec. 62. And see Central Nat. Bank v. 

Drosten Jewelry Co., 203 Mo. App. 646, 220 S. W. 511.

In Opinion 72a inserted on page 14 of Digest of Legal Opin ions of Thomas B. Paton, it is suggested that banks may protect themselves from the effect of the Illinois decision by using the form, "Certified, payable only if unaltered since originally drawn by the maker." ("Drawer" would be preferable to maker.") It is also stated that efforts will be made to have the 

 amended so as relieve banks from the responsibility placed upon them by the case. Such an amendment seems inadvisable. An immense amount of business is transacted in reliance upon certified checks, which are taken by men of affairs because they assume that the bank's certification is just as valuable as money and much safer and easier to carry. An amendment protecting the certifying bank in a situation like the Illinois case will benefit a few banks by saving them from a loss

§ 62 

which very rarely occurs, but this infrequent benefit will be vastly offset by a weakening of business confidence in certified checks, and this will injure all banks, since it is very advantageous to them that large transactions should be handled through checks with no cash drain. Even the special form of certification suggested by Mr. Paton is open to the objection that business men might be less willing to receive certified checks bearing such a clause. Consequently, it may be wiser for the banks to leave the  and their own practice unchanged, and rely upon forgery insurance and special paper which will make alterations obvious to the teller. A bank's duty to its depositor seems not to obligate it to certify a check not adequately safeguarded against alteration; the bank may elect to pay the check at once without committing any dishonor. 

If sec. 62 is to be amended at all, it should not be changed piecemeal, but comprehensive provisions should be enacted to make certain the rights of a bank which mistakenly honors checks held by an innocent purchaser for value in all the various situations discussed under sec. 62 in this book. 

Some analogous cases, which involve other questions than forgery, may be cited here, although most of them do not cite sec. 62. 

The acceptor of a check is clearly liable under sec. 62 and by the common law of certification, even although the depositor's account is insufficient to pay the check. At common law the authorities were divided on the question whether the holder of an uncertified check could retain the money paid him thereon despite the overdraft. 2 Daniel on Negotiable Instruments, sec. 1226; Woodward on Quasi Contracts, secs. 19, 182. The same conflict has continued since the N. I. L.

York, etc." It was held that this acceptance was conditional on delivery of genuine bills of lading and that upon discovery that the bills of lading were forged, the acceptor who had paid the draft could recover the money.

§ 62 of lading 

In Hannay v. Guaranty Trust Co. of New York, 187 Fed. Rep. Forged bills 

686, the plaintiff accepted generally a draft containing the provision, "charge the same to the account of R. S. M. I. 100 bales of cotton," with what purported to be a bill of lading for the cotton attached. The draft and the bill of lading were indorsed to the defendant bank and upon maturity of the draft it was paid by the plaintiff's bank. Upon discovery that the bill of lading was a forgery and that no cotton was shipped, the plaintiff sued the defendant for the recovery of the money. It was held on demurrer to the complaint that the acceptance and payment of the draft were conditional on the genuineness of the bill of lading and that the demurrer should be overruled. Only two cases were cited to support the decision, namely, Guaranty Trust Co. v. Grotrian, supra, in which the acceptance was quite different, and National Bank v. Merchants Bank, 91 U. S. 92, which does not seem to have any application. After the trial of this case, which resulted in favor of the plaintiff, the judgment was reversed by the Circuit Court of Appeals in Guaranty Trust Co. v. Hannay, 210 Fed. Rep. 810, on the ground that the rights of the parties were governed by the law of England, the draft having been drawn in the United States on the Bank of Liverpool, the agent of Hannay. It is to be observed that in neither of the two foregoing cases was the Negotiable Instruments Law referred to by counsel or by the court. 

Subsequently the Guaranty Trust Co. brought an action in 

England against Hannay claiming declarations that the bill was an unconditional bill of exchange by the Bills of Exchange Act, that its acceptance was unconditional and that they did not, by presenting the bill for acceptance with the bill of lading attached warrant the genuineness of the bill of lading by the law of England, and that they were not bound to repay the amount of the bill. Hannay counterclaimed for a declaration that the plaintiffs were liable to repay the money to the defendant. The Court of 

Appeals, in elaborate opinions by Pickford, Warrington and

Scrutton, JJ., rightly held that the acceptance was unconditional, both according to the Bills of Exchange Act and the Negotiable Instruments Law and that the acceptors could not recover the money paid to the holder of the bill. Guaranty Trust Co. v. Hannay [1918], 2 K. B. 623 (C. A.), revg. [1918] 1 K. B. 43. 

See review of this case and discussion of the subject, by Professor 

Chafee, in 32 Harv. L. Rev. 560. A shipper of cotton drew a draft upon the buyer reading, "charge the same to account of against 214 B. C.," attached forged bills of lading, and discounted the draft with the A bank which collected it from the buyer, who received the cotton from the carrier on surrender of the forged bills of lading. The shipper used the genuine bills of lading as collateral for other drafts discounted at the B bank, which recovered from the railroad for conversion of the cotton. Held, (1) the railroad can

§ 782 

Forged bills of lading recover from the buyer the amount which it paid for this conversion. The right of a common carrier to recover from a person who receives goods upon a forged bill of lading is not analogous to the position of a drawee of a bill of exchange, who must determine at his peril the genuineness of the signature of the drawer, or the position of the ostensible maker of a forged note who pays it and can not recover the amount. (2) The buyer can not recover the amount he paid on the draft from the A bank, inasmuch as the draft was not conditional on the genuineness of the bill of lading. Sec. 62 was not cited. Hubbard v. 

Southern Pacific Co., 256 Fed. 761, 168 C. C. A. 107 (La.). 

A draft issued in Kansas, with bill of lading attached, was indorsed by the defendant bank in Oklahoma, "Pay any bank or banker, all previous indorsements guaranteed." The plaintiff drawee paid the draft to a subsequent collecting bank in Texas and received the bill of lading, which was discovered to be forged. Held, the defendant bank was not liable on its indorsement, which guaranteed the genuineness of indorsements and not of the bill of lading. The , which was not cited, was then in force in Kansas and Oklahoma but not in Texas. 

Tradesmens State Bank v. Ft. Worth Elevators Co. (Tex. Civ. 

App.), 214 S. W. 656.

Sec. 63. When Person Deemed Indorser. 

A person placing his signature upon an instrument otherwise than as maker, drawer or acceptor, is deemed to be an indorser, unless he clearly indicates by appropriate words his intention to be bound in some other capacity.¹

Sonk, 201 Mich. 655, 167 N. W. 842.

See note on parol evidence to vary the liability of an irregular indorser in 28 Yale L. J. 187; also 87 Cent. L. J. 120.

In view of the preceding Michigan decision, the statement obiter in City Nat. Bank v. Price's Est., 225 Mich. 200, 196

N. W. 429, that an accommodation indorser of a note who waives presentment and notice was a joint maker, must merely mean that his liability was similar to that of a maker. Presentment to him would not have been necessary to charge other indorsers. 

The fact that the indorser was an officer of the payee's bank seems immaterial to the determination of the nature of his obligation.

An accommodation indorser is not jointly liable with the maker, and an action against them both does not fall within the long statute of limitations for actions "against defendants jointly liable upon contract. Macauley v. Feind, 179 N. Y. 

Supp. 469. 

An accommodation indorser who had waived demand and notice was held absolutely liable so that he could be sued in assumpsit on a money count like a maker, and not on a special count; Sed Quaere. Commercial Finance Corporation v. Gale, 

105 Vt. 3, 162 Atl. 899.

The defendant indorsers signed a judgment note with the following provisions, "I or we hereby guarantee the within note with the same rights to collect from me or us as the holder would have against the maker." Held that the entry of a joint judgment against them and the makers was error. First 

Nat. Bank of Moscow v. Kendrew, 105 Pa. Super Ct. 142, 160 

Atl. 227.

In Burke v. Jefferson Bank, 180 S. W. 500, affirmed without report in 121 Ark. 633, the court said that one who indorsed a note before delivery was "a joint maker and not entitled to notice of default," citing certain old cases. The attention of the court was probably not called to sec. 64 of the Negotiable Instruments Law which went into effect in the state several months before the date of the note. In Tancred v. First Nat. Bank, 124 

Ark. 154, 187 S. W. 160, it was held that one, indorsing a note before delivery, becomes, so far as the face of the note is concerned, a joint maker, but it may be shown by parol evidence that he signed as a surety, citing Vandeventer.v. Davis, 92 Ark. 

604. The note appears to have been made May 12, 1913. The

In Van Kleek v. Channon, 175 Ill. App. 626, it was held that one who writes his name on the back of a note prior to its delivery is presumed to be a guarantor. This case is wrong, if the note was made after 1907 (the date of the adoption of the Negotiable Instruments Law in Illinois), as it probably was, since the case was decided in 1912. No reference was made to the Act and the only case cited was an Illinois case in which the note was made fifteen years before the passage of the Act and therefore under the old law of the state. This decision seems overruled by the Illinois Appellate Court cases cited supra. 

Recovery can not be had against an anomalous indorser as maker even if the petition charges him to be a maker and parol evidence showing him to be such was admitted without objection. 

The court is not at liberty to give to the instrument other legal effect than the statute says shall be given to it and parol evidence will not be considered. Overland Auto Co. v. Winters (Mo. 

App.), 180 S. W. 561, affd. 277 Mo. 425, 210 S. W. 1. Accord, Kopf v. Yordy, 200 Ill. App. 409; Crane v. Downs, 108 Kan. 

599, 196 Pac. 600 (construing Missouri Act); Orthwein v. Nolker, 290 Mo. 284, 234 S. W. 787.

The intent to be bound in some other capacity must be indicated in the indorsement and can not be shown by parol. Busbee v. Creech, 192 N. C. 499, 135 S. E. 326, 13 Va. L. Q. 306; 

Smardon v. Broussard, 6 La. App. 579; First Nat. Bank v. 

Bickel, 143 Ky. 754, 137 S. W. 790. "The act does not merely raise a presumption that he is an indorser, but a status is absolutely fixed by it and can not be changed by parol proof." 

Lightner v. Roach, 126 Md. 474, 95 Atl. 62. "Sec. 63 is a statutory command that the legal effect of a blank indorsement can not be changed or varied by evidence from another source." 

First Nat. Bank v. Korn (Mo. App.), 179 S. W. 721. Accord, Cohen v. Ets-Hokin, 219 Ill. App. 340; Geller, etc., Hardware 

Co. v. Drozda, 203 Mo. App. 91, 217 S. W, 557. 

See also other cases and discussion under sec. 64.

But there seems to be no reason why the intent to be bound in some other capacity may not be found on the face of the instrument, and it was so held in Hibernia Bank v. Dresser, 132 La. 

532, 61 So. 561, in which case the note read, "We, the signers,

§ 63 

of anomalous indorsers, sureties and all of us in solido, promise to pay, etc." 

The signers on the back before delivery were held bound in solido indorser with those on the face and to the same extent and were not entitled to notice of dishonor, since the words quoted indicated an intention to be bound in some other capacity than as indorsers, Bonart v. Rabito, 141 La. 970, 76 So. 166, accord; see also Agri cultural Credit Ass'n. v. Jaccuzzo, 167 La. 230, 119 So. 31. 

But in Dresser Co. v. Hibernia Bank, 136 La. 314, 67 So. 

15, where another note in the same form was involved, it was held that one, who had signed his name upon the back of the note, could not be regarded as a maker in the sense that securities pledged by the maker signing upon the face to secure the payment of the note, and "any other indebtedness then due or thereafter to become due by the maker of this note," could be applied to other indebtedness of the one who signed upon the back. The court said, "If the Negotiable Instruments Act be applied to the case, Dresser's status is that of an indorser, though by having promised in solido with all the other parties and unconditionally to pay, he may have deprived himself of some of the rights of an indorser. 

Where a note read "X * does promise to pay" and was signed by X and defend t, it was held that defendant was deemed to be an indorser and not a maker, since the language on the instrument did not import an unconditional promise on his part to pay. O'Dess v. Gunter, 258 Mich. 667, 242 N. W. 804.

Where plaintiff was required to indorse a check payable to another before it was cashed by the bank, as he had previously been required to do on presenting checks payable to the same person, and as was also in accordance with the custom of the bank to require every person, who presented a check for payment to sign his name on the back for the purpose of holding him for the check, plaintiff's indorsement amounted to a contract to indemnify the bank if the check was not paid and the bank was entitled to charge the check back to plaintiff's account, if it was not paid. The  was not cited, although the check was dated after the passage of the act. Arkansas Nat. Bank V. 

Gunther, 127 Ark. 149, 191 S. W. 901.

This section abrogates the former rule in New Jersey that the signature of a third person upon the back of a negotiable instrument prior to its delivery to the payee creates per se no implied or commercial contract. Wilson v. Hendee, 74 N. J. Law 640, 66 Atl. 413. See also cases under sec. 64(1).

Upon a sale of property, the seller required the buyer to procure an indorser to a note to be given for part of the price. The buyer executed a note to the seller with the blank indorsement of the defendant. Held, that defendant was liable as an indorser and not as a maker. Roessle v. Lancaster, 130 App. Div. 1, 114 N. English common law. Steele v. M'Kinlay, 5 App. Cas. 754. anomalous indorser in England

The B. E. A. has no section corresponding to N. I. L., sec. 64, and the problem raised by subsec. 2 of this section of the N. I. L. has been decided in England under B. E. A., sec. 56,2 which corresponds to N. I. L., sec. 63, with additional use of other sections of the statute.

In Jenkins v. Coomber [1898], 2 Q. B. 168, it was held that, where A drew a bill on B, payable to his own order, which B accepted, and C, in accordance with a previous agreement to guarantee its payment, wrote his name on the back, and the bill was delivered to A, C was not liable to A as indorser, as the bill had not been indorsed by A before C put his name on the back. 

Steele v. M'Kinlay, 5 App. Cas. 754, was not changed by sec. 56, B. E. A., corresponding to sec. 63, N. I. L. cases It has, however, since been held in Glenie v. Bruce Smith [1908], 1 K. B. 263, where one T wrote his acceptance across the face of a blank bill form and the defendant indorsed it, and the bill was then delivered to plaintiff, who filled it up as drawer, payable to himself, and then indorsed it, that defendant was 2 Supra, p. 783, n. 1.

Liability of liable to plaintiff because under sec. 20 B. E. A. (sec. 14, N. I. 

Indorser in L.), the defendant was estopped from saying that his name was put on the bill as indorser before the drawer had made it a bill by indorsing it. Still later, upon a state of facts similar to those in Jenkins v. Coomber, that case was followed and Glenie v. Bruce Smith again distinguished on the ground that it was governed by sec. 20. Shaw & Co. v. Holland [1913], 2 K. B. 15. 

It thus appears that in England the indorsement of a blank bill is more efficacious in holding the indorser liable to the drawerpayee, who fills up and indorses the bill after he receives it, than is a bill indorsed and complete when delivered to the drawer-payee, except as to the drawer's indorsement. tainly an anomalous result. Cer- Glenie v.

Bruce Smith was followed in turn by Re Gooch 

[1921], 2 K. B. 593 (C. A.). Shaw v. Holland was distinguished, first because of evidence here that the indorser intended to be bound to the plaintiff payee, and secondly because there was no negotiation in that case whereas in Re Gooch the plaintiff indorsed the bill to a bank from which she took it up at maturity. 

The House of Lords has now held, in a case where there were no blanks upon the face of the bill at the time of its delivery, that the drawer-payee could recover from an anomalous indorser for the accommodation of the acceptor. McDonald 

& Co. v. Nash & Co. [1924], A. C. 625. Accord, Bernardi v. 

National Sales Corporation, Limited (1931), 2 K. B. 188, where the court held that if a third party signed the bill with the intention of being liable, the rights of the drawer could not be defeated merely because he signed below the signature of the third party. McCall Brothers v. Hargreaves (1932), 2 K. B. 423.

The view of the preceding cases that the indorser's liability depends on the application of sec. 20 B. E. A. (sec. 14 ) was continued by a majority of the Law Lords, who considered that the case was brought within that section by the fact that the defendant left a blank on the back of the bill above his indorsement, which was subsequently filled in by the indorsement of the drawer-payee before suit. They thought that the plaintiff could not have recovered without this subsequent indorsement, as necessary to complete the bill. 

A much more straightforward view, according with the business understanding of such an indorsement, was taken by the Lord Chancellor (Haldane). He considered that the plaintiff could have recovered without any indorsement by it, under the terms of sec. 56 B. E. A. (sec. 63 N. I. L.) since the defendant indorsed with the intention to be liable to the plaintiff.3 

Lord Haldane said, "I do not consider it necessary to resort 3 The Court of Appeal, whose decision is briefly reported in (1922) W. N. 272, had found that the defendant did not intend to be liable to the plaintiff but only to some third party, like a bank, who should buy the bill from the plaintiff; this finding was held inconsistent with the evidence by all the Law Lords.

§ 64 

to the authority given by s. 20, for it appears to me that the bills were, from the beginning, complete and regular on the face of them 

And s. 56 of the Act itself, which governs here, provides that where a person signs a bill otherwise than as a drawer or acceptor, he thereby incurs the liability of an indorser to a holder in due course. This section appears to me to make him become liable as an indorser if, as here, he has intended to become so." 

The decision is discussed in 69 Sol. J. 82, 58 Ir. L. T. 95, 40 L. Q. R. 387, 38 Harv. L. Rev. 681, which approves Lord 

Haldane's view.

It is hoped that Lord Haldane's view will hereafter prevail in the British Courts, and that Steele v. M'Kinlay, supra, will be distinguished because of the absence of evidence that the indorser in that case intended to be liable to the payee. The opinion of the majority of the Law Lords illustrates once more the astonishing reluctance of courts to carry out the plain understanding of business men as to the liability of the anomalous indorser. Indeed, in the absence of legislation the only common law jurisdiction in the world which decided this question on commercial principles unobscured by legal technicalities was the Republic of Hawaii. Yuen Lung v. Burke, 9 Haw. 142 

(1893). 

It would seem that since the payee may be a holder in due course there ought to be no difficulty, in England, in holding the anomalous indorser directly liable to the payee, under sec. 56 of the Bills of Exchange Act, without having the payee go through the form of first indorsing the instrument and delivering it to the intended backer to have him indorse it, and return it to the payee, so that the latter may sue as a subsequent indorsee, and without having the payee indorse before suit as in McDonald & Co. v. 

Nash & Co., supra.

Sec. 64. Liability of Irregular Indorser. 

Where a person, not otherwise a party to an instrument, places thereon his signature in blank before delivery, he is liable as indorser, in accordance with the following rules:-

ANNOTATIONS 

In Briscol v. American Southern Trust Co., 176 Ark. 401, 4

S. W. (2d) 912 the court held that a person placing his name on an instrument after maturity was not an indorser because it was not "before delivery" within this section. The case is clearly wrong, see secs. 63, 17(6) and (7).

Parole evi- dence to vary There has been considerable conflict over the question whether liability parol evidence was admissible to show the intention of the parties that anomalous indorsers should be bound in a manner different from the rules laid down in section 64. Most of the confusion on this point has been caused by a failure to distinguish those cases where the question of the nature of the liability of the parties is involved from those where the order of liability is in question.

It is the clear intention of the Act, as indicated by sections 

17(6), 31, 63 and 67, that one who fails to indicate, on the instrument, the capacity in which he intends to be bound shall be bound as an indorser. It is also the overwhelming weight of authority that parol evidence is not admissible to charge such a person on the instrument in any other capacity; see cases under sec. 63. But it is also equally clear, under sections 16, 68, 82(3), 109, 55 and 58, that the framers of the Act contemplated that, as between the immediate parties and persons other than holders in due course, evidence of any contracts was admissible so long as the contracts did not contradict the intention expressed by the plain words of the instrument. 

See the cases infra and under sec. 68.

An examination of the wording of section 64 itself will also show that the admission of parol evidence was not only contemplated but is necessary in the application of the rules of the section itself. Thus sub-section 3 lays down a rule different from sub-section 1, where the indorser signs for the accommodation of the payee. This difference of result is possible only by the admission of parol evidence to show the fact of accommodation. If the framers of the Act had intended section 64 to 

1 Not in B. E. A. See supra, p. 793.

§ 64 

state an absolute rule of liability it is hardly conceivable that they would have stated their rules in terms which required parol evidence to make them workable. 

If there could be any doubt as to this intention it is laid at rest by section 68, which permits a variation of order of liability as between indorsers, and the second sentence of section 16, which allows contracts between the immediate parties to be shown.

This position is further strengthened by the well-known rule of code construction that, unless there is a public policy, to the contrary, codified rules of law are applied only in absence of expressed intention of the parties.

Of course, it is clear that a holder in due course would be entitled to rely upon the instrument and the terms of rules laid down by the section. 

With these distinctions in mind one encounters little difficulty in the cases. See also pp. 801, 802, infra. ous cases on

The Negotiable Instruments Law governs a renewal note made after the passage of the act, although the original note was given before the act, especially where there were new indorsers on the renewal note making in law a new contract with different parties.

Presumption of time of

When an instrument in the payee's possession bears the dedelivery fendant's indorsement, and neither side offers evidence whether it was written before or after delivery, it appears much more probable that the defendant indorsed before delivery, since otherwise he would have performed an act largely futile. 

Whether a presumption to this effect arises from the mere production of the instrument, is not settled by the cases under the 

 The statement in 1 Daniel, Negotiable Instruments 

(6th ed.), sec.

713, that such a presumption in favor of signa-

The Massachusetts view on this point seems connected with the view in that state that the indorser was a comaker at common law. But the presumption appears to have been denied in other states, which demanded proof from the payee of the facts creating liability in the anomalous indorser. Marienthal v. Taylor, 2

Under the  it is arguable that the presumption follows from a broad construction of "delivery," in sec. 64, and from the provision of sec. 24, that every person whose signature appears on a negotiable instrument is presumed "to have become a party thereto for value." The difficulty with the narrow construction adopted by the cases marked quaere on p. 799, is that the payee must prove the promise to himself and that it was made before "original" delivery. A broader construction of "delivery" to include any delivery would obviate their difficulty, and would accord with the proposition that sec. 64 states a rebuttable presumption, see supra, p. 796. Sec. 65. Warranty Where Negotiation by Delivery, Etc. 

Every person negotiating an instrument by delivery or by a qualified indorsement, warrants,— 

Cross Reference: §§ 30, 38, 191, 7, 9, 16, 34, 36, 40, 49, 66. (1) That the instrument is genuine and in all respects what it purports to be; 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 13 to 16, 23, 124, 125. (2) That he has a good title to it;

Cross Reference: §§ 57, 13 to 16, 55. 

(3) That all prior parties had capacity to contract;

Cross Reference: §§ 22, 48, 50, 121. 

(4) That he has no knowledge of any fact which would impair the validity of the instrument or render it valueless. 

Cross Reference: §§ 23, 24 to 29, 55, 56, 19 to 22, 42, 119, 125.

But when the negotiation is by delivery only, the warranty extends in favor of no holder other than the immediate transferee. 

Cross Reference: §§ 30, 191, 9, 16, 34, 40, 49, 58.

The provisions of subdivision three of this section do not apply to persons negotiating public or corporation securities, other than bills and notes.¹ 

Cross Reference: § 30.

In section 49 there is a provision that the "negotiation" takes effect as of the time when the indorsement is actually made for the purpose of determining when the transferee becomes a holder in due course. Thus for one purpose actual indorsement is necessary to complete the negotiation. But legal title passes under section 

49 evidencing the legislative intent to make negotiation effective for other purposes. This legislative intent was carried over by the court to the "negotiating" in section 65 to cover the delivery of order paper without indorsement. Queensboro Nat. Bank of

But where the president acted as the sole representative of the purchaser and the bank, both principals were charged with the president's knowledge and the purchaser was not entitled to recover on the warranty. The state of Minnesota issued voucher warrants, i. e., drafts drawn by the state auditor upon the state treasurer who accepted them, payable to members of the National Guard who served on the Mexican border. Such warrants were payable through state depositories. A clerk, whose duty was to deliver these warrants to the payces, forged the indorsement of the payees upon several warrants, placed his own name beneath, and deposited them in his own account in the X bank. This bank indorsed these warrants in blank, and presented them through the clearing house to the Y bank, a state depository, which paid them. The 

Y bank indorsed them "Paid" with its own name beneath, and presented them to the state treasurer for redemption. The state sued both banks to recover the amounts paid. Held, both banks were liable to the state; the X bank was primarily liable, and if the Y bank was obliged to pay it could recover from the X bank the amount so paid. The X bank simply purchased the warrants, and its indorsement to the Y bank warranted, under sec. 65, that all previous indorsements were genuine and that it had good title to the paper. State v. 

Merchants Nat. Bank, 145 Minn. 322, 177 N. W. 135, see after sec. 198. 

Although the result is sound, the reasoning is open to question. 

The fact that the Y bank stamped the warrants paid shows that it was not purchasing them, but was paying them as agent of the drawee. Consequently, the so-called indorsement by the X bank was not a true indorsement for the purposes of transferring title but constituted a receipt by one presenting a check for payment. Sec. 65 therefore had no application. But the

X bank was liable to the Y bank on quasi-contractual principles, and under sec. 23, though not as indorser; it received money under a mistake in return for an instrument which it did not own, since the indorsement of the payees were forged. Similarly, the

Admissibility of parol 

In Smith v. Barner, 95 Oreg. 486, 188 Pac. 216, a trustee who evidence assigned to the plaintiff a note fraudulently obtained from the maker by the beneficiary was held not liable as a warrantor, in the absence of evidence that the note was negotiable, that it was indorsed even without recourse, and that the trustee knew of the fraud. Johns, J., for the court, said that there was a vital distinction under sec. 65 between the defenses which may be pleaded where the title passes by delivery and where it is acquired by indorsement without recourse. When a note is transferred by delivery only, the transaction rests in parol, and a defense in parol may then be made. An indorsement without recourse is a written contract into which the statutory terms and provisions are incorporated, and parol evidence is not admissible to vary the written indorsement. Sennett, J., concurring in the decision, denied the existence of this distinction, and considered that the implied warranties under an indorsement without recourse are always subject to parol evidence of the real agreement of the parties. 

A contemporaneous oral agreement is not admissible to show that an indorser without recourse was to be liable as guarantor. 

 Payette Nat. Bank v. Ingard, 34 

Ida. 295, 200 Pac. 344.

When notes were indorsed by one bank to another, without recourse, parol evidence that they were deposited as collateral and not sold was admissible. The evidence did not vary the terms of a written contract. It is true that the indorsement was contract by itself, but it was a part of the larger or whole contract between the banks. The N. I. L. was not cited. Northrup Nat. Bank v. Yates Center Nat. Bank, 98 Kan. 563. 159

Pac. 403.

Rescission of sale of defeccollectible 

An action for cancellation of a note because cashier's checks tive or non- received therefor were worthless is not an action for breach of instrument warranty in negotiation of the checks, and is therefore not governed by this section. Dille v. White, 132 Ia. 327, 109 N. W. 

909, 10 L. R. A. (N.S.) 510.

The right of the purchaser of a worthless or unenforceable instrument to rescind the purchase for fraud, misrepresentation, or mutual mistake of fact is independent of his right against the seller on an implied warranty. It depends on common-law principles of rescission, and may exist on grounds which do not create any liability for implied warranty under sec. 65, just as the similar right of the purchaser of a chattel to rescission for fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake, is not coextensive with his remedies under the Uniform Sales Act upon implied warranties. Hunt v. Sanders, 288 Mo. 337, 232 S. W. 456.

A note negotiable in form, payable to a foreign corporation which had not complied with Idaho law, was indorsed by the payee without recourse when overdue and after the Statute of Limitations had run. The lower court held the payee liable as warrantor to the indorsee. Held, reversed and new trial granted. 

Moody v. Morris-Roberts Co., 38 Ida. 414, 226 Pac. 278. One judge dissented and the majority were equally divided, on a rehearing, as to the grounds of decision. Two judges held that the warranties of a qualified indorser could not run to the plaintiff; first, because warranties are available only to a holder in due course; secondly, because the instrument, being transferred for the first time after the maker's obligation was barred with the transferor a mere assignor, was never "negotiable in its origin" within sec. 47, and consequently was governed by the law relating to ordinary contracts or non-negotiable instruments, and not by the , whialhas no application to a non-negotiable instrument. The two concurring judges held that the indorser would be liable to the plaintiff on a warranty of absence of knowledge of any fact impairing the validity of the instru ment, unless the indorsee also knew such fact, and that evidence as to the indorsee's knowledge should be submitted to the jury at a new trial. These judges stated that if the warranties under sec. 65 were express and part of the written agreement of transfer, parol evidence of the indorsee's knowledge would not be admissible to negative the indorser's obligation, but considered that the warranties were implied by law and hence not available to an indorsee with knowledge of defects. 

The opinion of these concurring judges seems preferable. 

Since the instrument complied with the requirements of sec. 1, it was governed by the N. I. L. regardless of subsequent transactions under sec. 47.

§ 66  Sec. 66. Liability of General Indorser. 

Every indorser who indorses without qualification, warrants to all subsequent holders in due course:- 

Cross Reference: §§ 17(6), 31, 33, 34, 52, 63, 67, 191, 196, 7, 16, 40, 58, 65, 68. (1) The matters and things mentioned in subdivisions one, two and three of the next preceding section; and 

Cross Reference: § 65. 

(2) That the instrument is at the time of his indorsement valid and subsisting.' 

Cross Reference: §§ 17(6), 31, 63, 67, 191, 7, 13 to 16, 19 to 23, 119, 120, 123 to 125. 2 And, in addition, he engages that on due presentment, it shall be accepted or paid, or both, as the case may be, according to its tenor, and that if it be dishonored, and the necessary proceedings on dishonor be duly taken, he will pay the amount thereof to the holder, or to any subsequent indorser who may be compelled to pay it. 

Cross Reference: 88 70 to 85, 88, 89 to 118, 143 to 160, 191, 7, 16, 36, 37, 45, 50, 51, 121, 124, 188, 192.

ANNOTATIONS 

The transferor of a non-negotiable instrument can not be subject to the warranties under this section, since they enure only to the benefit of a holder in due course, a term applicable only to a negotiable instrument. Farmers State Bank v. Blazek, 115 Kan. 178, 222 Pac. 748. Cf. Hayter v. Dinsmore, 125 Kan. 

749, 265 Pac. 1112.

A non-negotiable note was indorsed in blank by the defendant payee. Held, he can not set up a parol agreement that the indorsement was to operate only as a transfer without recourse, at least as against remote indorsee without notice of the agreement. Decisions under the  with respect to negotiable instruments were considered applicable, since the Act is a codification of common-law rules which in many instances are the same for negotiable and non-negotiable instruments. The indorser of a non-negotiable note promises to pay it, but can not require presentment to the maker and notice of dishonor; he is like the maker of a new note. The N. I. L. was cited, but without reference to any specific section. Berry v. Gross, 192 Ia.

B. E. A. s. 55 (2).

-Restrictive indorser The warranty of a maker who indorses a note, payable to his own order, is no stronger than his contract as maker, and if that is void for usury, so is his contract of indorsement. Sabine v. 

Paine, 166 App. Div. 9, 151 N. Y. Supp. 735, affirmed, 223 N. Y. 

401, 119 N. E. 849, 5 A. L. R. 1444, see also Consolidated Motors 

Co. v. Urschel, 115 Kan. 147, 222 Pac. 745, discussed under sec. 184. 

A single executor can not, without the concurrence of his coexecutors, indorse the name of a testator on a note, so as to bind the estate. The  was not cited on this point. Union Bank v. Sullivan, 214 N. Y. 332, 108 N. E. 558.

Where a forged instrument was negotiated by a party prior to the defendant indorser, it was held that his warranty did not run to the purchaser in due course. The court evidently overlooked the word "all" in this section. See discussion of the case under section 50. Ray v. Livingston, 204 N. C. 1, 167 S. E. 496, 17 Minn. L. Rev. 808.

An indorser "for collection" warrants that the instrument is genuine and that he has good title to it, etc. The court cited sec. 64, but evidently sec. 66 was meant. In re Ziegenhein (Mo. 

App.), 187 S. W. 893.

This holding seems correct where the indorser for collection receives value from the bank so that he can be considered a seller. Under such circumstances the restrictive nature of the indorsement should not negative the usual warranties of a seller of an instrument, for on correct principles it merely adds the promise that on presentation it will be honored, and is an obligation to protect subsequent holders for value from loss in the same manner as if there was no trust. This follows a fortiori where the trust is for a third person under sec. 36(3). It would even seem that in the absence of qualifying words like "without recourse" the restrictive indorser under subsecs. 2 and 3 of sec. 36 should be held, not under sec. 65, but under sec. 66, but it is possible that a holder for value under the restrictive indorsement may be "a holder in due course" within sec. 66 in view of the language of secs. 36, 37 and 47. See the discussion of this question under those sections. 

See the note in 36 Banking L. J. 71, which takes the opposite view from In re Ziegenhein, supra, and thinks that a banker receiving or paying a check indorsed restrictively should insist that the last preceding holder add the words, "Previous indorsements guaranteed." Such a guarantee would create liability even to the drawee bank. The note, however, fails to realize that the so-called "indorsement" on presentation for payment is

§ 66 

indorser only a receipt, although this proposition is correctly set forth in Restrictive 

First Nat. Bank v. City Nat. Bank, 182 Mass. 130, 65 N. E. 24, not citing the , which the editor quotes as contra to In re 

Ziegenhein, supra, without perceiving that the case did not involve a true indorsement. 

Such an indorsement was also held not to be a warranty in favor of the drawee in Citizens' Nat. Bank of Odessa v. San 

Angelo Nat. Bank of San Angelo (Tex. Civ. App.), 19 S. W. (2d) 388.  Contra, Farmers' State 

Bank in Merkel v. United States, 62 F. (2d) 178 (C. C. A. 5th), not citing the N. I. L.

The indorsement "Pay to the order of any bank, banker, or trust company, prior indorsements guaranteed" was held a warranty in favor of the drawee, the court stating that the same result would be reached in the absence of words guaranteeing all prior indorsements. The N. I. L. was not cited. Agricultural 

Ins. Co. v. North Texas Nat. Bank (Tex. Civ. App.), 57 S. W. (2d) 229; Guardian Savings & Loan Assn. v. Liberty State 

Bank (Tex. Civ. App.), 60 S. W. (2d) 823, affd., 127 Tex. 311, 94 S. W. (2d) 133.

Although section 66 states that the warranties of unqualified indorsers run to all subsequent holders in due course, it is significant that the word "only" is not used, thus the section is silent as to the rights of other holders. It is to be noted, however, that the warranties of section 65 run to any person to whom the instrument has been negotiated, and there is no reason why the same result should not be obtained under section 66. 

In cases where a holder in due course intervenes between the indorser and the party desiring to enforce the warranty, section 

58 gives him all the rights of the holder in due course. And if the instrument is unindorsed section 49 takes care of the rights; see Miller v. Shelby County Investment Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 30 S. W. (2d) 669, 9 Tex. L. Rev. 245. The only difficulty arises where the instrument is in the hands of an immediate transferee, not a holder in due course.

In such a case there is no reason why sections 66 and 65 can not be extended by analogy to cover the case. Such a result would conform to the intention of the parties, and the general commercial law covering implied warranties in sales of goods; see section 196. To hold otherwise would reach the grotesque result, suggested in the fourth edition of this book, p. 608, that a transferor of a qualified indorser would have greater rights than a transferor of an unqualified indorser. 

See State Exchange Bank v. Nat. Bank of Commerce, 70 

Okla. 234, 174 Pac. 796, 2 A. L. R. 211 and other cases cited under subsec. 4 of sec. 65, supra.

The statements in American Exch. Nat. Bank v. Yorkville

If the collecting bank were a warrantor under these sections, it would also warrant the genuineness of the drawer's signature, which is clearly not the case. 

The liability of the collecting bank to refund money paid on a forged indorsement rests on sec. 23 and the quasi-contractual duty to return money received under mistake, and not on any warranty, since there is no sale. 

In First Nat. Bank v. U. S. Nat. Bank, 100 Oreg. 264, 197

Pac. 547, 14 A. L. R. 479, the court stated that the indorsement of a collecting bank upon presentation for payment to the drawee does not create any warranty under this section, but that under clearing house rules the indorsement of the defendant operated as a guaranty of the genuineness of prior indorsements, though not of the signature of the drawer.

The indorsement with the clearing house stamp, under the rules, may operate as a guaranty of previous indorsements, and a suit by the drawee against a collecting bank to recover for a forgery does not come within the one year limitation placed by the California Code of Civil Proc., sec. 340, subsec. 3, upon a suit by a "depositor against a bank." Each successive indorser makes a separate contract with a remote indorsee and may be sued in a separate action even though a statute authorizes the joinder of all indorsers. Citizens Trust Co. v. Zoller, 121 Misc. 451, 201 N. Y. Supp. 179.

A statute providing that the maker and indorsers of negotiable instruments "may be sued in one and the same action" does not amend the Negotiable Instruments Law so as to make negotiable instruments joint contracts on the part of the maker and those secondarily liable. In a suit against one indorser it was held no defense that the maker and the other indorsers were not joined as defendants. Williams v. Peninsular Grocery Co., 73 Fla. 937, 75 So. 517. So. 516.

The payee of a note secured by a deed of trust, who has transferred the note and deed, is interested because of his contingent liability as indorser to bring a bill of review of a decree cancelling the deed of trust on behalf of the maker, but the indorsee is a necessary party. Bristow v. Tyler, 82 W. Va. 629, 96 S. E. 1052.

A made a note to the order of B, forged B's indorsement, then procured C's indorsement for A's accommodation, and negotiated the note. Held, C, by his indorsement, guaranteed the genuineness of B's signature, and was liable to a holder in due course. Packard v. Windholz, 88 App. Div. 365, 84 N. Y. 

Supp. 666, affirmed without opinion, 180 N. Y. 549.

In order to entitle the holder to sue the indorser on his warranty, he must give notice of the forgery within a reasonable time after its discovery. Ladd & Tilton Bank v. United States, 30 F. (2d) 334.

Where the indorsees of a check on which the payee's indorsement was forged acquired good title under the applicable foreign law, the words "previous indorsements guaranteed" used by the holder presenting for payment constituted a warranty not of the genuineness of prior indorsements, but of the authenticity of the holder's title. Thus payments made in reliance upon the warranty could not be recovered in spite of the prior forged indorsement.  United States v. Guaranty Trust Co. of New York, 69 F. (2d) 799, affd., 293 U. S. 

340, 79 L. Ed. 415, 55 S. C. 221, 95 A. L. R. 651 with note, 83

U. of Pa. L. Rev. 681, 12 N. Y. U. L. Q. Rev. 519, 2 U. of Chi. 

L. Rev. 479. 

A note payable to the maker's order, with the maker's name blank and indorsed by A and B, was brought by B to the defendant, with the request that he become maker. He declined, but indorsed the note on B's agreement that A should be maker. 

B, however, forged the defendant's name as maker and delivered the note to the plaintiff, a holder in due course. Held, the defendant was liable to the plaintiff as accommodation indorser. 

Under the terms of sec. 66, it was immaterial that the maker's signature was forged, although the defendant would not have been liable as maker. Shepherd v. Mortgage Sec. Corp., 139 

Va. 274, 123 S. E. 553.

In Little v. Peoples Bank, 209 Ala. 620, 96 So. 763, it was stated that an anomalous accommodation indorser warranted that all prior parties had capacity to contract and could not defend on the ground that the signature of the corporate maker was written by an unauthorized agent. The court, however, did not need to find a warranty in this case since the note had matured and the accommodation indorser was liable on her ordinary obligation to pay if the maker did not.

Conflict of laws A note secured by mortgage on land in California was executed, delivered and payable in California, but it was indorsed by defendant, the payee, in New Jersey, where, at the time of the indorsement, it would have been negotiable under the Negotiable Instruments Law, which had been there adopted, after the making of the note, but before the indorsement. By the law of 

California there can be only one action for the recovery of any debt or the enforcement of any right secured by a mortgage upon real estate. Held, that it was unnecessary to determine whether the note would have been negotiable in New Jersey prior to the adoption of the Negotiable Instruments Law; that notwithstanding the mortgage had been foreclosed and the land sold, the contract of the indorser was governed by secs. 63 and 66, , and that the defendant could be held for the unpaid balance. 

Mackintosh v. Gibbs, 79 N. J. L. 40, 74 Atl. 708 (Supreme Court). 

In the Court of Appeals, however, 81 N. J. Law 577, 80 Atl. 

554, Ann. Cas. 1912D, 163, it was held that, by reason of sec. 

195 of the Negotiable Instruments Law, that act did not apply to this note, but that under the former law of New Jersey the note was negotiable, although payable in installments and with. attorney's fees, and the judgment was therefore affirmed, the court stating its agreement with the Supreme Court upon the question of the effect of the proceedings in California for the foreclosure of the mortgage. In the syllabus of this case in the 

Supreme Court, it is stated that the note was "non-negotiable" by the local (California) law, but no reference is made in the opinion in either court to this fact. 

By the law of California at the time, a provision in the note for payment of attorney's fees rendered the note non-negotiable, Finley v. Pott, 131 Cal. 385; Meyer v. Weber, 133 Cal. 681.

The case must therefore be considered an authority for the proposition, that although a note is non-negotiable in the jurisdiction where it was made, delivered and payable, yet, if it is negotiable, by the law of the place where it is indorsed, the indorser's rights and liabilities will be those of an indorser of a negotiable note; otherwise, as stated by the Court of Appeals, p. 579, the defendant could not have been held, since in New Jersey an action can not be maintained against an indorser of a non-negotiable note.

§ 68 Sec. 67. Liability of Indorser Where Paper Nego tiable by Delivery.

Where a person places his indorsement on an instrument negotiable by delivery he incurs all the liabilities of an indorser.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 9, 17(6), 31, 34, 63, 64 to 66, 10, 16, 18 to 23, 30 to 47, 51, 57, 125(4), 192.

Sec. 68. Order in Which Indorsers are Liable. 

As respects one another, indorsers are liable prima facie in the order in which they indorse; but evidence is admissible to show that as between or among themselves they have agreed otherwise. Joint payees or joint indorsees who indorse are deemed to indorse jointly and severally.³

Defendant and plaintiff, in the order named, were indorsers on a note given by a corporation in which both were interested. 

The note was renewed several times, plaintiff being the first indorser on the renewals, the last of which he was compelled to pay in part, and he brought an action to recover the amount from defendant, alleging an agreement by defendant, when the first note was given, to pay it personally. There was evidence tending to support such allegation, and plaintiff testified that when he indorsed the renewal notes he did not know that the order of the indorsements had any legal significance, while it appeared that defendant did know such fact. Held, that the evidence was sufficient to require the submission of the case to the jury, as it would have justified a finding that the agreement of defendant to pay the original note impliedly extended to the renewals. Goldman v. Goldberger, 208 Fed. 877, 126 C. C. A. 35.

When automobile dealers employed an agent, who indorsed a customer's note payable to himself, which was then indorsed by the dealers and discounted at a bank, held, the agent on paying the note could not recover from the dealers on their indorsement. It was subsequent to his indorsement and they indorsed for his accommodation.  Ford v. 

Moreland, 96 W. Va. 225, 122 S. E. 652.

A and B, the principal stockholders in a corporation, indorsed successive renewals of the corporation's notes for its accommodation. For some time, no particular method was followed in the order of indorsement, but after a certain date, B insisted that A, the active manager of the corporation, should indorse first, on the ground that B would not indorse unless A became personally liable. Thereafter A always indorsed first but made no express agreement of liability. Held, B, after paying the note to a holder in due course, could recover the entire amount from A's estate; the action was not subject to the short Statute of Limitations for implied contracts of reimbursement but came within the longer statute for actions on negotiable instruments.

The evidence showed that joint liability was abandoned after a definite date and the liability was in accordance with the prima facie effect of the order of indorsement. Mann v. Bradshaw's 

Admr., 136 Va. 351, 118 S. E. 326.

The first of three accommodation indorsers, stockholders and officers in the corporation which made the note, was compelled to pay the note and sued the last indorser for contribution. The defendant claimed that he was a successive indorser because he had indorsed after the note had been handed to the bank, but evidence showed that the bank did not accept the note until it had been indorsed by the defendant. Held, the defendant was liable. The majority of the court relied on the presence above the first indorsement of the clause, "I hereby waive present-

Quigley, 180 Cal. 265, 180 Pac. 613. 

See discussion in 7 Cal. Law Rev. 343, approving the case because of additional circumstances indicating joint and several liability, though doubting any effect from the waiver. 

In this case, if the suit was on the indorsement the Statute of Limitations had run since maturity. The court held that it was an action for contribution, which accrued when the plaintiff paid, so that it was not yet barred. The court does not say that an action could not have been brought on the defendant's indorsement, if the statute had not run thereon. 

See also a note in 90 C. L. J. 216 on "Right of accommodation indorser to recover though action on note is barred." 

A promissory note was payable to the order of the maker and indorsed in blank by him and by several accommodation indorsers, who orally agreed among themselves as to the proportions for which they should be liable. One of the accommodation indorsers paid the entire amount due on the note, and wrote above the indorsements thereon the words: "Pay to the order of" an agent of such indorser. Semble, that an action in the name of the agent against another of the indorsers can not be maintained upon the note, the remedy of such indorser being by action upon the oral agreement of the indorsers for contribution. 

Shea v. Vahey, 215 Mass. 80, 102 N. E. 119.

In a suit by an assignee of an indorser, who had paid the note, against a prior indorser, evidence of an agreement between the two indorsers that the defendant was not to be liable to the plaintiff's assignor was held a good defense. Perrin v. Wheeler (Conn.), 151 Atl. 161.  

A note was indorsed by the payee and then successively by A and B. The holder obtained separate judgments against the maker and the three indorsers. A firm composed of A's sons paid the holder the amount due on the judgment and took assignments thereof. They allowed the judgment lien on A's land to lapse. Held, B's liability was not thereby discharged. While he had on the face of the note a right of recovery against A, his prior indorser, his means of protecting himself was to take up the no or to pay the debt and take an assignment of the other judgments. The holder was not bound to sue A at all, and B could not require it to proceed against him. While the relation between prior and subsequent indorsers bears some resemblance to that between principal and surety, they are not identical. 

So long as the holder of the judgment did nothing to release A's personal liability on the note or judgment, impairment of the

means of satisfying such liability is not a discharge. Lazaran v. 

Semans, 79 Pa. Super. Ct. 356.

§ 68 

"Joint payee or joint indorsees who indorse are deemed to indorse jointly and severally" 

Cross Reference: §§ 17(6), 31, 63, 67, 191, 11, 14, 16, 17(7), 24, 42, 45, 46, 59, 60, 63 to 67, 184.

Joint accommodation indorsers, being neither payees nor indorsees, are not jointly and severally liable under this section as it appears in the Uniform Act. When one joint indorser was notified, but not the other, both were discharged although the notified indorser waived demand and notice. Case v. McKinnis, 107 Oreg. 223, 213 Pac. 422, 32 A. L. R. 167. The court however, assumed for purposes of argument that the joint accommodation indorsers were jointly and severally liable. 

Accord, First Nat. Bank v. Michigan-Ark. Oil Corp., 231 

Mich. 597, 204 N. W. 719, stating that joint accommodation indorsers were jointly liable, and denying recovery to the payee against both the indorsers, who were not notified, since only one of them waived notice. See the note in 11 Corn. L. Q. 57.

But see sec. 109 which seems to indicate that a contra result is correct.

Since under sec. 68, joint payees or joint indorsees, who indorse, are deemed to indorse jointly and severally, an action lies against any of them individually, and parol evidence is inadmissible to show that they signed as guarantors only. Hodgens v. Jennings, 148 App. Div. 879, 133 N. Y. Supp. 584.

A corporation note contained on the back an accommodation "indorsement," beginning "I, or we, hereby guarantee" was signed seriatim by five individuals of whom M, was fourth. 

Held, M had no right to indemnification by the preceding indorsers under sec. 68, which does not determine the order of liability of joint indorsers among themselves. Sec. 68, in fixing the order of liability, contemplates successive negotiations of the instrument and successive indorsements. Kessel v. Murray, 197 Ia. 17, 196 N. W. 591, 33 A. L. R. 1346.

A surety indorser who pays the note can not recover contribution from other indorsing sureties without showing presentment and notice of dishonor. Bennett v. Kistler, 163 N. Y. Supp. 555. 

But if the plaintiff accommodation indorser was duly notified and paid the drafts, he can recover contribution from the other accommodation indorsers although they were not notified. The action is not upon the instruments themselves but is a suit for contribution, to which the provisions of the  as to notice. of dishonor and protest have no application because no question concerning liability upon commercial paper is involved, citing

§ 70 Sec. 69. Liability of An Agent or Broker. 

Where a broker or other agent negotiates an instrument without indorsement, he incurs all the liabilities prescribed by section sixty-five of this act, unless he discloses the name of his principal, and the fact that he is acting only as agent.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 19, 30, 31, 63, 65, 191, 9, 18 to 23, 34, 40, 42, 44, 67.

Parol evidence is not admissible to relieve a broker or other agent whose indorsement brings him within this section. Peoples 

Bank v. Baker (Mo. App.), 193 S. W. 632.

ARTICLE VI PRESENTMENT FOR PAYMENT Sec. 70. Effect of Want of Demand on Principal Debtor. 

Presentment for payment is not necessary in order to charge the person primarily liable on the instrument;2 but if the instrument is, by its terms, payable at a special place, and he is able and willing to pay it there at maturity, such ability and willingness are equivalent to a tender of payment upon his part. But except as herein otherwise provided, presentment for payment is necessary in order to charge the drawer and indorsers. 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 81, 61, 63, 67, 71 to 82, 85, 86, 109 to 

116, 157, 191, 192, 45, 60 to 66, 84, 87, 89, 120(4), 121, 143, 144, 147, 148, 150 to 152, 186, 194.

A note payable at a specified bank in a city is payable "at a special place" within this section, and if the maker supports his burden of proving tender there he is relieved of costs and interest subsequently accruing. His tender may be made con-

ditional on production and surrender of the note. Maddock v.

When a note was payable at a bank and the maker had sufficient funds on deposit in the bank at maturity, the holder, who failed to present the note at the bank could not include interest after maturity in a judgment confessed under warrant of attorney in the note. Forwood v. Magness, 143 Md. 1, 121

48 S. W. (2d) 687.

While failure to present a note at maturity at the bank where it was payable would relieve the maker from liability for costs and from his promise in the note to pay attorney's fees, if he was ready and willing to pay then and there; yet the maker was not relieved when he had no funds at the place of payment and was not present in person or by agent. His willingness and ability to pay if notified in another state where he was, was immaterial. Hostutler v. Alldredge, (Tex. Civ. App.), 235 S. W. 953. 

Although a note is payable at a special place, presentment at such place is not necessary to charge the maker, but merely to relieve him from liability for damages, if he is ready to pay there and there is no one there to receive the money. So it is no defense that the collateral was not there tendered. It is sufficient to tender the collateral at the trial. Gordon v. Benguiat, 95 Misc. Rep. 132, 159 N. Y. Supp. 1.

Contra is Cline v. First Nat. Bank, 67 Okla. 260, 170 Pac. 

472, that tender must be made before the commencement of the action and must be pleaded and proved at the trial. 

The constructive tender through readiness to pay at the place named does not relieve the maker of the necessity of actual tender in court when he is sued, and in the absence of such tender he is liable for costs. Bradshaw v. Saxton, 68 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 499.

Although a mortgage note did not state a place of payment, evidence was admissible to show that by an arrangement with the mortgagee lasting several years, the mortgagor had been accustomed to leave a check for interest at a bank drawn against sufficient funds therein, and such check was a sufficient tender of interest. Kuhlmeyer v. Butz, 215 Ill. App. 414.

When a seller retained title to the goods as security for notes given by the buyer, which were payable in Philadelphia, the seller could not, in the absence of proof of presentment there, claim that the maker was in default and resell the goods. O'Kane v. No. Am. Distilling Co., 171 N. Y. Supp. 275.

that sec. 70 is limited to the liability of primary parties and has not bearing on the liability of an indorser even of a time note, but that tender of payment by the maker through ability to pay at the place of payment would discharge the indorser of a time note under sec. 120(4), which taken in conjunction with sec. 87 renders recourse to sec. 70 unnecessary. Even if sec. 70 is applicable to an indorser's liability on time notes, the problem of demand notes is much more difficult. Sec. 70 does not make ability to pay at the specified bank equivalent to a tender unless it exists "at maturity." What is the maturity of a demand instrument for this purpose? If the note is considered to mature on delivery just as for purposes of the statute of limitations, the payee bank would be obliged to apply the maker's existing deposit at once or always discharge indorsers-an absurd result. 

If maturity means the expiration of a reasonable time, the bank is still in an undesirable situation because its decision that a reasonable time has not yet expired may not be accepted by the jury when suit is brought against the indorser, and the jury will find that the bank delayed too long. Consequently the note concludes that sec. 70 has no application to the liability of an indorser of a demand note. It is much easier to hold that there was no discharge in the principal case because of the express clause waiving indorser's defenses.

The same result, on similar facts, was achieved where a note payable "one day after date" was involved. Covely v. French, 154 Tenn. 672, 294 S. W. 513.

Proper presentment

Pleading 

Sec. 71. Presentment Where Instrument is not Payable on Demand and Where Payable on Demand. 

Where the instrument is not payable on demand, presentment must be made on the day it falls due. Where it is payable on demand, presentment must be made within a reasonable time after its issue, except that in the case of a bill of exchange, presentment for payment will be sufficient if made within a reasonable time after the last negotiation thereof.'

A notice to the makers before maturity, reminding them of the date when the note would fall due, is not a proper presentment. Willard State Bank v. Clark, 111 Kan. 439, 208 Pac.

In an action by a holder against an indorser on a demand note, made five years before the date of presentment for payment, the holder alleged in his petition that the note was duly presented for payment. The indorser in the trial court moved to dismiss the complaint for the reason that the note shows on its face that it was not presented within a reasonable time, as required by sec. 71, and the holder failed to allege any facts which would excuse the apparent delay. The trial court denied the motion. It was held affirmed, * in alleging that the note was duly presented the plaintiff (holder) has sufficiently set forth a plain and concise statement of his cause of action, which is all that is required. Whether or not five years is a reasonable time in this case can only be determined by the facts as shown on trial." Klemann v. Collins, 223 App. Div. 161, 227 

N. Y. B. E. A. s. 45 (2). "Where a note payable on demand has been indorsed it must be presented for payment within a reasonable time of the indorsement. Sec. 71 has abrogated the former distinction between inter- Demand est-bearing demand bills and notes and those payable without interest with reference to the time of presentment to charge an indorser. Under this section and sec. 193, the burden is on the holder to prove presentment within a reasonable time, and the defendant indorser need not plead failure to make due presentment. Where the facts are ascertained and not in dispute, reasonable time is a question of law. Sheffield v. Cleland, 19 

Ida. 612, 115 Pac. 20; Zaloon v. Gamin, 72 Misc. 36, 129 N. Y. 

Supp. 85; First Nat. Bank v. Korn (Mo. App.), 179 S. W. 721. 

See also cases under sec. 193, infra. Circumstances held to make three and a half years an unreasonable time. Commercial Nat. 

Bank v. Zimmerman, 185 N. Y. 210, 77 N. E. 1020. The case of Merritt v. Jackson, 181 Mass. 69, 62 N. E. 987, is in accord as to the burden of proof. See also, First Nat. Bank v. Star 

Watch Case Co., 187 Mich. 224, 153 N. W. 722, that burden of proof of notice of dishonor is on the holder. 

The case of German-American Bank v. Mills, 99 App. Div. 

312, 91 N. Y. Supp. 142, which held that this section is in effect a statute of limitations, and that the burden was upon the indorser of a demand note to plead and prove that presentment was unreasonably delayed, must be considered as overruled by Commercial Nat. Bank v. Zimmerman, supra.

This section does not extend the maturity of a demand note and the statute of limitations still runs from date of delivery. 

Broadway Bank & Trust Co. v. Longey, 116 Conn. 557, 165 Atl. 800. 

Presentation of a demand note twenty-three months after date is not within a reasonable time. Murray v. Grover, 80 

Pa. Super. Ct. 56.

Presentation of a demand note more than two years after its issue is not made within a reasonable time, so that indorsers are discharged. In re Redmond, 15 F. Supp. 923 (D. C. E. D. Pa.).

Notice to an indorser of a demand note two years and seven months after issue was held not sufficient to hold him. First

While dicta in the cases cited above have cast some doubt on the effect of this section (see previous editions of this book), a careful examination of the statute and the facts of the cases will disclose that the proper interpretation of the  is similar to the B. E. A. on the point involved here. 

The B. E. A. 45 (2) which covers this same section is worded as follows: "Where the bill is payable on demand, then subject to the provisions of this Act, presentment must be made within a reasonable time after its issue, in order to render the drawer liable, and within a reasonable time after its indorsement in order to render the indorser liable.”

It should be noticed that the B. E. A. differs from N. I. L. 71 in that it treats the drawer and the indorsers separately and makes the discharge of each depend upon a reasonable time after he became liable on the paper. The N. I. L., on the other hand, covers both situations in one sentence, and also includes therein the question of the liability of the indorser on the note, which in the B. E. A. is found in a separate section. 

So far as the liability of indorsers of a bill, which is our problem here, is concerned, under the N. I. L. two cases must be distinguished. (1) That of the indorser who himself holds the instrument an unreasonable length of time; (2) his immediate indorsee.

First, as to the indorser who holds the instrument too long it should be noted that the drawer is entirely discharged if it be a draft, or he is discharged to the extent of the loss if it be a check and the indorsers are entirely discharged (See N. I. L. 

186); under these circumstances such a person would have no rights on a draft except against an acceptor, Cf. N. I. L. 144, and on a check he could hold only the drawer to the extent to which he was not damaged.

§ 71 

Second, when such a person, having no rights on the instru- After the last ment, indorses it, the rights of his indorsee depend upon other sections of the Act. 

negotiation (a) If the indorsee takes the instrument within a reasonable time after issue, he is a holder in due course under section 53 and may hold all prior parties including the immediate indorsee, if he exercises due diligence. It should be noted in this respect that a reasonable time for collecting demand bills, which is measured from the last indorsement, may differ from a reasonable time for negotiating them, which is measured from issue. 

See cases involving checks under section 53, supra, and 186, infra. In this respect the  offers more protection to a holder in due course than does the B. E. A. (b) If the indorsee be not a holder in due course, taking it an unreasonable time after issue under section 53, then his rights are determined by section 58, which puts him in the position of an assignee of his indorser, and he will have the same rights against prior parties which the indorser had. Due diligence on his part in collecting would give him rights only against his indorser as provided in sections 71, 66, and 65(4). 

The Columbia Banking Company case, supra, turned on the holding in the lower court that the purchaser, having taken within a reasonable time after issue, was a holder in due course (N. I. L. 53; and see the opinion on rehearing, 113 N. W. 476) and so he was properly entitled to recover from all prior parties. 

The other cases cited above involve only the last point, that of the right of the indorsee to hold his indorser, which turns on the question of presenting the instrument through banks according to business custom. See cases on this point under section 186. None of them are authorities for the proposition that a purchaser of a check or draft long overdue because it has been held an unreasonable time has rights against any other prior parties than the immediate indorser. 

It would seem that the intent of the framers was to reach approximately the same result on these facts as that reached under the B. E. A. See Commissioners' note to section 71.

A check was held six months by a fraudulent payee, then cashed. Held, on the strength of this section, that the cashing bank could collect from a drawer who had stopped payment. 

Pan American Petroleum Corporation v. American Nat. Bank, 165 Tenn. 66, 52 S. W. (2d) 149, criticized in 17 Minn. L. Rev. 

319. The court entirely overlooked section 53. The case is a good example of the type of unreasonable results which can be reached by relying upon a single section without taking into consideration the rest of the Act. checks A postdated check is payable on demand, and presentment is Postdated sufficient when made three days after its date.
