§ 856 

Subsec. 2

Sec. 72. What Constitutes a Sufficient Presentment. 

Presentment for payment, to be sufficient, must be made.- (1) By the holder, or by some person authorized to receive payment on his behalf; (2) At a reasonable hour on a business day; (3) At a proper place as herein defined; (4) To the person primarily liable on the instrument, or if he is absent or inaccessible, to any person found at the place where the presentment is made.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 73 to 78, 88, 191, 192, 19, 79 to 84, 89, 111, 119 to 122, 145 to 147, 151, 152.

ANNOTATIONS 

Presentment of a promissory note for payment by a bank having it for collection is sufficient. Fowler Paper Co. v. Best 

Jones, etc., Co., 183 Ill. App. 310; Caine v. Foreman (Cal. 

App.), 289 Pac. 929.

The fact that the payee requested that different notes be substituted for the ones in the suit is no evidence of presentment and notice of dishonor. City Fuel Co. v. Brown, 254 Mass. 605, 150 N. E. 842.

This provision has reference to the general custom at the place of the particular transaction. So when presentment was made to a Chicago bank between 3 and 6 o'clock and the business day of banks continued after the closing of clearing-house transactions so as to enable banks holding paper for collection to present such as had been refused recognition in the clearings, such presentment was within reasonable hours on a business day. 

Columbian Banking Co. v. Bowen, 134 Wis. 218, 114 N. W. 451.

In case of presentment in a foreign jurisdiction what constitutes reasonable hours of a business day there is a matter of proof. Ib.

A notarial certificate of protest showing a due presentment raises a presumption that presentment was made at a proper time. Ib.

Subsec. 4 The defendant bank, not a member of the Minneapolis clearing house, arranged with a member bank to act as its agent to clear its checks through the clearing house. A check drawn 

1 "Either to the person designated by the bill as payee or to some person authorized to pay or refuse payment on his behalf, if with the exercise of reasonable diligence such person can there be found." B. 

E. A. s. 45 (3).

§ 73 against an ample deposit in the defendant bank was presented by the clearing house to the agent, which refused payment because it had not been supplied with enough funds by the defendant to cover the day's clearings. Held, a dishonor, for which the defendant bank was liable to the drawer. The presentment was sufficient, a further presentment at the drawee bank not being necessary in the absence of an express provision in the clearing house rules. Geibe v. Chicago-Lake State Bank, 160 Minn. 89, 199 N. W. 514. 

A note in 9 Minn. L. Rev. 67 distinguishes between presentment through the clearing house, held sufficient in this case, and presentment at the clearing house, which it considers insufficient since the clerks representing a bank there have no authority to refuse payment, but are only messengers to bring the checks to their bank where they will be examined. 

Presentment to the drawer with demand for repayment of money is not presentment for payment. Auerbach v. Barrett, 214 App. Div. 279, 212 N. Y. Supp. 141.

Sec. 73. Place of Presentment. 

Presentment for payment is made at the proper place,— (1) Where a place of payment is specified in the instrument and it is there presented; (2) Where no place of payment is specified, but the address of the person to make payment is given in the instrument and it is there presented; (3) Where no place of payment is specified and no address is given and the instrument is presented at the usual place of business or residence of the person to make payment;¹ (4) In any other case if presented to the person to make payment wherever he can be found, or if presented at his last known place of business or residence. 

Cross Reference: §§ 72, 87, 191, 6(3), 74 to 84, 87, 89, 108, 145, 168.

When a note was payable to a bank at a specified village, where the bank was located, but the corporate maker's place of business was elsewhere, presentment was sufficient to charge indorsers when the note was in the possession of a notary, the assistant cashier of another bank in the village, with authority to receive payment of the note or to protest it if not paid, although no notification was given to the maker at maturity.

Where a note is payable at a certain store, presentment for Place of payment at such store to a person connected therewith is sufficient, and no personal demand on the maker is necessary. Nelson v. Grondahl, 13 N. D. 363, 100 N. W. 1093.

When a note was payable at a specified place, where the payee resided, presentment at a different place, which was the domicile and place of business of the maker, was not sufficient to charge indorsers. Eagle Lumber Co. v. Oil States Lumber Co., 154 La.

Where a demand note is payable at the residence of the payee, mere possession of it at the place of payment is not a sufficient presentment to charge indorsers; some unequivocal act is necessary to show an election to declare the note due. In re Redmond, 15 F. Supp. 923 (D. C. E. D. Pa.).

Where a note is payable at a designated branch of a trust company, presentation at the principal office of the company on the date of maturity and at the branch after banking hours on the day following is not sufficient as against an indorser. Ironclad

Sec. 74. Instrument Must Be Exhibited. 

The instrument must be exhibited to the person from whom payment is demanded, and when it is paid must be delivered up to the party paying it. 

Cross Reference: 88 16, 88, 119, 191, 70 to 73, 75 to 84, 89, 96.

ANNOTATIONS 

When a note is payable to a bank at its place of business, the bank need not prove exhibition of the instrument as part of its prima facie case. Commercial Trust Co. v. New Eng. Macaroni 

Mfg. Co., 247 Mass. 366, 141 N. E. 285.

In an action on a demand note against the maker, it is not necessary to allege a demand for payment or that the note was exhibited to the maker. The note was due at the time of delivery, and demand is presumed to have been then made, and this is true even though the note bears interest. Church v. Stevens, 56 

Misc. Rep. 572, 107 N. Y. Supp. 310.

In an action by a holder in due course against an indorser, a finding that the holder demanded payment of the note from the maker, and the next day gave notice of such demand and

860 

refusal to the indorser, was held not sufficient to sustain a judg ment against such indorser, as there was no finding of an exhibition of the note, or that it was dispensed with. Grunstein v. 

Kucharski, 107 Conn. 269, 140 Atl. 482.

Where notes were, at maturity, not at the place provided for payment, but were in a bank, and so were not only not in readiness for exhibition and surrender, but could not have been surrendered if payment had been offered, there was no legal presentment for payment at the time and place specified in the note and no waiver being pleaded or claimed, the indorser was discharged. Greco v. Lo Monte, 162 N. Y. Supp. 982. 

Under the Negotiable Instruments Law, which, by sec. 70, makes presentment of a note necessary to charge the indorsers, and by sec. 74 requires the notes to be exhibited to the person from whom payment is demanded, a mere informal talk asking payment of a note, not accompanied with a presentment of it or intended as a formal presentment and demand, is not sufficient to put the note in dishonor. State of New York Nat. Bank v. 

Kennedy, 145 App. Div. 669, 130 N. Y. Supp. 412.

A statement by an assistant cashier of a bank, which was the holder of a note, to the person in charge of the maker's office, that he "had it [the note] here," and that it "is due and must be paid" is a sufficient demand and exhibition of the note to subsequently charge an accommodation indorser upon it. Toll v. Monitor Binding & Printing Co. (C. C. A. 8th), 26 F. (2d)

Presentment by telephone is not sufficient to charge an indorser. Robinson v. Lancaster Foundry Co., 152 Md. 81, 136

When the instrument is lost or destroyed the instrument need not be exhibited in order to get payment. Wooten v. Bell, 196 N. C. 654, 146 S. E. 705.

In an action against the acceptor of bills of exchange, production of the bills must be made at the trial or an excuse offered for their nonproduction, when the plaintiff's allegation that it was owner and holder of the bills had been put in issue and it offered no evidence of its ownership. Since formal demand is required only in order to charge the parties secondarily liable, it follows that any reasonable request to pay demand note with a clause for attorney's fees, is sufficient to put the maker in default if he fails to discharge the obligation. The maker waives exhibition of the note by not asking for it and refusing payment on the ground that he did not have the money and needed the sum to support his family. Hodges v. Blaylock, 82 Oreg. 179, 161 Pac. 396.

When the maker of a note told the cashier of the indorsee bank before maturity that he could not pay the principal, and repeated this statement on the day of maturity at his office very close to the bank to the cashier who had called to look over his books and who told him the note was due, and no demand was made by the maker for the production of the note, which was at the bank, this was a waiver by the maker of exhibition of the note, so that the presentment was sufficient to render the indorsers liable. Porter v. East Jordan Realty Co., 210 Mich. 398, 177 N. W. 987, 11 A. L. R. 963, with note on "Necessity of possession and exhibition of paper at time of demand in order to make a valid presentment."

The so-called waiver might perhaps be classified as estoppel, since the cashier was induced in reliance upon the maker's conduct to dispense with exhibition, to the bank's prejudice, since exhibition ceased to be possible after the day of maturity. Yet there is a difficulty in estopping the indorser by the conduct of the maker, so that "waiver" may be the best explanation. 

See J. S. Ewart, Waiver Distributed, Cambridge, 1917.

 Sec. 75. Presentment Where Instrument Payable at 

Bank.

Where the instrument is payable at a bank, presentment for payment must be made during banking hours, unless the person to make payment has no funds there to meet it at any time during the day, in which case presentment at any hour before the bank is closed on that day if sufficient.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 72, 73, 85, 87, 191, 70 to 74, 75 to 84, 89, 145.

ANNOTATIONS 

In a suit against the indorser of a note payable at a bank, the plaintiff must allege that the note was presented for payment at the bank during business hours or before the close of the bank. Deming Nat. Bank v. Baker, 83 W. Va. 429, 98 S. E. 438. 

The person to make payment has until the close of banking hours of the bank where the instrument is made payable in which to pay it, and if before the close of such hours he deposits money enough to pay it, a demand earlier in the day is premature. 

German-American Bank v. Milliman, 31 Misc. Rep. 87, 65 N. Y. 

Supp. 242.

Presentment where payable 

A promissory note payable at a bank and there presented on at a bank the day of maturity will be presumed to have been presented during business hours, where there is no evidence to the contrary, and it need not remain at the bank during all the day of maturity. Archuleta v. Johnston, 53 Colo. 393, 127 Pac. 134.

The same presumption was held to exist in Davis Nat. Bank v. 

Kight, 86 W. Va. 319, 103 S. E. 482.

When a note giving the street address of the maker, which was actually in Boston, was payable at "Mafs. Nat. Bk." and discounted in renewal of similar notes at the plaintiff bank in Lynn, which was the only bank of that name in Massachusetts, a presentment at the plaintiff bank was good, and the statement in the notarial certificate that payment was demanded there raises the presumption that the notary presented the note for payment during banking hours. Manufacturers Nat. Bank v. 

Simon, 245 Mass. 325, 139 N. E. 529.

It is sufficient presentment of a note payable at a bank if it is actually in the bank at maturity, ready to be delivered on payment. Sec. 87 was cited but the court must have had sec. 75 in mind. De La Vergne v. Globe Printing Co., 27 Colo. App. 

308, 148 Pac. 923. Accord, Doherty v. First Nat. Bank, 170 Ky. 

810, 186 S. W. 937; Nickell v. Bradshaw, 94 Oreg. 580, 183 

Pac. 12, 11 A. L. R. 623; Rosenthal v. Levine (Me.), 148 Atl.

Sec. 76. Presentment Where Principal Debtor is 

Dead. 

Where the person primarily liable on the instrument is dead, and no place of payment is specified, presentment for payment must be made to his personal representative, if such there be, and if, with the exercise of reasonable diligence, he can be found. 

Cross Reference: 88 72, 78, 191, 192, 6(3), 19, 20, 70 to 75, 77 to 

84, 89, 98, 148(2), 193.

Calling two or three times at the banking office of the administrator of a deceased maker, and again seeking him at a railroad station near the seat of his other business interests at a time when he might be expected to be there, warrants a finding of reasonable diligence to present a note for payment. Reed v. 

Spear, 107 App. Div. 144, 94 N. Y. Supp. 1007.

Where a note specifies a place of payment, the payee is not required to present the note for payment to the deceased maker's personal representative at maturity. Friedberg v. Mechanics' 

Bank of Brooklyn, 135 Misc. Rep. 194, 237 N. Y. Supp. 317. 

See sec. 73(1). 

Sec. 77. Presentment to Persons Liable as Partners. 

Where the persons primarily liable on the instrument are liable as partners, and no place of payment is specified, presentment for payment may be made to any one of them, even though there has been a dissolution of the firm.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 192, 6(3), 70 to 76, 78 to 84, 87, 99.

Sec. 78. Presentment to Joint Debtors. 

Where there are several persons, not partners, primarily liable on the instrument, and no place of payment is specified, presentment must be made to them all. 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 192, 6(3), 17(7), 41, 70 to 77, 79 to 84, 100, 128.

Under sec. 78, an informal demand on one of two joint makers is not a basis for charging indorsers. State of New York Nat. 

Bank v. Kennedy, 145 App. Div. 669, 130 N. Y. Supp. 412. 

1 Not in B. E. A., except inferentially from s. 45 (6), which is the same as  s. 78.

864 

The defendants, who signed a note on its face before delivery as sureties for B, who also signed, were primarily liable to the payee and could be charged without presentment to B. Sec. 78 must be read in connection with sec. 70, which does not require presentment to charge primary parties. Semble, if the defendants had not signed the note until after delivery, their liability would have been as indorsers, and presentment and notice would have been necessary to establish their liability. Colvin v. Glover, 143 Ark. 498, 220 S. W. 832. The correctness of the dictum is doubtful. The defendants would seem to have been comakers even if they signed after maturity. Furthermore, sec. 64 requires indorsers to sign before delivery if they are to be liable to the payee.

Sec. 79. When Presentment Not Required to Charge the Drawer.

Presentment for payment is not required in order to charge the drawer where he has no right to expect or require that the drawee or acceptor will pay the instru ment. 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 196, 61, 62, 70 to 78, 80 to 84, 89, 114(4), 150, 151, 152, 186.

ANNOTATIONS 

Presentment not necessary

Presentment is not required to charge the drawer of a check to charge upon which payment has been stopped. The  was not drawer cited. Sibree v. Thomas, 166 Ill. App. 422; Usher v. A. I. Tucker 

Co., 217 Mass. 441, 105 N. E. 360, L. R. A. 1916F, 826; Manos v. Eassy, 124 S. C. 154, 117 S. E. 222. Or it was issued in a kiting transaction. Tonne v. Horace State Bank (N. D.), 193 

N. W. 934.

Neither is presentment necessary to charge the drawer of a check, where his bank balance is less than the amount of the check. Gilman v. F. O. Bailey Carriage Co., Inc., 127 Me. 91, 141 Atl. 321, 24 Mich. L. Rev. 498, 1 Notre Dame Lawy. 93. Semble.

That the drawer of a bill has no funds in the hands of the drawee will not excuse failure to make presentment and notice of nonpayment, particularly when provision has been made for payment of any bill drawn by the drawer on the drawee. 

Simonoff v. Granite City Nat. Bank, 279 Ill. 246, 116 N. E. 636.

But where the drawer of a foreign bill of exchange, containing the words "Pay from balance," had no money on deposit with the drawee but expected to arrange with a broker to cover drafts, these facts were held to present a case for the jury, whether or not the drawer was entitled to notice of dishonor under section 79. Slaymen v. First Nat. Bank of Welch, 104 W. Va. 265, 139 S. E. 750.

§ 80 A complaint, alleging that a foreign draft was duly presented and the bank refused payment because the drawer defendant had no money on deposit with which to pay the check, was not defective for failure to allege protest, since this was dispensed with by the circumstances. Ellenbogen v. State Bank, 119 Misc.

Sec. 80. When Presentment Not Required to Charge the Indorser.

Presentment for payment is not required in order to charge an indorser where the instrument was made or accepted for his accommodation and he has no reason to expect that the instrument will be paid if presented. 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 29, 31, 63, 67, 132, 187, 191, 16, 60, 61, 63 to 68, 70 to 79, 81 to 84, 115(3), 119(2).

ANNOTATIONS 

The defendant was president and secretary of the maker corporation and as such he signed notes of the company as accommodation indorser. Later, before maturity of the notes, the company entered voluntary bankruptcy and the defendant signed the petition. The notes were subsequently dishonored and the defendant claims lack of presentment and notice. The court held, relying on  80 and 109, that the defendant's conduct amounted to a waiver because he could not possibly have expected the notes to be paid and suffered no change of position due to lack of notice. This is certainly an extension by analogy of section 80 and seems to reach an equitable result. 

See also 114(4) and 115(2). Atlantic Refining Co. v. Nucar 

Forwarding Corporation, 11 N. J. M. 541, 167 Atl. 677.

This section did not apply to the officers of a corporation who indorsed its note, when there was no evidence that the officers were accommodated or had reason to suppose the instrument would not be paid if presented. Engen v. Medberry Farmers 

Eq. Elev. Co. (N. D.), 203 N. W. 182, 39 A. L. R. 915.

Neither does this section apply to officers who knew that the corporation was insolvent and could not pay. Lane Cotton Mills 

Co. v. Kohler, 186 La. 469, 172 So. 530. 

In Clark v. O'Neal, 231 Ala. 577, 165 So. 853, and in previous decisions on the same case therein cited the court took the position that presentment was excused as to indorsers who were directors of the maker bank which was in liquidation at the time of maturity and the fact was well known to the indorser; but that such indorsers were entitled to notice. Note in this respect the difference between section 80 and section 115 (3). There is also an interesting analogy to section 79.

It is not necessary under this section and sec. 115, that a loan for which notes were given should have been made for the sole Presentment not required to charge indorser

Presentment accommodation of an indorser. It is enough if it was only partly not required to charge for his benefit. Bergen v. Trimble, 130 Md. 559, 101 Atl. 137. indorser Where the declaration set forth that the defendants were joint makers and the instrument shows them to be indorsers, the defense being that there was no presentment or notice, it was held that under sections 80 and 115 it was an error to exclude evidence that the note was made for their accommodation. Dankmer v. Wheeling Printing Co., 103 W. Va. 40, 136

S. E. 690. 

A president made and the directors and stockholders of a bank indorsed a note, payable to the bank, instead of charging off certain listed assets which were worthless, agreeing among themselves that all the signers should be liable, not separately, but collectively. Held, (1) that the note was supported by a sufficient consideration, and (2) that presentment to the maker for payment was not necessary to charge the indorsers. Union Bank of Brooklyn v. Sullivan, 214 N. Y. 332, 108 N. E. 558.

When a corporation assigned all its assets to the defendant for the benefit of creditors, and gave the plaintiff a note indorsed by the defendant, who had agreed orally, for consideration, to pay the debts of the corporation, presentment for payment was not required in order to hold the defendant as an indorser. The court states that the defendant became primarily liable on the note just like a maker, and that the note was taken by the plaintiff for the accommodation of the defendant because of the profit he derived from the contract of settlement. Weinreb v. 

Antzis, 192 N. Y. Supp. 644. The statement as to accommodation is questionable. The plaintiff also profited. 

The president of the X bank, upon the increase of the capital stock, took the unsubscribed amount, made a demand note for the amount to his own order, indorsed the note and the directors also indorsed it. The note was negotiated to the plaintiff bank, the proceeds paid to the X bank, the stock issued to the president, and pledged to plaintiff bank as security for the note. The president testified that the purchase of the stock was his individual transaction and so did the directors. There was no evidence to the contrary. Held, that the directors were not primarily liable, and the fact that they might be benefited by an increase in the value of the stock by the completion of the subscription for the increased issue, did not make the note one for their accommodation so as to dispense with presentment for payment in order to charge them. Murray v. Third Nat. Bk., 234 Fed. Rep. 481, 148 C. C. A. 247.

A firm was indebted to the defendant and accepted drafts drawn by and payable to him, which the plaintiff bank discounted on his indorsement in blank. When the acceptances matured, they were taken up by a note payable to the bank, signed by the firm, and indorsed by the partners and the defendant before

§ 82 (1) delivery to the bank. Held, the note was not made for the defendant's accommodation and he was entitled to presentment and notice. First Nat. Bank v. Bach, 98 Oreg. 332, 193 Pac. 1041.

Where a demand note was given in settlement of the corporate maker's debt and indorsed by its majority stockholder, it was held that he was not an accommodated indorser within sec. 80 since he had loaned his credit to the corporation. In re Redmond, 15 F. Supp. 923 (D. C. E. D. Pa.). 

Sec. 81. When Delay in Making Presentment is Ex cused. 

Delay in making presentment for payment is excused when the delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder, and not imputable to his default, misconduct, or negligence. When the cause of delay ceases to operate, presentment must be made with reasonable diligence. 

Cross Reference: 88 191, 193, 196, 61, 64 to 66, 70 to 80, 82 to 84, 113, 147, 148, 159, 194.

When the bank issuing a certificate of deposit was in the hands of the state agent for winding up, so that claims for payment could not legally be made, presentment to the bank was not necessary to charge an indorser. Engle v. Shepherd, 100 Okla. 200, 229 Pac. 208.

Insolvency of the maker, even if known to the indorser, will not excuse presentment for payment. Christina v. Mattenberger (Cal. App), 289 Pac. 934.

Presentment is not necessary to charge indorsers when at maturity the corporate maker is in receivership and its assets have been sold out by the receiver, to the knowledge of the indorsers, who had bought in the assets at the receiver's sale. 

Sunlite Co. v. Justice (Tex. Civ. App), 257 S. W. 579, disapproved in 2 Tex. L. Rev. 523.

The court says the indorsers "could have no reasonable expectation that such demand would be met by payment." This view incorrectly relies on sec. 80, which refers only to an accommodated indorser, whereas the defendants indorsed for accommodation. The Act does not specify the maker's insolvency as an excuse for failure to present. The decision must rest on the existence of waiver under sec. 82-3, or on the impossibility of presentment, under subsec. 1, since the corporation had virtually disappeared.

ENGLAND 

Presentment was excused of bills payable in Germany and Austria after the outbreak of war. Re Francke & Rasch [1918], 1 Ch. 470. (3) "By waiver of presentment, express or implied"

Cross Reference: §§ 5(3), 109 to 112. 

The facts excusing presentment or failure to give notice of dishonor or a waiver thereof must be specially pleaded. Proof thereof is not otherwise admissible. Galbraith v. Shepard, 43 

Wash. 698, 86 Pac. 1113.

To bind the indorser, his waiver must be with knowledge of the facts which release him, but ignorance as to their legal effect will not relieve him in the absence of fraud. Toole v. Crafts, 193 Mass. 110, 78 N. E. 775, 118 Am. St. Rep. 455. This case was again heard by the Supreme Judicial Court upon excep-

§ 82 (3) 

tions taken at a second trial, when it was further held that while Procedure a written waiver of demand made without limitation after the time for demand has expired can not, as a general rule, be limited by oral evidence, yet such evidence is competent to show fraud, mistake, or circumstances to aid the court to ascertain the construction of the agreement. So where on a demand note an indorsement was made more than sixty days after its date (see Merritt v. Jackson, 181 Mass. 69, 62 N. E. 987, waiving "demand, notice, and protest," evidence was admissible to show whether this waiver referred to a protest within said sixty days. or to a further protest, and that it was for the jury to say upon the evidence which of these two protests was the subject matter of the agreement, and that their finding for the indorser was conclusive. Toole v. Crafts, 196 Mass. 397, 82 N. E. 22.

In an action by the holder against the maker and indorsers of a demand note, waiving presentment, protest and notice of dishonor, eight years after date thereof, the defense was that no demand for payment was made for eight years. It was held that waiver of presentment and protest waived demand for payment, and indorsers are not discharged by the lapse of time. 

Morrison v. Frantz, 105 W. Va. 14, 141 S. E. 394.

Presentment of a bill is waived by any acts or conduct of the drawer calculated to lead the holder to believe that presentment is waived or to mislead or prevent him from treating the bill as he otherwise would. In this case the drawer promised from time to time to pay the bill, making no objection on the ground that the bill had not been presented to the drawee. Secs. 109 and 

111 were cited, but not sec. 82. Simonoff v. Granite City Nat. 

Bank, 279 Ill. 248, 116 N. E. 636.

The payee's negligent delay in presenting the check which operated to discharge the drawer was waived by the drawer's subsequent part payment of the debt and verbal promise to pay the remainder. Mary Couts Burnett Trust v. Samuels (Tex. 

Civ. App.), 59 S. W. (2d) 358.

In an action against an indorser of a note made by a corporation which was then insolvent, whose condition was known by the defendant, a director, it was held that the question of implied waiver of presentment and notice should have been submitted to the jury where the evidence showed that the defendant had helped to strip the corporation of its assets and had thereby disenabled it from paying the note. Rinehart v. Lucas (W. Va.), 190 S. E. 772. 

Defendant, the president of a corporation, indorsed its note.

Before maturity, the maker was adjudged a bankrupt partly upon the written admission of defendant of its inability to pay its debts with a willingness that it be adjudged a bankrupt. 

Held, that defendant had waived presentment and notice of dishonor. J. W. O'Bannon Co. v. Curran, 129 App. Div. 90, 113 

N. Y. Supp. 359.

Facts con- stituting waiver

§ (3) 870 

Facts con- stituting When the indorser of the note of a corporation was its presiwaiver dent and a majority stockholder, and, knowing of the insolvency of the corporation and that it could not pay the note, obtained a composition of the corporate debts under an agreement that he was to remain liable as indorser, presentment and notice were waived. Waterproof Paper & Board Co. v. Van Buren, 182 Wis. 640, 197 N. W. 338.

Where the indorsers of a note, payable at a bank, had assured the holder that it could not be paid at maturity and knew that the maker, a corporation, had not the money to pay it, they were not discharged by failure to present the note for payment. Bessenger v. Wenzel, 161 Mich. 61, 125 N. W. 750, 27 L. R. A. (N.S.) 516. 

Where payment on a check was stopped at the request of an indorser, it constituted an implied waiver of presentment to charge the drawer. Deitrick v. MacCarthy, 13 F. Supp. 850 

(D. C. D. Mass.). 

The defendant when indorsing a check to the plaintiff informed him that it was no good at the bank but that the plaintiff might be better able to get it paid by the drawer than the defendant. Also, long after the time when presentment should have been made, the defendant promised to pay the check. Held, presentment was dispensed with. Lieberman v. Fox, 160 Minn. 

449, 200 N. W. 468.

A firm made a note which was indorsed by one of the partners prior to its delivery. Shortly before maturity of the note, the indorser, during a consultation with the holder regarding a general assignment of the firm and the partners, which was thereafter made as a result of the conference, told the holder that neither the firm nor he could pay the note at maturity, and the holder therfore made no presentment for payment and gave no notice of nonpayment. Held, that both by the law merchant and under the statute there was an implied waiver of presentment and that under sec. 115-2 notice of dishonor was not required. 

In re Swift, 106 Fed. Rep. 65.

Evidence that defendant, who was an officer of the corporation which executed a note, and who was liable thereon as indorser, stated that if the holder would wait until 4 o'clock of the day on which the note matured, he would come to the bank and pay it, was held to be sufficient to require the submission to the jury of the question of waiver of protest and notice thereof. The 

 was not cited on this point. Second National Bank v. 

Smith, 118 Wis. 18, 94 N. W. 664. 

Where the indorser, president of the maker corporation, who was released by improper presentment, wrote the holder as follows "I will take care of it [the note] properly just as soon as I get the money" it was held that he had waived failure to present. Martin v. Traxler Realestate Co., 140 S. C. 505, 139

S. E. 165.

Where defendant-indorser assured the holder, before maturity Facts constiof the note, that a note for the same amount, with his indorsement, would be given in renewal, such assurance, if relied on by the holder, constituted a waiver of demand and notice. The 

 was not cited. Sweetser v. Jordan, 216 Mass. 350, 103

The defendant-indorser agreed with the plaintiff-indorsee to look after the collection of the note and prepared a notice to the maker to pay the note, which the plaintiff signed and sent to the maker. On the day of maturity the maker telephoned the plaintiff that he could not then pay the note. The plaintiff then telephoned the defendant who consented that the maker should be given further time. Held, that defendant had waived presentment and notice of dishonor. Moll v. Roth Co., 77 Oreg. 593, 152 Pac. 235.

Upon suit by a payee against an anomalous indorser, it appeared that the note was in the actual possession of the indorser from the time it was made until its maturity. This obviated the necessity of presentment and notice of nonpayment to the indorser. The indorser having the note in his possession, should have presented it for payment at maturity. Glesson v. Lichty, 62 Wash. 656, 114 Pac. 518.

Evidence of assurances by the indorser to the indorsee when indorsing and delivering a note, that the former would be responsible for principal and interest when due, and would look after the collection of the note and pay interest when it became due, is competent to show a waiver by declarations of the indorser calculated to mislead the indorsee and induce him to omit presentment and notice of dishonor. Torbert v. Montague, 38 Colo. 325, 87 Pac. 1145.

Where a note is payable at a bank, presentment and demand at a bank are necessary in the absence of some good and sufficient reason for failing to make presentment there. If the maker of such a note has no funds in the bank when it falls due, demand for payment there is unnecessary. The N. I. L. was not cited on this point. Myers Co. v. Battle, 170 N. C. 168, 86 S. E. 1034, semble. 

That the comaker of a note has a valid defense does not dispense with presentment to her in order to charge indorsers. 

Witte v. Broz, 111 Neb. 76, 197 N. W. 121.

Before maturity of a note, the holder informed defendant, an indorser, that the maker had denied liability and that the holder would look to defendant for payment. Defendant said that he was liable, but did not have the money to pay, that, if plaintiff would see the maker, defendant would pay, if plaintiff should fail to make the money out of the maker. Plaintiff was induced by these statements to omit presentment and notice of dishonor.

Sec. 83. When Instrument Dishonored by Nonpay ment.

The instrument is dishonored by nonpayment when,- (1) It is duly presented for payment and payment is refused or can not be obtained; or (2) Presentment is excused and the instrument is overdue and unpaid. 

Cross Reference: 88 71 to 82, 85, 86, 191, 84, 88, 89, 119, 122, 142, 148, 149, 150, 153, 186.

In an action by an indorsee against the indorser on a demand note, where the indorsee presented the instrument to the

§ 84  

maker for payment, who failed to pay it but promised to pay it five days later, it was held that there was a dishonor, in view of  section 83, when presentment was made, and notice given five days after presentment was too late, therefore the defendant was discharged. Bredow v. Woll, 108 Conn. 489, 143 

Atl. 849, 62 A. L. R. 293 and note.

In Commercial State Bank v. Harkrider-Keith-Cook Co. 

(Tex. Civ. App), 250 S. W. 1069, the court expressed the opinion that where a check was presented for payment and held more than 24 hours this was an acceptance, because otherwise, if it were a dishonor, the drawer and indorsers would be discharged by lack of notice. There is much to be said for this point of view. See discussion under sec. 137, also see sec. 150.

Sec. 84. Liability of Person Secondarily Liable- When Instrument Dishonored. 

Subject to the provisions of this Act, when the instrument is dishonored by nonpayment, an immediate right of recourse to all parties secondarily liable thereon accrues to the holder. 

Cross Reference: §§ 83, 89, 152, 170, 191, 192, 60, 61, 66, 70, 150, 151.

ANNOTATIONS 

Under this section an indorser whose liability has become fixed by demand and notice is, as to the holder, a principaldebtor. Pittsburgh-Westmoreland Coal Co. v. Kerr, 220 N. Y. 

137, 115 N. E. 465.

After a note has been dishonored at maturity and due notice given to the indorser, he becomes liable to the holder, not as a surety, but absolutely and independently of the liability of the maker and may set off his liability against a deposit in the holder bank, which has become insolvent, although the note matured subsequent to the bank's insolvency. Carnegie Trust Co. v. Kistler, 89 Misc. Rep. 404, 152 N. Y. Supp. 240; Curtis v. Davidson, 215 N. Y. 395, 109 N. E. 481. The N. I. L. was not cited in these two cases.

In a suit by the payee against the accommodation indorser, where presentment, demand for payment, etc., has been waived, it was held that the fact that the payee did not sue the maker while he was solvent, but waited three months until he became insolvent and then sued him was no defense. Owings v. Davenport, 143 S. C. 386, 141 S. E. 602.

And not being a surety, although indorsing for accommodation of the maker, he can not take advantage of a statute enabling a surety to require his creditor to proceed against the principal debtor. Bank of Conway v. Stary (N. D.), 200 N. W. 505, 37 

A. L. R. 1186.

 Foreign law of grace

Under this section and sec. 29, the payee of a note may sue an indorser for the accommodation of the maker, although known to be such, before realizing on security obtained from the maker. 

Miller v. Levitt, 226 Mass. 330, 115 N. E. 431.

The holder of a note need not proceed against the maker before suing the accommodation indorser. Kopf v. Yordy, 200 

Ill. App. 409. 

When a note was dishonored and protested, the last indorser could immediately resort to the collateral given as security for his liability as indorser without waiting until the holder sued him or parties prior to him. Halpern v. Cure, 173 N. Y. Supp. 385.

A note provided that if semi-annual interest was not paid, the holder might at his option declare the whole sum payable. After default of the installment of interest due two years before maturity of the principal, the holder for seventy days endeavored to make presentment to the maker and then notified the indorsers. 

Held, they were liable. Seventy days was not an unreasonable lapse of time in which to exercise the option to declare the whole note payable and charge the indorsers. Wagner v. Benjamin, 120 Wash. 532, 207 Pac. 1045.

Sec. 85. Time of Maturity. 

Every negotiable instrument is payable at the time fixed therein without grace. When the day of maturity falls upon Sunday, or a holiday, the instrument is payable on the next succeeding business day. Instruments falling due on Saturday are to be presented for payment on the next succeeding business day, except that instruments payable on demand may, at the option of the holder, be presented for payment before twelve o'clock noon on 

Saturday when that entire day is not a holiday.¹

Sec. 86. Time-How Computed. 

Where the instrument is payable at a fixed period after date, after sight, or after the happening of a specified event, the time of payment is determined by excluding the day from which the time is to begin to run, and by including the date of payment. 

Cross Reference: 88 4, 191, 194, 196, 6(1), 7, 11, 13, 17(2), 45, 147, 193. 

A note dated November 8, 1908, and payable twelve months after date, was presented for payment November 9, 1909. Held, that it should have been presented November 8, 1909. Lewry v. 

Wilkinson, 135 La. 105, 64 So. 1003. 

In an action on a promissory note dated April 5, 1923, due in three months, the due date was July 5, 1923. The writ was dated July 5, 1923. It was held that the action was prematurely brought, for, in view of  sec. 86, the maker was entitled to the whole of that day in which to pay the note. Krasnow v. 

Krasnow, 253 Mass. 528, 149 N. E. 321.

The plaintiff sued upon a note given pursuant to a contract containing the provision deferring the maturity of the note pending final determination of whether certain credit was allowable on the note. At the time of suit the matter had not been determined, but plaintiff, payee, agreed to allow the credit in full. It was held that the suit was not premature. McLain v. 

Robinson (Tex. Civ. App.), 269 S. W. 199.  

A typewritten note dated March 6, 1930, was payable three months after date. In the margin opposite the maker's signature was typed, "Due June 7, 1930." Held, that failure to present on June 6, 1930, discharged an accommodation indorser. 

E. E. Rivet & Sons v. Durand, 53 R. I. 48, 163 Atl. 476.

 Sec. 87. Rule Where Instrument Payable at Bank. 

Where the instrument is made payable at a bank it is equivalent to an order to the bank to pay the same for the account of the principal debtor thereon.¹

This section applies only where the instrument is made payable at a particular bank named. The fact that a note made payable at "any bank in Boston," was sent for collection to a bank there, in which the maker had a deposit when the note matured, did not authorize that bank to pay the note from such deposit. Carpenter v. National Shawmut Bk., 187 Fed. Rep. 1, 109 C. C. A. 55.

The bank becomes the agent of the maker for payment when it is designated as the place of payment, so that loss from failure of the bank falls upon the maker. John K. and Catherine

Since a note payable on demand is due and payable from the time of its delivery without demand, a bank holding a demand note may apply to its payment the deposit of the maker. Thomas v. Citizens' Bank, 27 N. D. 597, 147 N. W. 388, L. R. A. 1915A, 1728.

A bank has no authority to pay notes of a depositor made before the adoption of the Negotiable Instruments Law and payable at another bank. Elliott v. Worcester Trust Co., 189 Mass. 

542, 75 N. E. 944. When the depositor sues the bank, the bank can not claim the rights of a bona fide purchaser for value before maturity when it simply pleads a general denial and payment and files no claim in set-off. Ib. 

The provisions of this section may be waived by express provision in the note that the bank shall not apply funds on deposit to the payment of the note at maturity. Fitzpatrick's Adm'r v. Citizens' Bank & Trust Co., 231 Ky. 202, 21 S. W. (2d) 254.

The acceptance by the plaintiff drawee of a draft payable at its bank was equivalent to a direction by it to the bank to pay it for the plaintiff's account. The bank was not liable to the drawee for paying the draft in spite of a countermand, when this did not accurately describe the draft and was not given sufficiently soon to enable the bank in the exercise of reasonable diligence to stop payment. Davison Coal Co. v. Nat. Park Bank, 201 App. Div. 309, 194 N Y. Supp. 220.

cover the amount of the note from the holder, although a readjustment of the clearing-house accounts is not proper under the rules. Mt. Morris Bank v. Twenty-third Ward Bank, 172

Effect of non-payment maker, etc.

Failure of the holder of a note, payable at a bank, to present the note to the bank for payment at maturity, does not release of note on the maker, although he had sufficient funds in the bank for its payment, and the bank subsequently fails, since by sec. 70 no presentment is necessary to charge a party primarily liable. The rule applicable to a check does not apply, since the drawer of a check is only secondarily liable. First Nat. Bank of Birmingham v. Nagel, 227 Ala. 389, 150 So. 354; Stillman v. Justice, 100 Fla. 1679, 132 So. 107; Cosmopolitan Trust Co. v. Leonard 

Watch Co., 249 Mass. 14, 143 N. E. 827; Dubler v. Toscana

Straw Goods Corporation, 254 N. Y. Supp. 464 (a drawee of a draft); Federal Intermediate Credit Bank v. Epstin, 151 S. C. 

67, 148 S. E. 713, 29 Colum. L. Rev. 1023, 18 Cal. L. Rev. 56, 39 Yale L. J. 277, 16 Va. L. Rev. 183, 8 N. C. L. Rev. 184. Two 

Judges dissented; Binghampton Pharmacy v. First Nat. Bank, 131 Tenn. 711, 176 S. W. 1038, 2 A. L. R. 1377. Accord, Mershon v. Millerstown Borough (Pa. Sup.), 193 Atl. 328, where municipal bonds were payable at the office of the Treasurer of the Borough or at a named bank. 

But in New England Nat. Bank v. Dick, 84 Kan. 252, 114

Pac. 378, the court intimated that if the holder of a note payable at a bank fails to present it at the bank at maturity and the bank fails, the maker will be wholly discharged. 

And in Baldwin's Bank v. Smith, 215 N. Y. 76, 109 N. E. 138, Ann. Cas. 1917A, 500, Miller, J., said that, "It is incumbent on the holder of the paper to secure payment, and loss resulting from his neglect should fall on him, not on the drawer, who has no further duty to perform. I am unable to perceive why the same reason does not hold good in the case of a note, payable at a bank, where the maker has funds to meet it at maturity, espe cially since such a note is by statute made the equivalent of a check." In this case the defendant made a promissory note payable at the A bank. The plaintiff bank became the holder of the note and sent it to the A bank for "collection and remittance." 

On the day of maturity, the maker telephoned to the bank to

§ 880 

non-payment of note on maker, etc. 

Effect of charge the note to his account and was told that this would be done. But the bank did not charge the note to his account, made no entry crediting plaintiff and did not remit the money. Seven days later the bank failed. The maker during all this time had sufficient funds at the bank to pay the note. Held, that the note was paid and the maker discharged, and further, that, assuming the note was not paid, yet the A bank was plaintiff's agent to secure payment and that its failure to do so was negligence and that the loss must fall on the plaintiff, not on the maker. Sed quaere whether the facts justify a finding that the note was paid! 

See dissenting opinion of two judges and note in 29 Harvard 

Law Rev. 204. But since by sec. 87 a note, made payable at a bank, is equivalent to an order on the bank, the consequences of failure by the holder to present for payment at maturity or of failure to notify the maker of dishonor should be the same as in the case of the drawer of a check, and as failure by the bank to remit within a reasonable time indicates that the note had been dishonored, the maker might well have been held to be discharged by such failure to give notice, see sec. 186.

See also J. C. Peppin's comment on this situation in 18 Calif. 

L. Rev. 56.

The defendant made a note payable at the payee bank and authorized the bank to charge his account. At maturity thereof, in response to a notice from the payee bank, the defendant told the bank to charge his account, which was more than adequate, and return the note with his vouchers. After failure of the payee bank, the plaintiff sued, showing that it was a pledgee before maturity. Held, the defendant was liable, his account not being charged and the note not being marked paid. First

It is submitted that this is an unnecessary hardship on the defendant. The analogy of section 186 should apply here. See 

Baldwin's Bank v. Smith, supra.

Whether, when a note is payable to and at a bank, the existence of a sufficient deposit by the principal maker at maturity is equivalent to a tender of payment, so that if the deposit be not applied on the note indorsers and surety comakers will be discharged, see the discussion under secs. 71, 120-4, and the discussion of Little v. Peoples Bank, 209 Ala. 620, 96 So. 763, under sec. 70. 

The fact that an instrument payable one day after date was made payable at a certain bank, and that the maker had funds in that bank to pay the instrument at time of maturity is not a sufficient tender, under secs. 70 and 87, to discharge indorsers who waived presentment and notice when the holder failed to present the instrument for payment at maturity. Covely v. 

French, 154 Tenn. 672, 294 S. W. 513, citing secs. 66, 70, 82, 83, 84, 87, 120. Sed quaere? This seems to be contrary to the meaning of secs. 70 and 87, and certainly works a hardship on

the indorser for the benefit of a careless holder. See also sec. Effect of non-

In an action by the payee against the acceptor of a bill pay maker, etc. able at the bank at which the defendant had sufficient funds when the bill matured, but after a delay in attempt to collect it became insolvent, it was held that acceptor was primarily liable, and hence not released by failure to present for payment, in view of  secs. 62, 70, 87, 126, 127, 132, 138, 184, 192. 

Cashion Gin Co. v. Reisch (Okla.), 289 Pac. 701. The court in discussing the case entirely overlooked sec. 186 and said that delay in presentment would not discharge the defendant. If the case rested on these facts alone it would seem to be contra to the Meyer and Shaw cases infra, pp. 881, 882, and to the express intention of sec. 186. It should be noted, however, that the delay in this case was acquiesced in by one of the partners of the defendant company. This fact is really controlling and supports the decision.

A note payable at a bank was not paid and charged by the bank to the maker's account although there were funds sufficient to meet it. Held, the maker was liable to the holder. The negligence of the bank was not imputable to the plaintiff. Sec. 

87 merely creates the bank the agent of the maker and does not authorize it to receive payment for the holder. It was also held that the maker's check on the bank, which was subsequently dishonored because of the bank's insolvency, did not constitute payment of the note. U. S. Nat. Bank v. Shupak, 54 Mont. 542, 172 Pac. 324. 

Cf. Cosmopolitan Trust Co. v. Leonard Watch Co., 249 Mass. 

14, 143 N. E. 827, in which a note payable at the commercial department of a trust company was assigned to the savings department, and it was held to be a question for the jury whether the commercial department was constituted an agent of the savings department to collect the note. 

Placing money in the bank where a note is payable is sufficient tender of payment by maker, even though the bank fails to credit the account of the holder. Meyer & Kiser v. French (Tex. Comm. App.), 288 S. W. 405. 

Where a note with acceleration clauses was not at the bank where it was payable, the holder was held not entitled to sue for the entire amount on account of non-payment of the installment. 

Stegemann v. Emery, 108 Fla. 672, 146 So. 650.

A note, payable at the A bank, was deposited in the B bank for collection and sent by the B bank to the A bank for "collection and remittance," the latter bank being authorized to pay notes of the maker when made payable there. The A bank at the maturity of the note wrote a check on another bank for remittance of the amount, stamped "Paid" on the face of the note, cancelled the note by perforation and filed it with paid checks, but had made no entries of the matter on the books of the bank. Stamping other acts "Paid," and as payment

§ 882 

"Paid," and other acts as payment

Stamping At this point the A bank was notified that the maker had made an assignment for the benefit of creditors and was directed by the assignee to withhold the check drawn for remittance, which was done. Held, that the note was paid and that the A bank was liable to the B bank for the amount.  

Nineteenth Ward Bank v. First Nat. Bank, 184 Mass. 49, 67 N. E. 670. 

But in Hanna v. McCrory, 19 N. M. 183, 141 Pac. 996, orders drawn on a bank were presented by the payees for payment. 

The cashier received them and stamped on them, "Paid Oct. 16, 1916," and drew the checks to the payees, but retained the checks until the afternoon of the same day, when the bank was served with process of garnishment against the drawer. It was held that the orders were not paid and that the garnishor was entitled to the funds.

A distinction may be drawn in these cases, although it does not seem to have been made by the courts. As between banks, custom and usage may be such that the drawee bank is authorized by the collecting bank to credit the amount to the collecting bank and that such credit constitutes a payment even before a remittance of money or check is made, as in such cases as Consolidated Nat. 

Bank v. First Nat. Bank, 129 App. Div. 538, 114 N. Y. Supp. 

308, affd. 199 N. Y. 516, and by like custom and usage the stamping of the instrument as "paid" may have the same effect, as in Nineteenth Ward Bank v. First Nat. Bank, supra, and other cases. See Cohen v. First Nat. Bank, 22 Ariz. 394, 198

Pac. 122, 15 A. L. R. 701. In these cases the drawer of a check is, of course, discharged, and it is submitted that under sec. 87 the maker of a note payable at a bank should be discharged. But if a check or note payable at a bank is presented to the bank by the holder in person, stamped by the teller "paid," but before he had paid over the money, the teller is notified that the drawer had made an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or had not the money on deposit, or the deposit had been garnished, and the teller then erased the paid mark and returned the check, it could hardly be claimed that this was a payment so as to discharge the drawer. See Hanna v.

McCrory, supra. So also, if the instrument was sent by the holder to the bank by messenger or by mail. The instrument has not, in fact, been paid, but it may well be that the holder or the collecting bank, even in the absence of any custom or usage, should have the option of holding the drawee bank because of the manner in which it has dealt with the instrument, which was the holder's property, or of holding the drawer or maker because the instrument has not been honored. 

But in Shaw, Banking Commissioner v. R. C. Flick Mercantile Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 26 S. W. (2d) 1077, a note payable to

Y bank at Y bank was indorsed to W bank, who sent it back to Y bank for collection. At the date of maturity the maker had

§ 88 

more than enough money on deposit in the Y bank to pay the note. On the date of maturity the maker went to the Y bank and requested the note, but it could not be found. He left instructions to satisfy it out of his account. Two days later the 

Y bank failed. The amount of the note had neither been charged to the account of the maker nor credited to the account which the W bank carried with the Y bank. At the trial the note was produced, which was marked "Pd.", but that notation had been erased. It was held that the note was paid and the maker could not be held.

A series of checks drawn by the defendant were presented for payment through the Federal Reserve at his bank, marked "Paid," and returned to him. The bank paid the collecting bank by check which was subsequently dishonored. In a suit by the payee it was held that the checks were paid. Terminal Gas & Supply Co. v. Medford Auto Co., 285 Mass. 528, 189 N. E. 805.

A note, payable at a bank, was sent by a bank in which it had been deposited to the former bank for collection, and was presented to the maker who wrote across the face, "Charge to my account," and signed his name, which the cashier said was all right. The amount to the credit of the maker was slightly less than the amount of the note, but the next day the maker deposited money amounting to more than the note, and thereafter kept more than that amount to his credit. The bank did not charge the maker's account or remit the money, but held the note twelve days and then went into the hands of a receiver. 

Held, that though the bank had no authority to accept a part payment, yet under the circumstances the note was paid and the payee could not hold the maker. Peaslee-Gaulbert Co. v. Dixon, 172 N. C. 411, 90 S. E. 421.

In accordance with a notation on the margin of a note, the holder sent it for collection to a bank which held, as a special deposit, money of the maker. The cashier, at maturity, notified the maker, and the maker directed the cashier to pay the note out of his money. The cashier said, "All right, your note is paid," and asked what he should do with the note. The maker directed the cashier to hold the note until the maker should call for it. Held, that the note was paid at the time of this conversation.  Belk v. Capital Fire Ins. Co., 100 Neb. 260, 159 N. W. 405, 102 Neb. 702, 169 N. W. 262. 

See also, other cases under secs. 119 (3) and 136 as to the effect of stamping an instrument "paid."

Sec. 88. What Constitutes Payment in Due Course. 

Payment is made in due course when it is made at or after maturity of the instrument to the holder thereof in good faith and without notice that his title is defective.

The Arkansas case represents the better rule because it is impossible for the drawer or maker to protect himself if the paper has been negotiated.

The plaintiff at maturity was the holder of a note payable at the payee bank. The defendant, the maker, came to the payee bank and paid the note, and the bank credited the plaintiff's account. It is not clear that the plaintiff knew of the credit; but such transactions were customary. Upon failure of the payee bank the plaintiff sued the maker. It was held that the transaction constituted payment. Union Bank & Trust Co. of 

Helena v. Lynn, 73 Mont. 473, 237 Pac. 490; Koppler v. Bugge, 168 Wash. 182, 11 P. (2d) 236.

When the maker of a note paid the amount thereof at maturity to the payee as the authorized agent of the payee to accept payment, the maker's liability was extinguished, and he was held not liable to a purchaser after maturity. Semble, the reissue of a note after maturity and extinguishment will subject the party reissuing it to a liability, but the maker's liability is not revived unless he acquiesces or consents to the reissue. 

Manson v. Sutterer, 201 Ala. 81, 77 So. 375.

If the indorsee of a note tells the maker at maturity to see the payee, as the indorsee has nothing to do with it, and the maker thereupon pays the payee, the indorsee when afterwards suing on the note is estopped to dispute the defense of payment; or else there is evidence that the indorsee sues on behalf of the payee, who is barred.  Noble

Payment by the maker of a note to the payee when the note was in the physical possession of the payee did not discharge the note when the payee was not the actual or ostensible agent of the owner. The N. I. L. was not cited, and was not in force when the note was issued. Astoria State Bank v. Markwood, 37 S. D. 56, 156 N. W. 583; 38 S. D. 437, 161 N. W. 815; 41

But where the payee was the owner's agent for collection, and the fact was plainly stamped on the instrument, it was held that payment to payee in goods and services did not discharge the instrument. State v. Hanson, 55 N. D. 370, 213 N. W. 353. 

The N. I. L. was not cited.

An agent of a mortgagee, with authority to collect principal and interest, received from the mortgagor checks payable to the agent, which were cashed by the drawee bank and the proceeds misappropriated by the agent. Although a good payment to such an agent must be made in cash, still when the checks were actually paid in due course, this constituted an equivalent to a payment to him in cash. Two judges dissented. Potter v. Sager, 184

A resolution of a society required that its checks upon its deposit in the defendant bank be countersigned by the chairman of the board of trustees. Checks payable to the order of 

X, an employee of the society, for services rendered, were lost, and countermanded. Subsequently they were found, and a letter withdrawing the countermand sent to the bank. Although this was signed like the countermand, it was not countersigned according to the requirement for checks. The bank refused to recognize the letter, but afterwards paid X the checks. The society sued the bank for the amount of the checks. Held, the bank was liable, in the absence of any recognition by the society that the bank's action constituted payment to X, and the bank could not justify itself by showing that X was entitled to the money. A drew money from his account as executor in a bank and deposited it in his individual account, and then used the proceeds to pay his individual note to the bank. The maker of a note drew a check for the amount, payable to the order of a third person, which was indorsed by the payee and delivered to the bookkeeper of the holder of the note with instructions to apply it on the note. The bookkeeper had previously conducted other transactions between the parties. He promised to apply the check as directed and return the note, but in fact applied the check on a general account. Held, that this was a sufficient defense to an action on the note.  Rosenberg v. Segall, 159 N. Y. Supp. 152.

Where a seller gave a note to the buyer who had made advances on prospective shipments and at maturity the indebtedness of the buyer for goods shipped was sufficient to cover the note, the burden of proof rested upon the buyer to show that there was another indebtedness of the seller to which the buyer had the right to apply the proceeds of the goods sold. Notes provided for the payment by the maker of a reasonable attorney's fee if they were given after maturity to an attorney for collection. Held, the late mailing of the check did not constitute payment of the note, and the maker was liable for an attorney's fee. The N. I. L. was not cited. Aarons v. Dougherty, 79 Fla. 812, 84 So. 918.

A drawee bank was bound to pay to the holder a check duly indorsed by the payee and was not under a duty to inquire how the indorsee obtained the transfer or to know the amount of consideration paid therefor. The N. I. L. was not cited. Lincoln

A joint maker of a note, who was a surety, placed the amount of the note and costs on deposit in the bank, in the name of a trustee, to be transferred to the bank in exchange for an assignment of a judgment, when recovered against the defendant, the principal-maker. The rule that an agent's authority is revoked by the death of the principal, without notice, does not apply to payment of a check by the drawee bank having no knowledge of the drawer's death, even though the check was without consideration. Glennan v. Rochester Trust, etc., Co., 209 N. Y. 12, 102 N. E. 537, 52 L. R. A. (N.S.) 302.

In Massachusetts, by statute, "The death of the drawer does not operate as a revocation of the authority to pay a eheck if the check is presented for payment within ten days from the date thereof." G. L. 1923, c. 107, sec. 17. N. J. Laws 1916, c. 123, is similar.

The English Bills of Exchange Act, sec. 75, provides, "The duty and authority of a banker to pay a check drawn on him by his customer are determined by (1) a countermand of payment, (2) notice of the customer's death." Since the Negotiable

Instruments Law contains no provision upon this point, it must, as an omitted case, be governed by the rules of the law merchant under sec. 196.

ENGLAND 

The payee of a demand note held a mortgage to secure the debt. He sold and transferred the mortgage to one person for full value and afterwards indorsed the note to a holder in due course. Held, that the note was not paid by the sale of the mortgage. Glasscock v. Balls, 24 Q. B. D. 13. 

The payee of a bill drawn for a large sum accepted by E and payable at defendant bank, indorsed it in blank and handed it to X, its cashier, instructing X to take the bill to its own bank for collection. X, in fraud of the payee, presented the bill at defendant bank, which under a prior agreement with E paid X. 

After absconding with the proceeds, the payee sued the defendant for conversion. Held, that defendant was protected by sec. 59. The payment was in good faith and although presentment for payment across the counter was unusual in the case of bills for large sums, it was not sufficient in and of itself to excite a suspicion that something was wrong. Auchteroni and Co. v. 

Midland Bank Limited (1928), 2 K. B. 294.

§ 904 

 Checks ARTICLE VII  Sec. 89. To Whom Notice of Dishonor Must Be 

Given.

Except as herein otherwise provided, when a negotiable instrument has been dishonored by nonacceptance or nonpayment, notice of dishonor must be given to the drawer and to each indorser, and any drawer or indorser to whom such notice is not given is discharged. 

Cross Reference: 881 to 10, 17(6), 31, 63, 67, 83, 95, 96, 109 to 

115, 126, 133, 149, 184, 185, 191, 7, 61, 66, 70, 90 to 108, 137, 142, 152, 172, 186.

ANNOTATIONS 

This section repeats by implication a previous statute allowing suit at the next term of court without notice to indorsers. 

Wall v. Reimers (Tex. Civ. App.), 79 S. W. (2d) 142.

Where notice of dishonor to the drawer of a check is required it must be alleged in the complaint. Ewald v. Faulhaber Co., 105 N. Y. Supp. 114; Studebaker Sons Co. v. Fuether, 123 

N. Y. Supp. 118; Spear v. Assoc. Producing, etc., Corp., 120 

Misc. Rep. 518, 199 N. Y. Supp. 84. Contra, the drawer, in light of section 186, must allege absence of notice as an affirmative defense. Deal v. Atlantic Coast Line R. Co., 225 Ala. 533, 144 

So. 81, 86 A. L. R. 455, with note, 46 Harv. L. Rev. 845. So also, as to the indorser of a promissory note. Sykes v. Kruse, 49 Colo. 560, 113 Pac. 1013; Hall v. First Nat. Bank, 196 Ala. 

627, 72 So. 171; Gresham v. State Bank, 131 Miss. 20, 95 So. 

65; Carter v. Jennings, 134 Miss. 263, 98 So. 687.

But notice of dishonor is not necessary if the drawer had countermanded payment; and the complaint may be amended so as to conform to proof of such fact. Scanlon v. Wallach, 53 

Misc. Rep. 104, 102 N. Y. Supp. 1090.

Judgment for the payees of a check against the drawer can not be sustained in the absence of proof that notice of dishonor was given to the drawer. Kuflick v. Glasser, 114 N. Y. Supp. 870.

The drawer of a check is discharged by failure to give him notice of dishonor, the bank refusing to pay because it was short of funds, and subsequently proving to be insolvent. Bacigalupo v. Parrilli, 112 N. Y. Supp. 1040. It does not appear in the report of this case whether the bank paid any dividend or not. 

In Morris-Miller Co. v. Von Pressentin, 63 Wash. 74, 114 Pac. 

912, it was held that failure to give notice of dishonor of a check to the drawer will not discharge him unless it caused loss which he would not otherwise have sustained. But the

§ 89 

was not cited and the point, as affected by the statute, does not seem to have been considered. 

See also cases under sec. 186 infra.

To charge an indorser the complaint must allege presentment Pleading to the maker and notice of dishonor, unless the same are dispensed with under secs. 82 and 109 respectively, or is not required under sec. 118. First State Bank & Trust Co. v. Smoot 

& Co., 2 La. App. 793; Winn v. Batton (La. App.), 152 So. 349; 

Lynes v. Holt-Taylor Mercantile Co. (Mo. App.), 268 S. W. 702; 

Robinson v. Holmes, 57 Oreg. 5, 109 Pac. 754; First State Bank of Ovalo v. Ovalo Warehouse Assn. (Tex. Civ. App.), 276 S. W. 

773; Cities Service Oil Co. v. First Nat. Bank of Granbury 

(Tex. Civ. App.), 48 S. W. (2d) 348; Reisch v. Degnitz (Wis.), 228 N. W. 488.

In an action against the indorser of a note it is not sufficient to allege that upon maturity the note was duly presented for payment, and the indorser duly notified of nonpayment. The allegation and the evidence must show the demand and notice to have been upon such a day as will charge the defendant. 

The  was not cited on this point. Hoyland v. National 

Bank of Middlesborough, 137 Ky. 682, 126 S. W. 356. Sed quaere, whether this is not too technical? See next case.

An allegation that due notice of the protest of a note was duly given to an indorser is a sufficient allegation of notice of dishonor; the term "protest" including in a popular sense all the steps taken to fix the liability of an indorser, and the word "duly," in legal parlance, meaning "according to law," and relating not to form only, but including both form and substance. Sherman v. Ecker, 59 Misc. Rep. 216, 110 N. Y. Supp. 265, An allegation that a note was duly presented, dishonored, and protested, as to all of which the defendants had due and timely knowledge, is defective for failure to state that notice of dishonor was given to the defendant indorser. Kahnweiler v. Salomon, 107 Misc. Rep. 602, 177 N. Y. Supp. 739. This is much too technical.

Plaintiff must allege that notice of dishonor was given to the indorser of a note, or that it was waived. An allegation that the note was duly protested is not enough.  Wisdom & Levy v. Bille, 120 La. 700, 45 So. 554; but see comment on this case in Frank-Taylor-Kendrick Co. v. Voissement, 142 La. 973, 77 So. 895. 

But Gleason v. Thayer, 87 Conn. 248, 87 Atl. 790, Ann. Cas. 

1915B, 1069; Prudential Trust Co. v. Coghlin, 249 Mass. 184, 144 N. E. 283, are contra. Inasmuch, as by secs. 153 and 154, a protest appears to be only a formal statement in writing by a notary or other persons making it, of the fact of presentment, the time, place and manner thereof, etc., and does not include

§ 906 

Pleading a notice, which is a subsequent act, the first Louisiana decision has a technical correctness, but the overruling decision and the cases in other states sensibly adopt the business interpretation of protest, as including all the steps necessary to charge an indorser. See also sec. 111.

Burden of proof

Under the South Carolina Code a complaint which alleges that notes "became due and payable" by the defendant indorsers to the plaintiff is sufficient, although it does not allege presentment and notice. One judge dissented.  McCrae v. Spires, 121 S. C. 147, 113 S. E. 583. 

Where a statute authorized suit on a note by motion and notice, the notice must state a cause of action, and in a suit against an indorser it must show that the note was protested or notice of dishonor given. Security Loan & Trust Co. v. 

Fields, 110 Va. 827, 67 S. E. 342. The  was not cited in this case.

Although a complaint did not aver presentment and notice of dishonor or a legal excuse for failure, and the point was not raised by demurrer or answer, proof thereof must be made in order to recover from an indorser. Thompson v. Divine, 73 

Ind. App. 113, 126 N. E. 683.

The burden of proof is on the holder to show due notice, or that notice was waived or excused. Carter Lumber Co. v. Shupe

Terminal Corp., 101 N. J. Law 349, 127 Atl. 245. The N. I. L. 

was not cited. In re Tharp, 113 Misc. Rep. 199, 184 N. Y. Supp. 

232; National Bank of Rochester v. Erion-Haines Realty Co., 213 App. Div. 54, 209 N. Y. Supp. 522, affg. 123 Misc. Rep. 893, 206 N. Y. Supp. 452; Washington Horse Exch. Co. v. Bonner, 180 N. C. 20, 103 S. E. 907; Jones v. Carolina Nat. Bank, 114 

S. C. 11, 103 S. E. 27; McKee v. McGhee, 114 S. C. 183, 103 

S. E. 508; Williams v. Guaranty State Bank & T. Co. (Tex. 

Civ. App.), 264 S. W. 194.

The burden of proof of notice of dishonor was on the holder, and it was error for a charge to convey to the jury the impression that the indorser must prove not only that he never received notice of dishonor, but that such notice was never mailed to him, a burden impossible to carry unless he made the plaintiff a witness for himself. The uncontradicted testimony of the indorser that notice of dishonor was never received by him was sufficient proof on his part of want of notice. Casey v. Owens, 24 Ga. App. 91, 100 S. E. 42, construing Fla. N. I. L.

A notary's certificate stating that protest has been made; but with no mention of notice, is not enough to prove notice. Car ter Lumber Co. v. Shupe Terminal Corp., 101 N. J. Law 349, 127 

Atl. 245. The N. I. L. was not cited.

The notary's certificate stating due notice is presumptive evidence, which throws on the indorser the burden of proving the contrary, not by cross-examination of the plaintiff's wit-

§ 89 

nesses, but by producing affirmative proof. He may have the plaintiff and his agent ordered to submit to examination before trial. Marine Trust Co. v. Nuway Devices, 204 App. Div. 752, 

198 N. Y. Supp. 715.

Parol evidence is not admissible to show that one who appears as an indorser and who has been discharged by failure to give notice was to be bound as maker. Busbee v. Creech, 192 N. C. 

499, 135 S. E. 326, 13 Va. L. Rev. 306; Smardon v. Broussard, 6 La. App. 579. 

Unreasonable delay in giving notice of dishonor of a check will discharge the indorser whether such delay causes loss to him or not. Swift & Co. v. Miller, 62 Ind. App. 312, 113 N. E. 447.

A check drawn and indorsed in Indiana but payable in Illi-. nois is governed by the Illinois  as to the time within which notice of nonpayment must be given to an indorser. The 

N. I. L. was not in force in Indiana until after the dishonor. 

Wells Fargo & Co. Express v. First National Bank, 70 Ind. App. 

584, 123 N. E. 700. 

In Cahill v. Cahill, 205 Ill. App. 341, the odd statement appears that the N. I. L. requires demand of payment to be made upon an indorser. The court doubtless meant to say, notice of dishonor.

This section impliedly repeals a former Texas statute which permitted the holder of a negotiable instrument to fix the liability of a secondary party without protest and notice of dishonor by suing the primary party before the first term of the court after the right of action accrued. The allegation in a complaint that the defendant indorsers, though often requested, had refused to pay the demand, is insufficient to state the giving of notice of dishonor. First Nat. Bank v. Lee Cty. C. Oil 

Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 250 S. W. 313.

Failure to notify an indorser of an installment note of the nonpayment of previous installments does not affect his liability for later installments of the nonpayment of which he has been duly notified. Hopkins v. Merrill, 79 Conn. 626, 66 Atl. 174; 

Roberts v. International Bank (App. D. C.), 25 F. (2d) 214.

The notes did not appear to contain an option to declare the whole sum due for nonpayment of any installment. Cf. Galbraith v. Shepard, 43 Wash. 698, 86 Pac. 1113.

When each of eight notes maturing in successive months stated that it was one of a series, and that a default on any note would mature the entire series, due notice to indorsers of the dishonor of the first note was sufficient to charge them upon all the notes. 

The court thought that the acceleration was not automatic but optional, and that the holder had a reasonable time for the exercise of the option, but that starting suit against maker and indorsers constituted such exercise.

M made a note payable in installments to the defendant, who indorsed it to the plaintiff. The note contained the usual acceleration clause at option of the holder. When M had defaulted in several installments the plaintiff notified M that he exercised his option to accelerate, but the defendant was not notified until later. It was held that the defendant indorser is discharged because of lack of notice of presentment, and an attempt by the plaintiff to withdraw the notice and later again exercise his option and promptly notify the defendant was of no effect. Anderson v. Sperry (Wash.), 284 Pac. 102.

When acceleration by default is automatic, notice of dishonor must be given at once and it is not sufficient to give it upon commencement of the action. Bollenbach v. Ludlum, 84 

Okla. 14, 201 Pac. 982.

The indorser of a note payable by installments, with a provision for acceleration on dishonor of two or more installments, was entitled to notice of the dishonor of any installment. Semble, notice must also be given even in the absence of the acceleration provision, as each installment is equivalent to a separate note. 

Elworthy-Helwick Co. v. Hess, 9 Oh. App. 200. 

The defendant indorsed an installment note accelerable at the option of the holder on default providing for payments of $100 and later $125. The holder accepted payments of $100 when $125 was due. Later, after two defaults, he presented the note and gave defendant notice of dishonor. Held, since acceleration was at the option of the holder, the notice was sufficient to bind the defendant for the future installments; but as to the $25 balance of part installments he was discharged for lack of notice of dishonor. Berkowitz v. Kasparewicz (Conn.), 183 Atl. 

693, 104 A. L. R. 1326.

An action against an indorser after legal notice of dishonor is on notice not barred because judgment was rendered in his favor in a previous action solely for the reason that he had not been notified before that action was brought. Peck v. Easton, 74 Conn. 456, 51 Atl. 134.

Indorsers are discharged by failure to give notice although they subsequently took a mortgage from the maker to indemnify them against liability. A payment by the maker after the period of the Statute of Limitations does not toll the statute as to indorsers. Barber v. Absher Co., 175 N. C. 602, 96 S. E. 43.

When a notice of dishonor was mailed to the payee in care of the defendant accommodation indorser, this was not notice to the defendant. The notary's certificate is only presumptive evidence of notice. Sec. 89 was not cited. Greene v. Poz, 182 

N. Y. Supp. 900.

An indorser is entitled to notice of dishonor, even though he is an officer of the bank holding the instrument, unless it is his duty as officer to give such notice on behalf of the bank. First

Kane v. Eastman (Cal. App.), 288 Pac. 819, citing many authorities.

This section has no application to an action for contribution by an accommodation indorser who paid an instrument after notice, against his coindorsers who were not notified. It applies only to actions concerning liability upon commercial paper. 

Owens v. Greenlee, 68 Colo. 114, 188 Pac. 721, 9 A. L. R. 1184, with note, see also sec. 68, where conflicting cases are collected. 

When the stockholders of a corporation agreed to indemnify the indorser of its notes against liability, it was incumbent upon him to show that the notes had been duly protested, so that he became liable as indorser, before he paid the notes and looked to the stockholders for reimbursement.  

Moody v. Wise, 188 App. Div. 224, 176 N. Y. Supp. 515.

The defendants indorsed notes to the plaintiff to secure a debt. Held, failure to notify the indorser of the dishonor of the notes discharged him from liability pro tanto upon the debt, as well as upon the notes. Counts v. Burns (Tex. Civ. App.), 250

Contra, the plaintiff's failure to notify the defendant of the on notice dishonor of a note indorsed and pledged by him as collateral does not discharge him from liability on the principal debt.

A joint maker, though a surety, is not an indorser and is primarily liable, and, therefore, is not entitled to notice of dishonor.
