Sec. 90. By Whom Given. 

The notice may be given by or on behalf of the holder, or by or on behalf of any party to the instrument who might be compelled to pay it to the holder, and who, upon taking it up, would have a right to reimbursement from the party to whom the notice is given.' 

Cross Reference: 88 50, 95, 96, 102, 121, 191, 7, 56, 60 to 67, 70, 89, 91 to 118, 159.

A bank having a note for collection is a holder thereof entitled to give notice. Phillips v. Cunningham, 148 Tenn. 164, 253 

S. W. 354.

The showing to the indorser by the maker of a telegram demanding payment of the maker is not sufficient notice. Passaic 

Nat. Bank & Trust Co. v. Knapp (N. J. Super.), 158 Atl. 393.

Sec. 91. Notice Given By Agent. 

Notice of dishonor may be given by an agent either in his own name or in the name of any party entitled to give notice, whether that party be his principal or not. 

Cross Reference: 88 19, 90, 95, 96, 102, 56, 60 to 67, 89, 92 to 118.

ANNOTATIONS 

A note made by A to the order of B, indorsed by B and also by A, was protested for nonpayment. Notice addressed to B was sent to A, who forwarded it to B. Held, that although A could not give notice in his own behalf to B under sec. 90, since 

B was presumptively an accommodation indorser for A and not liable, yet A could forward it to B,.on behalf of the holder, and as his agent. Traders Nat. Bank v. Jones, 104 App. Div. 433, 93 N. Y. Supp. 768.

The cashier of the drawee bank which had refused to pay a check, gave the check to a notary to protest, which was done. 

Held, that the possession of the check by the cashier was evidence 1 "The notice must be given by or on behalf of the holder or by or on behalf of an indorser who, at the time of giving it, is himself liable on the bill." B. E. A. s. 49 (1).

§ 93 

of his agency of the holder to present it for protest. Hooper v. 

Herring, 14 Ala. App. 455, 70 So. 308.

A notary public may give notice as agent of the collecting bank holding the note. Phillips v. Cunningham, 148 Tenn. 164, 253 S. W. 354; Caine v. Foreman (Cal. App.), 289 Pac. 929.

A collecting bank is a proper party to give notice, and where it has done so, no notice from the owner is necessary. Bank of 

Alpena v. Meyers, 177 Ark. 214, 6 S. W. (2d) 22. 

When an indorsee presented the note for payment on the day of maturity, and on the same day gave the note to a third party with instructions to present to the defendant indorser the following day, and this was done according to instructions, and payment refused, it was held that proper steps had been taken to charge the defendant. Grenda v. Kitchen (Mass.), 170 N. E. 619.

Sec. 92. Effect of Notice Given on Behalf of Holder. 

Where notice is given by or on behalf of the holder, it enures for the benefit of all subsequent holders and all prior parties who have a right of recourse against the party to whom it is given. 

Cross Reference: 88 95, 96, 102, 191, 56, 61, 63 to 68, 70, 89, 91. 

93 to 118, 152.

Sec. 93. Effect Where Notice is Given by Party En titled Thereto.

Where notice is given by or on behalf of a party entitled to give notice, it enures for the benefit of the holder and all parties subsequent to the party to whom notice is given. 

Cross Reference: 88 90, 95, 96, 102, 191, 56, 61, 63 to 68, 70, 89, 91, 92, 94 to 118. 

Where the indorsers of a promissory note were promoters of a corporation, which made the note, and one or more of them received from the bank holding the note, as agent of the holder for collection, verbal notice of the dishonor of the note, and they all spoke together about the matter, the notice from the indorsers to each other enured to the benefit of the holder. Piedmont Carolina Ry. Co. v. Shaw, 223 Fed. 973, 138 C. C. A. 227.

§ 912 

 Notice by agents 

Sec. 94. When Agent May Give Notice. 

Where the instrument has been dishonored in the hands of an agent, he may either himself give notice to the parties liable thereon, or he may give notice to his principal. If he give notice to his principal, he must do so within the same time as if he were the holder, and the principal upon the receipt of such notice has himself the same time for giving notice as if the agent had been an independent holder. 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 19, 31, 61, 63, 66, 67, 83, 95, 96, 102 to 

104, 107, 149, 191, 36, 56, 60, 62, 64, 68, 89 to 93, 97 to 118.

ANNOTATIONS 

It is not necessary that notice of dishonor be given by the holder, at presentment, directly to the beneficial owner, disregarding all intervening indorsees for collection. Blue Ribbon 

Garage v. Baldwin, 91 Conn. 674, 101 Atl. 83.

Where an agent for collection of a note does not know an indorser's address and mails to the principal a notice addressed to such indorser in blank with postage for forwarding, the agent is not guilty of negligence in collecting. Brill v. Jefferson Bank, 159 App. Div. 461, 144 N. Y. Supp. 539.

And under such circumstances the notice is received on time even though the principal received it four days late, due to a delay in mail, but immediately remailed it to the indorsee. City 

Trust & Savings Bank v. Edson, 202 Ia. 671, 210 N. W. 898.

In an action by a holder against a collecting bank because recourse against indorsers was lost, due to the bank's failure to properly give notice, the bank at which the note was payable was non-existent and upon notice of that fact the collecting bank notified the holder, who failed to notify the indorsers. It was held that the bank was excused. The obligation to give such notice was on the holder, not the collecting bank. Lewis v. Chelsea Exchange Bank, 241 N. Y. Supp. 639.

Where a bank, holding a note for collection, sent notice of dishonor to the bank from which it received the note on the day after dishonor, and it was received the next day, and notice of dishonor was mailed at once to the prior indorser, both banks used due diligence. Gleason v. Thayer, 87 Conn. 248, 87 Atl. 

790, Ann. Cas. 1915B, 1069.

Plaintiff indorsed and deposited a check for collection in bank on the 28th. On the 29th he was notified of the dishonor of the check, and on the 30th he notified the defendant indorser by telegraph. Held, that the notice was in due time. Jurgens v. 

Wichmann, 124 App. Div. 531, 108 N. Y. Supp. 881.

The plaintiff pledgee of a note indorsed by B, sent it to the defendant bank for collection. The defendant forwarded it to the X bank, which presented it to the Y bank in the same

§ 95 

agents town, at which the note was payable. The notary who pro- Notice by tested the note made out separate notices for each of the indorsers, including the plaintiff and defendant, and mailed the notice for B to the defendant bank. The defendant failed to forward this notice to B or notify the plaintiff that it had not done so. In a previous suit by the pledgee on the principal debt, Farmers Nat. Bank v. Nelson, 255 Pa. 455, 100 

Atl. 136, L. R. A. 1917E, 506, not citing , it had been held that the discharge of B, the only solvent party on the pledged note, released the principal debtor (the pledgeor), the court saying that the pledgee owed the pledgeor a duty of care to collect collateral and was responsible for the negligence of its agent (the present defendant). The plaintiff then sued the defendant for negligence. Held, not liable. The defendant was simply the agent of the plaintiff for collection, and discharged its duty by selecting the X bank as sub-agent and notifying the plaintiff of the dishonor. It was no part of its duty to forward the notice to B or send it to the plaintiff. The plaintiff had not advised the defendant of B's address. The plaintiff should either have given the defendant specific directions to notify B or notified B itself in the time allowed it for that purpose by sec. 94, as the principal holder. Despite the statement in the previous case, the negligence was the plaintiff's, and not the defendant's. Farmers Nat. Bank v. Peoples Nat. 

Bank, 263 Pa. 266, 106 Atl. 311.

ENGLAND 

A branch of a country banking company sent to a London bank for collection a bill bearing several indorsements. Upon dishonor the London bank sent notice by post on the next day to another branch of the forwarding bank. The next day notice was sent by telegraph to the right branch, and the subsequent notices of dishonor to other parties were given in due time. Held, that sufficient notice of dishonor was given and the first indorser was liable. Fielding v. Corry [1898], 1 Q. B. 268. 

Sec. 95. When Notice Sufficient. 

A written notice need not be signed, and an insufficient written notice may be supplemented and validated by verbal communication. A misdescription of the instru ment does not vitiate the notice unless the party to whom the notice is given is in fact misled thereby. 

Cross Reference: §§ 96, 196, 10, 23, 56, 97 to 118, 153, 154, 162, 172. 

Where the notice of protest described the note correctly and the envelope was correctly addressed and was received and opened by the indorser, the notice was sufficient, although the

§ 914 

 Form of notice notice was on its face by mistake addressed to the maker. Wilson v. Peck, 66 Misc. Rep. 179, 121 N. Y. Supp. 344. But it was held otherwise where both the notice and the envelope containing it were addressed to another party. Marshall v. Sonneman, 216 

Pa. 65, 64 Atl. 874, in which case the  was not cited.

A notary's certificate of protest was held a sufficient notice, although it lacked the notary's seal. Cohen v. Sovalsky, 124 

Misc. Rep. 368, 208 N. Y. Supp. 46.  

See sec. 153 infra, and discussion of the case there.

Sec. 96. Form of Notice. 

The notice may be in writing or merely oral¹ and may be given in any terms which sufficiently identify the instrument, and indicate that it has been dishonored by nonacceptance or nonpayment. It may in all cases be given by delivering it personally or through the mails." 

Cross Reference: §§ 83, 149, 191, 10, 89 to 95, 97 to 118, 153.

ANNOTATIONS 

Oral notice of dishonor, given personally or through an agent, is enough to charge the indorsers. Kelly v. Theiss, 77 App. Div.

Following receipt of his notice of dishonor, the owner of the note at once notified a prior indorser by telephone and, on the following day, visited and orally notified another indorser. Held, that these notices complied in all respects with the requirements of law. Blue Ribbon Garage v. Baldwin, 91 Conn. 674, 101 Atl. 83. 

Notice by service of process against the indorsers is sufficient where process was served within the time prescribed by the Act. 

Winn v. Batton (La. App.), 152 So. 349; Winn v. Perryman (La. App.), 160 So. 804. 

Notice of dishonor may be given by telephone if it be clearly shown that the party to be notified was really communicated with, that is, fully identified as the party at the receiving end of the line. American Nat. Bank v. Nat. Fertilizer Co., 125 Tenn.

Notice by telephone is sufficient under this section. Caine v. 

Foreman (Cal. App.), 289 Pac. 929.

Sec. 97. To Whom Notice May Be Given. 

Notice of dishonor may be given either to the party himself or to his agent in that behalf.

Leaving the notice at the window of the cashier of a hotel corporation is not sufficient service, it not appearing that any one's attention was drawn to the notice, or that any one was present, and the president and managers having testified that it was not brought to their attention. Am. Exch. Nat. Bank v. Am. Hotel

Both the notice of dishonor and the envelope containig it were addressed to the second indorser and delivered by a notary public to the first indorser. Oral notice of dishonor given by telephone to a clerk of an indorsing commercial corporation, is not notice to the corporation, especially when it does not appear that the clerk had communicated the notice to any one connected with the management of the business of the corporation. American Nat. Bank v. Nat.

When any party is dead, and his death is known to the party giving notice, the notice must be given to a personal representative, if there be one, and if with reasonable diligence he can be found. If there be no personal representative, notice may be sent to the last residence or last place of business of the deceased.¹

Second Nat. Bank v. Smith, 91 N. J. L. 531, 103

Sec. 99. Notice to Partners.

Where the parties to be notified are partners, notice to any one partner is notice to the firm even though there has been a dissolution.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 95, 96, 191, 77, 89 to 94, 97, 98, 100 to 118.

Notice to one partner is notice to all the firm although it was fraudulently suppressed by the partner receiving it. Kensington Nat. Bk., v. Ware, 32 Pa. Super. Ct. 247.

This section has no application to a note made by one partner and indorsed by another. Deffler v. Loudenback, 233 Ill. App. 240.

Sec. 100. Notice to Persons Jointly Liable. 

Notice to joint parties who are not partners must be given to each of them, unless one of them has authority to receive such notice for the others. 

Cross Reference: §§ 95, 96, 17(7), 68, 78, 89 to 99, 101 to 118.

Joint indorsers, to whom notice of dishonor has been given, are not discharged by reason of failure to give notice to the other joint indorsers. Doherty v. First Nat. Bank, 170 Ky. 810, 186

S. W. 937. But in this case the indorsers were joint payees and so were jointly and severally liable under sec. 68. Aliter, if they are accommodation indorsers, Case v. McKinnis, 107 Oreg. 223, 213 Pac. 422, 32 A. L. R. 167, semble, stated under sec. 68. The 

Kentucky case relies on the earlier decision in Williams v.

Paintsville Nat. Bank, which, as stated under sec. 68, was affected by the special wording of that section in one revision of the Kentucky statutes.

Four defendants indorsed a note for the accommodation of the maker, before delivery to the payee. They indorsed jointly. 

None of the indorsers were given notice of dishonor, but two of them later waived such notice. It was held that the common law rule applies; that all joint indorsers are discharged, if no notice was given to all and no waiver by all applies. First Nat. 

Bank of Ludington v. Mich.-Ark. Oil Corp., 231 Mich. 597, 204 

N. W. 719, 11 Cornell L. Q. 57.

This unnecessarily narrow interpretation of section 68 is unjustifiable, in light of the plain meaning of section 109.

Sec. 101. Notice to Bankrupt.

Where a party has been adjudged a bankrupt or an insolvent, or has made an assignment for the benefit of creditors, notice may be given either to the party himself or to his trustee or assignee.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 95, 96, 89 to 94, 97 to 100, 102 to 118.

This section settles a conflict. It had been held that notice of dishonor to an assignee for the benefit of creditors was sufficient.² 

The contrary was held in Ohio in a case making a distinction between bankruptcy and a voluntary assignment for the benefit of creditors.

Sec. 102. Time Within Which Notice Must Be 

Given.

Notice may be given as soon as the instrument is dishonored; and unless delay is excused as hereinafter provided, must be given within the times fixed by this Act.*

ANNOTATIONS 

The sending of notice before maturity of a note to all the parties is not a sufficient notice of dishonor. Case v. McKinnis, 107 Oreg. 223, 213 Pac. 422, 32 A. L. R. 167.

Oral notice to the indorser's son the day before the note matures is not sufficient.  Horton v. 

Wilson, 175 N. C. 533, 95 S. E. 904.

A letter sent by the holder to the indorser before maturity stating that the note had not been paid is premature and ineffective as notice of dishonor. Kelly v. Ford, 115 W. Va. 435, 176 S. E. 705.

Defects in the allegations of notice of dishonor and waiver of notice in the petition, are cured by a finding of the jury that notice of dishonor was given to defendant in writing in proper time, and that defendant declared his intention to pay. Doherty v. First Nat. Bank, 170 Ky. 810, 186 S. W. 937.

Sec. 103. Where Parties Reside in Same Place. 

Where the person giving and the person to receive notice reside in the same place, notice must be given within the following times:- (1) If given at the place of business of the person to receive notice, it must be given before the close of business hours on the day following; (2) If given at his residence, it must be given before the usual hours of rest on the day following; (3) If sent by mail, it must be deposited in the post office in time to reach him in usual course on the day following.¹

notice The specific words of this section can not be modified by the Time for definition of a reasonable time in sec. 193, which has no application to this section but applies to cases like those described in sec. 144 and perhaps others. Jones v. Carolina Nat. Bank, 114 S. C. 11, 103 S. E. 27. 

Notice given "two or three days after the note was due" is too late. Solomon v. Cohen, 94 N. Y. Supp. 502; Siegel v. Dubinsky, 56 Misc. Rep. 681, 107 N. Y. Supp. 678.

The plaintiff, holder of a demand note, presented it to the maker on the seventeenth of the month and was told to return on the twenty-second and he would be paid. The plaintiff complied with the request; but on the twenty-second the maker had - absconded. On that day notice was given to the defendant indorser. Such notice was held not within the time limit, the dishonor having occurred on the seventeenth. Bredow v. Woll, 108 Conn. 489, 143 Atl. 849, 62 A. L. R. 293. 

Where the note matured on January 2nd and the notices were mailed and dated January 4th, it was held that they were given too late. First Nat. Bank of Ludington v. Mich.-Ark. Oil

The paper in question was dishonored May 13th and the letter containing notice was postmarked May 14th. Held, this constituted sufficient evidence of notice. Rice Growers Credit

The holder's agent called at defendant's place of business to give him notice of dishonor of the note and found that he was absent from the city. The word "may" in sec. 96 is to be construed as "must" and the impossibility of giving oral notice does not excuse delay; notice by mail being practicable. Price v. Warner, 60 Oreg. 7, 118 Pac. 173.

A notice placed in a mail chute on the day of protest, but not postmarked until the next day at noon, is mailed in time and it will be presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the notice reached its destination by 5 o'clock, which would be before the close of business hours, both parties residing in Manhattan. The indorser swore that he did not get the notice until the following day, but did not testify that he was at his office on the day it was mailed. This was not enough to show that the notice was not received in time. Wilson v. Peck, 66

Sec. 104. Where Parties Reside in Different Places. 

Where the person giving and the person to receive notice reside in different places, the notice must be given within the following times:- (1) If sent by mail, it must be deposited in the post office in time to go by mail the day following the day of dishonor, or if there be no mail at a convenient hour on that day, by the next mail thereafter.¹ (2) If given otherwise than through the post office, then within the time that notice would have been received in due course of mail, if it had been deposited in the post office within the time specified in the last subdivision."

Proof of notice of protest properly addressed, stamped and mailed in time to go by mail on the day following the dishonor, is due notice, under secs. 104 and 105, and the fact that the notice was addressed to one, as treasurer, who indorsed the note in his individual capacity does not affect the validiy of the notice. 

Farmers Nat. Bank v. Howard, 71 W. Va. 57, 76 S. E. 122.

In an action by the indorsee against the indorser on certificates of deposit, where the notary testified that he mailed notice of dishonor, addressed to the defendant, in care of the plaintiff holder, within the time required by  section 104, but it was received by the indorsee four days later than the regular mail and was immediately remailed to the indorser, it was held that the mere delay in receiving notice was not sufficient to submit the question whether notice was mailed within time to the jury. City Trust & Savings Bank v. Edson, 202 Ia. 671, 210 N. 

W. 898; see also sections 94 and 105.

Plaintiff received in Boston, Oct. 2d, notice of dishonor of a note. Plaintiff's notice to defendant indorser in Somerville, Mass., was mailed in Boston, Oct. 4th, postmarked 8:30 P. M.

There were twelve daily mails between Boston and Somerville. 

Held, that the words "go by mail" mean an actual departure in the course of mail from the post office in which the notice was deposited, in case there is a mail from that post office to the destination of the notice at a convenient hour on the required day, and that it could not be ruled, as a matter of law, that plaintiff had sustained the burden required by the statute. Harris v. Baker, 226 Mass. 113, 115 N. E. 292.

When the notice of dishonor to an indorser living at a different place from the holder was deposited in the mails the afternoon of the day following dishonor, the burden was on the holder to show whether there was a mail train on that day, and if so, that it did not leave before the mailing. Nickell v. Bradshaw, 94 Oreg. 580, 183 Pac. 12, 11 A. L. R. 623.

Oral notice given by the holder who lived at Denver, to an indorser residing in Colorado Springs on the day following the day the holder received notice from his agent for collection is within time, the agent having given his principal notice the day after the dishonor. De La Vergne v. Globe Printing Co., 27 

Colo. App. 308, 148 Pac. 823.

Where drafts were dishonored in Shanghai and the holder's New York office notified the drawer, by mail, which notice was received before mail could have arrived from Shanghai, the notice was held sufficient. Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. 

V. Lazard-Godchaux Co. of America, 207 App. Div. 174, 201 

N. Y. Supp. 771; affd. 239 N. Y. 610, 147 N. E. 216.

Sec. 105. When Sender Deemed to Have Given Due Notice. 

Where notice of dishonor is duly addressed and deposited in the post office, the sender is deemed to have given due notice, notwithstanding any miscarriage in the mails. 

Cross Reference: §§ 95, 96, 106, 70, 89 to 94, 97 to 104, 107 to 118. 

ANNOTATIONS 

The effect of the holder's knowledge that, although the notice is properly deposited in the post office, it will not seasonably reach the indorser through the mail, because of war or other reasons, is discussed by Professor K. N. Llewellyn, 23 Colum. 

L. Rev. 156 n. 

Where a statute provides that the notary's certificate shall constitute evidence of the facts stated therein and the certificate shows mailing, the mere statement by the indorser that he did not receive the notice was held not sufficient to go to the jury. 

Trusts & Guarantee Co. v. Bernhardt, 270 N. Y. 350, 1 N. E. (2d) 459.

A notice addressed to the indorser without any address is not a proper notice. Peoples Bank & Trust Co. v. Allen, 94 N. J. L. 

355, 110 Atl. 704. 

Where the president of a corporation and the corporation were both indorsers, a mailed notice of non-payment addressed to the corporation, attention of the president, was held not to be duly addressed to the individual indorser so as to give rise to the presumption of due notice. Bovay v. Fuller, 63 F. (2d) 

Where notice of dishonor is addressed to an indorser at an address other than the one given on the note and is not received by him, he is discharged from liability. Century Bank v. Breitbart, 89 Misc. Rep. 308, 151 N. Y. Supp. 588.

Notice addressed to an indorser at the address of the maker which appeared on the note, when the correct address of the maker could have been found in the city directory, was held not duly addressed. H. H. Dickinson Co. v. Hickey, 235 Mich. 638, 209 N. W. 848.

Although non-receipt of a duly mailed notice of dishonor does not discharge an indorser, evidence of such non-receipt is competent on the question whether the notice was actually mailed. 

Union Bank of Brooklyn v. Deshel, 139 App. Div. 217, 123 N. 

Y. Supp. 585; Cakins v. Vaughan, 217 Ala. 56, 114 So. 570.

A notary public having produced his certificate showing demand and refusal and notice to defendant indorser, and also testified that he gave notice to defendant by letter duly stamped, addressed, and mailed, it was not error to exclude defendant's

§ 106 

evidence that he had not received the notice. First Nat. Bank v. Mailing notice 

Delone, 254 Pa. 409, 98 Atl. 1042.

A statement by the clerk in charge that it was the custom of the collecting bank to give written notice without production of copy of the notice, is not sufficient evidence to support a finding that notice had been given. McMillan v. Montgomery, 121 

Oreg. 28, 253 Pac. 879.

A plaintiff suing on an indorsement of a dishonored negotiable note has the burden of proving notice of dishonor. Where the notary, who testified that within due time he mailed notice of non-payment of a note, was cashier of the plaintiff bank, and therefore an interested witness, and the indorser denied receiving notice, and the president of the maker testified that, three days after maturity, he saw the note and that the alleged indorsement of protest was not written on the note, the question whether notice of dishonor was given was for the jury. First Nat. Bank v. Star Watch Case Co., 187 Mich. 224, 153 N. W. 722.

Proof of execution of notices of dishonor, of inclosing them in stamped envelopes and placing them with other mail matter carried to the post office by a clerk, whose business this was, is enough without calling the clerk, to justify a finding that the notices were duly mailed, in an action against the indorser. 

Central Nat. Bank v. Stoddard, 83 Conn. 332, 76 Atl. 472; Wolf v. Union Trust Co., 150 Md. 385, 133 Atl. 121.

When the person charged with the duty of giving notice to indorsers testified that he signed the notices and gave them to his mailing clerk to mail, and the clerk testified that it was his invariable practice to collect and deposit all such letters in the mail, a finding that the notices were mailed will not be set aside. 

Prudential Trust Co. v. Hayes, 247 Mass. 311, 142 N. E. 73;

Commercial Trust Co. v. New England Macaroni Mfg. Co., 247 

Mass. 366, 141 N. E. 285.

Notice of protest was addressed to "S. H. (the indorser), 24 

E. Market St., Wilkesbarre, Pa." It was found by the referee that defendant's place of business was at "Nos. 22 and 23 E. 

Market St., Wilkesbarre, Pa.," that there was another S. H. residing and doing business in Wilkesbarre to whom defendant's letters were often delivered by mistake and that defendant never received notice of the protest. Held, these facts were insufficient to warrant a conclusion of law that due notice had been given to the indorser. Siegel v. Hirsch, 26 Pa. Super. Ct. 398. 

Sec. 106. Deposit in Post Office-What Constitutes. 

Notice is deemed to have been deposited in the post office when deposited in any branch post office or in any letter box under the control of the post office department.' 

Cross Reference: 88 95, 96, 70, 89 to 94, 96 to 105, 107 to 118.

926 Mailing notice 

ANNOTATIONS 

Deposit in a mail box is equivalent to deposit in the post office. Prudential Trust Co. v. Coghlin, 249 Mass. 184, 144 N. E. 283. 

Deposit of a note of protest in a mail chute under the control of the post office is sufficient. Wilson v. Peck, 66 Misc. Rep. 179, 121 N. Y. Supp. 344.

In an action by a holder in due course against an indorser, it was held that under Massachusetts G. L., c. 107, section 13, providing that a notarial seal on a protest shall be prima facie evidence of the facts therein, and of the giving of notice to the drawer and indorsers, a prima facie case was made against the indorsers by such protest, even though the notary did not himself place the notices in the mails, but left them with his stenographer to do so. Holmes v. Cabot, 262 Mass. 152, 159 N. E. 615.

A notice of protest properly addressed and left in the place in the notary's office where mail was usually collected by the postman was not a mailing of the notice as required by the statute. Friedman v. Maltinsky, 260 Pa. 312, 103 Atl. 731. Contra Wolf v. Union Trust Co., 150 Md. 385, 133 Atl. 121; see also Myers v. Moore-Kile Co., 279 Fed. 233; Federal Asbestos 

Co. v. Zimmermann, 171 Wis. 594, 177 N. W. 881, see valuable note 25 A. L. R. 9.

Sec. 107. Notice to Subsequent Party-Time of. 

Where a party receives notice of dishonor, he has, after the receipt of such notice, the same time for giving notice to antecedent parties that the holder has after the dishonor. 

Cross Reference: §§ 95, 96, 103, 104, 56, 70, 89 to 94, 97 to 102, 108 to 118.

ANNOTATIONS 

When the answer alleges that the indorser had no notice of dishonor, the burden is on the holder to show that due notice was given. It is not shown by testimony of a notary that, not know. ing the address of the indorser, he inclosed the notice of dishonor to a subsequent indorser with postage for forwarding the notice. to the prior indorser. Fuller Buggy Co. v. Waldron, 112 App. 

Div. 814, 99 N. Y. Supp. 920. The  was not cited in this case.

A bank holding an indorsed note for collection may give notice of its dishonor to all parties liable thereon or only to its principal, from whom it received the note, leaving the latter to notify in turn its principal or antecedent indorser and so on down the line. Gleason v. Thayer, 87 Conn. 248, 87 Atl. 790, Ann. Cas. 1915B, 1069. 

1 The English Act interpolates "due." B. E. A. s. 49 (14).

§ 108 

The plaintiff, after receiving notice of dishonor, delayed six days to notify the defendant indorser, during which he was attempting to ascertain why the defendant's indorsement had been crossed out by a line in ink drawn through it. Held, the defendant was discharged, the delay not being excused. Emerson & Buckingham Bank & T. Co. v. German Am. T. Co., 65 

Colo. 398, 176 Pac. 472.

A joint indorser who has received notice of dishonor and would be entitled to contribution, may give notice to his coindorsers under this section. Antecedent parties means antecedent in liability and each joint indorser is an antecedent party as to his part of the debt. Williams v. Paintsville Nat. Bank, 143 Ky. 781, 137 S. W. 535, Ann. Cas. 1912D, 350. See the comment on this case under sec. 68.

But a joint indorser who paid the holder and received an indorsement without recourse can not recover either on the note or in an independent action for contribution against his coindorser who was not notified either by the original holder or by the indorser who paid, especially when he was under no legal obligation to pay the original holder. The plaintiff can not, by waiving the want of notice to him, pay and render his co-indorser liable to contribute. Case v. McKinnis, 107 Oreg. 

223, 213 Pac. 422, 32 A. L. R. 167. Contra, Owens v. Greenlee, 68 Colo. 114, 188 Pac. 721, 9 A. L. R. 1184, with note, stated under sec. 68, which has a special form in Colorado. 

Sec. 108. Where Notice Must be Sent. 

Where a party has added an address to his signature, notice of dishonor must be sent to that address; but if he has not given such address, then the notice must be sent as follows:¹ (1) Either to the post office nearest to his place of residence, or to the post office where he is accustomed to receive his letters;¹ or (2) If he live in one place, and have his place of business in another, notice may be sent to either place;¹ or (3) If he is sojourning in another place, notice may⚫ be sent to the place where he is so sojourning.¹ 

But where the notice is actually received by the party within the time specified in this act, it will be sufficient, though not sent in accordance with the requirements of this section.¹

ANNOTATIONS 

This section possibly changes the Massachusetts law laid down in Wamesit Bank v. Buttriek, 11 Gray 387, which held that when notices of dishonor, addressed to all the indorsers respectively and enclosed in a letter to the last indorser, never reached him, the prior indorsers were not discharged. Contra at common law, that they were discharged: Aldine Co. v. Warner, 96 Ga. 370; 

Stix v. Mathews, 63 Mo. 371, 375. AMES thought that the N. I.

L. did not deal with this point (see the last page of his first article). In view of this uncertainty it seems unwise to send all the notices to the last indorser; to be safe they should be separately mailed to the respective indorsers. 

A notary's certificate of notice of protest, being by statute prima facie evidence of the facts therein stated, and in the absence of contradictory proof, conclusive, it is not necessary to show, in addition, that the notice was sent to a proper place, even though there was evidence that it was mailed to a certain post office station. This will be presumed to be the right place in the absence of contradictory evidence. Scott v. Brown, 240 

Pa. 328, 87 Atl. 431.

The indorser lived at the place where the note was dated, but moved from said place at some time not stated. Held, that notice of dishonor mailed to said place was sufficient, the court assuming that there had been no change of residence up to that time. 

Mohlman v. McKane, 60 App. Div. 546, 69 N.Y. Supp. 1046.

Notice addressed to an indorser at a place which at the time of the execution of the note was stated by him to be his residence, is sufficient. Archuleta v. Johnston, 53 Colo. 393, 127 Pac. 134. 

Defendant indorsed a note, made payable in New York City, without adding an address. Upon dishonor the notary spent three-quarters of an hour in inquiring of the maker and of several other persons likely to know defendant's address, but without success, and then mailed the notice to an address given in the last issue of a standard city directory, but the defendant having moved to another street and number never received the notice. Held, as a matter of law sufficient diligence on the part of the notary and that defendant was not discharged. McGrath v. Francolini, 92 Misc. Rep. 359, 156 N. Y. Supp. 981.

The maker of a note, who added an address to his signature, also indorsed the note after the indorsement of defendant, and in the presence of defendant added a different address to his signature as indorser. Held, from these facts and other circumstantial evidence, that the jury were warranted in finding that the purpose of the maker in adding an address when he indorsed the note, was to designate the place to which notice to defendant should be sent, and that defendant ratified the act and adopted the address as his own. Lankonfsky v. Raymon, 217 Mass. 98, 104 N. E. 489.

Where a notary sent notice of dishonor and nonpayment to the address given him by officers of the bank at which the note was payable, and the notices were never returned by the post office, and the indorser testified that possibly he may have received notice, but he cannot remember, it was held that a motion by the defendant indorser for a directed verdict or nonsuit was properly overruled. Liberty Title & Trust Co. v. Sweeten 

(N. J.), 150 Atl. 422.

The burden of proof of notice is on the holder; and proof that notice was mailed to the defendant at 2277 West Twenty- Third St., Los Angeles, when his business address was 727

Assn. v. Century Land & Water Co., (Cal. App.), 65 P. (2d) 110.

Notice of protest addressed merely, "Clarence Hartman, New York City, New York," is not sufficient where there is no evidence that the indorser lived or ever had lived, or was sojourning in New York, or that any inquiry was made to ascertain the fact. 

Fonseca v. Hartman, 84 N. Y. Supp. 131.

The indorser of a promissory note, not having added an address after his indorsement, notice of dishonor addressed to him, "New York City," was sufficient under sec. 108(1), although his street address could have been found by consulting the telephone directory. McGrath v. Francolini, 156 N. Y. Supp. 980. In this case is a dictum contra to McGrath v. Francolini, 92 Misc. Rep. 

359, 156 N. Y. Supp. 981, supra, "if the holder goes further and attempts to add a particular address, he takes the risk that the address so chosen may be wrong, in which event the statute gives him no protection." But the court cited only cases on instruments made prior to the enactment of the Negotiable Instruments Law.

The indorser's office was in Brooklyn, in the building occupied by the Fulton Savings Bank, notice addressed to the "Fulton Building, Brooklyn," was not received although the indorser had his office there for eighteen years. It was held that the notice was improperly addressed. The court took the position that if the notice had been addressed to the post office

Such a result seems impractical in the absence of proof of negli gent addressing.

Pleading 

Plaintiff, the payee of a dishonored note, knew that the defendant indorser lived in New York City, but claimed that he did not know his address. Defendant testified that plaintiff had frequently corresponded with defendant at his New York address. The notice of dishonor was mailed to defendant in the care of the maker, but not delivered to defendant. Held, that this was not sufficient notice, and that defendant was discharged. 

E. I. Dupont, etc., Powder Co. v. Rooney, 63 Misc. Rep. 344, 117 

N. Y. Supp. 220.

Notice to an indorser, who has added no address to his signature, mailed to the post office of his place of residence, is good, but not if addressed to a house where the indorser does not reside or do business or receive his letters, even though he owned the house and his sons did business there. Ebling Brewing Co. v. 

Reinheimer, 32 N. Y. Misc. Rep. 594, 66 N. Y. Supp. 458.

Where a notary inquired of several persons as to the post office address of an indorser, all of whom seemed to have some information and stated their belief that a certain town was the nearest town to the farm where the indorser lived, and a much larger place than the town where the indorser actually received his mail, a notice of dishonor sent to such nearest town was sufficient, although the indorser did not receive it within a reasonable time. 

Vogel v. Starr, 132 Mo. App. 430, 112 S. W. 27. The  was not cited in this case.

Sec. 109. Waiver of Notice. 

Notice of dishonor may be waived, either before the time of giving notice has arrived, or after the omission to give due notice, and the waiver may be express or implied. 

Cross Reference: 88 95, 96, 102 to 104, 110, 111, 5(3), 56, 61, 66, 70, 82(3), 89 to 94, 97 to 101, 112 to 118, 159.

ANNOTATIONS 

An averment of demand and notice in the indorsee's pleadings is proved by evidence of facts showing a waiver thereof. 

 Bromberg v. Self, 16 Ala. App. 

627, 880 So. 631; Sandler v. Scullen, 290 Mass. 106, 194 N. E. 

827; Bobin Zill Sash & Door Co. v. Lyons, 37 Ohio App. 139, 174 N. E. 156. Contra, Hallowell & Brownlee v. Benitz, 38

Civ. App.), 103 S. W. (2d) 246.

Where notes waived notice of non-payment, a complaint with the notes attached and reciting that they were part thereof was held sufficient to state a cause of action without alleging notice of dishonor or waiver thereof. G. & H. Inv. Co. v. Raymond, 113 Conn. 386, 155 Atl. 497. 

The "makers * * * and indorsers waive presentment for payment, protest and notice" appearing on the face of the note sued on, was held sufficient proof of waiver of notice of dishonor, in the absence of other pleadings and proof. Sibley v. 

Continental Supply Co. (Tex. Civ. App.), 290 S. W. 769, writ of error denied, 116 Tex. 402, 292 S. W. 155.

The facts constituting waiver must be alleged and proved. 

Galbraith v. Shepard, 43 Wash. 698, 86 Pac. 1113; Congress

Pofcher v. Fisher (Mass.), 172 N. E. 94. waiver

But a waiver of "notice of presentment, dishonor, and protest," is not a waiver of presentment. Hayward v. Empire

Waiver after maturity 

A collateral undertaking worded as follows, "I have deposited with you as collateral security for the payment of any note or notes discounted by you made by myself or/and bearing my indorsement (Notice of presentation, demand and protest being hereby waived) the following property:", was held to waive notice and protest on another note not part of that transaction. 

Passaic Nat. Bank & Trust Co. v. Simon, 108 N. J. Eq. 268, 154 

Atl. 827.

A waiver of notice of dishonor before maturity does not require consideration. Quaere as to a waiver after maturity. 

Deere & Weber Co. v. Britzius, 46 S. D. 597, 194 N. W. 834.

An indorser who, after the time for giving notice of dishonor, declares his intention to pay the note, waives notice of dishonor, whether he had knowledge of his discharge by failure to give notice or not, and no consideration is necessary to support a waiver. James v. Ward, 80 Colo. 293, 250 Pac. 1097; County 

Sav. Bank v. Jacobson, 202 Ia. 1263, 211 N. W. 864; Hansen v. Bowers (Ia.), 223 N. W. 891; Doherty v. First Nat. Bank, 170 Ky. 810, 186 S. W. 937; Johnson v. Anderson, 172 Minn.

But see, Aebi v. Bank of Evansville, 124 Wis. 73, 81, 102 N.

The same view is taken in Hurlburt v. Bradley, 94 Conn. 

495, 109, Atl. 171; the new promise must be made with intent to relinquish a known right. It is enough, however, if the indorser knows of the want of notice, though he is ignorant of the want of presentment. See the note on this case in 29 Yale L.

The president of a corporation wrote a letter on corporate stationery signed as president saying "your note will be taken care of." Held, it was not a waiver to bind him individually. 

Rees Taylor Co. v. Kullman, 9 N. J. Misc. 857, 155 Atl. 893, 30

§ 109 

A promise to substitute other notes for the ones in suit is a waiver where it was made with knowledge of default and lack of notice. Vigen v. Castle Building Co. (Cal. App.), 65 P. (2d) 1340.

Waiver is the intentional abandonment of a known right, not a trick to catch the indorser napping. The burden is on the holder to prove waiver. Sec. 109 was not cited. McKee v. McGhee, 114 S. C. 183, 103 S. E. 508.

Where an indorser, knowing he was discharged from liability for want of proper notice of dishonor, promised that if the maker does not pay the note, he will, he waives his discharge. The 

 was not cited. Richardson v. Kulp, 81 N. J. L. 123, 78 Atl. 1062; Fashion Hat Frame Co. v. Ringel, 81 Cal. App. 

556, 254 Pac. 275.

When a note was dishonored and no notice was given to the indorsers, but the indorsers procured the holder to consent to an extension of the time of payment and to accept a renewal note, the indorsers waived notice on the original note. Burton v. McCaskill, 79 Fla. 173, 83 So. 919.

A letter from the indorser to the holder after dishonor, admitting liability, is a waiver of lack of notice. First Nat. Bank v. Tamaqua Mfg. Co., 71 Pa. Super. Ct. 39.

After dishonor of notes, an indorser who had not been notified admitted liability and authorized a plan of settlement. 

Held, he waived notice of dishonor. First Nat. Bank v. Anderson, 125 Va. 102, 99 S. E. 561.

A finding of waiver is sustained when the indorser, on default by the maker, took a renewal note from the maker, indorsed it, and then upon the holder's rejection of the note did not deny liability as an indorser but requested the holder to let the matter rest awhile. Goffe & Carkener v. Gurley (Kan.), 72 

P. (2d) 964.

Where the indorser, receiving no notice of dishonor, after maturity continually made statements to the holder that he was endeavoring to have the matter cleared up, and by his conduct induced the holder to stand by and defer action, it was held that the indorser is estopped to urge want of notice of dishonor. 

Kuhl v. Schlichtemeier (C. C. A.), 14 F. (2d) 593.

Where the drawer of a dishonored draft, without receiving notice of dishonor, authorizes the sale of chattels, "for my account," given as security for the money advanced by the payee on the draft, it amounts to an implied waiver of notice of dishonor. Biggers v. Bank of Ringgold, 38 La. App. 521, 144 S. 

E. 397.

While presentment and notice are not waived by conversations of the drawer which do not involve a clear admission of liability or a distinct promise to pay, but are consistent with the view that the defendant is merely seeking to avoid or postpone a suit against himself, an offer by the drawer of a bill of Waiver after maturity

934 maturity Waiver after exchange payable in Russia and dishonored to refund the value of rubles in our money at current exchange or to deliver rubles constituted a waiver of protest and notice. Carmen v. Higginson, 245 Mass. 511, 140 N. E. 246.

Want of proper notice of dishonor to the drawer corporation was waived by a resolution of the corporation to make demand upon a bank which had guaranteed payment of the draft. The resolution necessarily recognized the liability of the drawer since the guarantor would not be liable otherwise. Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. v. Lazard-Godchaux Co., 207 App. 

Div. 174, 201 N. Y. Supp. 771. The court also held that proper notice was given. If not, it seems questionable whether the drawer by its own waiver could affix a liability upon the guarantor which would not otherwise exist. 

Checks payable to the defendant corporation were indorsed by its agent and discounted by the plaintiff bank. After dis honor and notice to the agent, he requested the plaintiff to return the checks for collection to the various drawee banks and promised that he would see they were paid. Held, a waiver of notice of subsequent dishonor, binding upon the principal corporation. The court considered that the discount was for the accommodation of the corporation and that sec. 115-3 would also apply. Armour & Co. v. Guaranty State Bank (Tex. Civ. 

App.), 253 S. W. 1110, discussed under sec. 115(3), where the application of that section is questioned. 

While a waiver of an indorser's right under Vt. G. L. [1917] sec. 2864, to presentment of an overdue note within sixty days after his indorsement, will not be inferred from doubtful acts or language, the indorser's request that the indorsee should not press the maker for payment during six months constitutes a waiver of demand and notice. Foundry Mfg. Co. v. Farr, 96 

Vt. 382, 119 Atl. 885. On a later appeal, the court decided that the waiver dispensed with demand and notice altogether and did not merely postpone the time. (Vt.), 126 Atl. 548, noted in 9 Minn. L. Rev. 279.

Defendants were corporate directors who had indorsed the corporation's note as individuals and to whom on default at maturity no notice of dishonor was given. Thereafter they signed an agreement in "their respective rights" and "official capacity" as directors to an instrument assigning corporate rental to the payee, their signatures as directors being unneces sary to make the assignment effective. Held, that they had thereby waived the failure to give notice. Kramer v. Stryker, 274 Mich. 179, 264 N. W. 618.

Plaintiff, an indorser of a check deposited by him with defendant bank, was not given due notice of its dishonor. With knowledge thereof, plaintiff gave his own check for the dishonored check and sued defendant for its failure to give him due notice of such dishonor. Held, that plaintiff had waived

§ 109 

the bank's laches and could not recover. Weil v. Corn Exchange Waiver after 

Bank, 63 Misc. Rep. 300, 116 N. Y. Supp. 665. Quaere, whether maturity sec. 109 has any application to the case. See dissenting opinion of Lehman, J.

Mere advice, after dishonor, to the holder by an agent of the indorser, telling how to collect, does not constitute a waiver of notice. McMillan v. Montgomery, 121 Oreg. 28, 253 Pac. 879.

Negotiation about payment is not sufficient to constitute a waiver. First National Bank of Morristown v. Turner (N. J. 

Sup.), 157 Atl. 665, 30 Mich. L. Rev. 967.

A mere oral promise to renew a note, made after its maturity by an accommodation indorser, is not a waiver of the failure to give notice of dishonor; such promise is not an acknowledgment of liability. Mechanics and Farmers Savings Bank v. Katter john, 137 Ky. 427, 125 S. W. 1071, Ann. Cas. 1912A, 439.

But a promise to pay if given time is a waiver. Weinbergen v. McConnell, 192 Wis. 539, 213 N. W. 313.

Where the instrument in question was transferred without indorsement it was held that indorsement after maturity with knowledge of dishonor amounted to waiver of notice. Bobin Zill 

Sash & Door Co. v. Lyons, 37 Ohio App. 139, 174 N. E. 156; 

Benoit v. Damour, 53 R. I. 317, 166 Atl. 550.

Waiver is a question of fact for the jury. Boggs v. Farmers' Proof of 

Fund of Texas (Tex. Civ. App.), 37 S. W. (2d) 205. 

waiver The burden of proof is on the holder to show that notice was waived. In re Tharp, 113 Misc. Rep. 199, 184 N. Y. Supp. 

232. See other cases under sec. 89.

Waiver of notice after maturity must be proved by clear and unequivocal evidence.  Keiser v. 

Butte Creek, etc., Co., 48 Cal. App. 38, 191 Pac. 552. "I am endeavoring to arrange funds for the (maker) to pay their note" held not a waiver. West Virginia Coal Co. v. Gaine, 112 Pa. Super. Ct. 158, 170 Atl. 416.

A waiver of notice of dishonor may be implied by any conduct or words of the indorser whereby the holder is reasonably induced to believe that such waiver is intended and this is a question for the jury. Linthicum v. Bagby, 131 Md. 644, 102 Atl. 

997; Simonoff v. Granite City Nat. Bank, 279 Ill. 248, 116 N. E. 636. 

But waiver of notice will not be inferred from doubtful acts or language of the indorser. Worley v. Johnson, 60 Fla. 294, 53 So. 542, 33 L. R. A. (N.S.) 639; Cochran v. Howard, 11 La. 

App. 219, 123 So. 428.

An agreement between the indorsers and the holder that a demand note was not to be collected until the maker corporation became solvent was held no waiver of notice. Lane Cotton Mills 

Co. v. Kohler, 186 La. 469, 172 So. 530.

936 Waiver at or before A custom in the course of dealing between the parties, that maturity the defendant indorser paid instruments without notice of dishonor, is sufficient to constitute a waiver. Citizens Nat. Bank v. Jennings (Ga. App.), 127 S. E. 656; id. 33 Ga. App. 659, 

The indorser at the time of negotiation promised the indorsee to look after the note and that the money would be in his hands, and on the day of maturity again promised to look after the note. 

Held, that the indorser had waived presentment and notice of dishonor. Dillon v. Brion, 96 Kan. 189, 150 Pac. 553.

Notice of dishonor to an indorser was waived by an agree ment between him, the maker, and the holder by which all parties understood that the instruments were not to be paid at maturity. Whitney v. Chadsey, 216 Mich. 604, 185 N. W. 826.

Some time before the note was due the holder wrote the indorser that the note was falling due and that the holder wanted and expected prompt payment. On the date the note fell due the indorser went to the holder's office, asked for the holder and remarked that he was on his way to get money to pay the note. The note was not paid and no notice of nonpayment, etc., given the indorser. It was held that the indorser was discharged. No notice was given and his acts did not amount to a waiver. Mellen-Wright Lumber Co. v. McNett, 242 Mich. 369, 218 N. W. 709.

If the indorser of a note, knowing that the maker would not pay it at maturity, agreed before maturity that he would pay the note or othewise take care of it if the payee would wait until after the time for presentment and notice of dishonor would necessarily be passed, he must be held to have waived presentment and notice. Orthwein v. Nolker, 290 Mo. 284, 234

S. W. 787. 

The facts that the indorser knows that the money deposited in the bank by a person, primarily liable on the instrument, for the purpose of paying the instrument was diverted to another purpose, and such action was acquiesced in by the indorser were held not to constitute a waiver of lack of notice. 

Rauchmen's State Bank v. Cooper, 123 Kan. 21, 254 Pac. 364.

The mere fact that both the holder and the indorser know that the maker is insolvent and that the holder must look to the indorser does not constitute a waiver of presentment and notice. 

Lucas v. Swan, 67 F. (2d) 106 (C. C. A. 4th). 

A letter from the indorser at the time of indorsement, agreeing to collect the note, is evidence of waiver. The burden of proving waiver is on the holder.  

Washington Horse Exch. Co. v. Bonner, 180 N. C. 20, 103 S. E. 907.

Before maturity of a note the indorser was notified that the note was due and unpaid and that he would be held liable. Where evidence showed that defendant had helped strip the corporation of its assets, implied waiver was held a question for the jury. Rinehart v. Lucas (W. Va.), 190 S. E. 772. 

A letter from the indorser to the holder stating that the maker had died and requesting the holder to keep the security pledged for payment intact was held not to be a waiver of notice of dishonor although coupled with the fact that the maker's insolvency was known to the indorser. ENGLAND 

A bill was drawn by the A Company to its own order on the B Company and accepted and indorsed to the C Company. All three companies knew that the bill would be dishonored. No notice of dishonor was given to the drawer, because the secretary of the C Company, who was also secretary of the other two companies, knew it never was intended to make the drawer liable. Held, that it was not the duty of the secretary of the 

C Company to communicate his knowledge of the dishonor to the drawer, that his knowledge was therefore not notice to the drawer, and that the latter was discharged. In re Fenwick [1902], 1 Ch. 507. 

Sec. 110. Who Affected by Waiver.

Where the waiver is embodied in the instrument itself, it is binding upon all parties; but where it is written above the signature of an indorser, it binds him only.¹

A printed waiver on the back above the indorsements is emof the bodied in the instrument and binds all indorsers appearing below it. Costello Bros. v. Buckley (R. I.), 148 Atl. 414; Central

The majority considered that in order to give some meaning to the second clause, the first clause must be limited to waivers on the face of the instrument. They considered that the division provided for by the two clauses of sec. 110 is one of time rather than of place. Sec. 111. Waiver of Protest. 

A waiver of protest, whether in the case of a foreign bill of exchange or other negotiable instrument, is deemed to be a waiver not only of a formal protest but also of presentment and notice of dishonor.¹ 

Cross Reference: 881 to 10, 72, 95, 96, 109, 126, 129, 153, 184, 185, 191, 5(3), 61, 66, 70, 82(3), 89 to 110, 112 to 118, 159.

A waiver of protest written on the face of a negotiable promissory note before it was indorsed, is deemed to be a waiver on the part of an indorser, not only of a formal protest, but also of presentment and notice of dishonor. Frank-Taylor-Kendrick 

Co. v. Voissement, 142 La. 973, 77 So. 895.

A waiver of "notice of protest" on the face of a note was held not to include a waiver of presentment. Sed quaere. 

Harris v. Schafler, 149 Misc. 1, 266 N., Y. Supp. 701.

A waiver of "presentment for payment and protest" is sufficient to waive presentment and notice of dishonor. Brooks v. 

American Nat. Bank of Beaumont (Tex. Civ. App.), 103 S. W. (2d) 246.

An allegation in the declaration that the defendant "waived demand, protest and notice of demand, nonpayment and protest," is not an allegation of a conclusion of law. Williams v. 

Peninsular Grocery Co., 73 Fla. 937, 75 So. 517.

A declaration that alleges protest of an acceptance but which does not specifically allege that notice of dishonor and nonpayment thereof was given the indorser, is sufficient, as "protest" means all the steps accompanying dishonor necessary to charge an indorser. Maury v. Winlock & Toledo Logging & R. Co., 148 

Wash. 572, 269 Pac. 815. 

Sec. 112. When Notice is Dispensed With. 

Notice of dishonor is dispensed with when, after the exercise of reasonable diligence, it can not be given to or does not reach the parties sought to be charged. 

Cross Reference: 88 61, 66, 95, 96, 70, 82(1), 89 to 111, 113 to 

118, 148(2), 159, 193.

The differences in phraseology in secs. 82(1), 112 and 148(2), are discussed by Professor K. N. Llewellyn, "Supervening Im-

Reasonable diligence depends upon the circumstances of the case, and is a question for the jury. Brewster v. Shrader, 26

But when the facts are undisputed, reasonable diligence is a question of law. Plaintiff, an indorser who has been notified of the dishonor of the note and, being ignorant of the address of defendant, a prior indorser, sent a notice addressed to him in care of the maker with whom plaintiff understood defendant sometimes stayed, but the notice never reached the defendant. 

Held, that there was not due diligence to ascertain defendant's residence. A junior indorser should inquire of the other parties for information, Two judges dissented.  University Press v. Williams, 48 App. Div. 188, 62 N. Y. 

Supp. 986.

The notary testified that he mailed notice of dishonor, the contents of which were not of record, to the indorser, at a certain address in the city, that he did not know whether he looked for the indorser's address in a city or telephone directory. The indorser testified that he never lived, did business or received mail at this address. Held, not the exercise of such reasonable diligence as to dispense with notice of dishonor. Mechanic v. 

Elgie Iron Works, 98 Misc. Rep. 620, 163 N. Y. Supp. 97. 

Notice of dishonor addressed to a town where the indorser had never lived, and which was not received, is ineffective to charge the indorser. Ib., Passaic Nat. Bank & Trust Co. v. 

Knapp (N. J. Sup.), 158 Atl. 393.

Where the notary examined the telephone directory and the city directory for the address of the defendant and, failing to find it, mailed the notice to a co-indorser whose address he knew, but failed to inquire of the co-indorser, it was held that reasonable diligence had not been exercised. Bost v. Rexine Co., 56 

App. D. C. 34, 8 F. (2d) 795, 55 A. L. R. 670.

Where the indorsers denied due diligence, because notices were not received for a month, the plaintiff replied that notice. was given in due course. The notary was allowed to testify that he inquired of the payee and mailed the notices to the address given, then later he learned of the indorsers' address and mailed a second set of notices. It was held that such evidence was properly admitted and showed due diligence. First Nat. Bank of 

Belmar v. Gray, 101 N. J. Law 179, 127 Atl. 201. The  

was not cited. 

Where the maker of the note was a brother of the holder, and the only inquiry the latter made to discover the residence of an indorser was at the place where the indorser had formerly worked, this was not sufficient diligence to dispense with notice. 

Plaintiff should, at least, have applied to the other parties to the

§  

946 note for information. Silver v. Loucheim, 84 Misc. Rep. 234, 147 

N. Y. Supp. 29.

When a time note was indorsed by the defendant to the plaintiff after maturity, even if presentment to the maker was excused because it was impossible to find him, notice of dishonor given to the defendant 60 days after the indorsement was not sufficient to charge him in the absence of evidence of the facts excusing want of notice. Carter v. Jennings, 134 Miss. 263, 98 

So. 687.

Sec. 113. Delay in Giving Notice-How Excused. 

Delay in giving notice of dishonor is excused when the delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder,' and not imputable to his default, misconduct, or negligence. When the cause of delay ceases to operate, notice must be given with reasonable diligence. 

Cross Reference: 88 95, 96, 191, 196. 61, 66, 70, 81, 89 to 112. 114 to 118, 148, 159, 193, 194.

ENGLAND 

Delay in giving notice of dishonor caused by the necessity of making inquiries as to the address of the party to be notified is excusable, the holder being ignorant of the address. The Elmville [1904], p. 319. 

Failure, after the exercise of reasonable diligence, to find the drawer of a dishonored bill at the address given by him, does not dispense with notice if an address at which he is to be found comes to the holder's knowledge before action brought. Studdy v. Beesty, 60 L. T. Rep. 647.

Sec. 114. When Notice Need Not Be Given to 

Drawer.

Notice of dishonor is not required to be given to the drawer in either of the following cases:- (1) Where the drawer and drawee are the same person; (2) Where the drawee is a fictitious person or a person not having capacity to contract; (3) When the drawer is the person to whom the instrument is presented for payment; (4) Where the drawer has no right to expect or require that the drawee or acceptor will honor the instrument;2 

1 B. E. A. s. 50 (1) uses "party giving notice" instead of "holder." 

2 "Where the drawee or acceptor is, as between himself and the drawer, under no obligation to accept or pay the bill." B. E. A. s. 50 (2) (c) (4).

§ 114 

(5) Where the drawer has countermanded payment.

The plaintiff purchased from the defendant bank a draft drawn by it on a bank in Lomza, Poland. The defendant had no funds in the Lomza bank, but maintained a deposit in a bank in Warsaw, of which the Lomza bank was a correspondent. 

The defendant notified the Lomza bank that the draft had been drawn and asked it to charge the amount against the Warsaw bank. The defendant had followed this procedure in previous drafts on the Lomza bank, and it was the regular practice of New York banks with relation to drafts on smaller foreign towns. The draft was dishonored and no notice given to the defendant bank. Held, the defendant was discharged, being entitled to notice of dishonor. One judge dissented. Mazukiewicz v. Hanover Nat. Bank, 240 N. Y. 317, 148 N. E. 535, revg. 209 App. Div. 674, 205 N. Y. Supp. 278, and 122 Misc. 

Rep. 290, 203 N. Y. Supp. 526; certiorari denied, 270 U. S. 643.

The court points out that the method pursued was the only practical course, since New York banks could not keep accounts with banks in each of the smaller foreign towns. It was sufficient if the defendant had a right to expect that the draft would be paid when presented, although it had no funds in the drawee bank. The court evidently construed "right" as equivalent to "reason" in sec. 80, and not in a strictly legal sense as denoting the credit side of a chose in action. On the embarrassing effect to international banking of a contrary decision, see the note in

The court suggests that the defendant's knowledge prevented the draft from being negotiable, since the essence of a negotiable instrument is that it evidences a bona fide transaction. This reasoning is open to serious question, since negotiability depends on the face of the instrument, and furthermore, if the draft was not negotiable, the provisions of the  could have had no application.

Sec. 115. When Notice Need Not be Given to In dorser.

Notice of dishonor is not required to be given to an indorser in either of the following cases:- (1) Where the drawee is a fictitious person or a person not having capacity to contract, and the indorser was aware of the fact at the time he indorsed the instrument; (2) Where the indorser is the person to whom the instrument is presented for payment; (3) Where the instrument was made or accepted for his accommodation.

A note made by a corporation and indorsed by the defendants was delivered to the payee in renewal of a similar note. The corporation was insolvent both at the issue and the maturity of the renewal note. Held, the indorsers were not discharged for want of notice of dishonor. Fosdick v. Govt. M. S. Hotel Co., 115 Wash. 127, 196 Pac. 652.

It is clear that the indorsers were accommodation parties and that the note was not made for their accommodation. The court, however, took the extraordinary view that the note was "accepted" for their accommodation by the payee; the word clearly does not refer to the receiving by a holder but to the acceptance of a bill of exchange by the drawee. The decision might better have been rested on the ground that notice of dishonor was waived under the circumstances of the renewal, so that the case fell under sec. 109. See Lucas v. Swan, 67 F. (2d) 

106 (C. C. A. 4th), approving this comment.

The Washington court distinguished the preceding case in 

Black v. Emporium D. G. Co., 129 Wash. 100, 224 Pac. 591, and held the indorser discharged for want of notice on the ground that here the maker did not become insolvent until after issue of the note. If the indorser was actually accommodated in this

§ 116 

indorser case and not an accommodation party, he was not entitled to Accommodated notice regardless of the maker's solvency. The court, however, read into this section on notice of dishonor the last clause of sec. 80 on presentment: "and he has not reason to expect that the instrument will be paid if presented," and considered the time that the insolvency began material in judging whether there was such "reason." In view of the different phraseology of the two sections, this construction is very questionable. It seems probable that in this case as in the preceding, the indorser was an accommodation party, and hence entitled to notice at all events, unless waived.

When a bank taking checks for collection from the payee pays to it the face value minus the usual commissions, the transaction can be considered for the accommodation of the indorser-payee and notice to it is unnecessary under sec. 115-3.

The indorsement by the defendant company of its debtor's note, the proceeds being used for payment of debt, was held not for accommodation of the indorser, within  sec. 115, therefore directed verdict for the plaintiff was an error. Commercial Nat. Bank v. Ashley Corp., 133 S. C. 304, 130 S. E. 890.

Where due notice of dishonor by nonacceptance has been given, notice of a subsequent dishonor by nonpayment is not necessary, unless in the meantime the instrument has been accepted.

Sec. 118. When Protest Need Not be Made-When 

Must be Made.

Where any negotiable instrument has been dishonored it may be protested for nonacceptance or nonpayment, as the case may be; but protest is not required except in the case of foreign bills of exchange. 

Cross Reference: 881 to 10, 83, 126, 129, 149, 153, 184, 185, 191, 61, 66, 70, 89, 152 to 160, 167, 170, 172, 173.

ANNOTATIONS 

The mere fact of a protest is not conclusive upon the dishonor of the instrument and due notice to the indorser; other evidence is competent on these questions and they must be left to the jury. 

Where no formal protest is necessary, and defendant admitted having received notice of dishonor, and did not ask to have the questions of presentment and payment submitted to the jury, he was not aggrieved by the court allowing the notary to amend his certificate of protest by annexing his seal or by the admission of his certificate in evidence. Demelman v. Brazier, 198 Mass. 458, 84 N. E. 856.

In a foreign attachment proceeding against the indorser of a note, the plaintiff's allegation that the note was duly protested is insufficient. He should have alleged due presentment and notice. Especial strictness is required in attachment proceedings. Deming Nat. Bank v. Baker, 83 W. Va. 429, 98 S. E. 438.

In many states statutes made the certificate of the notary prima facie evidence of the facts of presentment, demand, nonpayment and notice of dishonor. Therefore, while protest is not required in cases of promissory notes and inland bills, it is usual to protest these instruments also, when dishonored, since the notary's certificate of protest is the most convenient and certain mode of proving the facts. Prudential Trust Co. v. Coghlin, 249 Mass. 184, 214 N. E. 283; Eaves v. Keeton, 196 Mo. App. 

424, 193 S. W. 629; Leonard v. Raleigh Co-op. Mercantile Co. (N. D.), 196 N. W. 102; Scott v. Brown, 240 Pa. 328, 87 Atl. 431. 

The presumption created by such a statute is not conclusive, and it is arguable that upon the appearance of proof of nonservice, the statutory presumption entirely disappears. The

§ 119 

 was not cited. Latham v. Sheff, 193 App. Div. 576, 185 

N. Y. Supp. 278.

Although the West Virginia prima facie statutes are superseded by the N. I. L., the same prima facie effect is given to the notary's certificate. This effect is not lost although the notary corrects the certificate by reference to his memoranda made at the time of protest. Thorn v. Aler, 92 W. Va. 290, 114 S. E. 741, 28 A. L. R. 536, with note on "Right of notary who protests paper to change or contradict his certificate."

When a third party furnishes the whole or part of the consideration for the surrender of a secured note, though acting at the instance of the maker, and the note is then indorsed and delivered over by the holder and held by the third party, the presumption is that a purchase and not a payment was intended.

Although stamping an instrument "Paid" or other cancellation is not conclusive evidence of discharge, yet, where a bank intentionally and not influenced by fraud, accepted its depositor's check on his account in payment of the note of a third party, marked the note "Paid" and surrendered it to the depositor, charged the check against the depositor's account and stamped it "Paid," the note was discharged, notwithstanding a check on another bank previously credited to the depositor's account turned out to be uncollectible, so that the depositor's account was insufficient to pay his check given for the note.

AMES: 

Subsec. 4 is a startling innovation and should be cancelled. Under it payment before maturity will discharge the instrument, for such would be the effect as to a simple contract. Yet it has always been the case that if a negotiable instrument is transferred before maturity to a holder in due course the instrument is not discharged by such payment. 

BREWSTER: Subsec. 4 relates to acts between the parties. 

AMES: The subsection declares just the opposite. If a negotiable instrument is "discharged" the maker can never be charged upon it. 

MCKEEHAN: Professor Ames' criticism is justified. Yet it is unbelievable that this subsection will be permitted to upset the rule that declares payment before maturity to be no defense against a holder in due course, although to limit the meaning of the subsection the courts will probably be obliged to take the ground that any other interpretation would be revolutionary, unjust and absurd.

All fail to see that discharge under the act is not a real defense. 

See supra, p. 618, also secs. 57, 117, 121 (original heading), and 122.-Ed. 

Mr. McKeehan's prophecy was fulfilled in Manchester v. 

Parsons, 75 W. Va. 793, 84 S. E. 885, the court holding that although a literal interpretation of sec. 119 (4) might indicate that payment to a prior holder will discharge a negotiable instrument in the hands of a holder in due course, yet such a construction would defeat sec. 57 and other provisions of the Act and was clearly not intended. That the acts referred to in the subsection must be limited to such acts as relate to and affect the holder demanding payment.

Held, that although plaintiff was constructive trustee of the note for the maker, the defendant could not set up as a defense "the independent cause of action" of the maker. The result reached by terming the defense personal seems clearly inequitable, since the wrongdoing plaintiff is thereby enabled to throw the entire loss occasioned by the maker's insolvency on the innocent defendant. § 119 (4) 10 11 So far as concerns the questions involved in secs. 119-120, there is no longer any hope of uniformity. Not only have several states made changes in these sections before adopting the Act,¹ but in Iowa ¹¹ it has been held that under sec. 58 providing that "in the hands of any holder other than a holder in due course, a negotiable instrument is subject to the same defenses as if it were non-negotiable," a maker, known to the payee to be a surety, was discharged by an extension given to the principal maker without the consent of the surety, the court considering the provision of secs. 119 and 120 as applicable only to holders in due course. So also in Missouri.12 And the Court of Appeals of New York, having already declined in National Citizens Bank v. Toplitz, 178 N. Y. 464, 71 N. E. 1, to consider the effect of these sections in an action at law, held, that, even if it be assumed that in an action at law the makers of a note must arbitrarily be treated as primarily liable thereon, it does not prevent the court in an action in equity from determining and enforcing the rights of the parties as the same are found as a matter of fact. Therefore, where the accommodated payee of a promissory note discounted it at the defendant bank, which had knowledge of the facts, and the bank became insolvent before the note fell due, the court held, that, in a suit brought by the payee in equity to compel the receiver to offset his credit balance in the bank against the amount of the note, the receiver must do so, thus relieving to that extent the accommodation makers.13 

There is really no more reason for abrogating the rule, which discharges a surety because a binding extension of time is given to the principal when the creditor is the holder of a negotiable note than in the case of any other form of contract, since in no case does the rule apply unless the creditor knows of the relation when he grants the extension. The negotiability of the instrument and its availability for circulation are therefore in no wise impaired. It is true that the rule has been criticized as being unfair to a creditor who is ignorant of the effect of his act, yet the rule has been almost universally adopted as the more equitable one. But, whatever may be said of the question where the prejudicial act is the giving of time, there can be no excuse for permitting the creditor to release the security given by the principal and yet to hold the surety. But even in this case secs. 119 and 120 have been interpreted as giving this very right to the holder of a negotiable instrument even with knowledge of the suretyship, because such release of security is not specifically mentioned in the Act as a cause of discharge of the instrument.¹ 14

The confusion and ambiguities caused by these sections in attempting to deal with some cases of suretyship and omitting others, have been pointed out by Professor Hening," and also by Professor Greeley.18 The confusion is much increased by the absence of any definition in the Act of the words "principal debtor" which are used both in sec. 119 and sec. 120. These words may mean either a party primarily liable or a party who, as between himself and another party or parties to the instrument, ought to pay it. And it is not always clear in which sense they are used in these sections. Professor Hening argues that secs. 120 and 192 should be totally repealed because, unless all defenses of the surety are codified, none should be, and that all can not be successfully codified owing to the diversity of the suretyship rules under both the decisions and the statutes of the different states. It would seem, however, that it is advisable in an act dealing with negotiable instruments to have some provision dealing with the modes of legal discharge of the instrument and of a party or parties, leaving the instrument otherwise still in force.19 Suretyship defenses- As indicated by the above discussion, the cases dealing with Interpretation the question of suretyship defenses of parties primarily liable of the act on the instrument have been very unsatisfactory and their results far from uniform.

The cases to the contrary which are cited and criticised on p. 968 supra ff. and said by the A. L. R. note infra to be the weight of authority at that time, rely entirely upon sections 29, 192 and an exclusive interpretation of section 119, ignoring 119 (4). The first two sections merely state the liability arising on the instrument and have nothing to do with defenses to, or discharge of, such liability. The argument that suretyship defenses of the principal maker are not included in section 119 (4) ignores the plain words of that section and the clear implication of section 196. It rests upon the fallacious assumption that section 119 is the only section of the act covering the question of discharge of the instrument, see secs. 51, 122, and 124.

It seems equally clear that under section 57 a holder in due course who did not know of the suretyship agreement, either at the time he purchased the instrument or at the time of the alleged discharge, would not be subject to any of the defenses of suretyship. Kuhn v. Groel, 118 Wash. 285, 203 Pac. 44.

Suretyship defenses- So also a payee is not subject to defenses when not party to 

Interpretation suretyship agreement. Continental Mutual Bank v. Elliot, 166 

Wash. 283, 6 Pac. (2d) 638. of the act The case that causes the real difficulty is that in which the holder in due course at the time the instrument was negotiated to him had no knowledge of the suretyship relation but later learned of it before he gave time to the principal debtor or did the other acts alleged as defenses. In such a situation should he be allowed to enforce the instrument according to its terms as he bought it; or should he be subject to the suretyship defenses growing out of facts which were later brought to his attention?

There is much to be said in favor of the cases which hold that in this situation the suretyship defenses should not be available. The original parties by making, drawing and accepting the instrument under sections 60, 61 and 62 undertake to pay it "according to its tenor" and the holder in due course under section 57 "may enforce payment" free from all defects of title and defenses. It seems that his contract rights arise from the face of the instrument and should be enforceable as there appearing. This is especially desirable and necessary for the protection of the holder, where he may have learned later of the suretyship relationship but does not know of the legal effect of his acts.

The only objection under the act is that section 119 (4) allows as discharge "any act which will discharge a simple contract" and in such cases at common law the surety is discharged even if the creditor does not know of the legal effects of his acts. 

It should be observed, however, that the holder in due course is in a different position from an assignee of a simple contract. 

The assignee's contract is that of his assignor, which is subject to the suretyship relationship; but the contract of the holder arises from the face of the instrument, and it is by definition and the provisions of the act quoted above totally severed and distinct from the agreement of suretyship.

Since a negotiable instrument is not a single contract but an aggregate of contracts the defenses set up under section 119 (4) should be only those which could be pleaded against the particular contract of the person against whom the defense of discharge is offered. Thus the holder in due course and his transferees should be free from the suretyship defenses which otherwise might be pleaded under this situation. Such is the result of the majority of the cases, though the reasoning by which it is often reached is very properly criticised in the passages quoted above.
