In an action by the payee against the accommodation maker of the original note, where the plaintiff innocently accepted renewals from the principal maker, that contained the forged indorsement of the defendant, and on later discovering the forgery accepted a chattel mortgage from the principal maker on condition that the notes on which the signature was forged should first be paid, it was held that the defendant was primarily liable on the instrument, and was not discharged by the acceptance of renewals that brought about the extension of time, since there was no intention to destroy the old obligation. The plaintiff's action in respect to accepting a chattel mortgage from the principal maker on condition that the renewal notes which contained the forged signature of the defendant should first be paid did not bar recovery on the original note, since the principal maker, being owner of the property, had legal title and could mortgage it and use the proceeds to pay any valid obligation. The defendants were makers of a note payable July 1, 1909.

Before the maturity of the note one of the makers made a contract with G and C whereby G and C assumed and agreed to pay the note when due. The next day G and C made a contract with X whereby X in turn assumed and agreed to pay the note. Said C, who was cashier of the plaintiff bank, the holder of the note, to induce X to assume its payment, agreed to extend the time of payment to September 1, 1909, and the plaintiff bank did so extend the time, without the knowledge and consent of the makers. Held, that secs. 119 and 192 of the 

 were inapplicable, since the relation of suretyship created by the said agreements arose independently of the original in-

§ (4)  

978 -Missouri strument, and that the makers were discharged by the said extension of time. Citizens Bank of Senatti v. Douglas, 178 Mo. 

App. 664, 161 S. W. 601. -Kentucky

Where defendants, surety-makers of a note, were assured by plaintiff, the holder, that he had sufficient funds of the principal debtor to satisfy all claims, and the holder extended the note, without defendants' consent, and defendants were prevented by such assurances from paying the note and pursuing the principal debtor, who was then solvent, the plaintiff was estopped from asserting the defendants' liability, the principal debtor having become insolvent. Bank of Neelyville v. Lee, 193 Mo. App. 537, 182 S. W. 1016, 196 Mo. App. 496, 196 

S. W. 43, (Mo. App.), 208 S. W. 143.

In Farmers State Bank v. Schelin (Mo. App.), 264 S. W. 

427, it was held that the effect of extension of time to the principal debtor upon the liability of accommodation makers must, in an action between the original parties, be determined without any reference to the , and that all defenses that would be open to the defendant on any other form of written contract might be set up against the payee in this case. 

But in Night & Day Bank v. Rosenbaum. 191 Mo. App. 559, 177 S. W. 693, it was held that an accommodating indorser is not discharged by a binding agreement of extension of time to the maker, without the consent of the indorser. This peculiar result is reached by holding an accommodation indorser to be a party primarily liable because sec. 29 makes an accommodation party, whether he is maker, drawer, acceptor or indorser, liable to a holder for value. But sec. 29 does not enact that all accommodation parties are liable as principal debtors or otherwise than according to the liability usually attached to their position on the paper. Such a construction of sec. 29 is also in the teeth of sec. 192, which defines the person "primarily" liable on an instrument as the person who, by the terms of the instrument, is absolutely required to pay the same and "all other parties are 'secondarily' liable." The two cases cited 20 by the court for its surprising proposition do not sustain it. In both of these cases the accommodating party was a maker and it was held in the one case that such maker was not released by time given to the accommodated indorser, and in the other, that an accommodating maker was not released by time given to his accommodated comaker.

This case is no longer the prevailing rule as pointed out by Newkirk v. Hays, 220 Mo. App. 514, which says it was overruled by Long v. Mason, supra.

In an action by the holder of a note against the maker the defense was payment. The indorsee of a note and a check, pledged to him for a loan to the payee, collusively delivered this collateral and the pledgeor's own note, when all three instruments were overdue, to the person who was maker of the pledged note, and drawer of the check. In return the pledgee took the amount of the loan, which was much less than the face of the collateral. He was held liable in conversion for the difference to the pledgeor. 

Aulwes v. Farmers Bank of Humboldt, 44 S. D. 92, 182 N. W. 528.

The court said that the pledgee was not selling the debt and transferring the collateral to the purchaser, but was discharging the collateral instruments by making the principal debtor the holder thereof after maturity, which left the pledgeor without redress except for conversion by the pledgee. The result is clearly sound. But quaere, was the collusive maker and drawer a holder "in his own right?"

The Aulwes case on this point was overruled in Buek v. First

The plaintiff, payee of a note for the sum of $4000, indorsed it before maturity as collateral security for a note for $700 which it had executed to X bank. A note made by A, B and C, payable "on or before August 1st," and indorsed by the payee to his wife, was paid by A in July through checks on the X bank which greatly overdrew A's account. B was cashier of the X bank and knew of this transaction, but C did not. Instead of cancelling the note, the payee's wife indorsed it to B to deposit in the X bank to A's credit to cover the checks. B put the note in the Y bank of which he was also cashier, crediting the X bank with the amount thereof, and the X bank credited A. No other officer of either bank had knowledge of these transactions. Long after August 

1st, the X bank obtained actual possession of the note, which was found among its papers when it became insolvent. The bank commissioner sued the three makers alleging that the X bank was a holder in due course. Held, A and B were liable whether the banks were holders in due course or not, since they got credit on the note against their own obligations; but C was not liable, since the X bank did not hold in due course. Even though the Y bank was a holder in due course, the X bank could not shelter itself under Y's title by reacquisition when it did. not originally hold in due course. "In his own right" is not used merely in contradistinction to a right in a representative capacity, but indicates a right not subject to that of another person, and good against all the world.

The payee of three notes delivered them for safe-keeping to his agent, who forged the payee's indorsement and pledged the notes as collateral for his own debt to the H bank. When the payee sought to raise money on the notes, his agent told him that it would be necessary to indorse them, and presented to him three exact duplicates of the true notes, on which the agent had forged the maker's signature. These were indorsed by the payee in ignorance of the deception. One of these forged notes was negotiated by the agent to the plaintiff, who also believed it to be genuine. The payee later made a written statement to the H bank that his indorsements on the notes held by them were genuine. The maker applied to the C bank for money with which to take the notes over from the H bank. 

He gave a new note to the C bank, and after taking up the unmatured genuine notes with forged indorsements held by the II bank, he pledged two of them to the C bank to secure the loan as had been pre-arranged. One of these reissued notes was the genuine counterpart of the false instrument which had been genuinely indorsed by the payee to the plaintiff. The writing given by the payee to the H bank was known to the maker but not to the C bank. The plaintiff holder of the note forged by the maker but genuinely indorsed brought replevin against the C bank to recover the note actually made by the maker bearing the payee's forged indorsement. Held, he could not recover. He did not have legal title to the genuine note as it had not been delivered to him. Even if the indorsement of the forged note would constitute an equitable assignment of the valid instrument, an equitable assignee could not maintain replevin. Moreover, it would not be equitable to protect him as assignee in this case. The maker on re-acquiring the notes before maturity did not extinguish the instruments but was a purchaser and could reissue. Sec. 119 (5) makes reacquisition "at or after maturity" a discharge, thus indicating that a discharge precluding renegotiation does not result from reacquisition before maturity. Sec. 50 also sanctions renegotiation. The maker, therefore, relying on the payee's representation of the validity of the indorsements, had the status to invoke estoppel against the plaintiff, who claimed in the right of the payee. The estoppel in favor of the maker inured to the benefit

BREWSTER: This subsection evidently means a discharge of a prior party by the holder.

The Supreme Court of Oregon has adopted Judge Brewster's view, that sec. 120-3 applies only to a discharge by the act of the creditor, and therefore does not include discharges by operation of law, for example, bankruptcy, and does not embrace a situation where, after a trial on the merits, the note is in effect destroyed because of a vice inherent in the transaction. Everding v. Toft, 82 Oreg. 1, 160 Pac. 1160.

Bankruptcy of a prior party is not a discharge. Brooks v. 

American Nat. Bank of Beaumont (Tex. Civ. App.), 103 S. W. (2d) 246.

In this case the maker was discharged by a judgment based on fraud in the note and bad faith on the part of the holder, and under this construction of sec. 120-3, the indorser would not be discharged by the discharge of the maker and therefore recourse to the general principles of suretyship was necessary in order to hold that the indorser was discharged. No answer was made to Dean Ames' other illustrations, viz., the discharge of a first indorser by the act of the holder in failing to give him notice of dishonor, which discharge would, under this subsection entail the discharge of subsequent indorsers, although they had had due notice, and the illustration of the discharge of an accommodation maker by a holder knowing of the accommodation which would discharge the accommodated indorser, although he is the party ultimately liable. The discharge of the maker of a note by the Statute of Limitations does not discharge accommodation indorsers. “Discharge" in subsec. 3 contemplates some affirmative act of release on the part of the holder and not a discharge by his mere failure to act. Romero v. Hopewell, 28 N. M. 259, 210 Pac. 231.

A judgment for the maker when sued by the indorsee does not discharge the payee-indorser. Sec. 120-3 is merely declaratory of the previous law, and "discharge" does not mean a discharge by operation of law but by some act or neglect of the creditor. Highleyman v. McDowell Motor Car Co., 202 

Mo. App. 221, 216 S. W. 52.

A note by Stanley H. Udy in U. Mo. Bull. Law Series 20, p. 44, considers that this decision would follow from the wording of subsec. 3 as adopted in other states, but that the court has overlooked the Missouri form of the subsection. The added

§ 120 (3) 

phrase, "except when such discharge is had in bankruptcy pro- Judgments ceedings," implies that "discharge of a prior party" includes discharges by operation of law. If it includes only discharges by the creditor, why should the Missouri legislature expressly provide that it does not include bankruptcy? Despite this criticism, it may be possible to justify the decision. It is clearly just, and accords with the common law and the interpretation of subsec. 3 in other states. The peculiar Missouri addition may be regarded as an inartistic attempt of the legislature to limit "discharge" to releases by the creditor; they expressed this intention by excluding the kind of discharge by operation of law which was most familiar. Their omission of other kinds was an accident, which should not expand "discharge" in the main portion of the subsection so as to alter the common law and effect a very unfortunate result.

Nuzman v. Bennett, 115 Kan. 766, 224 Pac. 900. -"Agreement binding upon

The agreement for extension of time may be express or implied, may be by parol or in writing, but must be a binding the holder" contract enforceable at law or in equity, supported by a valuable consideration and for a definite period. The burden of proving the agreement is on the indorser alleging it. If the facts and circumstances are all ascertained it is a question of law whether they constitute such an agreement. In the absence of offered evidence of the intention of the maker and holder the payment and acceptance of interest in advance is sufficient evidence of an intention to extend the time of payment. Cape Charles Bank v. Farmers Mut. Exchange, 120 Va. 771, 92 S. E. 918; Maghone v. Penta (Mass.), 165 N. E. 424.

Where the indorser's signature on the renewal notes was forged it was held that such renewal did not discharge his obligation on the original instrument. Droege v. Hoagland State 

Bank, 86 Ind. App. 236, 156 N. E. 592.

Where the note in suit was renewed by later notes containing the forged indorsement of the original indorser, and the original note had been returned to him as paid, it was held that the indorser was discharged by the extension of time without his consent. Worster v. Perry (Mass.), 170 N. E. 115. It is submitted that this case is wrong because it is hard to see how such an instrument would constitute an "agreement binding upon the holder.”

When a series of notes maturing in successive months contained a provision that default on one note would mature the entire series, and on the day after the first note had been defaulted and protested the maker gave to the holder a check which was unpaid, held, even if this constituted such an extension of time as would discharge the indorsers on the first note, they remained liable on the succeeding notes. Statutes allowing Waiver 

Where the indorser subsequent to release promised to pay the note and also made payments, it was held that he had waived the defense. Mortgage Investment Inc. v. Natal, 181 La. 651, 

160 So. 128.

An offer to prove a change made by the cashier of a bank, holding a note, on which defendant claimed to be a surety, by altering to a later date a marginal notation of the due date made by the cashier when the note was discounted, and making a like change in the entry as to the maturity of the note in the bank's index book of notes, was rightly refused in the absence of evidence to show that these acts of the cashier were within his authority or were ratified by the bank. Vanderford v. Farmers Bank, 105 Md. 164, 66 Atl. 47, 10 L. R. A. (N.S.) 129.

When the first indorser of a note bearing several indorsements obtained the note from the holder and wrote "Without recourse" after his name, this was a material alteration, which if ratified by the holder discharged subsequent indorsers; but he was held not to have become a party to the alteration, so that there was no discharge. It was also held that the subsequent indorsers were entitled to the benefit of a set-off by the first indorser against the holder, so that they were only liable to the holder for the balance of the note, and if forced to pay would be entitled to recover over from the first indorser. Freile v. Rudiger, 89 N. J. Eq. 91, 104 Atl. 142, modified in 90 N. J. 

Eq. 248, 106 Atl. 410.

Variation of the original note by the substitution of another and different obligation discharges the indorser. The N. I. L. was not cited. Maltby v. Longoria, 124 Tex. Comm. App. 428, 78 S. W. (2d) 176.

Subsec. 1 

There is a slight ambiguity in this section. The first clause 

Payment contains the provisions, (1) that the bill is not discharged and (2) that it may be further negotiated. If the exception applies to both clauses then it might be argued that under subsec. (1) the bill was discharged when paid by the drawer. Such interpretation might work a hardship on the drawer. (See fifth edition of this book, p. 924.) The punctuation would seem to indicate, however, that the exception was intended only to apply to the second, the right to negotiate. This conclusion is strengthened by the reference in the Commissioners' notes to Daniel on 

Negotiable Instruments (4th edition, 1891), where that writer, secs. 1239 to 1241, points out the reasons why the drawer should not be allowed to renegotiate where it is payable to a third person; but at the same time suggests that the instrument is not discharged. This is also the specific provision of B. E. A. 59(2) (a), which the notes also cite. The matter of discharge in the 

 is covered by sec. 119(2) and (4). If the exception be so limited, any difficulty with the section is removed. The rights of a transferee of a drawer who cannot negotiate are adequately covered by N. I. L. 49.

Payment by accommo- The drawer of a certified check which he had drawn payable to the United States Government for taxes was required to take up the check because of failure of the drawer bank. He then sued the liquidator of the bank claiming subrogation to the preferred rights of the Government granted by federal statute. 

Held, the drawer plaintiff was subrogated to the rights of the Government and can recover in full. Cuesta, Rey & Co. v. Newsom, 102 Fla. 853, 136 So. 551, 45 Harv. L. Rev. 389, not citing

Where the payee of a check obtained it by false pretenses and the consideration never passed to the drawer, and the payee indorsed it to the plaintiff, a holder in due course, it was held, ondary party that the transaction was for the accommodation of the payee, that dated sec- he was the party actually primarily liable to the indorsee, so that a payment by him to the indorsee, who retained the check and sued the drawer, discharged the check as against all parties. 

Josephsohn v. Gens, 85 Misc. Rep. 372, 147 N. Y. Supp. 451.

The result was right, but it is submitted that the reasoning is wrong. The instrument was not made for the accommodation of the payee, but as the indorsee after payment to him held the title in trust for the payee, to whose benefit recovery by the indorsee from the maker would inure, and as the payee would be liable over to the drawer, in order to prevent circuity of action, recovery by the indorsee should not be permitted.

§ 122 Sec. 122. Renunciation by Holder. 

The holder may expressly renounce his rights against any party to the instrument, before, at or after its maturity. An absolute and unconditional renunciation of his rights against the principal debtor made at or after the maturity of the instrument discharges the instrument. 

But a renunciation does not affect the righs of a holder in due course without notice. A renunciation must be in writing, unless the instrument is delivered up to the person primarily liable thereon.

ANNOTATIONS 

An agreement for immediate payment of part of a promissory note is sufficient consideration for the release of a surety from obligation to pay the residue. But under sec. 122, , such release must be in writing, "renunciation" being there used in the sense of "release." Baldwin v. Daly, 41 Wash. 416, 83 Pac. 

724; Pitt v. Little, 58 Wash. 355, 108 Pac. 941; Whitcomb v. 

National Exchange Bank, 123 Md. 612, 91 Atl. 689; see also note 10 Oreg. L. Rev. 401 and cases there cited; Portland Iron 

Works v. Siemens, 135 Oreg. 219, 295 Pac. 463, 10 Oreg. L. Rev. 401.

The term "renunciation" describes the act of surrendering a right or claim without recompense, but it can be applied with equal propriety to the relinquishing of a demand upon an agreement supported by a consideration. Therefore this term includes. the release of a claim by virtue of an accord and satisfaction, as well as a gratuitous waiver of liability. Whitcomb v. National 

Exchange Bank, 123 Md. 612, 91 Atl. 689; Kohn v. Zaludek (Tex. Civ. App.), 38 S. W. (2d) 110.

The cases cited above represent an improper interpretation of the act. When secs. 119, 120 and 122 are read together it appears that sec. 122 applies only to renunciation by a unilateral act of the holder in cases where the instrument is not delivered up to the person intended to be released. McGlynn v. 

Granstrom, 169 Minn. 164, 210 N. W. 892, 25 Mich. L. Rev. 782.

This section deals with express renunciation, and does not apply to or prevent a discharge by oral novation, under which the obligation of other persons is accepted in lieu of that of the maker of a note. Nelson v. Hudson, 221 Mo. App. 211, 299 S. 

W. 1111, overruling Engle v. Brown, 202 Mo. App. 345, 216 S. 

W. 541; Gannon v. Bronston, 246 Ky. 612, 55 S. W. (2d) 358, 80 A. L. R. 324 with note, 22 Ky. L. J. 445, the case also contains an exhaustive collection of authorities; Hazlehurst Oil Mill & Fertilizer Co. v. Booze, 160 Miss. 136, 133 So. 120; Johnston tion on con-

Sec. 123. Cancellation-Unintentional-Burden of 

Proof.

A cancellation made unintentionally, or under a mistake or without the authority of the holder, is inoperative; but where an instrument or any signature thereon appears to have been cancelled the burden of proof lies on the party who alleges that the cancellation was made unintentionally, or under a mistake or without authority. 

Cross Reference: 88 19, 191, 10, 48, 50, 55, 59, 119(3), 120(2), 121, 122, 124.

This section contains no matter not embraced in the title of the Act, and hence does not contravene a provision of the Constitution that no law shall embrace more than one subject, that subject to be expressed in the title. Gilley v. Harrell, 118 Tenn.

The president made, and the directors and stockholders of a bank indorsed, a note payable to the bank. Subsequently, certain of the indorsers erased their names and each gave a new note to the bank for a proportionate share of the amount. This was done without the authority or knowledge of the board of directors. Held, that the cancellation of the indorsements was inoperative, and also that the validity of the indorsement of another indorser who did not take part in the unauthorized cancellation of the other indorsements was not thereby affected. 

Union Bank of Brooklyn v. Sullivan, 214 N. Y. 332, 108 N. E. 558. 

After the drawer's death, the payee collected a check, which was marked paid by the drawee, but afterwards the payee returned the amount to the drawer's estate under advice of counsel. Held, the mistaken cancellation was inoperative. 

Gleason v. Brown, 129 Wash. 196, 224 Pac. 930.

Sec. 124. Alteration of Instrument—Effect of. 

Where a negotiable instrument is materially altered without the assent of all parties liable thereon, it is avoided, except as against a party who has himself made, authorized, or assented to the alteration, and subsequent indorsers. 

Cross Reference: 881 to 10, 125, 126, 184, 185, 191, 13, 14, 15, 17, 19, 23, 34, 35, 43, 48, 59, 121, 122, 133, 153, 188.

But when an instrument has been materially altered and is in the hands of a holder in due course, not a party to the alteration, he may enforce payment thereof according to its original tenor.¹

The plea of non est factum by the maker, denying execution of the note in such an amount, and alleging that it was not his obligation and was never signed by him or any person authorized to sign for him, raised only the issue of whether the instrument was actually signed by the maker, and does not raise the defense of material alteration. But the defendant does not have the burden of showing that the plaintiff knew of the alteration. Schram v. Johnson (Ia.), 225 N. W. 369.

In an action on a promissory note which is regular on its face, the burden of establishing a defense that the instrument had been fraudulently altered by the holder after its execution and delivery is upon the defendant.  Teske v. Baumgart, 99 Neb. 479, 156 N. W. 1044.

Where the defendant admitted his signature to a note but pleaded alteration of the note after delivery and the note was regular on its face, it was properly admitted in evidence, and the burden of proof that it was altered without his consent and after delivery was held to be on the defendant. The  was not cited. Cavitt v. Robertson, 42 Okla. 619, 142 Pac. 299.

Fraudulent alteration, although a crime, need be proved in an action on the note only by a preponderance of the defendant's evidence. Foundry Mfg. Co. v. Farr (Vt.), 126 Atl. 548.

Since alteration is an affirmative defense, the burden of establishing it by a preponderance of the evidence is on the defendant and never shifts. Forgery being a crime, the presumption of innocence is in favor of the plaintiff, and the defendant's evidence, to be preponderating, must be sufficient to overcome this presumption as well as the plaintiff's evidence. 

The court, without deciding whether the burden of proof was different when there was suspicious evidence of alteration on the face of the instrument, held that the existence of such evidence was a question for the court, not the jury, and sustained the finding of the trial judge that the note was not obviously altered. Wood v. Skelley, 196 Mass. 114, 81 N. E. 872.

The maker of a note secured by a deed of trust on land sold the land to the plaintiff, who before maturity paid the full amount of the note to the payee but did not take back the note. 

The payee indorsed the note in blank and fraudulently sold it to the defendant, a bona fide purchaser for value before maturity. In Anderson v. Foglesong, 201 Ia. 481, 207 N. W. 562, the court was of the opinion that an instrument which had been altered by the erasure of words, which were subsequently reinserted, was perfectly valid. Sed quaere. If this is sound any altered instrument could be returned to validity by correcting the alteration. Such a result seems contrary to the purpose of this section, which is to prevent tampering with instruments. 

The Canadian case infra represents the proper interpretation. 

CANADA- 

A joint note signed by several makers was avoided when the plaintiff-payee inserted the words "jointly and severally," although these words were afterwards cancelled by him. Banque

Provinciale v. Arnoldi, 2 Ont. L. R. 624 (C. A.). 

An accommodation indorser of a note, completed but so drawn as to leave spaces, which can be filled in so as to increase the amount, and which were so filled in by the maker, without the indorser's consent, is not liable, even to a holder in due course, for such increased amount, but only for the original amount. 

National Exchange Bank v. Lester, 194 N. Y. 461, 87 N. E. 779; 

Laseter v. Hill, 218 Ala. 240, 118 So. 252. The Alabama Supreme Court disapproved the decision of the same case by the 

Alabama Court of Appeals, 22 Ala. App. 501, 118 So. 250, which was of the opinion that negligence of the maker was a question for the jury. The decision of the Supreme Court is approved in a note 42 Harv. L. Rev. 572, but see note 23 Mich. L. Rev. 775, 778, see also 4 Ala. L. J. 115.

But the drawer of a check, negligently drawn by leaving spaces which can be and are filled in to an increased amount, without exciting suspicion, and which is paid in good faith by the drawee bank, can not recover the amount from the bank. 

The question of negligence is for the jury. Sec. 124 does not cover the case and under sec. 196 the rule of the law merchant must prevail. Young v. Grote, 4 Bing. 253, was approved. 

Timbel v. Garfield Nat. Bank, 121 App. Div. 870, 106 N. Y. 

Supp. 497.

The conflicting American common-law cases on these two points are collected in 31 Harv. L. Rev. 781 nn.

The plaintiff at various times wrote out in pencil checks for small amounts aggregating $60 and delivered them to the payee's agent, who raised the checks either by filling blank spaces or by changing the amounts, so that they aggregated $680. He indorsed the payee's name and had the checks collected from the defendant drawee bank. The payee credited the drawer with the original amounts of the checks. In an action by the drawer against the drawee bank for the total amount of the checks, it was held that an instruction was properly refused by the trial court that the plaintiff's negligence, if proved, would bar recovery. A note in 3 Cornell L. Q. 274, considers that the decision on the second point, allowing the drawee to retain the original amount of the checks, impliedly holds the drawee a holder in due course. The note thinks that the sweeping language of the first sentence of sec. 124 prevents the drawee from relying on the checks to any extent unless it is a holder in due course; but doubts whether it can be such, inasmuch as it is not a purchaser but a payor of the check, except perhaps in a case like Allen Grocery Co. v. Bank of Buchanan County, supra, where the original amount of the check caused an overdraft of the drawer's account. This was not true in the case at bar although the payment of the raised amounts of the checks caused overdrafts. 

This criticism of the case at bar seems unsound. The court does not expressly say that the drawee was a holder in due course and such a holding is unnecessary to the result. The bank was not endeavoring to enforce payment of the checks according to their original tenor, so that the second sentence of sec. 124 need not apply. The bank was defending an action for money had and received, which rests on equitable considerations, and it would be inequitable, as the court points out, for the depositor to recover from the bank money which had been paid out in settlement of his debts to the payee. The deduction from the amount recovered rests on familiar principles of equitable set-off. 

The case represents a minority view in denying that negligence is immaterial in an action by the depositor against the drawee bank. Such an action is not brought on the check but on the contract between bank and depositor; it is doubtful if sec. 124 should apply. The court, in stating that the  had changed the previous Kentucky recognition of negligence, cited only cases where a holder in due course recovered on a note from a negligent maker; it did not discuss the special factors in the bank and depositor cases, which have led the House of Lords and the New York courts to recognize negligence under the Acts in that situation though treating it as immaterial in suits by purchasers of instruments. 

The drawee bank was also held liable to the drawer despite the latter's negligence in facilitating alteration in Glasscock v. First Nat. Bank, 114 Tex. 207, 266 S. W. 393, 36 A. L. R. 320.

A cashier's check for $3.00, otherwise properly drawn, was negligently stamped with a protectograph, "Not over five hundred dollars. The drawer was under no duty to use a protectograph. Without it the forger could have raised the check and then stamped it with a protectograph. The use of the device by the bank may be regarded as an unrequired precaution to safeguard the bank's own interests, which should not make it liable to a purchaser who placed an uninvited reliance upon the same safeguard. 

On the other hand, it is arguable that although the bank was under no duty to use the protectograph, it must use it carefully, if at all, because the presence of the stamp made the deception of a purchaser somewhat more probable.

ENGLAND 

A bill for £500 was accepted. The drawer afterwards changed the amount to £3,500 by filling spaces left by himself when he drew the bill. A holder in due course can recover only £500 from the acceptor. Scholfield v. Londesborough [1896], A. C. 514. 

The mere leaving of spaces in a check which can be filled in is not by itself a violation of duty by a customer to his banker, even though the jury find that the check was drawn negligently and that the bank was not guilty of negligence in paying the check. Scholfield v. Londesborough followed. Colonial Bank of Australasia v. Marshall [1906], A. C. 559, Privy Council. 

But in London Joint Stock Bank v. Macmillan [1918], A. C. 

777, a member of the plaintiff firm signed a check payable to the firm or bearer at the request of a clerk who said he wanted the money for petty cash. The check was blank as to amount except that there were figures "2.0.0." in the space intended for figures. The clerk wrote the words "one hundred and twenty pounds" in the space left for words and the figures "1" and "0" on either side of the figure "2," drew the money from the defendant bank and absconded. Plaintiffs sued the bank for the amount charged against their account. 

The House of Lords held, reversing the Court of Appeals [1917], 2 K. B. 439, that defendant was not liable on the ground that the customer owed a duty to the bank to exercise reasonable care in drawing checks to prevent the banker from being misled. That the loss to the bank was a natural and direct cause of the failure to exercise such care. That Young v. Grote was correctly decided and that it was not inconsistent with Scholfield v. Earl of Londesborough. See a note on this case in the 

House of Lords in 145 Law Times 208. See also the contrary decision of the court below criticized in a note on the doctrine English negligence cases on

The present English law, cases like those of New York, supra, p. 1033, find a duty of care owed to the drawee bank but not to holders in due course. The conflicting Privy Council view may be modified when the question next arises, since that tribunal, unlike the House of Lords, is free to overrule its decisions.

The United States, as a depositor in the defendant bank, brought an action to recover the amount of two checks paid by the defendant and charged to the plaintiff's account, in each of which the payee's name had been unlawfully changed by a swindler after the checks had been signed. The bank teller had exercised reasonable care in paying the checks, and the cancelled checks together with a statement of account were returned to the plaintiff within one week after they had been cashed, with a notice that if no error was reported within ten days after their delivery, the account would be considered correct. The plaintiff discovered the forgery a few days later during the prosecution of the swindler, but did not give notice of it to the bank until six months thereafter. Meanwhile, the plaintiff had seized all the available property of the swindler so that it was too late for the bank to protect itself. Held, that the plaintiff by failing to give the bank notice of the forgery within a reasonable time after its discovery discharged the bank from liability. Quaere, whether a material alteration by a stranger will Spoliation avoid a negotiable instrument? Jeffrey v. Rosenfeld, 179 Mass. 

506, 61 N. E. 49. The language of sec. 124 leaves little room for doubt on this question. 

There is dictum in Swartz v. Bank of Haileyville, 169 Okla. 

22, 35 P. (2d) 701, 8 U. of Cin. L. Rev. 547, to the effect that the doctrine of spoliation is still in effect under the ; but the case clearly rests on assent by the maker to the alteration. 

Professor Ames, Judge Brewster and Mr. McKeehan all agree that sec. 124 abrogates the American doctrine of spoliation and substitutes the English rule.

Professor Ames regrets the return to archaic formalism, but 

Judge Brewster approves the change.

Although under the first paragraph of the section a spoliation will avoid the instrument, yet the second paragraph leads to the same result as under the former law, if the instrument is in the hands of a holder in due course, that is, he may recover according to the original tenor. This is true not only of a subsequent holder in due course but of the holder at the time of the spoliation, if he is a holder in due course. Wright v. O'Brien, 67 Ind. 

App. 521, 119 N. E. 469, semble, not citing the N. I. L.; Bowman v. Berkey, 259 Pa. 327, 103 Atl. 49, 262 Pa. 411, 105 Atl. 557, semble, not noting the N. I. L. But if the holder at the time of the spoliation is a donee of the instrument or a purchaser after maturity, it would seem that he could not recover, if his predecessor in title was also not a holder in due course. See Pensacola State Bank v. Melton, supra.

Illinois and South Dakota preserve the common-law doctrine of spoliation by their phraseology of sec. 124, supra, p. 67. In 

Fry v. Jenkins, 173 Ill. App. 486, a change of date by one not a party, without the consent of the holder, was held not to prevent recovery if the original tenor can be clearly shown. And similarly if a guarantee was written over the defendant's accommodation indorsement by the collecting bank without the holder's consent, the defendant was held liable on his indorsement though not on the guarantee. The instrument is avoided when "materially altered," which seems to include innocent changes, and the innocent holder seems "a party to the alteration," who is excluded by the second sentence from recovering according to the original tenor of the instrument. Where an instrument has been innocently altered it is discharged; but the innocent party can sue upon the original debt for which it was given. First Nat. Bank of Sparta v. Yowell, 155

This was so even though the instrument was given as payment, and the previous instrument was cancelled and plaintiff allowed to invoke sec. 123.

This case seems to reach the proper solution of the apparent difficulty arising under the wording of this section. It may in some cases work a hardship on the person who makes the alteration; but it is in line with the policy of the act to prevent tampering with instruments. 

In National Bank of Topeka v. Davies, 143 Kan. 542, 56 P. (2d) 82, the court took the attitude that a holder in due course guilty of innocent alteration could recover according to the original tenor. Sed quaere. 

Any of the material changes enumerated in the statute, without the consent of the maker, will avoid the instrument and render it unenforceable, without regard to the motive or the purpose. Holloway v. Gano, 125 Kan. 3, 262 Pac. 573. This seems the preferable view because it is within the apparent words and intent of the statute.

The payee altered the interest provisions of a note given for a chattel to make them conform to the original agreement of the parties, but without the maker's consent. At maturity, without disclosing the alteration, he took a renewal note conforming to the agreement and the altered form of the old note. 

The maker set up want of consideration for the new note, but did not offer to return the chattel. Held, the maker was liable to the payee on the renewal note. The innocent alteration avoided the original note but did not discharge the debt; the legal and moral obligation to pay for the chattel furnished consideration for the renewal note. Two judges dissented on the ground that the material alteration vitiated all subsequent trans actions. Born v. Lafayette Auto Co. (Ind.), 145 N. E. 833, superseding 139 N. A check for $37.98 had on it a printed clause, "Not good for more than $15." A line was drawn through these words but they were plainly discernible. Kerschbraun & Louis, 100 Neb. 876, 161 N. W. 577, L. R. A. 1917E, 788. In this case the alteration was made by an agent of defendant, who was authorized to make the draft for an amount not in excess of $15.00, and the defendant had received the consideration. The case may therefore be distinguished from the preceding cases.

When a note not given in a commercial transaction was partly in print and partly in three different handwritings, it was incumbent upon the plaintiff, a copayee, to offer evidence in addition to the note to show that he had no notice of defects or infirmities. The  was not cited. Reinhart v. Echave, 43 Nev. 323, 185 Pac. 1070, 187 Pac. 1006. 

Cf. Fleming v. Drew, 88 Okla. 160, 212 Pac. 306, where typewritten alterations of a printed form of note were held not to be sufficient evidence for the jury, that the purchaser was put on inquiry as to the possibility of alteration after delivery to the payee. The N. I. L. was not cited. 

When a note which originally called for interest from maturity was altered before delivery so that interest ran from date, without the consent of one comaker but by the direction of the other comaker, and the amount was altered by strangers to the instrument, each comaker was held liable to an innocent purchaser for value before maturity according to the tenor of the note at the time he signed, although the alterations seem to have been apparent on the face of the instrument. The N. I. L. was not cited. Gould v. Gould, 99 Wash. 204, 169 Pac. 324.

For the effect of apparent alteration on the ability to be a holder in due course, see cases under sec. 52 supra.

The defendants indorsed a note for the accommodation of the name maker who wrote it on a bank form, making it payable to and at the bank, where he expected to get it discounted. When the bank refused to discount it for the maker's agent, he drew a line through the name of the bank as payee and place of payment, and substituted the name of the plaintiff, who took the note for value. The evidence was conflicting as to the consent of the indorsers to this alteration. The trial judge directed a verdict for the plaintiff. Held, they were not liable unless they consented, and a new trial must be had to determine that fact. 

Muse v. Clark, 112 S. C. 82, 98 S. E. 850.

The court assumed for the purposes of the case that the plaintiff was a holder in due course, although inclined to believe that the apparent nature of the alteration prevented this, and held that he could not enforce the note according to the original tenor, under sec. 124, since the plaintiff would have no title to the note as it first read, and the alteration "deprived the contract of all legal validity in its inception." It is not necessary to agree with this last reason in order to regard the decision as right on the facts, for the plaintiff was not within the description of the original instrument and so could not enforce it. However, the opposite result might have been reached on the doctrine of such cases as Sutherland State Bank v. Dial, 103 Neb. 136, 170 

N. W. 666, stated under sec. 49. See 28 Yale L. J. 695. It seems harsh to regard the note as avoided by the alteration since the person who advanced the money upon it was immaterial to the indorsers. But where the indorsers designate one person only it is clear that the instrument should be avoided by such alteration. Upton v. Bush, 141 Miss. 660, 107 So. 284. 

In Munroe v. Stanley, 220 Mass. 438, 107 N. E. 1012, as the maker was willing to pay the note according to the original tenor, the court declined to decide whether the purchaser of a note altered as to amount and negotiated to the purchaser, who filled in the blank for the name of the payee with his own name, could recover according to the original tenor. 

But in Tower v. Stanley, 220 Mass. 429, 107 N. E. 1010, where a note, blank as to the name of the payee, was delivered to one with authority to fill in his own name, but he fraudulently altered the instrument and negotiated it with the blank unfilled, and the purchaser filled the blank with his own name, the purchaser was held not a holder in due course and was not entitled to recover according to the original tenor of the note. 

So, also, in Stone v. Sargent, 220 Mass. 445, 107 N. E. 1014, in which case the note was altered by the payee erasing his name, leaving the space blank, and increasing the amount, it was held that the note was not enforceable against the maker even according to its original tenor since the transferee having taken the note in an incomplete state was not a holder in due course.

Although the alteration of the payee's name without the maker's consent discharged him, he waived this defense by giving renewal notes payable to the original payee after he knew, or with reasonable exercise of care could have known, of the alteration. Farmers & Merchants Bank v. Parker, 150 Tenn. 184, 263 

S. W. 84, 35 A. L. R. 1253, with note on "Renewal as precluding defenses available against the original instrument." The opinion also states that the addition of a comaker without the consent of the first maker discharges him but the added comaker would be liable.

Defendant signed a note for $15,000 for the accommodation of G, with a blank for the name of the payee, because it was not known from whom the money could be obtained, and upon condition that the note should also be signed by R and others. A bank to which application was made would lend only $11,000 and on condition that R guarantee the payment. The bank filled in R's name as payee and had him indorse the note and took his personal guaranty of its payment. The bank indorsed a payment of $4,000 on the back of the note and gave R $11,000, less the agreed discount, and R gave the money to G. Held, a material alteration as to the amount and as to the effect of the instrument and the bank being a party to the alteration could recover nothing from the defendant. Washington Finance Corp. v. Glass, 74 

Wash. 653, 134 Pac. 480, 46 L. R. A. (N.S.) 1043.

It is submitted that this case was decided on wrong grounds. 

The result might have been reached on the ground that the bank was not a holder in due course, because it knew that the instrument was not complete when it was offered to it for discount and the failure to secure the other signatures would therefore operate as a defense. But the court passed over this ground of defense and based its conclusion solely on the defense of alteration. The decision is against the weight of authority at common law 3 and there is nothing in secs. 124 and 125 to effect a change in this respect. The formal character of the instrument was unchanged and the defense of alteration arises only when the form is altered, not when a collateral matter is added, whatever may be the substantial effect thereof.

It has been suggested, moreover, that the change in the law made by the second paragraph of 124, whereby a holder in due course of an altered instrument may recover according to the original tenor, necessarily limits the operation of the first clause. to alterations which are prejudicial to the non-assenting party. 

Otherwise if the plaintiff had bought the instrument bona fide for $11,000 after the indorsement of payment of $4,000, the note would be avoided by the first paragraph and yet the plaintiff

The plaintiff delivered two notes for $500, blank as to payee, and a policy of insurance upon his life with an assignment thereof, blank as to assignee, to W to secure a loan of $1,000. 

W raised one note to $1,500 and delivered it with the other note and the policy and assignment to S as security for a loan of $2,000, which W afterwards paid and received back the notes and policy. Later the policy and a forged assignment thereof were again transferred by W to S with a note for $3,000 bearing the forged signature of the plaintiff maker. W having died, the genuine $500 note and the raised $1,500 note were found among his papers. Plaintiff sued S and the administrators of W. 

Held, that the defendant S must deliver the policy, the forged assignment and forged $3,000 note to plaintiff and that the administrators of W upon payment by plaintiff of the genuine $500 note must deliver to him that note and the raised note for $1,500. Sherman v. Connecticut Mut. Life Ins. Co., 222 

Mass. 159, 110 N. E. 159.

The court points out that the original tenor of the instrument put the plaintiff's purchase after the maturity of the first two installments, and suggested that if these were unpaid, he took the whole note as overdue paper. It is not clear whether the court thought that this fact alone would render the plaintiff not a holder in due course, even if he had no notice of the alteration from the face of instrument. Such a result may necessarily follow from sec. 124, since by the original tenor of the instrument he was a purchaser after maturity. Nevertheless, if the alteration was completely concealed, so that he had no actual notice from the instrument that it was overdue, he should be treated as a holder in due course at least with respect to installments not yet due at the time of his purchase.

Later he consented to an extension of the note. Held, the indorser was discharged. That the alteration was beneficial to him is immaterial. His consent to the extension did not ratify the alteration unless done with full knowledge thereof. Johnson 

Farm Loan Co. v. McManigal, 288 Fed. 185 (C. C. A., Neb.).

The addition of an agreement to pay interest on interest is a material alteration, which discharges nonassenting surety comakers if binding. But they were not discharged when the agreement between the payee and the principal maker was without consideration. Forbearance of the payee to sue for interest was not such consideration in the absence of proof that it was pursuant to a request by the principal maker. Schroyer v. Thompson, 262 Pa. 282, 105 Atl. 274. The holding is questionable. The alteration ought to discharge the nonassenting parties regardless of its ultimate enforceability. They should not be made to bear the risk as to whether consideration will be proved or not on a contract to which they did not agree.

The plaintiff corporation lent money on a note signed by the borrower and several accommodation comakers. The note was made out on a printed bank form and was originally payable to the bank, but the corporation's name had been inserted as payee and the provision as to interest changed so that it would run from date instead of maturity. § (4)  

1058 Alteration although made after the accommodation comakers signed. Johnof payee's name son v. Dover Mercantile Co., 164 Ark. 371, 261 S. W. 913.

The court stated that the corporation was not a holder in due course because the note was not indorsed to it by, the bank, but that the corporation was subject only to such defenses as were available against the bank, and the bank was a holder in due course because it had no notice of the alteration. This argument is not entirely satisfactory, since the bank gave no value. It would also seem that inasmuch as the alterations, although made before delivery, were without the consent of the accommodation comaker, the latter were liable only according to the original tenor of the instrument. At this point, the theoretical difficulty arises that the original tenor of the instrument made the bank payee, so that as to these accommodation makers the plaintiff was not an indorsee or a payee. If the bank could not recover, how can the corporation recover? See the cases contra on p. 1046, supra, under sec. 124. It seems reasonable, however, to support the decision on the ground that the bank was a holder in due course of the note in its original tenor although disguised by the alteration. The bank was a holder, for it was the payee of the original note and had possession of it before delivery to the corporation; took without notice of the defenses; and the value paid by the corporation can be linked with the bank's possession and legal title to make it a holder in due course in trust for the corporation.

ENGLAND 

The acceptor of a bill payable to the drawer or order, when accepting, struck out the words "or order" and wrote over his acceptance the words "in favor of F (the drawer) only." Held, that the alteration was immaterial, the bill being still payable to order under sec. 8(4) B. E. A., and the acceptance was a general acceptance of a negotiable bill. Meyer v. Decroix [1891], A. C. 520. This case depends, of course, on the English Act which does not require that the instrument must be payable to order or to bearer in order to be negotiable."

A completed bill of exchange purportedly drawn in London was altered apparently in Germany without the knowledge or consent of the acceptor by the obvious substitution of a German city as the place of drawing. In an action against the acceptor it was held that the bill was avoided as to him because the alteration of an inland bill to a foreign bill was material. Also that plaintiff had failed to sustain the burden of proving that by the German law the rights and liabilities of the parties thereupon had been unaffected. Koch v. Dicks (1933), 1 K. B. 307.

Comm. App.), 276 S. W. 664.

An order for the payment of money, addressed to no one in particular, but generally to anyone for whom the drawer might be employed or who owed him money, is too indefinite and uncertain to be binding on anyone. Dugane v. Hvezda Pokroku 

No. 4 (Ia.), 119 N. W. 141. 

A voucher draft containing a statement of indebtedness, a receipt in the following form: "Notice, Receipt only by those having authority to sign and in ink. Paying bank will not accept unless conditions are complied with. No alterations

§ 126 exchange allowed," and a statement that when properly receipted this Bills of voucher becomes a draft on the debtor payable through a certain bank, is not negotiable but becomes so when receipted, as required, but as the signature of the payee was in pencil and not in ink the instrument was not negotiable. The  was not cited except as "the statute." Van Blatz Brewing Co. v.

Interstate Ice Co., 161 Mo. App. 531, 143 S. W. 542. The court seems to have overlooked the fact that the instrument not being payable to the order of the named payees was for that reason not negotiable and could not have been made negotiable by a proper receipt, even if such receipt would otherwise have made it negotiable. "Spiketon, Wash., 1911, Coast Coal Co. You are hereby authorized to deduct one dollar per month from my monthly pay to pay for the services of Dr. Skeets as mine doctor." Orders in the above form were given by miners to plaintiff. Held, that they were substantially bills of exchange and not binding on the drawee unless accepted in writing. Skeets v. Coast Coal Co., 74 Wash. 327, 133 Pac. 433. It is submitted that these instruments not being payable to order or bearer and having no equivalent words of negotiability were not negotiable and therefore not governed by the N. I. L.

A draft with the notation "This draft will not be honored unless receipted bill is attached" was held not a bill of exchange. 

Camp v. Oakland Mortgage & Finance Co., 128 Cal. App. 238, 17 P. (2d) 151.

Defendant gave to plaintiff a bill of exchange payable to the plaintiff's order for work done by plaintiff. The drawee refused to pay the order. Defendant knew that the order would not be paid. The lower court held that the plaintiff could not recover from the defendant, as the order operated as an equitable assignment of the defendant's claim against the drawee and was accepted in full settlement. The judgment was reversed, because the defendant had knowledge that the order would not be paid. and there was no evidence sufficient to show an express agreement on the part of the plaintiff to take the same as absolute payment and that the order did not operate as an equitable assignment. American Luxfer Prism Co. v. Bartolicius Star Iron Works, 152 N. Y. Supp. 1014. 

ENGLAND 

The acceptor of bill payable to drawer or order, when accepting struck out the words " or order" and wrote over his acceptance the words "in favor of F (the drawer) only." Held, that the alteration was immaterial, the bill being still payable to order under sec. 8(4) supra, p. 1065, n. 1, and the acceptance was a general acceptance of a negotiable bill. Meyer v. Decroix [1891], A. C. 520. See also Bavins v. London & S. W. Bank

Sec. 127. Bill Not An Assignment of Funds in Hands of Drawee. 

A bill of itself does not operate as an assignment of the funds in the hands of the drawee available for the payment thereof and the drawee is not liable on the bill unless and until he accepts the same.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 185, 189, 191, 3, 18, 60, 61, 130, 135, 137.

ANNOTATIONS See Ralph W. Aigler: "Rights of Holder of Bill of Exchange 

Against the Drawee," 38 Harv. L. Rev. 857.

An unaccepted draft cashed by a bank at the drawer's request is not an assignment of the drawer's funds in the hands of the drawee. Jones v. Crumpler, 119 Va. 143, 89 S. E. 232.

A holder in due course of a dishonored bill has no cause of action against the drawee, either at law or in equity, as an assignee of the drawer's contractual rights underlying the bill. 

State, ex rel., Macon Creamery Co. v. Mix, 222 Mo. App. 426, 7 S. W. (2d) 290.

A bill of exchange given to the payee as a gift and never collected from the drawee could not be enforced against the drawer's estate, since it was an uncompleted gift. It could not operate as an equitable assignment of funds in the drawee's hands, on the theory that the delivery of the draft to the donee was a sufficient delivery to complete the gift. Gardner v. 

Moore's Admr., 122 Va. 10, 94 S. E. 162.

An unaccepted order drawn upon a debtor is not effectual as an equitable assignment, unless it is drawn upon a particular fund, and not to be payable generally. Izzo v. Ludington, 79 

App. Div. 272, 79 N. Y. Supp. 744. "Please pay to S. G. Co. at the end of each month the amount due me for boarding your horses until otherwise notified." Held, that the above instrument does not amount to an equitable assignment of the fund or render the drawee liable thereon until accepted in writing. The court cited secs. 126 and 127, but overlooked the fact that the instrument was not negotiable and that therefore the statute did not apply. Frederick & Nelson v. Spokane Grain Co., 47 Wash. 85, 91 Pac. 570. 

Contra, Taylor v. Dollins, 205 Mo. App. 246, 222 S. W. 1040.

Bills were drawn in Argentina upon a New York bank by its Buenos Aires branch and delivered to the payee in good faith, but in return for money which he was alleged to have obtained from various persons by fraud. The Court of Criminal Proceedings of Buenos Aires, having jurisdiction over the particular crime and the defendant, issued an order enjoining the bank from paying the draft anywhere in the world unless presented by bona fide holders for value. The bank pleaded this injunction as a defense in an action brought in New York by an indorsee, but the defense was held demurrable as not binding the plaintiff, even if not a holder for value. The defendant had leave to plead the actual facts of the alleged fraud, which the court intimated would be a good defense, but this seems doubtful in an action at law in view of the principle presented on p. 741 ff, supra (which is followed in New York cases, Warren v. Haight, 65 

N. Y. 171; City Bank v. Perkins, 29 N. Y. 554; Brown v. Penfield, 36 N. Y. 473; contra, Owen v. Evans, 134 N. Y. 514, 31 

N. E. 999), that a maker, drawer, or acceptor can not set up in a law court the equities of other persons. If, however, the defense could be raised, it would seem that the Argentine adjudication of the payee's equitable liability should have been conclusive on the plaintiff, if not a holder in due course, because he would then be privy to the payee. The court said that title to the money paid for the draft must be determined by Argentine law, which presumably was in accord with the law merchant as recognized in New York, but it might be that Argentine law was different.  Scura v. Nat. City Bank, 107 Misc. Rep. 93, 177 N. Y. Supp. 75.

Sec. 130. When Bill May be Treated as Promissory Note. 

Where in a bill drawer and drawee are the same person, or where the drawee is a fictitious person, or a person not having capacity to contract, the holder may treat the instrument, at his option, either as a bill of exchange or a promissory note.

Sec. 131. Referee in Case of Need. 

The drawer of a bill and any indorser may insert thereon the name of a person to whom the holder may resort in case of need, that is to say, in case the bill is dishonored by nonacceptance or nonpayment. Such person is called the referee in case of need. It is in the option of the holder to resort to the referee in case of need or not, as he may see fit. 

Cross Reference: 88 83, 126, 149, 185, 191, 17(6), 31, 61, 63, 66, 67, 161, 171.

This provision is rarely inserted in English or American bills. 

No case involving such a provision has been found in the United States. The usual form is, "In case of need apply to A B at X." 

If the referee pays the bill the drawer will be liable to him for the amount. See Story on Bills, sec. 65; Daniels, Negotiable 

Instruments, sec. 11; Chalmers, Bills of Exchange, sec. 15.

ARTICLE II ACCEPTANCE Sec. 132. Acceptance-How Made, Etc. 

The acceptance of a bill is the signification by the drawee of his assent to the order of the drawer. The acceptance must be in writing and signed by the drawee. It must not express that the drawee will perform his promise by any other means than the payment of money.¹ alone as

Signature The signature of the drawee without more is a sufficient acacceptance ceptance. Lawless v. Temple, 254 Mass. 395, 150 N. E. 176, 48 

A. L. R. 758, 24 Mich. L. Rev. 605. This is the proper interpretation of the act; see the fourth edition of this book, p. 821, and for the weight of authority see note "Drawee's mere writing of his name on a bill as acceptance thereof," 48 A. L. R. 760. 

Cross Reference: 88 62, 126, 185, 187, 191, 1 to 7, 10, 12, 17 to 21, 23, 24, 31, 61, 63, 70, 133 to 142, 161, 181, 188, 189, 192.

A complaint which fails to allege a written acceptance of a bill of exchange does not state a cause of action against the drawee. Wadhams v. Portland Ry. Co., 37 Wash. 86, 79 Pac. 

597. Faircloth-Byrd Mercantile Co. v. Adkinson, 167 Ala. 344, 52 So. 419, is contra on a bill made before the  took effect in Alabama, but under a former statute which also required an acceptance of a bill of exchange to be in writing. 

But a plea which does not affirmatively disclose the fact that the contract was made by parol is a plea of a written agreement. 

So even though the statute required the acceptance of a bill to be in writing, a plea that the drawee "agreed to pay the order" is sufficient. Barnsdall v. Waltemeyer, 142 Fed. Rep. 415, 73

C. C. A. 515.

Clayton Town Site Co. v. Clayton Drug Co., 20 N. M. 185, 147

X, a depositor in defendant bank, gave an order on the bank Payment to Y, who presented the order to the bank. The cashier marked the order, "presented Oct. 16, 1912, 9:05," and stamped on it, "Paid Oct. 16, 1912," and drew a check to the order of Y, but withheld it because of garnishment by a creditor of X. This case was settled, but thereafter the plaintiff, another creditor of X, instituted garnishment proceedings against X and the defendant bank. The defendant thereafter delivered and paid its cashier's check to Y. Held, that stamping the order given by X, "Paid," was not a payment or an acceptance thereof nor an assignment of funds of X in the bank, but that the funds still remained to the credit of X and subject to garnishment by Y, who was entitled therefore to recover of the defendant bank. 

Hanna v. McCrory, 19 N. M. 183, 141 Pac. 996. Accord, Hall v. First Nat. Bank (Tex. Civ. App.), 252 S. W. 828, 254 S. W.

The plaintiff, a Chicago bank, in accordance with the banking custom in that city, had a notice in its pass books that checks on the plaintiff, when deposited, would be credited conditionally, and if not found good at close of business, would be charged back to the depositor's account. All checks were stamped by the receiving teller when received and were then handed by the teller to the bookkeeper who advised as to the condition of the account. 

A check drawn on the bank by another depositor was deposited in it by the defendant and so stamped and treated. Held, the check was not accepted or paid by the bank, so as to entitle the defendant to a set-off. The notice of its method of doing business negatived the intention to make an unqualified acceptance.

 Sec. 133. Holder Entitled to Acceptance on Face of Bill. 

The holder of a bill presenting the same for acceptance may require that the acceptance be written on the bill, and, if such request is refused, may treat the bill as dishonored.¹

Sec. 134. Acceptance by Separate Instrument. 

Where an acceptance is written on paper other than the bill itself, it does not bind the acceptor except in favor of a person to whom it is shown and who, on the faith thereof, receives the bill for value.'

Letters of credit 

Sec. 135. Promise to Accept-When Equivalent to Acceptance. 

An unconditional promise in writing to accept a bill before it is drawn is deemed an actual acceptance in favor of every person who, upon the faith thereof, receives the bill for value.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 3, 25, 27, 126, 132, 185, 187, 191, 10, 31, 62, 133 to 142, 188.

ANNOTATIONS 

It should be noted that section 134 provides that an extrinsic acceptance must be in writing and is good only to persons to whom it is shown; while section 135 provides that a promise to accept is good to any person who "upon faith thereof receives the bill for value." There has been considerable criticism among legal writers because of this variance in wording. All this seems to be based on a dictum in a lower New York court in Bank of 

Michigan v. Ely, 17 Wend. 508, 511, discussing the old New

York Act from which the  was copied. 

This distinction between the sections was common to the statutes which were adopted in many states prior to the N. I. L., and seems to refer to letters of credit. An extrinsic acceptance is part of the contract contained in the bill and as such should go along with it. Section 134, therefore, requires it to be shown to one who wishes to claim under it. A letter of credit, on the other hand, is often intended to stay with the drawer and to cover a series of bills which, of course, immediately return to the drawee. Under such circumstances the promise to accept, the letter of credit, and the bill are necessarily separated, so section 135 properly requires, merely, that the holder take on "faith thereof."

It has been suggested that subsequent holders who take drafts issued under letters of credit would be in precarious positions, so far as the drawee was concerned. Such rights are fully covered under the N. I. L. by sections 49 and 58. It is a policy of the N. I. L. that bona fide purchasers should be allowed the rights appearing on the face of the paper; therefore, a person taking a bill drawn in compliance with a letter of credit, but knowing nothing about it, relies only on the bill itself, and under such circumstances he should get no better rights against the drawee, whose acceptance does not appear thereon, than his transferee had. If there is any commercial necessity for giving 

1 Not in B. E. A.

§ 135 

ACCEPTANCE 

credit greater rights to a holder, it can be accomplished by the simple Letters of expedient of writing on the face of the draft, "Drawn in accordance with letter of credit from the drawee, or some similar reference to the promise, which would in no way affect negotiability. See sec. 3(2), supra.

The plaintiff purchased a draft in accordance with a letter of credit issued by a bank on behalf of the drawer. On presentation of the draft to the bank, the bank wrote a letter to the plaintiff stating that it was remitting the amount of the draft to a New York bank to the plaintiff's credit. This remittance was never sent. The bank was held liable for the amount of the draft. The court spoke of the letter as an acceptance. The 

 was not cited. Bank of Eclectic v. Sturdivant Bank, 203 Ala. 458, 83 So. 321. The second letter was not an acceptance, inasmuch as it was not written on the instrument and the draft was not purchased in reliance upon this letter. However, the bank seems clearly liable on the contract to accept contained in its letter of credit. It seems doubtful if the second letter added anything to the liability of the bank. 

Defendant wrote to a bank that it would be satisfactory for the bank to honor drafts made against defendant by S. covering shipments of poultry, if with shipping documents attached, until further advice. Plaintiff, after seeing the correspondence, accepted an order from S. for poultry to be shipped to defendant. A draft drawn by S. upon defendant, payable to plaintiff, was purchased by the bank, with shipping documents attached, but was dishonored by defendant, who paid S. directly. 

The bank obliged plaintiff to take up the draft. Held, defendant was liable as acceptor of the draft. Wilson & Co. v. Niffenegger, 211 Mich. 311, 178 N. W. 667. See the note in 25 Colum. L. Rev. 

819, on virtual acceptances by letters of credit.

The plaintiff, after seeing the telegram, sold cattle to A, which were consigned to the defendant, and took A's drafts in favor of the bank, which held a mortgage on the cattle. After dishonor the bank transferred the draft to the plaintiff. Held, the defendant was liable on an agreement to accept, although the draft was not accurately described; and the drawer was not a necessary party. Sigel- 

Campion Co. v. Davis, 69 Colo. 511, 194 Pac. 468, not citing the N. I. L. 

"We agree to sign packing house acceptance" was held not a promise to accept. Pacific Coast Coal Co. v. Lindsay Co operative Citrus Assn., 112 Cal. App. 207, 296 Pac. 919. Sed quaere.

A bank telephoned to a live stock commission company, in- Acceptances quiring if it would pay drafts issued by M for the net proceeds of any stock shipped to it by M. A bank certifying a check has doubtless the same right.

Sec. 136. Time Allowed Drawee to Accept. 

The drawee is allowed twenty-four hours after presentment in which to decide whether or not he will accept the bill; but the acceptance if given dates as of the day of presentation.¹

Sec. 137. Liability of Drawee Retaining or Destroy ing Bill. 

Where a drawee to whom a bill is delivered for acceptance destroys the same, or refuses within twenty-four hours after such delivery, or within such other period as the holder may allow, to return the bill accepted or nonaccepted to the holder, he will be deemed to have accepted the same. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 185, 191, 16, 18, 31, 61, 62, 70, 71, 83, 85, 88, 102 to 104, 119(3), 127, 133 to 136, 138 to 142, 143 to 152, 155, 160, 186 to 189, 194.

For an excellent discussion of the problems arising under this section see L. W. Feezer: "Acceptance of Bills of Exchange by Conduct," 12 Minn. L. Rev. 129.

ACCEPTANCE § 137 acceptance It has been suggested that there is a conflict between sections Retention as 136 and 137 because section 136 allows the drawee twenty-four hours in which to accept, while section 137 provides that refusal to return the bill "within" twenty-four hours or such time as the holder may allow amounts to acceptance. The conflict is more apparent than real, and is based on the assumption that the drawee is entitled under section 136 to keep the bill while he makes up his mind. Section 136 makes no such provision. The bill is at all times the property of the holder, and he is entitled to have it when he wants it, and section 137 so provides. If the holder should demand return before twentyfour hours, the drawee would be required to comply on pain of being held as an acceptor; but return within twenty-four hours unaccepted would not be a dishonor. See  149 and 150.

The drawee could still accept by notification within the twentyfour hours. See section 191. Here an extrinsic acceptance, section 134, would play an important part. If the drawee after returning the bill still refused to act after the expiration of the time allowed, the holder then would be required to treat the bill as dishonored or lose his rights against prior parties. See section 

150. See also, the Commissioners' note to section 150. 

In Westberg v. Chicago Lumber Co., 117 Wis. 589, 94 N. W. 

572, it was said that the mere retention of a bill by the drawee is not an acceptance. Either destruction or a refusal to return to the holder should be shown. The Wisconsin statute adds the words "mere retention of the bill is not an acceptance.

These cases represent the overwhelming weight of authority under the act, and in the interest of uniformity they should be followed. It is submitted also that, although they do not follow the proper historical interpretation of earlier acts, they reach a convenient and workable result which insures uniformity in all cases involving presentment of instruments. As pointed out in the fourth edition of this book, p. 839 ff, the act, in secs. 136 and 137, covers only presentment for acceptance, and presentment for payment is not mentioned. But it does not necessarily follow that because the act is silent as to presentment for payment that the result should be different from the case of presentment for acceptance. The considerations involved in both cases are the same, the act in other sections has provided that upon presentment immediate action must be taken, the drawee has twenty-four hours in which to accept, secs. 136, 137, and his failure to do so must be treated by the holder as dishonor, or the drawer and indorsers are relieved, sec. 150; notice of protest and notice of dishonor must be given within one business day, secs. 155, 103 and 104, and it has been held that a delayed promise to pay is dishonor. See cases under secs. 83 and 88. Although the act seems silent on the point of how long the drawee may take to pay, the rule of the Wisner case fills this gap by requiring promptness on the part of the drawee, thus he must return the instrument or be liable for its face

for payment value as acceptor. These cases properly draw an analogy from Presentment secs. 136, 137, 150, 102, 104 and 188, and remove all doubt as to the rights of the parties secondarily liable, and seem to conform to the clearing house custom that items be honored or returned at once. 

In Standard Trust Co. v. Commercial Nat. Bank, 166 N.

In Commercial State Bank v. Harkrider-Keith-Cook Co. 

(Tex. Civ. App.), 250 S. The court bases this reasoning on secs. 89, 102, 103 requiring notice to be given the day after dishonor, and on the fact that section 115 does not include delay in payment as one of the excuses for delay in giving notice. The court might also have drawn an analogy from sec. 150.

Sec. 138. Acceptance of Incomplete Bill. 

A bill may be accepted before it has been signed by the drawer, or while otherwise incomplete, or when it is over-due, or after it has been dishonored by a previous refusal to accept, or by non-payment. But when a bill payable after sight is dishonored by non-acceptance and the drawee subsequently accepts it, the holder, in the absence of any different agreement, is entitled to have the bill accepted as of the date of the first presentment. 

Cross Reference: 88 4(1), 83, 126, 132, 149, 185, 187, 191, 7, 13 to 21, 53, 62, 71, 86, 133 to 137, 151, 161, 188, 189, 196.

This section does not mean that one to whom the bill is transferred while incomplete may become a holder in due course. 

Clay & Funkhouser Banking Co. v. Dobyns, 213 Mo. App. 468, 255 S. W. 946.

Sec. 139. Kinds of Acceptances. 

An acceptance is either general or qualified. A general acceptance assents without qualification to the order of the drawer. A qualified acceptance in express terms varies the effect of the bill as drawn. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 185, 187, 191, 18, 33, 62, 133 to 138, 140 to 142, 161, 188, 189.

Sec. 140. What Constitutes a General Acceptance. 

An acceptance to pay at a particular place is a general acceptance unless it expressly states that the bill is to be paid there only and not elsewhere. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 185, 191, 38, 62, 70, 73, 87, 133 to 

139, 141, 142.

Sec. 141. Qualified Acceptance. 

An acceptance is qualified, which is: (1) Conditional, that is to say, which makes payment by the acceptor dependent on the fulfilment of a condition therein stated;

ACCEPTANCE § 141 

(2) Partial, that is to say, an acceptance to pay part only of the amount for which the bill is drawn; (3) Local, that is to say, an acceptance to pay only at a particular place; 1 (4) Qualified as to time; (5) The acceptance of some one or more of the drawees, but not of all.

Law Rev. 183, which considers that since a conditional acceptance is recognized by the statute, it should be treated like an ordinary negotiable instrument and no defenses except the nonfulfillment of the condition should be admitted. 

The transferee of a check without indorsement had it presented to the defendant drawee bank for payment through the clearing house. The defendant gave conditional credit for the amount to the collecting bank, but upon examination discovered that the payee had not indorsed, and returned the check for his indorsement, after certifying it in compliance with the clearing-house rule requiring certification of all checks over $500 returned for indorsement or informality. The transferee sued on the certification, without procuring the payee's indorsement. Held, the drawee bank was not liable. The certification was equivalent to a conditional acceptance, in effect a promise to pay when the check was properly indorsed, and the plaintiff can not recover without showing performance of the condition. 

The court did not decide how long the drawee bank might be obligated to hold the funds to enable the plaintiff to obtain the payee's indorsement. Lipten v. Columbia Trust Co., 194 App. 

Div. 384, 185 N. Y. Supp. 198. For adverse criticism of some of the reasoning of the court, see the discussion of this case under secs. 49, 186. The decision is approved in 30 Yale L. J. 759.

Sec. 142. Rights of Parties as to Qualified Accept ance.

The holder may refuse to take a qualified acceptance, and if he does not obtain an unqualified acceptance, he may treat the bill as dishonored by non-acceptance. 

Where a qualified acceptance is taken, the drawer and indorsers are discharged from liability on the bill, unless they have expressly or impliedly authorized the holder to take a qualified acceptance, or subsequently assent thereto. When the drawer or an indorser receives notice of a qualified acceptance, he must within a reasonable time express his dissent to the holder, or he will be deemed to have assented thereto. 1 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 141, 149, 185, 191, 193, 5(3), 66, 70, 89, 107, 111, 120, 144, 152, 188.

The payee of a bill took an acceptance, payable when lumber was inspected and placed to the credit of the payer, but gave no notice thereof to the drawer. Held, that the drawer was discharged. Lewis Hubbard & Co. v. Morton, 80 W. Va. 137, 92 

S. E. 252.

ARTICLE III PRESENTMENT FOR ACCEPTANCE Sec. 143. When Presentment for Acceptance Must 

Be Made. 

Presentment for acceptance must be made: (1) Where the bill is payable after sight, or in any other case, where presentment for acceptance is necessary in order to fix the maturity of the instrument; or (2) Where the bill expressly stipulates that it shall be presented for acceptance; or 

1 The English Act adds: "The provisions of this subsection do not apply to a partial acceptance whereof due notice has been given. Where a foreign bill has been accepted as to part, it must be protested as to the balance." B. E. A. s. 44 (2).
