(3) Where the bill is drawn payable elsewhere than at the residence or place of business of the drawee. 

In no other case is presentment for acceptance necessary in order to render any party to the bill liable.

Sec. 144. When Failure to Present Releases Drawer and Indorser.

Except as herein otherwise provided, the holder of a bill which is required by the next preceding section to be presented for acceptance must either present it for acceptance or negotiate it within a reasonable time. If he fail to do so, the drawer and all indorsers are discharged. 1 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 143, 147, 148, 191, 193, 61, 66, 70, 79, 89, 111, 120, 132, 145, 146, 149 to 152, 157, 186. 

Where an instrument was payable "30 days after arrival" of the car, and there was a local custom at the point of arrival that such drafts were presented as sight drafts, it was held that presentment for acceptance before the arrival of the car was a proper presentment within the instructions. New York, N. H. & H. R. Co. v. First Nat. Bank, 105 Conn. 33, 134 Atl. 223, 36 

Y. L. J. 139, 40 Harv. L. Rev. 508.

Sec. 145. Presentment-How Made. 

Presentment for acceptance must be made by or on behalf of the holder at a reasonable hour, on a business day and before the bill is overdue, to the drawee or some person authorized to accept or refuse acceptance on his behalf; and: (1) Where a bill is addressed to two or more drawees who are not partners, presentment must be made to them all, unless one has authority to accept or refuse acceptance for all, in which case presentment may be made to him only. 3 (2) Where the drawee is dead, presentment may be made to his personal representative;

A bill may be presented for acceptance on any day on which negotiable instruments may be presented for payment under the provisions of sections seventy-two and eighty-five of this act. When Saturday is not otherwise a holiday, presentment for acceptance may be made before twelve o'clock noon on that day."

Sec. 147. Presentment Where Time is Insufficient.

Where the holder of a bill drawn payable elsewhere than at the place of business or the residence of the drawee has not time with the exercise of reasonable diligence to present the bill for acceptance before presenting it for payment on day that it falls due, the delay caused by presenting the bill for acceptance before presenting it for payment is excused and does not discharge the drawers and indorsers.

Sec. 148. Where Presentment is Excused. 

Presentment for acceptance is excused and a bill may be treated as dishonored by non-acceptance, in either of the following cases: 

(1) Where the drawee is dead, or has absconded, or is a fictitious person or a person not having capacity to contract by bill;¹ (2) Where, after the exercise of reasonable diligence, presentment cannot be made; (3) Where, although presentment has been irregular, acceptance has been refused on some other ground.2

Sec. 149. When Dishonored By Non-acceptance. 

A bill is dishonored by non-acceptance: (1) When it is duly presented for acceptance and such an acceptance as is prescribed by this act is refused or cannot be obtained; or (2) When presentment for acceptance is excused and the bill is not accepted. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 132, 133, 142 to 148, 185, 187, 191, 71 to 78, 89, 134 to 141, 150 to 152.

Sec. 150. Duty of Holder Where Bill Not Accepted. 

Where a bill is duly presented for acceptance and is not accepted within the prescribed time, the person presenting it must treat the bill as dishonored by non-acceptance or he loses the right of recourse against the drawer and indorsers.

§ 152 

PROTEST Sec. 151. Rights of Holder Where Bill Not Accepted. 

When a bill is dishonored by non-acceptance, an immediate right of recourse against the drawers and indorsers accrues to the holder and no presentment for payment is necessary. 

Cross Reference: 88 61, 66, 126, 149, 185, 187, 191, 70 to 78, 89, 143 to 150, 152.

ARTICLE IV PROTEST Sec. 152. In What Cases Protest Necessary. 

Where a foreign bill appearing on its face to be such is dishonored by non-acceptance, it must be duly protested for non-acceptance, and where such a bill which has not previously been dishonored by non-acceptance is dishonored by non-payment, it must be duly protested for nonpayment. If it is not so protested, the drawer and indorsers are discharged. Where a bill does not appear on its face to be a foreign bill, protest thereof in case of dishonor is unnecessary. 

Cross Reference: 88 83, 126, 129, 142, 148, 149, 153 to 160, 170, 185, 191, 61, 66, 70, 89, 109 to 111, 112 to 118, 147, 150, 167, 172, 186.

A dictum in Amsinck v. Rogers, supra, that the obligation of the drawer of a check is determined by the law of the place where it is payable, was rejected in Hennenlotter v. De Orvanos, 114 Misc. Rep. 333, 186 N. Y. Supp. 488, which held that the law of the place of drawing governs, as in bills of exchange, since under sec. 185 a check is only a species of bill of exchange. 

The  has changed the common-law rule laid down in 

Hibernia Nat. Bank v. Lascombe, 84 N. Y. 367.

But where a bill drawn by defendant in Kansas City on a bank in London, England, was paid by the drawee in good faith and in the ordinary course of business but on a forged indorsement of the payee, and under sec. 60 of the Bills of Exchange 

Act (Appendix I) such payment is deemed to have been made in due course, the payee can not recover from the drawer the amount paid for such bill. The question as to what constituted a legal payment was governed by the law of the place of performance and it is to be assumed that the drawer issued the bill and the payee took it with a view to that law.  Belestin v. First Nat. Bank, 177 Mo. App. 300, 164 

S. W. 160. 

The former statute whereby promissory notes, payable and negotiable at a bank and discounted by a bank, are placed on the same footing as foreign bills of exchange is repealed by the 

Negotiable Instruments Law. Therefore protest of such a note is not required. Williams v. Paintsville Nat. Bank, 143 Ky. 

781, 137 S. W. 535, Ann. Cas. 1912D, 350. But the Negotiable

Instruments Law which makes a note negotiable by indorsement or delivery, ipso facto, places it on the same footing as a bill of exchange and subject to the Statute of Limitations of five years for actions on bills of exchange or promissory notes placed upon the footing of bills of exchange. Pensacola Bank v. Thornberry, 226 Fed. Rep. 611, 141 C. C. A. 367, and cases cited. 

The Negotiable Instruments Law making no provision as to the damages recoverable in actions on foreign bills of exchange, this subject is relegated to the Law Merchant under sec. 196. 

The subject has been considered in the following cases. 

The damages recoverable by the payee of a negotiable foreign bill of exchange protested for nonpayment against the drawer may be deemed to be made up as follows: (1) The face of the bill; (2) interest thereon; (3) protest fees; (4) re-exchange, i. e., the additional expense of procuring a new bill for the same amount payable in the same place on the day of dishonor; or a percentage in lieu of such re-exchange in jurisdictions where it is permitted by statute. Pavenstedt v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co., 203 

N. Y. 91, 96 N. E. 104, Ann. Cas. 1913A, 805.

A bill drawn in Columbia and payable in New York in United States money was dishonored. Subsequently the drawee paid in

§ 152 foreign bills

New York the principal sum with interest and protest fees, with- Damages on out prejudice to the right of the holder to recover re-exchange. 

In an action by the holder against the drawer, who was also drawee, held, that the measure of damages to the payee upon its refusal to pay is the amount of the draft, with interest and protest fees. This is true although the currency of the country in which the bill was drawn depreciated after the date of the bill and its dishonor, so that the holder was required to pay a larger number of dollars in such depreciated currency for the amount of American money for which the bill was drawn than he was able to realize upon the draft in the country where it was drawn in the first instance. Ibid.

By the law merchant the holder of a dishonored foreign bill of exchange is entitled to recover of the drawer re-exchange, which is the price that the holder must pay on the date of dishonor, in the currency of the country where the original bill was drawn, payable where the original bill was payable, for a good bill, of the same amount of money, and this rule is not changed by the fact that at the date of the trial the value of the foreign currency had depreciated in the market of the country where the bill was drawn. Simonoff v. Granite City Nat. Bank, 279 

Ill. 248, 116 N. E. 636.

The defendants, residing in England, accepted bills drawn by and payable in marks to the plaintiff, at Leipzig, Germany. In an action on the bills, held, that the plaintiffs are entitled to recover a sum in United States money sufficient to purchase the marks at the time of maturity of the bills with protest fees and interest at six per cent. until the entry of judgment, and not the value of the marks at the time of the trial.  Gross v. Mendel, 171 App. Div. 237, 157 N. Y. Supp. 357.

The master of a Norwegian vessel, on purchasing coal in Virginia, signed a blank draft and delivered it to the seller, who filled in the date, his own name as payee, the Norwegian owner of the vessel as drawee, the amount, and the time of payment as thirty days after sight. The draft was presented to the drawee in Norway for acceptance and was protested for nonacceptance. Thirty days later it was duly protested for nonpayment. During the thirty-day interval, the krone had risen in the exchange market. In an action by the payee against the drawer, he was held liable for re-exchange at the current rate on the day of dishonor by nonpayment and not on the day of dishonor by nonacceptance. The reasons given were: (1) Reexchange relates to the time when a bill ought to be paid, not when it ought to be accepted; and (2) when the drawer makes a draft on himself, that is a virtual acceptance, and he is liable as drawee without formal acceptance. Consequently the draft needed no acceptance, and the only effect of the first presentment was to fix the day of maturity as thirty days later. The

Sec. 153. Protest-How Made. 

The protest must be annexed to the bill, or must contain a copy thereof, and must be under the hand and seal of the notary making it, and must specify: (1) The time and place of presentment; (2) The fact that presentment was made and the manner thereof; (3) The cause or reason for protesting the bill; (4) The demand made and the answer given, if any, or the fact that the drawee or acceptor could not be found.¹

Sec. 155. Protest-When to Be Made. 

When a bill is protested, such protest must be made on the day of its dishonor, unless delay is excused as herein provided. When a bill has been duly noted, the protest may be subsequently extended as of the date of the noting.2

B. E. A. s. 94. A form of protest which may be used in such case is given in the first schedule to the Act.

Sec. 156. Protest-Where Made. 

A bill must be protested at the place where it is dishonored, except that when a bill drawn payable at the place of business, or residence of some person other than the drawee, has been dishonored by non-acceptance, it must be protested for non-payment at the place where it is expressed to be payable, and no further presentment for payment to, or demand on, the drawee is necessary. 

Cross Reference: 88 83, 126, 149, 152, 153, 185, 191, 62, 70, 87, 89, 142, 150, 154, 155, 157 to 160. 

Sec. 157. Protest Both for Non-acceptance and Nonpayment.

A bill which has been protested for non-acceptance may be subsequently protested for non-payment.

118, 150, 152 to 156, 158 to 160, 185 to 187.

Insolvent.

Where the acceptor has been adjudged a bankrupt or an insolvent or has made an assignment for the benefit of creditors, before the bill matures, the holder may cause the bill to be protested for better security against the drawer and indorsers.¹

Sec. 159. When Protest Dispensed With. 

Protest is dispensed with by any circumstances which would dispense with notice of dishonor. Delay in noting or protesting is excused when delay is caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder and not imputable to his default, misconduct or negligence. When the cause of delay ceases to operate, the bill must be noted or protested with reasonable diligence. 

Cross Reference: 88 109 to 112, 114 to 117, 126, 153, 154, 185, 191, 193, 79 to 82, 89, 94, 102 to 107, 113, 118, 147, 148, 152, 155 to 

158, 160, 188, 194. 

See the article by Professor K. N. Llewellyn, "Supervening

Impossibility of Performing Conditions Precedent in the Law of Negotiable Paper," 23 Colum. L. Rev. 142, 154-161.

Protest of a check payable abroad is dispensed with if the drawer has no funds with the drawee bank to pay the check. 

Ellenbogen v. State Bank, 119 Misc. Rep. 711, 197 N. Y. Supp. 278.

Protest of a check payable abroad is not dispensed with if the drawer bona fide believed a sufficient credit had been established at the drawee bank to pay the check. Kardynal v. Grezezinski, 255 Mich. 421, 238 N. W. 213.

Where the plaintiff's assignors purchased a check from the defendant bank on Austria in 1914, the war intervened and the check was not dishonored until 1921, it was held that protest was not dispensed with, even though the bank knew the fact that the purchasers were interned in France. Gorsche v. 

First Nat. Bank of Manistique, 233 Mich. 428, 206 N. W. 992.

Where the drawee was a non-existent bank it was held that protest was not necessary. Lewis v. Chelsea Exchange Bank, 137 Misc. Rep. 153, 241 N. Y. Supp. 639.

Sec. 160. Protest Where Bill is Lost, Etc. 

Where a bill is lost or destroyed or is wrongly detained from the person entitled to hold it, protest may be made on a copy or written particulars thereof. 

Cross Reference: §§ 126, 136, 137, 150, 152, 153, 185, 191, 70, 89, 118, 119(3), 120(2), 123, 154 to 159.

Where checks indorsed without restriction and deposited in the defendant bank, which credited the amount to the depositor's account and mailed them to its correspondent for collection, were lost in the mail, and not found until after the drawer became bankrupt, the bank must stand the loss and can not charge the amount of the checks to the depositor's account, because the defendant held the checks as owner and not as mere agent for collection and, although it might have charged back

§ 162 

ACCEPTANCE FOR HONOR 

the amount if the checks had been dishonored, they were not dishonored and the loss was due to the failure of defendant to attempt to collect them as lost paper. Heinrich v. First National 

Bank of Middletown, 219 N. Y. 1, 113 N. E. 531.

Even if the defendant bank took the check, not as cash, but for collection, it was held liable for the loss when the depositor was unable to replace the check through ignorance of the drawer's name.  Stark v. Public Nat. 

Bank, 123 Misc. Rep. 647, 206 N. Y. Supp. 8.

ARTICLE V ACCEPTANCE FOR HONOR Sec. 161. When Bill May Be Accepted for Honor. 

Where a bill of exchange has been protested for dishonor by non-acceptance or protested for better security and is not overdue, any person not being a party already liable thereon may, with the consent of the holder, intervene and accept the bill supra protest for the honor of any party liable thereon or for the honor of the person for whose account the bill is drawn. The acceptance for honor may be for part only of the sum for which the bill is drawn; and where there has been an acceptance for honor for one party, there may be a further acceptance by a different person for the honor of another party.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 85, 126, 149, 152, 153, 158, 162, 191, 17(6), 32, 61 to 63, 66, 132, 138, 141, 150, 163 to 170, 171, 187.

Sec. 162. Acceptance for Honor-How Made. 

An acceptance for honor supra protest must be in writing² and indicate that it is an acceptance for honor, and must be signed by the acceptor for honor. 

Cross Reference: 88 161, 31, 132 to 135, 163 to 170.

A promise by telegram to accept a draft for the account of the person who was named therein as drawee is not an acceptance for honor. Renfrow v. Citizens' State Bank, 87 Ind. App. 

318, 158 N. E. 919, 26 Mich. L. Rev. 567, 3 Ind. L. J. 562. 

1 The provision in the last clause for a further acceptance by a different person for the honor of another party is not in the English Act; see s. 65 and s. 65 (2). 

2 The English Act reads, "must be written on the bill." B .E. A. s. 65 (3).

 Sec. 163. When Deemed to Be An Acceptance for 

Honor of the Drawer. 

Where an acceptance for honor does not expressly state for whose honor it is made, it is deemed to be an acceptance for the honor of the drawer.

Cross Reference: §§ 161, 162, 61, 62, 164 to 170. 

Sec. 164. Liability of the Acceptor for Honor. 

The acceptor for honor is liable to the holder and to all parties to the bill subsequent to the party for whose honor he has accepted. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 161, 191, 64, 68, 162, 163, 165 to 170.

Sec. 165. Agreement of Acceptor for Honor. 

1 The acceptor for honor by such acceptance engages that he will on due presentment pay the bill according to the terms of his acceptance, provided it shall not have been paid by the drawee, and provided also, that it shall have been duly presented for payment and protested for non-payment and notice of dishonor given to him. 2

Sec. 166. Maturity of Bill Payable After Sight-Ac cepted for Honor.

Where a bill payable after sight is accepted for honor, its maturity is calculated from the date of the noting for non-acceptance and not from the date of the acceptance for honor. 

Cross Reference: §§ 4(1), 126, 155, 161, 162, 191, 163 to 165, 167 to 170.

§ 170 ACCEPTANCE FOR HONOR Sec. 167. Protest of Bill Accepted for Honor, Etc. 

Where a dishonored bill has been accepted for honor supra protest or contains a reference in case of need, it must be protested for non-payment before it is presented for payment to the acceptor for honor or referee in case of need. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 131, 152 to 156, 161, 162, 191, 70, 83, 89, 163 to 166, 168 to 170.

Sec. 168. Presentment for Payment to Acceptor for Honor-How Made. 

Presentment for payment to the acceptor for honor must be made as follows: (1) If it is to be presented in the place where the protest for non-payment was made, it must be presented not later than the day following its maturity; (2) If it is to be presented in some other place than the place where it was protested, then it must be forwarded within the time specified in section one hundred and four.¹ 

Cross Reference: §§ 85, 86, 104, 126, 156, 182, 183, 165, 194, 71 to 78, 89, 164, 166, 167, 169, 170.

Sec. 169. When Delay in Making Presentment is Ex cused.

The provisions of section eighty-one apply where there is delay in making presentment to the acceptor for honor or referee in case of need. 

Cross Reference: 88 81, 131, 161, 162, 168, 71 to 78, 89, 159, 165.

Sec. 170. Dishonor of Bill By Acceptor for Honor. 

When the bill is dishonored by the acceptor for honor it must be protested for non-payment by him. 

Cross Reference: 88 83, 126, 152, 153, 161, 162, 191, 70, 89, 118, 154 to 160, 163 to 169.

 ARTICLE VI PAYMENT FOR HONOR Sec. 171. Who May Make Payment for Honor. 

Where a bill has been protested for non-payment, any person may intervene and pay it supra protest for the honor of any person liable thereon or for the honor of the person for whose account it was drawn. 

Cross Reference: 88 83, 126, 152, 153, 185, 191, 17(6), 61 to 63, 66, 88, 118, 119, 121, 154 to 160, 161, 172 to 177. 

In Hooper v. Herring, 14 Ala. App. 455, 70 So. 308, the drawer of a dishonored check paid the amount to the payee and took up the check. The court, citing this section, said that the drawer had a right to intervene and pay it to protect his honor. 

This seems an improper application of the section. The drawer did not pay for honor but to discharge his obligation to the payee. This would give him no rights against the drawee on the check, but only for damages for the dishonor of the check and it was for this that he sued. 

Sec. 172. Payment for Honor-How Made. 

The payment for honor supra protest in order to operate as such and not as a mere voluntary payment must be attested by a notarial act of honor which may be appended to the protest or form an extension to it. 

Cross Reference: 88 152, 153, 154, 171, 49, 50, 58, 118, 121, 155 to 

160, 161, 173 to 177.

Sec. 173. Declaration Before Payment for Honor. 

The notarial act of honor must be founded on a declaration made by the payer for honor or by his agent in that behalf declaring his intention to pay the bill for honor and for whose honor he pays. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 171, 172, 185, 19, 88, 161 to 170, 173 to 177.

Sec. 174. Preference of Parties Offering to Pay for 

Honor.

Where two or more persons offer to pay a bill for the honor of different parties, the person whose payment will discharge most parties to the bill is to be given the preference. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 171, 185, 191, 64, 68, 88, 172, 173, 175 to 177.

PAYMENT FOR HONOR § 177 Sec. 175. Effect on Subsequent Parties Where Bill is 

Paid for Honor.

Where a bill has been paid for honor, all parties subsequent to the party for whose honor it is paid are discharged, but the payer for honor is subrogated for, and succeeds to, both the rights and duties of the holder as regards the party for whose honor he pays and all parties liable to the latter. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 171, 172, 185, 191, 50, 51, 57, 58, 64, 68, 70, 88, 89, 120, 121, 152, 173, 174, 176, 177.

AMES: This section codifies, as does the English Act, evidently by an oversight, the overruled case of Ex parte Lambert, 13 Ves. 179. It should be amended by substituting for "liable, the fourth word from the end, the word "prior." 

BREWSTER: Ex parte Lambert was the law in several states, and seems just.

MCKEEHAN: It is doubtful whether the change in the English rule was inadvertent. The rule enacted by this section is probably the more just one.

CHAFEE: The rule codified in this section has the advantage of preventing circuity of action, since if the party for whose honor the payment is made, should, as between himself and the party sued, be the one who ought to pay the bill, the party sued, upon payment to the payer for honor could recover against the party for whose honor the bill was paid. It also seems more logical that one who pays for the honor of a particular party should put himself in the place of that party. 

Sec. 176. Where Holder Refuses to Receive Payment Supra Protest.

Where the holder of a bill refuses to receive payment supra protest, he loses his right of recourse against any party who would have been discharged by such payment. 

Cross Reference: 88 84, 126, 151, 171, 172, 175, 185, 191, 61, 66, 120(4), 173 to 175, 177.

Sec. 177. Rights of Payer for Honor. 

The payer for honor, on paying to the holder the amount of the bill and the notarial expenses incidental to its dishonor, is entitled to receive both the bill itself and the protest.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 152, 171, 172, 185, 191, 50, 118, 121, 153, 161, 162, 173. 

1 The English Act adds, "If the holder do not on demand deliver them up, he shall be liable to the payer for honor for damages." B. E. A. s. 68 (6).

ARTICLE VII BILLS IN A SET Sec. 178. Bills in Sets Constitute One Bill. 

Where a bill is drawn in a set, each part of the set being numbered and containing a reference to the other parts, the whole of the parts constitute one bill. 

Cross Reference: 88 126, 185, 191. 

See Note, Duplicate or substitute drafts, notes or checks following Samland v. Ford Motor Company, 123 Neb. 819, 244 

N. W. 404, 87 A. L. R. 1475, 1480.

Sec. 179. Right of Holders Where Different Parts 

Are Negotiated.

Where two or more parts of a set are negotiated to different holders in due course, the holder whose title first accrues is, as between such holders, the true owner of the bill. But nothing in this section affects the rights of a person who in due course accepts or pays the part first presented to him. 

Cross Reference: §§ 30, 52, 88, 132, 178, 191, 57, 62, 119, 180 to 183.

Sec. 180. Liability of Holder Who Indorses Two or More Parts of a Set to Different Per sons.

Where the holder of a set indorses two or more parts to different persons he is liable on every such part, and every indorser subsequent to him is liable on the part he has himself indorsed, as if such parts were separate bills. 

Cross Reference: 88 17(6), 30, 31, 63, 67, 126, 178, 185, 191, 57, 64, 66, 68, 179, 181 to 183.

Sec. 181. Acceptance of Bills Drawn in Sets. 

The acceptance may be written on any part and it must be written on one part only. If the drawee accepts more than one part, and such accepted parts are negotiated to different holders in due course,' he is liable on every such part as if it were a separate bill. 

Cross Reference: 88 52, 126, 132, 178, 185, 187, 191, 57, 62, 133 to 142, 179, 180, 182, 183, 188. 

1 The English Act reads, "get into the hands of different holders in due course.' B. E. A. s. 71 (4).

§ 184 

 Sec. 182. Payment by Acceptor of Bills Drawn in 

Sets.

When the acceptor of a bill drawn in a set pays it without requiring the part bearing his acceptance to be lelivered up to him, and that part at maturity is outstanding in the hands of a holder in due course, he is liable to the holder thereon. 

Cross Reference: 88 52, 85, 86, 88, 119, 132, 178, 191, 57, 126, 179 to 181, 183, 185, 187.

Sec. 183. Effect of Discharging One of a Set. 

Except as herein otherwise provided where any one part of a bill drawn in a set is discharged by payment or otherwise the whole bill is discharged. 

Cross Reference: §§ 57, 88, 119, 122, 124, 178, 182, 191, 126, 179 to 182, 185.

Two parts of a bill of exchange drawn in a set in New York on a drawee in Paris were mailed in separate covers to the payees in Spain. Only the second part of the bill was received. This was indorsed by the payees, negotiated and presented to the drawee and payment refused, because the first part, which was apparently regularly indorsed by the payees and several other persons, had been previously presented and paid in good faith. 

One notice of dishonor was given to the drawer and the indorsee of the payees sued the drawer. The French Code of Commerce provided that "The party who pays a bill of exchange at its maturity and without opposition is presumably discharged." 

Held, that as the validity of the payment was governed by the law of the place of performance and as by the French Code the payment of the first part of the bill was valid although the indorsements were forged, and the drawer was therefore discharged, a complaint which set forth the above facts was demurrable. Caras v. Thalmann, 138 App. Div. 297, 123 N. Y. Supp. 

97; Casper v. Kuhne, 159 App. Div. 389, 144 N. Y. Supp. 502, accord.

 Miscellane ous instru- An instrument promising to pay money to the payee's order ments and conveying as security specified personal property and future crops and rents, and authorizing the payee to seize and sell these in his discretion after or before maturity, was not a negotiable promissory note. Caton v. First Nat. Bank, 20 Ala. App. 384, 102 So. 369, reversed on another point in Ex parte First Nat.

A promise to pay a certain sum of money to the order of the plaintiff with an option in the defendant to deliver potatoes instead is not a negotiable note. Parker v. Baldwin, 216 Mich. 

472, 185 N. W. 746.

An instrument translated "pay to order of A $1,300" with no date of maturity or drawee is not a negotiable note, since it contains no unconditional promise to pay. It is not a bill of exchange or check since no drawee is named or otherwise indicated. Ayub v. Saloman (Tex. Civ. App.), 252 S. W. 291.

An instrument reading "Having been cause of a money loss to my friend X, I have given her three thousand dollars. I hold this amount in trust for her and one year after date or thereafter, on demand, I promise to pay to the order of X, her heirs. or assigns, three thousand dollars with interest" is a valid promissory note. As it does not appear upon the face that there was no consideration or an invalid consideration, it will be presumed that there was a valid consideration. In the absence of evidence to the contrary the court must assume that the money loss referred to was legally chargeable to the maker. Hickok v. 

Bunting, 92 App. Div. 167, 86 N. Y. Supp. 1059.

A dated note, which read, "On demand after date I promise to pay," etc., was a promissory note.  

Kinkela v. Booras, 194 N. Y. Supp. 850.

Agreements to extend ment, etc.

A provision in a note whereby maker, surety, guarantor, and time of pay- indorser consent that the note or any part of it may be extended without further notice does not make it non-negotiable. Polk 

County Nat. Bank of Bartow v. Shelton, 69 F. (2d) 352 (C. 

C. A. 5th).

A note is not rendered non-negotiable by (1) a stipulation whereby the makers, indorsers, guarantors and sureties consent that the time of payment may be extended without notice; (2) a stipulation that the note shall immediately become due and payable, if the maker should fail in business or ask a respite or become bankrupt before the maturity of the note; or (3) a stipulation that, if the note be not paid at maturity, any money, stocks, bonds, or other property on deposit or otherwise to the credit of the maker or any indorsers on the books of the bank at which the note is made payable shall at once stand applied to its payment. Hibernia Bank & Trust Co. v. Dresser, 132 La. 

538, 61 So. 569; explained and qualified, Bonart v. Rabito, 141 

La. 970, 76 So. 166.

The indorser was not released because more than one extension was made, since the agreement did not deprive him of the right at maturity of the note or of any extension thereof to pay the note and become subrogated to an action against the maker. Ib. 

Accord as to right to apply bank balance, Mechanics & Metals 

Nat. Bank v. Warner, 145 La. 1022, 83 So. 228.

A clause in a note consenting "that the time of payment may be extended without notice thereof" is satisfied by one extension. If more than one is given without consent of the surety he will be discharged. A complaint on a note payable to the maker's order which maker's fails to allege indorsement by the maker is defective. Simon order v. Mintz, 51 Misc. Rep. 670, 101 N. Y. Supp. 86; Edelman v. 

Rams, 58 Misc. Rep. 561, 109 N. Y. Supp. 816.

Notes payable to the maker without indorsement were incomplete as negotiable instruments, and therefore not entitled to the statutory presumption under sec. 11 that they were signed on the day of their date, but they were entitled to the benefit of the common law presumption that facts which usually and regularly co-exist in business affairs co-exist in the particular case in the absence of evidence to the contrary. Sugar v. Silverman, 105 Misc. Rep. 293, 173 N. Y. Supp. 182.

Contra. In Cassetta v. Baima (Cal. App.), 288 Pac. 830, it was held that a note payable to the maker's order and in the hands of a third person was entitled to the benefit of the presumption of sec. 14 of authority to fill in blanks.

A note to the maker's own order is not valid until indorsed and a mortgage supporting it is void. Kaufman v. Federal Nat. 

Bank, 287 Mass. 97, 191 N. E. 422. 

A transfer of a note, payable to the maker's own order, and not indorsed by him is not a transfer in due course of business and the transferee is not a holder in due course. Nat. City 

Bank v. Titlow, 233 Fed. Rep. 838.

A transferee without indorsement can recover on such an instrument from the maker. Achee v. Williams, 6 La. App. 316.

In an action on a note payable to the makers and indorsed by only one, it was held that the transferee was not entitled to reformation of the note in the form of the acquisition of the indorsement of the other maker, because the instrument was incomplete and therefore a nullity. In re Divelbess' Estate, 216 Ia. 1296, 249 N. W. 260.

The fact that such a note is not indorsed does not prevent recovery on the debt for which it was given. Armato v. Ross 

(La. App.), 170 So. 400. 

In an action by the accommodation indorsee, who paid the maker's "my order" note that was signed but not indorsed by the maker, against another accommodation indorser, it was held that the instrument was incomplete and not a note under  sec. 184, and there can be no liability under N. I. L. sec. 68. Prestenbach v. Mansur (La. App.), 129 So. 445.

While a note payable to the maker's own order is not a good legal contract until indorsed, yet a note in which the payee is one of two or more makers is not invalid. Although for technical reasons the payee can not maintain an action at law on it, there is a remedy in equity. Reid v. Windsor. 111 Va. 825, 69 S. E. 1101.

Such an instrument was admitted to probate against the estate of one of the co-makers in In re Talbott's Estate, 200 Ia. 585, 203 N. W. 303.

What are checks? 

A note in 22 Mich. L. Rev. 728 points out that if a contrary decision had been made, it is difficult to see what defenses other than forgery, etc., would be open to a maker of an instrument payable to the order of himself. Since the indorsement by the maker-payee is not part of a sale of the note, it should not give rise to any warranty. In the absence of such warranties, it seems immaterial whether the defendant is sued as an indorser or as a maker, since in either event he may set up the defense of fraud against the plaintiff, unless a holder in due course. The court stated that even if warranties existed, they would under the express language of sec. 66, run only to a holder in due course, so that the plaintiff must establish such a holding; but the court recognized that a different rule might prevail with respect to warranties under sec. 65.

The maker of a note payable to himself, who indorses it, is not liable as indorser, but only as maker. Farmers & Merchants Sav. Bank v. Hudson, 62 Utah 131, 218 Pac. 93.

Sec. 185. Check Defined. 

A check is a bill of exchange drawn on a bank payable on demand. Except as herein otherwise provided, the provisions of this act applicable to a bill of exchange payable on demand apply to a check. 

Cross Reference: 88 7, 126, 186, 188, 191, 1 to 10, 61, 62, 87, 127 to 160, 170 to 177.

Effect of forms receipt

§ 

1132 

 Effect of receipt 

In Capital & Counties Bank v. Gordon [1903], A. C. 240, forms 252, 88 L. T. R. 574, it was held that checks drawn payable to X and crossed payable only upon signature by the payees of a form of receipt at the foot of the instrument were not bills of exchange within the meaning of the Bills of Exchange Act. 

The fact that the checks were payable to X, without words of negotiability, would not under the English Act render them non-negotiable. Therefore the judgment may be regarded as an authority to the effect that the requirement of a receipt by the payees upon the instrument impairs its negotiability. 

In Underwood, Ltd. v. Bank of Liverpool & Martins [1924], 1 K. B. 775 (C. A.), and B. E. A. s. 82, Scrutton, L. J., at p. 792, held that the protection given by B. E. A. s. 82, to bankers paying crossed checks, did not extend to documents which, though in form checks, are no unconditional promises to pay, because the order to pay is conditional on a receipt on the check being signed by the payee.

But a check which bore at the foot the words "The receipt at the back hereof must be signed, which signature will be taken as an indorsement of the check," and on the back of which was a receipt form, is negotiable, since the order to pay is unconditional, the words at the foot not being addressed to the bankers and not affecting the order to them. Nathan v. Ogdens (K. B. 

Div., Aug., 1905), 21 T. L. R. 775, 93 L. T. Rep. 553, 94 L. T. 

Rep. 126 (semble).

The defendant gave the plaintiffs a check written on a blank sheet of paper on the face of which he wrote "to be retained." 

The defendant promised to send a check on one of his banker's printed forms in substitution for this check. The defendant did not do this and the check was dishonored on presentment. 

In an action on the check, held, that the addition of the words, "to be retained" merely imported a condition between drawer and payee, not addressed to the bankers and not binding on them and that the order as regards the banker was an unconditional order to pay. The said words are only requests to the payee, and the check was an unconditional order to pay within the meaning of sec. 73 B. E. A. [sec. 185 ] and plaintiffs were entitled to sue upon it, citing Nathan v. Ogdens, supra. 

Roberts & Co. v. Marsh [1915], 1 K. B. 42.

This case seems clear: the words "to be retained" can fairly be regarded merely as a request to the payee. But it is submitted that Nathan v. Ogdens is wrong since the words at the foot of the check plainly imply that the drawer did not intend the drawee to pay unless the receipt was signed. 

Compare with these cases Berenson v. London & Lancashire 

F. Ins. Co., 201 Mass. 172, 87 N. E. 687; Val Platz Brewing Co. v. Interstate Ice Co., 161 Mo. App. 531, 143 S. W. 542. This 1 Supra, p. 1065, n. 1.

§ 186  

requirement of a receipt on checks is becoming frequent in the Effect of United States. Notwithstanding Professor Brannan's opinion receipt forms in the preceding paragraph that the negotiability of the check is impaired by the condition, the courts may possibly hold that it is reasonably incidental to the drawee's obligation, like surrender of the check by the holder. The question resembles the equally unsettled problem of the drawee's right to require the holder merely to sign his name on presentation for payment.2 

Such a receipt-signature, however, merely acknowledges the payment of money, i. e., the amount of the check, whereas the special clauses on checks exemplified in the preceding cases require the holder to acknowledge that this money is in full payment of his claim to a dividend or for the price of merchandise or services itemized on the check. Such a release of indebtedness is much more than a recital of the performance of a transaction in the life of the check. The question is further complicated in 

England by the Stamp Acts, which impose on the holder the additional burden of putting a revenue stamp on the check when he signs his name to a receipt. See 59 Ir. L. T. 46.

A check may be drawn by a bank upon itself. Ross v. Lon don County Westminster & Parr's Bank, [1919] 1 K. B. 678. 

Sec. 186. Within What Time a Check Must Be Pre sented.

A check must be presented for payment within a reasonable time after its issue or the drawer will be discharged from liability thereon to the extent of the loss caused by the delay.³

Facts excus ing delay and loss

When the payee of a check presented it the day after he drawer's received it and the drawer's account was sufficient, the drawer was not discharged if the bank asked the payee to return on the following morning when the bank would have more money on hand, although the payee did not so return and the bank failed before the check was again presented through a collecting bank; but the drawer would be discharged if the bank tendered bills of small denominations which the payee declined to receive. Empire-Arizona Copper Co. v. Shaw, 20 Ariz. 471, 181 Pac. 464, 4 A. L. R. 1229, with note on "Conduct of holder of check at time of presentation for payment as affecting drawer's liability."

If the holder of a check is induced by the drawer to delay presentation while the deposit is sufficient to cover it, the drawer may be precluded from setting up injury caused by the delay.

 Tarasek v. Kosciuszko Bldg. & L. 

Assn., 218 Ill. App. 487.

In an action by the vendor of land against the purchaser, where the vendor instructed the purchaser to pay the consideration to the mortgagee, but the purchaser made a check payable to both the vendor and the mortgagee, and the mortgagee received same on November 5, 1926 and left it at the bank with

Board of Directors of St. Francis'

The plaintiff-payee of a check presented it to the drawee twenty days after issue and it was returned for lack of funds. 

Held, the delay, though unreasonable, did not discharge the drawer, since it would have caused no injury to him if he had allowed funds to remain in the bank until presentment. Bodner v. Rotman, 95 N. J. Eq. 510, 123 Atl. 529.

Action on a check given by a firm in which defendant was a partner for money loaned by plaintiff to the firm. The other partner thereafter drew out the firm's deposit and the defendant settled with him without ascertaining whether the check had been paid. Held, that sec. 186 has no application, the efficient cause of the loss to plaintiff not being the delay in presenting the check but the drawing out of the money and subsequent settlement between the partners. The drawer of a check is not released from liability thereon by reason of delay in presentment, where even if there had been no delay the check would not have reached the drawer bank in time to be paid. Daw v. Cowan (C. C. A.), 23 F. (2d) 646. The 

N. I. L. was not cited.

Where the bank on which the check is drawn and all the parties interested reside in the same city, it is the duty of the holder to present it to the bank for payment on the day the check is received or at furthest, the next day, even in the case of a large city like Chicago. The holder has the burden of proving that his delay has not resulted in loss to the drawer.

Nat. Plumbing & Heating Supply Co. v. Stevenson, 213 Ill. 

App. 49.

The plaintiff, a Buffalo manufacturing company, maintained a sales office in Chicago from which goods were sold to the defendant, who always sent checks on his Chicago bankers to the local office, despite a printed request on each invoice to make payment direct to Buffalo headquarters. The plaintiff kept a Chicago bank account in which it placed funds sufficient for Chicago expenses and in which Chicago cash payments were also deposited, but Chicago payments by check when received by the local office were forwarded to Buffalo headquarters and there deposited for collection. A check drawn by the defendant was thus forwarded and deposited in Buffalo. Before presentation, the drawee bankers closed their doors. The check would have been paid if it had been deposited in the plaintiff's Chicago bank. The plaintiff acted quickly in each step of the course taken. Held, the drawer was discharged.  Republic Metalware Co. v. Smith, 218 Ill. App. 130. 

The notes in 31 Yale L. J. 187, 4 Ill. L. Q. 142, approve the decision, considering that while the "send-checks-to-headquarters" practice is commercially desirable to prevent losses from the juggling of large local sales revenues by dishonest local sales managers, any risks incident to protecting the principal from the possible crime of its agent should fall on the party protected and not on the local customers. The result would be otherwise if the local establishment were merely a warehouse from which deliveries of merchandise were made.

From there it was sent to the drawee bank where it arrived one day after the bank closed. Had plaintiff deposited it in a Chicago bank immediately, it would have been forwarded on the next business day after the first business day on which it came into plaintiff's possession directly to the drawee in time for payment. Semble, the drawer of a check contracts that it will be paid on presentment but not that it will be certified. This is the theory on which the law discharging the drawer and indorsers upon certification is based. Lipten v. Columbia Trust Co., 194 App. Div. 384, 185 N. Y. Supp. 198. Sed quaere? Under sec. 61 the drawer of a bill of exchange engages that it will be accepted, and by sec. 185 the provisions applicable to a bill of exchange payable on demand apply to a check unless otherwise provided. That the discharge of the drawer by certification under sec. 188 rests on other grounds and does not imply an exception to sec. 61 is shown by the fact that the drawee's refusal to certify constitutes dishonor and renders the drawer liable upon due notice. 

In Wachtel v. Rosen, 249 N. Y. 386, 164 N. E. 326, affirming 

223 App. Div. 416, 228 N. Y. Supp. 476, 62 A. L. R. 374, it was held that a petition stating that certification on a check had been refused and due notice given did not state a cause of action. The court relies on the old common law before the act and refuses to give effect to secs. 61 and 185 suggested above; see also sec. 89. The reasoning of the court seems highly artificial, contrary to the plain meaning of the sections and business custom. It is hard to conceive of a bank which was willing to pay a check, refusing to certify it, but, if such a situation existed, it is equally hard to conceive that the holder would refuse the cash. The plea that the check was not certified clearly falls within the drawer's undertaking under secs. 61 and 185; and, if not, then as a practical matter of pleading it inferentially indicates dishonor by non-payment. The case is adversely criticized in 38 Yale L. J. 112; but see 77 U. Pa. L. Rev. 126; and 

28 Mich. L. Rev. 74; see also 6 N. Y. L. Rev. 70, and 15 Va. L. 

Rev. 683. 

Certification simply makes the banker the debtor of the holder.

There is no assignment of funds or special preference created by certification. Downey v. Citizens State Bank of Noblesville, 100 

Ind. App. 158, 194 N. E. 743.

So far as concerns the liability of the certifying bank, it is immaterial whether the drawer of a check had a deposit in the bank.  Security State Bank v. 

State Bank of Brandtford, 31 N. D. 454, 154 N. W. 282.

But a bank certifying a check without funds is not liable thereon except to a holder in due course. National City Bank v. Titlow, 233 Fed. Rep. 838.

If the cashier of the drawee bank certifies a check, it is no defense against a holder in due course that the cashier violated the banking laws because the drawer had no funds. Semble, a certified check is not expected to be presented so promptly as an ordinary check. The  was not cited. Smith v. Hubbard, 205 Mich. 44, 171 N. Be of certifying bank and holder A certifying bank can not set up, when sued by a holder in due course, the fact that the drawer of the certified check is indebted to the bank for more than the amount of the check. 

Nat. Mechanics Bank v. Schmelz Nat. Bank, 136 Va. 33, 116 

S. E. 380.

The treasurer of a corporation drew a corporate check to the order of the defendant bank, stating on its face that it paid the personal debt of the treasurer, and had the check certified by the drawee bank. The defendant payee bank collected the check. Held, it was not liable to the receiver of the corporation. The certification of the check protected the defendant bank from any liability. The certifying bank became responsible for its payment, and the defendant was not concerned as to the relation between the treasurer and his corporation. 

Schmitt v. Mellon Nat. Bank, 67 Pa. Super. Ct. 453.

Defendant bank certified a check at the request of the payee who failed. The drawer stopped payment of the check. In an action on the check by the payee's representative the defendant set up a right of set-off which the drawer had against the payee. 

Held, that by the certification the drawer was discharged, that neither he nor the drawee could thereafter enforce the set-off against liability on the check. Carnegie Trust Co. v. First Nat. 

Bank, 213 N. Y. 301, 107 N. E. 693, L. R. A. 1916C, 186.

Accord, McAdoo v. Farmers State Bank, 106 Kan. 662, 189 

Pac. 155, stating that certification operates as if the money had actually been paid out on the check by the bank to the holder, and redeposited by him to his own credit in exchange for a certificate of deposit issued by the bank. 

But where the drawer gave a check to the plaintiff as a loan for a definite purpose, who had the check certified and sued to recover the amount from the certifying bank for his own benefit after he had made it impossible to accomplish the purpose for which it was given, held, the drawee bank as assignee of the drawer's claim for a return of money lent could set it up by way of counterclaim, in the action on the check.  Marie Antoinette Realty Co. v. Yorkville Bank, 123 Misc. Rep. 522, 205 N. Y. Supp. 395.

The payee of a check given to him for value, transferred it, also for value, to plaintiff, but without indorsing it. The payee died the next day, and the drawer, although having no equities against the check, stopped payment. Plaintiff subsequently sent the check to the drawee bank, and the teller certified it without asking any questions. Held, that under sec. 49, , the title of the payee vested in plaintiff, and that the bank was liable to him upon its certification. Meuer v. Phenix Nat. Bank, 94 

App. Div. 331, 88 N. Y. Supp. 83.

The holder's agent in bad faith procured the plaintiff's certification of a forged check drawn upon it. Held, the plaintiff could recover from the holder. Banca Commerciale Italiana

§ 187 

Trust Co. v. Clarkson, 274 N. Y. 69, 8 N. E. (2d) 281, 110 

A. L. R. 1105 and note.

Where the drawer of a check before delivery to the payee procures its certification and the bank fails before presentation for payment, the bank is not liable on the check to the drawer, but only to the holder, and therefore the drawer on receiving the check from the payee can not set it off against a debt to the bank. Schlesinger v. Kurzrok, 47 Misc. Rep. 634, 94 N. Y. 

Supp. 442.

Notice to a bank by a depositor that his certified check, indorsed in blank, had been lost and to stop payment, would not justify the bank in refusing payment to a holder in due course. Poess v. Twelfth Ward Bank, 43 Misc. Rep. 45, 86 N. Y. 

Supp. 857, semble. See also, Unaka Nat. Bank v. Butler, 113 

Tenn. 574, 83 S. W. 655. Cf. Elliott v. Worcester Trust Co., 189 

Mass. 542, 75 N. E. 944, and Pease & Dwyer v. State Nat. Bank, 114 Tenn. 692, 88 S. W. 172.

The drawer of a check payable to his creditor had it certified and delivered it to a messenger for transmission to the payee, whom it never reached. The payee's name was apparently indorsed on the check by some unauthorized person, who received payment from the certifying bank. The true payee having received the returned voucher from the drawer, after the forgery was discovered, presented it to the bank for payment, which was refused; and the bank also refused the drawer's demand that certification be withdrawn and the funds set apart be restored to the drawer's account. The payee and the drawer joined in one action on the check against the certifying bank, under sec. 

209 of the Civil Practice Act, which authorizes joinder of plaintiffs in whom any right to relief arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally, or in the alternative, when, if such persons brought separate actions, any common question of law or fact would arise. Held, a misjoinder of plaintiffs. The rights of the two plaintiffs were mutually destructive. If the payee had title to the check, the deposit was forever withdrawn from the control of the drawer; but if the check had been reassigned to the drawer who was now the lawful holder, the right to have the funds belonged to the drawer alone. Semble, the bank was not liable to the payee. Two judges dissented on the ground that there was a liability in the alternative and common questions affecting both plaintiffs.  Olsen v. 

Bankers Trust Co., 205 App. Div. 669, 199 N. Y. Supp. 700. 

The minority opinion seems preferable. If two separate actions must be brought, the two juries may take divergent views and the bank escape liability to the plaintiff. But see the discussion of this case by J. L. Rothschild, "Civil Practice in New 

York," 23 Colum. L. Rev. 618, 632. The dictum is also open

Where a check was given in payment of a gambling debt and certified at the application of the holder, it was held that the drawer could not stop payment on the check because he had been discharged from liability and had lost his right to the money on deposit. B paid A for a horse by a check drawn by B & Co. to B's order and certified by procurement of B, who indorsed the check to A, who deposited it in the X bank, which credited him with the amount. Payment was stopped by B because of fraudulent representations of A which induced the purchase of the horse. 

There was no showing that B had repudiated the trade and tendered the horse to A. The X bank sued the drawee which interpleaded B but not A. Held, that neither the drawer nor the indorser could stop payment of a certified check after it had been delivered, that the X bank was a bona fide holder, though not for value, and that the X bank could recover against the drawee. Blake v. Hamilton, etc., Bank, 79 Ohio St. 189, 87 

N. E. 73.

If in this case and in the preceding case of Times Square 

Automobile Co. v. Rutherford Nat. Bank, the defrauded drawer had rescinded the contract and offered to return the property and the bank had been notified of this fact and instructed not to pay the check, it would have no right to do so. The fraudulent payee became constructive trustee of the check for the drawer, whether the check was certified or not, and payment to a constructive trustee after notice of the trust would be a wrongful payment. When the bank is sued it should interplead both the drawer and the payee or under reformed procedure bring them into the action. Greenberg v. World Exchange Bank, 227 App. 

Div. 413, 237 N. Y. Supp. 200, 43 Harv. L. Rev. 825. In some cases it has been held that the bank could defend in the action at law at the instance and in the interest of the defrauded

A typewritten letter of countermand, signed in typewriting, is also sufficient, and renders the bank liable for its subsequent certification of the check. Sarantopoulos v. Mid-City T. & Sav. 

Bank, 222 Ill. App. 24.

Since a check is not an assignment of the drawer's funds, the drawee bank is liable to him for paying it after countermand, and it is sufficient if he gives notice of the countermand to the cashier of the bank at his residence on Sunday, when the cashier did not refuse to act on a notice given outside of business hours. The N. I. L. was not cited. Hewitt v. First Nat.

The editor considers that the bank should be liable only for negligent payment, and that such liability can not be abrogated by agreement.

But a depositor is liable to a bank for an overdraft which was paid inadvertently after the depositor had stopped payment, when the order of countermand contained a printed form releasing the bank from liability for accidental payment, although the depositor did not read these words. A check drawn by the plaintiff upon the defendant bank was entrusted for delivery to the payee to an agent, who instead forged the payee's indorsement and obtained money on the check. Subsequently, the check was certified, and after several indorsements, was paid by the drawee. The drawer sued the drawee bank for the amount of the check alleging that it was certified "at the request of some person other than himself, the payee or bona fide holder." The court said that the payment to a holder under a forged indorsement did not constitute an acceptance because there was no writing; and that if the certification was without the knowledge and consent of some party to the check, it did not constitute an acceptance so as to change the relation of the parties and effect an assignment of the drawer's funds in the bank. However, the plaintiff could not recover upon his petition since it did not affirmatively allege that the certification was made without the knowledge or consent or authorization of the drawer, holder or payee. Gasper v. Security State Bank, 109 Neb. 495, 191 N. W. 654.

 General effect of sec. 189 on former minor ity view that check is assignment The doctrine formerly recognized in Kentucky that a check operates as an assignment, has been abrogated by this section and the bank is not liable to the holder on an uncertified-or unaccepted check or in damages for refusal to pay it. First 

Nat. Bank v. Hargis, etc., Bank, 170 Ky. 690, 186 S. W. 471.

A check is not an assignment of funds of the drawer, nor does the drawee bank become liable in equity to the holder by stating to him that the check is good and will be paid on presentation. Superior Nat. Bank v. National Bank of Commerce, 99 Neb. 833, 157 N. W. 1023; Rambo v. First State Bank, 88 

Kan. 257, 128 Pac. 182. Nor is a check an assignment of the drawer's cause of action against the bank for the deposit. Marks v. First Nat. Bank, 84 Oreg. 601, 165 Pac. 673.

Where a depositor issues a check against his general deposit account, such check is not an equitable assignment of the fund standing to the credit of the depositor, although the depositor made the deposit for the purpose of paying the check, and a garnishment of the bank in a suit against the depositor prior to presentation of the check to the bank, creates a lien on the deposit superior to any rights of the check holder. Kaesemeyer v. Smith, 22 Ida. 1, 123 Pac. 943, 43 L. R. A. (N.S.) 100 note; 

Boswell v. Citizens Savings Bank, 123 Ky. 485, 96 S. W. 797, semble; Catanzaro & Sons v. Hellman Commercial Trust & Sav. 

Bank, 281 Pa. 468, 126 Atl. 812. 

Contra, Farrington v. F. E. Fleming, etc., Co., 94 Neb. 108, 142 N. W. 297, 47 L. R. A. (N.S.) 742; but see this case properly criticized in 77 Central L. J. 200, and 27 Harvard Law Rev. 177. 

Also, contra, is McClain & Norvet v. Torkelson, 187 Ia. 202, 174 N. W. 42, 5 A. L. R. 1665, with note on "Effect of  upon the theory as to a check being an assignment of the drawer's funds." The view of this decision that sec. 189 merely denies the holder a right against the drawee bank and does not prevent the check from being otherwise an assignment is adversely criticized by a note in 9 Ia. L. Bull. 64, 70, on the ground that sec. 189 expressly provides that the check does not operate as an assignment of funds and is not subject to any such limitation as the Iowa court suggests. The decision is also adversely criticized in 5 Ia. L. Bull. 262; 5 Corn. L. Q. 305; and by Professor Aigler in 38 Harv. L. Rev. 857, 870, n. 48.

The authority of the decision is considerably weakened by In re 

Knapp's Est., 197 Ia. 166, 197 N. W. 222, which concerned the mutual rights of holder and drawer and did not involve any liability of the drawee bank, and by Murray v. American Sav. 

Bank, 197 Ia. 318, 197 N. W. 69, infra, p. 1167, which declares that a portion of what was said in McClain & Norvet v. Torkelson was dictum only, and that the only point decided was that the N. I. L. would not operate in favor of the garnisher against a check holder where the interest of the drawee bank would be in no manner affected. It is to be hoped that even the holding

§ 189 

as so limited will be regarded as wholly overruled in later decisions. Such is the conclusion of 9 Ia. L. Bull. 210.

A check or a draft is not an equitable assignment as between the drawer and the payee, so the receiver of an insolvent drawer bank is entitled to the balances in the correspondent banks at the time of the failure, and the payees of outstanding checks drawn on such balances are not preferred creditors. Union 

State Bank of Lancaster v. People's State Bank of Lancaster, 

192 Wis. 28, 211 N. W. 931. The court, in an excellent decision, discusses the conflict and points out that the  changed the law of Wisconsin.

A bank held a note made by a depositor, A, who tendered in payment a check drawn to his order on the bank by another depositor, X, but was told by the cashier that he was too busy to tend to the matter and was asked to come in on a later day. 

The next day the maker of the note came and found the bank's doors closed on account of insolvency. Held, the maker, A, could offset the amount of the check against his liability to the bank on the note. The court expressly held that the check did not constitute an assignment of funds of the drawer, X, distinguishing McClain & Norvet v. Torkelson, supra, but stated that the maker of the note had in legal effect made a good tender of payment, since the cashier had made no objection to the offer of a check instead of currency. Murray v. American 

Sav. Bank, 197 Ia. 318, 197 N. W. 69. See the discussion of this case by Prof. Aigler in 38 Harv. L. Rev. 857, 871. 

In Gruenther v. Bank of Monroe, 90 Neb. 280, 133 N. W. 

402, it was held that where plaintiff accepted a check on the defendant bank on the statement of the bank that the check was good and would be paid, and the drawer thereafter withdrew his deposit, but left with the bank the exact amount of the check, the bank was liable to the plaintiff, the payee, without reference to the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Law. 

The remark of one of the three dissenting judges that, "The majority are insensibly controlled by the former decisions of this court with respect to the rights of a check holder," is the only explanation of a decision which is contrary to the plain language of the statute. 

In Elgin v. Gross-Kelly Co., 20 N. M. 450, 150 Pac. 922,

L. R. A. 1916A, 711, a bank paid a check on it, without notice of the death of one of the partners in the drawer firm. The administrator of the partnership sued the holder for the money. 

The court held that the payment to the holder was good because the death of the drawer of a check does not revoke the authority of the bank to pay it to a holder for value, at least, if the drawer's estate is solvent, if the bank has no notice of the death. 

The court might have left its decision on the authorities cited by the court on this point to which may be added the later case of Glennan v. Rochester Trust, etc., Co., 209 N. Y. 12, 102 N. E. 

537, 52 L. R. A. (N. S.) 302, Ann. Cas. 1915A, 441, and see also,

But as plaintiff relied also on sec. 189, , the court check is considered that section and limited its operation to questions assignment arising between the bank and the holder of the check, that is, that under this section, a check is not of itself an assignment as against the drawee bank, but is an assignment as against the drawer. It is submitted that this distinction is unsound, and like 

Gruenther v. Bank of Monroe, supra, another example of the tendency of some courts to take a narrow view of the statute and hark back to the old law of the state. 

Before the Negotiable Instruments Law, the question whether a check was an assignment of any part of the drawer's deposit had been considered by the courts, both with respect to the rights of the holder against the drawee and the rights of the holder against the drawer or the latter's creditors or estate, and there had been differences of opinion on both questions. Before the statute, the weight of authority was that a check was not an assignment in either respect. The purpose of the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Law was to abrogate this conflict, and when the statute declares that a check of itself does not operate as an assignment, to say that it does so operate in any case is to declare the exact opposite of the statute. 

The certification of a check procured by the drawer operates as an assignment of the fund in favor of the owner of the check. 

McIntire v. Raskin, 173 Ga. 746, 161 S. E. 363.

Miscellane ous assign- When bankers who had contracted to sell sterling drew ment cases checks in favor of the buyer which were not delivered, held, no property was created which was held by the bankers in trust for the buyer, so that he could not claim as a preferred creditor. 

Samuels v. Drew & Co., 296 Fed. 882 (C. C. A., N. Y.).

The maker of a mortgage note gave the mortgagee a check in payment. Because of illness the mortgagee did not present the check for ten days, during which the funds in the bank were garnished by a creditor of the mortgagor. Held, the foreclosure of the mortgage would not be enjoined. It had not been paid, as the check gave the mortgagee no valid claim to the funds in the bank. The drawer was not discharged by the delay as he suffered no injury through the use of the funds to pay the garnishing creditor. Wileman v. King, 120 Miss. 

392, 82 So. 265, 5 A. L. R. 584.

A check drawn against a sufficient deposit was not paid in full on presentation because of the bank's mistake. The bank, on discovering it possessed excess funds and before locating the cause, issued a certificate of deposit payable to itself for the amount of the shortage according to its practice. Held, the depositor was not a preferred creditor for the amount of the certificate. Since the check was not an assignment of the drawer's funds, the whole transaction left the parties in the

§ 189 assignment same relation with respect to the unpaid portion of the check Miscellaneous that they sustained to each other before the check was pre- cases sented. Dahl & Penne v. State Bank, 110 Oreg. 68, 222 Pac. 1090. 

A debtor sent a telegram to the defendant bank to pay to his creditor, S, a specified sum. A swindler impersonating S received a cashier's check from the bank, which was collected. 

Held, S had no cause of action against the bank. The telegram was a check which did not operate as an assignment of funds. 

 Southern Trust Co. v. Am. Bank of Commerce & T. Co., 148 Ark. 283, 229 S. W. 1026, 14 A. L. R. 

761, with note, "Payment of check upon forged or unauthorized indorsement as affecting the right of true owner against the bank."

If the telegram was a check, it was non-negotiable, but it seems not a check, only an instruction to the bank as agent to pay money. On the assumption that it was a negotiable check, an acceptance by the bank was properly denied. The mere act of payment of a check was not an acceptance, because not in writing under sec. 132. Although the cashier's check was a writing, which perhaps imported a promise to pay the telegram, such a collateral promise, under sec. 134, was not an acceptance except in favor of one who took the telegram in reliance on the promise, and S did not do so. See the comment in 22 Colum. L. Rev. 182, 278.

Farmers' & 

Merchants Bank v. Talley, 24 Ala. Gifts of checks

The gift of a check is automatically revoked by the death of the drawer before payment or certification by the drawee. In re 

Ludlam's Estate, 158 Misc. 283, 285 N. Y. Supp. 597.

A gift causa mortis of a check on a savings bank for part of the drawer's deposit is not effective even if the pass book was delivered with the check. A gift to be effective must place the thing donated beyond the control of the donor, but the drawer of a check may stop payment at any time before the check is cashed, and it makes no difference what prevents the check from being cashed. Provident Inst. for Sav. v. Sisters of St. Francis, 87 N. J. Eq. 424, 100 Atl. 894, not citing the

 For adverse criticism of the court's reasoning, see 

91 Cent. L. J. 109; but the decision seems sound.

A depositor in contemplation of suicide drew a check upon the bank payable to the order of his betrothed for an amount a few cents less than his entire account, and killed himself immediately after mailing the check to the payee. Held, that the check could not be enforced against the bank or the estate of the drawer. Not being an assignment of any part of his bank account it was not a valid gift inter vivos, and being in contemplation of suicide, it was against public policy and not a valid gift mortis causa. Love and affection did not constitute a sufficient consideration to support it. Bainbridge v. Hoes, 163 App. Div. 870, 149 N. Y. Supp. 20.

Cashier's checks drawn by the defendant upon a New York banker were purchased by a woman with the intention of sending them as gifts to the payees named. The drawer advised the drawee of the drafts and credited its account. The purchaser died before delivering the checks. Held, her executrix could recover the price of the checks from the issuing bank. 

The payees had acquired no rights upon the checks before the donor's death and delivery to them thereafter would be improper. One judge dissented. Gellert v. Bank of California, 107 Oreg. 162, 214 Pac. 377. See the valuable note, "Transmission of Money and Sale of Credit," 33 Yale L. J. 177. 

In Carter v. Greenway, 152 Ark. 339, 238 S. W. 65, it was held that checks for part of the drawer's account in a bank could be made the subject of a valid gift causa mortis, although not collected during his lifetime.  

The decision is adversely criticized and numerous cases contra collected in 1 Wis. L. Rev. 504.

Where a check was delivered as a gift causa mortis, the whole transaction between the parties is admissible with the check to determine whether a valid assignment of the fund was made.

 TITLE IV GENERAL PROVISIONS ARTICLE I Sec. 190. Short Title. 

This act shall be known as the Uniform Negotiable

Instruments Law.¹ 

The pamphlet published by the Commission on Uniform Laws in 1928 contains the following comments: "Section 190 as originally drafted reads "This act shall be known as the Negotiable Instruments Law." In order to bring the language of this section into harmony with the language of the Uniform Sales Act (sec. 79), the Uniform Warehouse Re ceipts Act (sec. 62), the Uniform Transfer of Stock Act (sec. 

26), and the Uniform Bills of Lading Act (sec. 57), the language has been slightly changed.

The Uniform Sales Act (sec. 74), the Uniform Warehouse Receipts Act (sec. 57), the Uniform Transfer of Stock Act (sec. 

19) and the Uniform Bills of Lading Act (sec. 52) provide that: "This act shall be so interpreted and construed as to affectuate its general purpose to make uniform the law of those states which enact it." While the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act does not contain this section, yet the courts have interpreted it in harmony with the principles of this section. Rockfield v. First 

National Bank of Springfield, 77 Ohio St. 311; Downey v. 

O'Keefe, 26 R. I. 571; Thorpe v. White, 188 Mass. 333; Toole v. 

Crafts, 193 Mass. 110; Gibbs v. Guaraglia (N. J.), 67 Atlantic 

Rep. 81; Baumeister v. Kuntz (Fla.), 42 South Rep. 886; Farquahar Co. v. Higham (N. D.), 112 N. W. Rep. 557; Vander 

Ploeg v. Van Zunk (Iowa), 112 N. W. 807; in Rockfield v. First 

National Bank, supra, Mr. Justice Spear said (pp. 329-331): "It is so much a matter of common knowledge as to make it proper to take judicial notice of the fact, that the act herein considered was enacted because of an effort on the part of the Bar of many, if not all of the states of the union, to bring about a uniform system of law respecting negotiable instruments...

That this purpose was prominent in the minds of the members of our General Assembly in the enactment of the Ohio act is shown by the title of the act itself which: 'An act to establish a law uniform with the laws of other states on negotiable instruments.' The desirability of such legislation had been long felt by commercial people of our state as well as by the judiciary and the Bar at large. *The purpose of the act is to bring 

Ohio into harmony with the other states of the union on so im-

Cicero (in de Re Publica) said: "Nec erit alia lex Romae, alia Athenis, alia nunc, alia posthac; sed et omnis gentis, et omni tempore, una les, et sempiterna et immutabilis continebit."

It should be noted that the Uniform Limited Partnership Act phrases the corresponding section as follows: "(1) The rule that statutes in derogation of the common law are to be strictly construed shall have no application to this act. (2) This act shall be so interpreted and construed as to effect its general purpose to make uniform the law of those states which enact it."

§ 191 revocable placed it on a pointed file, and, without making a charge on Mailing as its books to the drawer's account, drew a draft on Chicago to the order of the plaintiff bank and placed it in the mails the same evening. Subsequently that evening or next morning, the drawee bank learned that the drawer's account was overdrawn. After receiving from the plaintiff bank an unsatisfactory reply to a request by telephone for the return of the draft, the drawee bank arranged with the local postoffice to have the draft intercepted in the mail and returned, so that it never reached the plaintiff. In an action to recover the amount of the check, held, the drawee bank was not liable. The delivery which completes acceptance did not take place, for it involved a loss of control over the subject matter, and under the postal regulations, the drawee bank was entitled to reclaim the letter from the mail before it reached the plaintiff. Semble, in ordinary cases when the power of recall is not exercised, the mailing of a letter amounts to a delivery of its content to the addressee. Traders Nat. Bank v. First Nat. Bank, 142 Tenn. 

229, 217 S. W. 977, 9 A. L. R. 382, with note "Withdrawal of, or right to withdraw letter from mail as affecting consummation of contract.' 

No acceptance was involved, since the transaction constituted a payment if anything. Nevertheless, since payment could by custom be made by a substituted executory contract, such a contract was analogous to an acceptance of the check, and similar questions arose.

It is submitted that the decision was incorrect, and that the draft was delivered. In other branches of the law delivery may take place without loss of control over the subject matter. 

Talbot v. Talbot, 32 R. I. 72, 78 Atl. 535. The objective act of mailing is sufficient to complete the contract expressed in the writing. Furthermore, the dictum, which is settled law (see under sec. 16), that mailing is delivery of a negotiable instrument when it is not regained from the postoffice, is inconsistent with the decision. A promise is not binding so long as it is open to revocation by the unfettered choice of the promisor.

Mailing can not be both a delivery and not a delivery, according to what happens later.

Contra to the decision is Canterbury v. Bank of Sparta, 91 

Wis. 53, 64 N. W. 311, 30 L. R. A. 845, 51 Am. St. Rep. 870, before the  See 1 Williston on Contracts, sec. 86. Cf.

Sec. 192. Person Primarily Liable on Instrument. 

The person "primarily" liable on an instrument is the person who by the terms of the instrument is absolutely required to pay the same. All other parties are “secondarily" liable.¹ 

Cross Reference: 88 60, 62, 191, 10, 17(6), 18, 61, 63 to 68, 70, 89, 121, 165.

ANNOTATIONS 

In addition to the cases hereunder cited, secs. 119 and 120 should be consulted for other cases applying to this section. 

1 Not in B. E. A.

GENERAL PROVISIONS § 192 

Under this section both principal and surety (comaker) are primarily liable on the note. Roberson-Ruffin Co. v. Spain, 173 N. C. 23, 91 S. E. 361.

And the rule is the same, although the note recites that one of the two makers was a principal and the other a surety. In re 

Nashville Laundry Co., 240 Fed. Rep. 795; Hardesty v. Young (D. C.), 34 F. (2d) 310.

An accommodation maker is a person primarily liable, even though he add the word "surety" to his signature, or the fact that he signed for accommodation is otherwise known to the holder. See cases under sec. 119.

The defendant and her husband signed as comakers a note payable to the plaintiff. A state statute provided that a married woman should not become surety for her husband's debts. 

The trial court admitted evidence that she signed the note as such a surety and found for the defendant. Held, error and judgment for the payee. By the terms of the note she was primarily liable, and parol evidence was not admissible to vary this liability, which she was estopped to dispute. Two judges dissented on the ground that a new trial should be held to ascertain whether the payee had knowledge of her suretyship, since reliance on her representations was necessary to an estoppel. Barton Sav. Bank & T. Co. v. Bickford, 97 Vt. 166, 122 Atl. 582. The decision is adversely criticized in 72 U. Pa. L. 

Rev. 332; 10 Va. L. Rev. 397.

A wife signed note as comaker with her husband for his accommodation, secured by a mortgage on her property. The payee pledged the note and mortgage with other collateral to the defendant, a holder in due course. Although the Alabama statute forbidding a wife from becoming a surety for her husband was held not to give her a defense on the note against a holder in due course, she sued to compel the defendant to exhaust the other collateral pledged by the payee before resorting to her property or liability, on the theory that she was a surety as to the defendant. This marshaling was refused. She was primarily liable with her husband to the defendant, whose bona fide purchase made the note free from any qualities of suretyship so far as the defendant was concerned, even if an ordinary surety would have been entitled to compel the creditor to exhaust the assets of the principal. Davies v. Simpson, 201 

Ala. 616, 79 So. 48.

The accommodation comaker of a note payable to the plaintiff placed the word "surety" after his name. Afterwards, the principal maker executed a mortgage to the plaintiff to secure this note and any other indebtedness. Subsequent advances were made to him by the plaintiff. Held, the accommodation maker could not compel the plaintiff to apply the collateral upon his note rather than to other indebtedness of the principal maker. Semble, the accommodation maker was not Surety makers

Although an indorser may be only an indorser or surety, as to the maker, entitled to reimbursement from the maker if the indorser pays the note, yet as to the payee he is primarily liable if the note, on its face, recites that the signers, indorsers, guarantors and sureties are liable in solido. Bonart v. Rabito, 141 La. 970, 76 So. 166. 

The holder of a check may join in one action the drawee bank which took the check, marked it "Paid" but did not pay it, and the drawer who was alleged to have prevented the bank from remitting the money. The N. I. L. was not cited. 

McGhee v. Milburn, 85 Okla. 17, 204 Pac. 279. 

A statute allowing the joinder of maker and indorser in one action is permissive and not mandatory, and they may be sued in separate actions. An action against the maker pursued to judgment does not bar a subsequent action against the indorser, one being primarily and the other secondarily liable. Marine
