Sec. 198. Time When Act Takes Effect. 

This chapter shall take effect on A number of the states add sections defining public holidays; making provisions as to notes given for a patent right; authorizing a bank to send a collection item direct to the drawee, and to receive the drawee's draft in payment; fixing the damages on protested bills; and regulating the liability of a bank to a depositor for mistakenly dishonoring checks. 

New York, by amendment, adds the following section, numbered 328 (Laws, 1904, c. 287): "No bank shall be liable to a depositor for the payment by it of a forged or raised check, unless within one year after the return to the depositor of the voucher of such payment, such depositor shall notify the bank that the check so paid was forged or raised."

Similar provisions have been adopted in some other states, but not as amendments to the Negotiable Instruments Law.

Although no attempt has been made to collect in this work all the cases construing such forgery statutes, the following decisions have been noted as of interest. 

This additional section is a general statute which promulgates a rule of substantive law and can be relied on as a defense, although not pleaded. Shattuck v. Guardian Trust Co., 204 

N. Y. 200, 97 N. E. 517.

Forged indorsements are not included in "a forged or raised check" under this statute. Also, it relates exclusively to the liability of a bank to its own depositor, and does not apply in an action by the drawee bank against a collecting bank to recover money paid on checks with forged indorsements. Limitations for forged or raised checks

Quaere, if this statute applies to checks with forged indorsements. Pannonia Bldg. & Loan Assn. v. West Side Trust Co., 93 N. J. L. 377, 108 Atl. 240.

Checks were held to be forged within this statute when originally payable to the agent of a corporation, and a swindler erased the name of the corporate payee and forged the indorsements of the agent. Union Tool Co. v. Farmers & Merchants 

Nat. Bank, 192 Cal. 40, 218 Pac. 424, 28 A. L. R. 1417.

This statute begins to run upon return of the vouchers and not upon discovery of the forgery. California Vegetable Union v. Crocker Nat. Bank, 37 Cal. App. 743, 174 Pac. 920. The depositor was held barred by negligence. See the note on this point in 32 Harv. L. Rev. 287. Accord, as to the accrual of the cause of action, Glassell Development Co. v. Citizens Nat. Bank, 

191 Cal. 375, 216 Pac. 1012, 28 A. L. R. 1247, which held that the words "action *** by a depositor against the bank for the payment of a forged or raised check" necessarily meant his action against the bank to recover the money deposited with it.

A notice on a bank pass-book requiring forgery to be reported within ten days, which was not specially called to the depositor's attention, was not effective in view of a statute requiring notice within sixty days. Denbigh v. First Nat. Bank, 102 Wash. 546, 174 Pac. 475.

Federal courts decisions 

The famous case of Swift v. Tyson, 41 U. S. (16 Pet.) 1, 10 

L. Ed. 865 (1842), which held that the federal courts were not and state bound to follow the decisions of the supreme court of the states on matters pertaining to general commercial law, was overruled by the Supreme Court of the United States in Erie Railroad v. 

Tompkins, U. S. No. 367, Oct. Term, 1937, on April 23, 1938, after this book went to press. 

Under this decision the federal courts are now bound to follow state decisions both in matters of common law and statutory interpretation, which includes all cases of negotiable instruments.

I. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS 

Little in the way of direct amendment to the N. I. L. seems to have developed since the publication of the fifth edition of this book. The amendments are still in the hands of a committee of the conference of Commissioners on Uniform Law, but their adoption seems no more likely or necessary than it was at the time of the last edition.

The Uniform Bank Collection Act also is still before the conference, while its counterpart, the American Bankers Association's Bank Collection Code, luckily, has failed of adoption in any other states. The nature and desirability of this legislation, which constitutes a substantial change in the law as developed under the N. I. L., is fully discussed in the following articles: 

BEUTEL, Bank Collections Act, 9 Tulane L. Rev. 378 (1935).

BOGART, Failed Banks, Collection Items and Trust Pref erences, 29 Mich. L. Rev. 545 (1931). 1192

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS DONLEY, Some Problems in Collecting Checks, 38 W. Va. 

L. Quar. 195 (1932). 

PATON, Uniform Bank Collections Code, 21 Am. Bankers 

Assn. Jour. 907 (1929).

STEFFEN, The Check Collection Muddle, 10 Tulane L. 

Rev. 537. 

TOWNSEND, Bank Deposits of Commercial Paper, 7 N. Y. 

U. L. Q. Rev. 293, 618 (1929-1930).

TOWNSEND, The Bank Collection Code of the American 

Bankers Association, 8 Tulane L. Rev. 21, 236, 376 (1933-1934). 

Notes, 40 Yale L. Jour. 802 (1931), 33 Col. L. Rev. 125 (1933).

The discussion of amendments which appeared in the fifth edition, p. 1099 ff., has been deleted for the purpose of conserving space; but it is submitted that the policy there advocated of avoiding amendment should be continued until the time is ripe for complete re-codification.
